News.title: Raging Crufts competitor drove van into show ring at posh dog show & attacked shocked judge in row over her pets’ entry
News.content:
Next

A DOG show competitor went barking mad and drove her van into the ring to confront a shocked judge, a court has heard.

Furious Marianne Hunter, 63, flew into a four-letter racist rant against the official who barred her pets from a contest at the country event.



Mother-of-two Hunter had travelled 270 miles from Kent to Narberth in South West Wales so her prized pooches could compete at the annual Snooty Fox charity show.

But the court heard she lost her temper before hurling insults at show judge Tracey Hodges, calling her a “Welsh c***”.



Hunter, a business manager with Public Health England, then drove her white Ford Transit van into the show ring — knocking over one of the participants while children were playing nearby.

Prizes at the event included a modest £100 for each champion.

But the court heard it was enough for her to go on the attack when her dogs were stopped from entering a pair of categories.

Prosecutor Sian Vaughan said Hunter had “no regard for anyone else” when she drove the van, before she was stopped by her husband taking the keys.

Miss Vaughan told Haverfordwest magistrates: “There was a difficulty with the defendant’s dogs when she was told they were unable to enter two categories at the same time.

“Marianne Hunter lost her temper and called Tracey Hodges a ‘Welsh c***.”



Hunter can be seen online proudly posing with her black and white lurcher at world-famous dog show Crufts after receiving a good citizen training award.

She is listed as a committee member of the Kennel Club- registered Aylesford and District Dog Training Society in Kent.

But she had to be kept under control herself during the incident.

Miss Vaughan added: “The keys were taken from the vehicle by her husband, and if he had not done that, it could have become a lot worse.”

Hunter, of Crockenhill, Kent, admitted racially aggravated ­intentional harassment on June 1 last year and was fined £1,115.



She denied dangerous driving but was found guilty by magistrates and fined an additional £2,676.

She was also handed a 12-month road ban and must pass an extended test before she can drive again.

News.title: Woman, 27, charged after police officer ‘blasted in foot with sawn-off shotgun’ in Nottingham shooting
News.content:
GUN HORROR Woman, 27, charged after police officer ‘blasted in foot with sawn-off shotgun’ in Nottingham shooting







Next

A WOMAN has been charged after a cop was reportedly shot in the foot with a saw-off shotgun in the Nottingham city centre.

Aisha Zaman, 27, faces two firearm offences following the horror incident in the early hours of Sunday morning.



The woman has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of a firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence.

Nottinghamshire Police says Zaman has been remanded in custody.



She is due to appear before Nottingham Magistrates’ Court on Friday.

The on-duty officer was shot at a bus stop on Angel Row at around 4.50am on October 18 after approaching two people acting suspiciously.



The suspects fled the scene and the injured cop was rushed to hospital, where he remains receiving treatment.

The force then launched a major hunt for the suspects.



A firearm – believed to be a saw-off shotgun – was recovered from the scene as detectives launched their major investigation.

Several other people have been arrested in connection with the incident.

This includes two men, aged 24 and 30, and two women, aged 25 and 21, who have been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

A 35-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender – both remain in police custody.

Terrifying images from the site of the shooting show what appears to be a sawn-off shotgun discarded on the street.



Footage later emerged showing the aftermath of the shooting with members of the public spotted rushing to assist the wounded cop.

Detective Chief Superintendent Rich Bull, who is leading the investigation, said: “We would just like to take this moment to thank the public.

“The outpouring of support for the injured officer has been greatly appreciated.



“We continue to support him as he undergoes further treatment in hospital and are keeping him and his family fully informed of the developments in this investigation.

“He has asked for privacy during this incredibly difficult time.

“We have now charged a 27-year-old woman in connection with this incident.

“We hope this offers the public some reassurance.

“Our investigation team are still following a number of lines of inquiry to ensure those responsible are arrested, charged, and put before the courts.”

News.title: OAP nearly dies after eating too much BEETROOT in first known case of its kind
News.content:
VEGGIE SHOCK OAP nearly dies after eating too much BEETROOT in first known case of its kind







Next

A MAN nearly died after eating too much beetroot in what doctors believe may be a world-first.

The American national, 82, ploughed through a whopping six pounds of the root veg per week and was even drinking the cooking water.

He had been trying to stay healthy – but the veggie bonanza completely backfired.



While eating dinner one evening the man suddenly became dizzy and passed out, according to The Journal of Emergency Medicine.



Emergency services scrambled to the scene and found his blood pressure dangerously low and his skin slate grey.

He was rushed to A&E and pumped with oxygen.

But his oxygen levels failed to rise – dropping to a critical 88 per cent rather thna a usual 96 to 100 per cent rate.

Eventually doctors cracked the mystery illness – the pensioner was suffering from methemoglobinemia – a rare blood disorder which can be caused by consuming too much nitrate.

Beetroot is high in nitrate and the OAP had also been taking heart medication which was also loaded with the chemical.

Doctors suspect that the enormous quantities of the purple veg combined with the heart meds triggered the dangerous blood problem.

He was treated with the antidote of methylene blue – and his oxygen levels soared back up to 99 per cent with his skin returning to a normal colour in just 90 minutes.



A doctor commenting on the unusual case online said the pensioner nearly died of beetroot.

The purple veg has been touted by some as a “natural Viagra”, according to Dr Stefan Buntrock.

The case of the 82-year-old beet victim was “the perfect example of a fundamental misunderstanding when it comes to nutrition and the health benefits of certain foods”.

He added: “A rule of thumb [is] focusing excessively on a single supposedly healthy ingredient is unlikely to give you additional benefits.

“And in extreme cases it may even become dangerous.”



It comes after a horrifying spate of food poisoning infected huge batches of a popular green veggie – and ended up killing a man.

Luigi Di Sarno, 52, died after taking a fatal bite of a broccoli and sausage sandwich amid a growing botulism outbreak.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Nine others were hospitalised in 2025 after eating broccoli from the same food truck in Italy.

News.title: Trump ‘asks Elon Musk to reverse Starshield blackout’ that left Ukraine defenceless against Putin’s missiles blitzes
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump asked Elon Musk to reverse restrictions on Ukraine’s Starlink service after last week’s blackout left Kyiv defenceless against Russian strikes.

The US president told the SpaceX founder he was frustrated that speeds had remained capped at around 100mph over a Wednesday night call.



US and Ukrainian officials said the system was almost back up to speed on Thursday, shortly after the conversation, the Wall Street Journal reports.

It comes after the outlet revealed that Musk ordered the slowdown last Tuesday, in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel hubs and rising fuel prices.



Kyiv’s military depends on the satellite system to guide drone fleets including interceptors used to down deadly Russian attacks.

But the tech mogul restricted the speeds that Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network.



The outage struck without warning overnight as Russian forces unleashed a deadly salvo of ballistic missiles on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

Trump told aides and allies this week that he wanted to reverse the slowdown, the officials said.



It follows a week of questions about why Starlink was throttled and whether the move was ordered by the White House.

Musk initially blamed Trump for disruption, writing on X: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” an acronym for the president of the United States.

Trump had accused Kyiv of “seriously hurting the world diesel markets” by continuing to launch strikes on Russian oil refineries.

He also blocked numerous sanctions against the Kremlin on Friday and struck a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin earlier this month.



Zelensky’s complaints that Ukrainians would die if the service wasn’t restored led to further confusion over who ordered the directive.

He said: “It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side.”

But Trump has repeatedly denied giving the order or knowing who did.



The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Trump spoke with Musk hours after the outage became public.

Asked about Musk’s decision on Thursday, Vice President JD Vance said: “I don’t think this is about Elon. I think it’s fundamentally about what America’s policy in Ukraine and Russia is going to be.”

Ukraine and its European allies slammed Musk for last week’s outage.

“Let me be blunt: the blood of Ukrainian children will be on the hands of the owner and the entire team of this American company,” Ukrainian human rights lawyer Oleksandra Matviichuk said.

Military analyst Giorgi Revishvili previously told The Sun the restrictions exposed a major weakness in Kyiv’s battle plan.



He said: “Kyiv lacks a viable replacement capable of filling that gap of Starshield’s protection.

“This will be very hard to do in the short term when winter is coming and Ukraine will face more bombardments.”

Russia continued to pound Kyiv on Wednesday night, unleashing 21 ballistic missiles and 210 drones across the capital.



At least two people were killed and 34 were left injured in the horror blitz targeting residential areas, power plants and medical facilities.

The salvo struck just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations after talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

As the war grinds into its fifth year, Russia has ramped up mass attacks to wipe out Ukraine’s critical infrastructure to cut off heat and water.

Suffering a critical shortage of air defences, Ukraine’s economy is being pushed to the brink by Russian strikes.

News.title: Pregnant woman, 27, ‘dissolved in acid by ex & girlfriend’ ID’d by tattoo reading ‘when I die you’ll love me’
News.content:
DEPTHS OF EVIL Pregnant woman, 27, ‘dissolved in acid by ex & girlfriend’ ID’d by tattoo reading ‘when I die you’ll love me’







Next

A PREGNANT woman has been identified by a tattoo reading, “When I die you’ll love me” after being dissolved in acid and buried in a shallow grave in Brazil.

Beatriz Vitoria Aparecida Neves Mota, 27, was found buried in a wooded area near Jaboticatubas, in the region of Belo Horizonte on Wednesday – 12 days after she went missing.



Her ex-boyfriend, Samuel Castro Melo, 18, who may have been the father of her unborn child, and his now girlfriend, Carla Luiza da Silva, 23, have been arrested on suspicion of involvement in her murder.

When the victim’s current boyfriend, Yuri Gabriel Guedes Lopes, saw her remains, he could not recognise her.



It was only through the distinctive tattoo near Beatriz’s collarbone that she was identified.

“They beat her, tied her up with wire and even poured caustic soda over her body. There were clumps of hair beside her,” he said.



“Probably they used caustic soda to dissolve the body. I recognised her through a tattoo. What they did was absolutely disgusting.”

Beatriz is believed to have been three-onths pregnant when she was killed.



Her brother, Maxwell Sergio Marques Mota, 29, said the family had only discovered that Beatriz might have been pregnant after she vanished.

He said: “My younger sister told me that Beatriz had taken pregnancy tests and one came back positive. She would have been around three months pregnant, and there is a chance it was Samuel’s. We are all very sad.”

Beatriz had reportedly been in a relationship with Samuel for a month, but her family said the pair had separated about three months before her death.

Yuri, who had been dating the victim for around four weeks, described her as a generous young woman who was always willing to help others.

“She was capable of giving the whole world if she could. She was a very humble girl, always ready to help,” he said.



Beatriz was last seen by friends at a bar in Jaboticatubas on the evening of October 9.

A car pulled up nearby at around 7pm and she went outside to speak to the driver.

Her sister, Giovanna Neves de Castro, said Beatriz had become extremely nervous after receiving a telephone call while at the bar.



“She asked for five minutes to go down to the next street to meet someone and said that, if she didn’t come back, they should go after her,” she said.

“When she didn’t return, her friends went looking for her but could no longer find her.”

According to local reports, Beatriz briefly returned inside and told people she was frightened because there was a woman inside the car who she did not recognise.

She then left again, and was never seen alive again.

Local media reported that a teenager, Maria Eduarda, told police that she had accompanied Samuel and Carla when they drove to pick up Beatriz that same evening.



She recalled that Samuel then drove to an area of vacant plots known as Terra dos Portugueses.

Samuel and Carla got out and went further into the area with Beatriz while Maria Eduarda remained inside the vehicle.

About 30 minutes later, the couple allegedly returned without the victim.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The teenager later guided police to the area , where investigators found her remains.

The investigation is ongoing.

News.title: Trump ordered to sit for deposition over $10bn BBC Panorama doc lawsuit or face defamation case being dismissed
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump has been ordered to answer questions under oath over his $10billion lawsuit against the BBC.

The US President risks his defamation case being dismissed if he does not sit for the deposition by December 11.



Trump is suing the broadcaster for a misleading Panorama edit of his speech on the day of the US Capitol attack on January 6, 2021.

He claims the Corporation defamed him and violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.



The BBC denies the claims and has apologised for the error.

Charles Tobin, the BBC‘s lawyer, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”

Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing “matters of national importance” while he was campaigning in Georgia.

A deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to a series of questions.

In a filing on Wednesday, Trump’s lawyers said the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year.

They said the BBC was “wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action.”



It comes just months after the BBC demanded to see Trump’s tax returns as part of the legal proceedings.

The move aimed to show if Trump really suffered “direct harm to his professional and occupational interests” as is claimed in his lawsuit.

The BBC’s lawyers said in March: “Plaintiff (Mr Trump) put his financial condition at issue the moment he filed this case.”

They also want financial records from the President’s vast real estate and media empire, including companies in Bali, Hungary, Vietnam, Ireland and the UK, as well as the US.

If the corporation does gain access, it could give unprecedented insight into his wealth.



Trump pushed back and called the BBC’s request a “fishing expedition”.

A judge granted the request in July but another judge then agreed to an emergency motion filed by Trump’s lawyers to pause the disclosure.

The BBC has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

Trump’s lawyer conceded this summer that they had no evidence the documentary was available in the US as they originally claimed.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The US president agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, after the BBC argued its commercial arm had “no role in creating or producing” the doc.



Depositions are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials.

News.title: Range Rover demolishes quiet town’s historic cross in crash as pedestrian taken to hospital
News.content:
'A REAL MESS' Range Rover demolishes quiet town’s historic cross in crash as pedestrian taken to hospital







Next

A RANGE Rover smashed into a historic market cross in the middle of a quiet town with one pedestrian rushed to hospital.

The reckless driver demolished the local landmark of Howden, East Yorkshire, just after 10.30 am today.



The 4×4 drove into the medieval monument, mounting its base and causing the five-metre-high cross to topple over.

The impact of the car crash sent parts of the Grade II listed landmark flying across the ground.



Pictures of the incident show the car’s punctured tyres and bumper hanging off the front.

Emergency services raced to the scene with on pedestrian taken to hospital for further examination.

But thankfully there have been no reports of any serious injuries.

The vehicle has since been recovered and removed from the site.



Local officials are now investigating the damage and working out how best to conserve and fix their town’s important monument.

David Howard, a local independent councillor, was alerted of the incident and went to see the dramatic scene.

He said of the cross: “It’s in a real mess. It marks the centre of the town and it needs to be put back in some form – restored, repaired, replaced.

“It does look like a very, very interesting art installation at the motor show at the moment.

“In fact, it’s almost an album cover from an early 1980s rock band.”



A Humberside Police spokesperson said the collision said: “Officers were deployed to a reported road traffic collision in the area of Market Place, Howden, involving a car and a pedestrian this morning.

“Thankfully, nobody is believed to have sustained serious injuries as a result of the collision.

“The vehicle has since been recovered and the road closure that was put in place whilst emergency services attended has now reopened.”

News.title: Horror in Spain as man dies after walking into fishmongers and taking his own life after grabbing blade from shop
News.content:
BLADE TRAGEDY Horror in Spain as man dies after walking into fishmongers and taking his own life after grabbing blade from shop







Next

A MAN has died after walking into a fishmongers, snatching a knife from the counter and slashing his throat.

The incident happened in Seville earlier today in front a horrified shoppes.



The victim first walked into a bar that had just opened – but was thrown out after requesting a knife to take his own life.

He then headed to to the fishmongers, called Pescaderia Susana, where he stabbed himself multiple times.



People desperately attempted to disarm him but the man eventually collapsed in a pool of blood.

An unnamed eyewitness said: “I saw him stab himself at least six times in the chest and several more times in the neck, but he was still standing.



“He just kept stabbing himself. He wouldn’t fall over so we could take the knife away from him. It was horrific, absolutely harrowing.

“I heard the screams of the horrified fishmongers. My legs are still shaking. I know it was only a few minutes, but it felt like an eternity to me.”

Police and paramedics rushed to Luis Montoto Street, where the incident happened, after receiving multiple 999 calls.

Nothing could be done to save the victim and he was pronounced dead at the scene and a screen was put up around his body.



Residents have told police they did not recognise the man, believed to be aged around 40.

His identity and nationality have not yet been made public.

Owner of the fishmongers, Susana Calvo, was slightly injured after a brief struggle with the man.

She said his only words were, “One moment, one moment” as he walked behind the counter without permission to take the weapon he used on himself.

He then started stabbing himself inside the premises before continuing to harm himself outside on the pavement.



How to get help EVERY 90 minutes in the UK a life is lost to suicide It doesn’t discriminate, touching the lives of people in every corner of society – from the homeless and unemployed to builders and doctors, reality stars and footballers. It’s the biggest killer of people under the age of 35, more deadly than cancer and car crashes. And men are three times more likely to take their own life than women. Yet it’s rarely spoken of, a taboo that threatens to continue its deadly rampage unless we all stop and take notice, now. News.title: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns public
News.content:
Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting says.

Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.

He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.

Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El NiÃ±o event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean.

Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.

He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and with flooding expected this winter.

Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".

"How would we cope if the payment systems at the local supermarket went down?" he said.

"Those are the sorts of everyday challenges and threats that we could well face. And it's right that we ask the country to be ready for those things and to ask everyone to do their bit."

News.title: AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened
News.content:
Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain a massive flaw in internet technology, after AI discovered issues that could be exploited by hackers.

Developers of the PHP platform - which powers more than 70% of websites, including Wikipedia and digital shopping sites - rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

Cyber-security firm Wiz described the issue as the "most severe" ever detected, while OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

But how did AI discover a massive cyber-security risk in the internet, and what does it mean for you? The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy reports.

Read more on the cyber-security threat here.

News.title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".

The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.

Statements from the woman's parents were also heard in court, saying their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, and that she had been "very worried about HIV".

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

The witness said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre, and that he then sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.

She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after", she said she "was just crying - really upset".

The witness said Brand had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually.

"He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her.

"He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".

The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.

News.title: Woman charged after police officer injured in shooting
News.content:
A 27-year-old woman has been charged after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer was shot in the foot after he approached a man and a woman at a bus stop in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The male officer remains in hospital receiving treatment, the force added.

Aisha Zaman, of Collison Street, Hyson Green, has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence.

Nottinghamshire Police has said on Friday the charge comes after "consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service".

Zaman has been remanded into custody and will appear before Nottingham Magistrates' Court on Friday, police added.

Several other people have been arrested in connection with the incident, including two men, aged 24 and 30, and two women, aged 25 and 21, who have been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

A 35-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender. Both remain in police custody.

Det Ch Supt Rich Bull, who is leading the investigation, said the "outpouring of support" for the officer had been "greatly appreciated".

"We would just like to take this moment to thank the public", he added.

"We continue to support him as he undergoes further treatment in hospital and keeping him and his family fully informed of the developments in this investigation."

He said officers were "still following a number of lines of inquiry", and anyone with information has been asked to contact the force.

News.title: Two storms in two days as Austen and Boelo head for UK
News.content:
Gusts of wind will widely reach 60-70mph, and perhaps 80mph in exposed locations.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts.

Some buildings could potentially be damaged by the strongest winds, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm.

Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places.

As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre.

That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph.

The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph.

All schools have been told to close on Friday because of the high winds predicted to be caused by Storm Austen, the Government of Jersey has said.

Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday.

News.title: Watch: Ukraine hit by strikes after Russia agrees to new peace talks
News.content:
Kyiv has been hit by another round of missile strikes hours after Russia agreed to resume peace talks on Wednesday.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said the three waves of missiles were launched by "Russian humanitarians".

This comes after US envoy Steve Witkoff called Russia's President Vladimir Putin a "humanitarian" following a meeting in St Petersburg on Wednesday.

Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks with the US and Ukraine.

The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from the scene of a destroyed retail park.

More on this story.

News.title: Caroline Flack's brother 'never recovered' from her death, inquest hears
News.content:
The brother of TV presenter Caroline Flack took his own life having "never recovered" after his sister's death, an inquest heard.

Paul Flack, 55, was found unresponsive at his home in Sandringham Road, Norwich, on 21 June, and died later in hospital.

His partner told Norfolk Coroner's Court how he had struggled with his father developing dementia and his younger sister's death in 2020.

Area Coroner Johanna Thompson gave a narrative conclusion, stating Paul Flack died while under the influence of alcohol and that his "intent in doing so is unknown".

He was described as "everyone's favourite person" by his partner Joanna Millington, but she said this "took its toll".

His sister, the ex-Love Island and X Factor host, was found dead at her home in Stoke Newington, east London, on 15 February 2020.

"We then went into lockdown for Covid," said Millington, who provided a written statement to the court.

"I do not think Paul ever recovered from this."

An inquest later established Caroline Flack took her own life, aged 40, having feared press intrusion ahead of her trial accused of assaulting her boyfriend.

News.title: Dame Judi Dench: 'I can't do a play, a film or read anymore'
News.content:
Dench also discussed meeting American actor Sidney Poitier, who became the first black man to win the Academy Award for best actor in 1964.

She was appearing in Amy's View in New York when Poitier came backstage after a performance. She recalled that director Richard Eyre was in her dressing room, giving her notes, when there was a knock at the door.

Dench said she felt as if she were in a wind tunnel when Poitier walked in, adding: "It was thrilling."

Asked what she had said to him, Dench replied: "Not much, a bit of an open mouth. So charming. Very tall."

The conversation then turned to Dench's love of Shakespeare. She recalled watching her brother play King Duncan in Macbeth when she was nine and said the moment sparked her passion for the playwright.

"He walked on and he said 'What bloody man is that?' I thought, 'oh my God, this is for me'. He said 'bloody', did you hear that?"

She also admitted to being " besotted" by Shakespeare's sonnets: "I just love them."

"It's the rhythm of it. It's the rhythm of your heart," she added, "it's the way he's summed up so simply the way that any of us feel about, well, anything."

News.title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
News.content:
Barclays is cutting around 5,000 staff as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.

The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce.

The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.

Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.

Although not all of the cuts are due to AI, their scale will prompt further concern over the impact of the new technology.

Company spending on AI is increasing along with claims new tools can replace some of the basic tasks currently done by staff such as administrative and programming work.

HSBC, Standard Chartered and Danske Bank have also flagged AI-related job cuts this year.

"It is a hot button topic," said AJ Bell investment analyst, Russ Mould.

However, banks had not yet made big moves towards the widespread introduction of AI and they would be considering the implications for security and customer service before implementing AI technology to make financial savings, he said.

"Any company at any time needs to keep on top of its cost base," he said.

"It will be intriguing to see what other banks say in their results in the coming weeks.

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union that represents banking sector workers said the company was "using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce".

"Employers should be focussed on upgrading employees' skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach," she said.

Barclays is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.

AJ Bell's Russ Mould said despite "reaching for the AI lever" Barclays had failed to match expectations with its financial results.

Barclays also revealed it made Â£2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.

Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business.

"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future.

"We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake.

"Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."

Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers.

Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".

"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.

Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further Â£1.1bn of savings in 2027.

News.title: Tommy Robinson hired detectives to find journalists, court told
News.content:
Political activist Tommy Robinson has told a court he hired private detectives to track down and photograph two reporters to "put pressure" on them.

The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, told Southwark Crown Court he was "shocked and scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".

He has denied two charges of harassment causing fear of violence to reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber after the 2024 Southport attacks.

Robinson is accused of writing posts on X, sending direct messages and making phone calls that made the two journalists fear the risk of vigilante attacks.

He denied wanting to expose the journalists to threats of violence, and said he felt his actions were "totally reasonable... under the circumstances".

News.title: Map thief leads 'merry dance' with return promises
News.content:
Defence barrister Jessica Flain said West had partly paid a man to restore the map, but he would not hand it back until the full fee was settled. She asked for sentencing to be adjourned for seven days so a friend could pay the balance and West could take the map to Charing Cross Police Station.

Judge Charlotte Welsh refused, saying she did "not believe a word of it".

She said West had told the court in June that he could return the map within seven days, and in August that it was with a friend and he would retrieve it once he had recovered from heart surgery.

"Again, that appears to have been a lie," she said. "You were charged in February. You have had eight months to return the map."

The judge said she believed West had a buyer in mind and had stolen the map "to order".

The court heard he had 27 convictions for 107 offences in the UK and abroad, mostly for dishonesty and including 41 thefts. They included a burglary conviction in Hungary in 2011 and a theft conviction in France in 2013, and he had also been convicted under various identities.

Flain said West, a father of two, was "ashamed and embarrassed" and had been in debt and unable to meet basic living costs. She described the offence as "a short-term, pressured decision by an elderly man living in difficult circumstances".

Judge Welsh said the map was of "international cultural significance" and the damage had "permanently diminished what can be learned from it". The court was told the two digital copies of the atlas are incomplete.

West was jailed for three years for criminal damage, with concurrent sentences of 16 months for theft and six months for possessing a bladed article. The judge refused to suspend the sentence, saying immediate custody was needed "to deter other people from doing precisely what you have".

News.title: Police should not be scared to wade in to stop wrongdoing, says Badenoch
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised punishments for people who intervene to "do the right thing" in a speech at the Police Federation conference.

Telling delegates she was "not scared to wade in", she called for more support for members of the public as well as police officers who step in to stop wrongdoing.

Badenoch also criticised Labour for failing to send a minister to the conference for two years in a row.

The prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman rejected the claims, stating the police have the government's "full backing" and are benefitting from investment. The BBC has contacted the Home Office for comment on ministerial attendance at the police conference.

In a speech at the conference, Badenoch said: "Too often these days, we fail to recognise sacrifice and service.

"Whether it's hounding brave and elderly veterans through the courts, hounding police officers who try to do the right thing, or even ordinary members of the public who step in to help only to find that they're in trouble themselves.

"It's no wonder the people in this country are becoming too scared to wade in, too scared to do the right thing. Well, I am different. I am not scared to wade in, and I am not scared to back the police."

The Conservative leader listed police officers who have been killed in the line of duty, such as PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough who died in the Cleveland A66 crash, and PC Andrew Harper, killed investigating a quad bike theft.

She also attacked police being investigated following controversial cases, including the case of 24-year-old Chris Kaba, who was shot by Sgt Matthew Blake in 2022 after he tried to ram his way past police cars.

The police officer was put on trial for murder before being cleared, with Badenoch saying his "job was made harder because he didn't get the backing he deserved".

Badenoch also attacked Labour, saying: "I think it is telling that for two years in a row, the Labour Government has not sent anyone to address this conference â not the policing minister, not the Home Secretary.

"You are the ones who enforce the law. You are the ones who ensure there are consequences for bad behaviour. That's why, if we want law and order back in our country, back on our streets, we need to back the police."

Responding, the prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman said: "I would reject those claims.

"The police have the government's full backing and as you will have seen from various reports this morning, we are continuing to invest in our police and we are bringing forward reforms following the Bernard Hogan Howe report in due course."

The Home Office has been contacted for comment about ministerial attendance at the conference and whether the government is still planning to recruit 13,000 police officers.

News.title: Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists
News.content:
The energy minister has insisted she backs Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's immigration reforms after she made what she described as a "light-hearted remark".

Miatta Fahnbulleh was repeatedly asked in an interview on Wednesday whether she supported the government's plans to increase the time it takes for migrants to gain permanent UK residency, but refused to.

Referring to that exchange, she joked to reporters on Thursday that she did not explicitly answer the question because she had told herself she would "never lie".

In a later statement, she said: "Today I made what was meant to be a light-hearted self-deprecating remark. I didn't get it right and it hasn't come off as I intended."

She added: "I fully support our home secretary and the government's position on migration reform."

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

The government wants to double the time it takes most migrant workers to qualify for permanent residence from five years to 10 years, while in the case of refugees it could take 20 years.

Mahmood told Labour Party conference in September the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country".

But a significant number of Labour MPs and trade unions want her to water down the proposed policy.

Downing Street has repeatedly insisted that Mahmood is considering responses to a consultation exercise before finalising the reforms.

On Wednesday, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to make sure we get this right."

Asked earlier on the same day on Sky News, whether she backed the proposed reforms, Fahnbulleh said: "We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution."

She was pressed several more times on the issue, saying the government was consulting on the proposals and would "will come out with the measures that we take forward".

At a lunch with political reporters on Thursday, Fahnbulleh said: "I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge [on Sky] yesterday, but nevermind."

In her later statement, she said this was a joke and suggested it was not intended to show she did not support Mahmood's reforms.

"As I said earlier this week, it's absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship," Fahnbulleh said.

It comes after another Cabinet minister, Angela Rayner, criticised the proposed changes ahead of Labour's conference in Liverpool.

Rayner warned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules.

She later denied there was a split within the heart of government over the issue.

News.title: Man, 61, charged with murder after 'stabbed' woman dies following crash
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder after a woman who had suffered "stab wounds" died following a crash.

Housing association worker Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to the crash in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision", which the BBC understands were sustained in a stabbing.

Clifford Foster, 61, from Bridgend, has been charged with murder and is due to appear at Newport Magistrates' Court on Friday.

The Welsh Ambulance Service (WAS) has denied Barnfield was driving because of ambulance wait times, saying it was aware of "misleading rumours" circulating online.

It said medics were called to the crash in Coity Road at about 12:44 BST and a response unit arrived seven minutes later.

In a statement issued later on Thursday, WAS said that from initial investigations it had been "unable to identify" any calls from Barnfield's phone numbers.

"Enquiries are ongoing to establish if any calls were received by other means," it added.

Reports in some media had claimed Eleanor had crashed her car while driving herself to hospital.

Ger-y-Nant retirement housing complex, where police arrested Foster on Tuesday, is a few minutes' drive from the Princess of Wales Hospital, with Coity Road the main road in between.

Senior Investigating Officer Claire Lamerton said her thoughts were with Barnfield's loved ones, who were being supported by specialist officers.

"This is not being investigated as a domestic incident, and I encourage the public to not speculate about the circumstances as court proceedings are now active," she said.

News.title: UK plans emergency powers to protect undersea cables
News.content:
The government has outlined new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables amid increased fears of Russian interference.

Ministers are set to gain powers to order telecom companies to remove or disable services during national security emergencies, as well as granting officials access to sites including cable landing stations.

The government has also outlined plans for stronger criminal penalties for those convicted of tampering with either undersea internet cables or energy pipelines.

The new powers would be backed up with prison sentences of up to 14 years for intentional conduct, 10 years for reckless conduct and two years for grossly negligent conduct, alongside unlimited fines.

It comes amid growing fears of suspicious activity in UK waters, and concerns that legal powers over the network have not kept pace with its growing importance to national security.

An extensive network of undersea cables and pipelines owned and operated primarily by the private sector are thought to carry almost all the UK's international data traffic and three-quarters of its gas supplies.

The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report last year, external to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.

The UK and its Nato allies are concerned about the risk Russia poses to offshore infrastructure.

In April, the government accused Russian submarines of conducting a covert operation over cables and pipelines in waters north of the UK.

The UK has also accused Russia of mapping undersea infrastructure using spy ships. Last year, it revealed the Royal Navy had tracked one such suspected ship, the Yantar, after it passed near UK waters.

Russia has denied the claims, and accused the UK of stirring up tensions through "anti-Russian alarmism".

News.title: Retired decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m
News.content:
A retired decorator has become a millionaire after selling a collection of PokÃ©mon cards at auction.

The man, from Woking, said he had no idea the cards had any value until he read in his local newspaper about a single card fetching more than Â£6,000.

His collection, which had been in an attic for 15 years, was auctioned off at Ewbank's on Wednesday for Â£1.56m.

The Surrey auction house claimed it was the UK's most valuable trading cards auction ever and suggested it could be a European record.

"I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true," said the man, who asked not to be identified.

"When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school.

"I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment.

"He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say."

PokÃ©mon is a Japanese franchise best known for its trading cards, video games and animated television series.

The man said he had bought some complete sets of the cards from someone in Malaysia on eBay.

One set which cost him Â£300 at the time went for Â£75,000 at Wednesday's auction.

The cards, all filed into bespoke PokÃ©mon binders while still sealed, were stored in the attic after his son lost interest in the franchise.

News.title: Top Gun star Tom Skerritt dies aged 93
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Tom Skerritt, the Emmy-winning actor who starred in Top Gun and the TV series Picket Fences, has died at age 93.

Skerritt died on Wednesday of natural causes, according to his family. In his work, he embodied a solid, wry authority figure, whether as a flight instructor in Top Gun, a tough-but-fair sheriff in Picket Fences or the doomed captain of Alien.

“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives. He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices,” his family wrote.

Skerritt was nominated for an Emmy twice, both for Picket Fences, and won outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993.

open image in gallery Tom Skerritt with his wife, Julie Tokashiki, at the IWC Schaffhausen Top Gun Gala Event on January 17, 2012 in Geneva, Switzerland ( Getty Images for IWC )

Other career highlights include playing Shirley MacLaine’s patient husband in Turning Point, Sally Field’s husband in Steel Magnolias and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster’s attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in Contact.

“A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man’s body, and I’ve always loved that. It’s a nice compliment. I’ve been able to walk the line between television and features,” he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997.

Onstage, he was the narrator in Our Town at Seattle’s Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham's A Time to Kill, in which The Associated Press wrote he “nicely pulls off a charming disgraced and drunken lawyer.”

Tom Skerritt’s early life

Skerritt grew up in a middle-class Detroit family, his father a small businessman and his mother a housewife. He had two brothers; a sister died as a child. He spent four years in the Air Force, attended Wayne State University and then switched to the University of California, Los Angeles, to study filmmaking, inspired by a viewing of Citizen Kane.

His performance in a Los Angeles theater production of The Rainmaker led to his first film role — a supporting role as a sergeant in the 1962 scrappy, $250,000 independent Korean War film War Hunt. The movie marked the debuts of Skerritt, Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola.

Redford and Skerritt were vying for the same lead role, with the former winning out. Years later, Redford, now directing, paid Skerritt back with compound interest in A River Runs Through It, handing him the plum role of the stern Rev. John Maclean, a minister whose governing passions are his faith and fly-fishing. The New York Times was impressed by his “halting, thoughtful manner.”

open image in gallery Tom Skerritt and Jenifer Lewis at the 26th Satellite Awards Presentation at W Hollywood on April 02, 2022 in Hollywood, California ( Getty Images )

Redford, who died last year, became a lifelong friend. “There was such a deep connection we made with each other that it matured into a level-headed friendship,” Redford told the Seattle Times in 2007. “His values were close to mine, and he kept his integrity.”

‘Alien’ and ‘Top Gun’

After War Hunt, however, Skerritt still struggled for screen time, landing a small role in M.A.S.H. and Thieves Like Us for Robert Altman, and doing a bit part as a motorcycle cop in Harold and Maude for Hal Ashby.

Things changed with The Turning Point, which earned him a National Board of Review win. Then came Alien, with Skerritt playing the beleaguered and doomed captain of the ship Nostromo, crouched in a dark, claustrophobic duct, hunting the alien with a sputtering flamethrower. He told the Seattle Times that what appealed to him in the script was that the lead actor disappeared and “the woman becomes the hero. I really like that idea.”

Things shifted again after that, including a memorable role as Tom Cruise’s instructor in the landmark Top Gun: “Gentlemen, you are the top 1% of all Naval aviators. The elite. The best of the best. We’ll make you better,” he told the students. “This school is about combat. There are no points for second place.”

Skerritt achieved perhaps his best notices as the kindly sheriff in Picket Fences, a comedy created by David E. Kelley that won 14 Emmy Awards — one for Skerritt — and a Golden Globe over its four-year run from 1992 to 1996.

Skerritt co-starred opposite Kathy Baker, playing his doctor wife in the community of Rome, Wisconsin, a place with bizarre happenings, like having a robber leaving a trail of frogs or the pope becoming the primary witness to a murder.

open image in gallery Picket Fences creator David E. Kelley (center) poses with actors Tom Skerritt and Kathy Baker after the show won best drama series during the 45th annual Emmy Awards in Pasadena, Calif., on Sept. 19, 1993 ( AP Photo/Douglas C. Pizac )

“It was written by the best writer on television,” he told the A.V. Club in 2019. “That was the magic and brilliance of it. Because I wasn’t trying to do a series, but then they said Kathy Baker was going to do it, and I thought, ‘She’s fabulous — what do they want me for?’”

Also on the small screen, Skerritt played William Walker on ABC’s Brothers and Sisters, Jimmy Ford on TNT’s Leverage and he had the recurring character Evan Drake on Cheers. He starred in the Hallmark movie What the Deaf Man Heard, co-starring Matthew Modine, Judith Ivey and James Earl Jones. He also modeled for Guess jeans.

Directing and writing — his initial dream — had been overtaken by a career in front of the camera, though he managed to direct and star in the 1997 television movie Divided by Hate.

“Things happen,” he told The Ottawa Citizen in 1992. “You get hired for a film and the roles kept coming for me. I kept telling myself that if I stuck with acting it would be a really good training for what the problems are in directing. Then the family came along and I had to support them. The years flew by and there was a time when I said I would give up acting and really try to get into directing. But it hasn’t worked out that way and I have no regrets.”

He is survived by his third wife, Julie Tokashiki, and five children.

News.title: Trump counted on young voters to win in 2024. They are now switching to Democrats in droves
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Almost two years into President Donald Trump’s second administration and young Americans -who helped him win the White House in 2024 - are shifting their support to Democrats, polling suggests.

Just weeks ahead of the midterm elections, the number of voters aged 18 to 29 who identified as Democrat or leaned that way has jumped from 55 percent in 2024 to 70 percent, according to the latest New York Times/Siena poll of likely voters.

Across the country, young voters are more likely to cast their ballot for the Democratic candidate in their district by 44 percentage points, compared with a 10-point margin in 2024, the poll found.

While Trump made gains with young voters two years ago, only 16 percent of voters aged 18 to 29 now approve of his job performance, compared to 79 percent who disapprove. In another blow, 86 percent of those 18 to 29 disapprove of how the president has handled the economy.

Trump’s war in Iran is also proving deeply unpopular with younger voters, with 87 percent saying they disapprove.

open image in gallery Young Americans are signaling a shift to the Democratic party ahead of the midterms after two years under President Donald Trump’s second term ( AFP via Getty Images )

Young male voters flocked to Trump in 2024, with more than half (55 percent) of the demographic signaling their support for him, according to the NYT/Siena poll. Now, Democrats hold a 1 percent advantage over the president with young men.

Support for Trump and Republicans among young women, who lean more liberal, has also dropped since 2024.

Still, younger voters are not massively impressed with the Democrats either. The poll found that 41 percent said the party was not focused on the right issues. Still, the Republican Party fared worse among the demographic—77 percent said the GOP had the wrong focus.

Overall, the NYT/Siena poll found that the majority of voters, aged 18 to 29, believed Democrats had a better handling of the economy, the cost of living, immigration, foreign wars, healthcare, AI, gas prices and corruption than Republicans.

The Harvard Youth Poll, released Thursday, had similar findings. Democrats lead Republicans 63 percent to 26 percent among likely voters ages 18–29, with 10 percent undecided, it found.

Half of young Democrats (50 percent) said that they will definitely vote in November, compared with 34 percent of young Republicans. Among young people who say they will definitely vote, 63 percent describe their vote as opposition to Trump and his policies, compared with 14 percent who describe it as support.

open image in gallery Despite the bump, younger voters are not massively impressed with the Democrats either - 41 percent said the party was not focused on the right issues. But young people were even more damning of Republicans, with 77 percent saying the party had the wrong focus ( AFP via Getty Images )

“Young voters are poised to deliver a sharp rebuke to President Trump, while the broader generation is sending a message to everyone in power,” said John Della Volpe, director of polling at the Institute of Politics.

“Young people feel economic pressure, and they’re holding the current administration responsible — making the midterms a critical referendum on Trump and his policies,” added Sophia Robertson, student chair of the Harvard Public Opinion Project.

Trump’s approval rating has languished near historic lows for months but the White House has brushed off the unfavorable polls.

“President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a previous statement.

Trump himself has acknowledged that the president’s party historically tends to lose seats in Congress in the midterms.

“For whatever reason, I don't understand it, nobody does. Nobody's been able to explain it. Whoever wins the presidency, Republican or Democrat, automatically does poorly in the midterms,” he told reporters earlier this month.

News.title: Jury deliberates in trial of New Yorker who became a teen bride to an Islamic State fighter
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A New York woman accused of receiving weapons training from the Islamic State group was tricked by her father into traveling to Syria, where she became an unwilling teen bride to a militant fighter, her lawyer told a jury Thursday.

Halima Salman, a U.S. citizen born in Brooklyn, was 17 when her father took the family to Turkey in 2017, then put her in a van without saying where they were going and drove into Syria, where the van was surrounded by men with guns, according to her lawyer, Mia Eisner-Grynberg.

There, she became caught up in the Syrian Civil War. She spent three months locked in a room while the sound of bombs striking nearby targets could frequently be heard. Her father, an Islamic State sympathizer, died after he was injured in a bombing in 2018, but not before arranging for her to marry a member of the group when she turned 18. She was then detained in Baghouz, Syria, in 2019 by forces opposed to the Islamic State.

When Salman returned to the U.S. in 2024, she was arrested and charged with willingly undergoing military training with the Islamic State in 2018, when she was 18.

“Find her not guilty,” Eisner-Grynberg told a jury Thursday as Salman used her clothing to wipe away tears. She said Salman had “been through hell and back" since leaving New York, where she had been in the Girl Scouts and studied sewing and craft making.

Prosecutors insist Salman had more agency in Syria than she claims.

In her closing arguments Wednesday, Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda Shami portrayed Salman, now 27, as dishonest and manipulative.

She said Salman had pledged loyalty to the Islamic State and sent her then-husband a photograph of her with the group's flag. She had also been filmed by her husband with an assault rifle she had been trained to use. Jurors were shown the brief video clip.

During the trial, Salman took the witness stand and testified that her marriage was bad before she left Syria and divorced her husband. The prosecutor, Shami, disputed that account of a poor marriage, citing two loving text messages Salman sent to her husband.

“Her statements on the stand don't make sense,” Shami said.

Eisner-Grynberg said the government was right to investigate Salman after her time in Syria but should not have brought charges after failing to find anyone who had seen her undergoing weapons training. She said prosecutors could not show that Salman ever took a serious interest in the Islamic State, which has been designated by the United States as a terror group.

“You can come back here in five minutes with a not-guilty verdict,” Eisner-Grynberg told jurors. “This is a grave miscarriage of justice,” she said of the prosecution.

The jury began deliberating Thursday.

News.title: Woman, 27, charged after police officer shot in Nottingham
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A woman has been charged in connection with the shooting of a police officer in Nottingham city centre on Sunday.

Aisha Zaman, 27, of Collison Street, Hyson Green, has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence, Nottinghamshire Police said.

She has been remanded into custody and will appear before Nottingham Magistrates' Court on Friday.

The incident happened at a bus stop in Angel Row at around 4.50am on Sunday.

The officer approached two people acting suspiciously and received a gunshot wound to the foot.

He remains in hospital receiving treatment.

The force said officers stopped a vehicle in the Radford area of the city on Sunday evening and arrested a 27-year-old woman on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm with intent and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

A 24-year-old man and a 25-year-old woman inside the vehicle were also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender, police said.

They were later released on conditional bail pending further enquiries.

Late on Wednesday, police said Nottingham Magistrates’ Court had granted detectives a warrant of further detention, allowing them to continue questioning the 27-year-old suspect.

A 30-year-old man who was arrested in Bedfordshire early on Monday was also questioned on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Police said he has since been recalled to prison for breaching the terms of his licence.

A 21-year-old woman was detained in southeast London on Tuesday on suspicion of assisting an offender.

open image in gallery The incident happened at a bus stop in Angel Row at around 4.50am on Sunday ( AFP/Getty )

She was later released on conditional bail pending further enquiries.

On Wednesday afternoon, a 35-year-old man was arrested in the Bulwell area of Nottingham on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender.

Later that evening, a seventh person was arrested when a 33-year-old woman was detained in Aspley also on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender. Both remain in custody.

Detective Chief Superintendent Rich Bull, who is leading the investigation, said: "We would just like to take this moment to thank the public. The outpouring of support for the injured officer has been greatly appreciated.

"We continue to support him as he undergoes further treatment in hospital and are keeping him and his family fully informed of the developments in this investigation.

"He has asked for privacy during this incredibly difficult time.

"We have now charged a 27-year-old woman in connection with this incident.

"We hope this offers the public some reassurance.

"Our investigation team are still following a number of lines of inquiry to ensure those responsible are arrested, charged, and put before the courts."

The Police Federation of England and Wales sent best wishes to the officer and said it was a “stark reminder of the dangers police officers face every day”.

Anyone with new information that could help our inquiry are being urged to call 101 quoting incident 106 of 18 October 2026 or Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

More to follow...
