Sports.title: Next in line? Main contenders for the Manchester United hot seat
Sports.content:
Julian Nagelsmann (unattached)

The German was of interest to Manchester City while Omar Berrada was part of the hierarchy on the other side of town. He is highly thought of and would come with an impressive CV for a 39-year-old, having taken charge of Bayern Munich and Germany. Nagelsmann is regarded as an innovator who is very demanding of his players and builds teams to press relentlessly, a concept not currently used at United, as Bruno Fernandes will testify. His spell with Germany was underwhelming, concluding with a 2026 World Cup last-32 defeat by Paraguay, and at Bayern – with an exceptional squad – he won the Bundesliga in his only full season and was sacked the following March with the team second and still in the Champions League.

Unai Emery (Aston Villa)

The King of the Europa League is tactically astute and knows about working on a budget. If he is intrigued by the prospect of managing United, it would come down to whether he believes they have more potential than Villa, who are one point and place above them in the Premier League and faring much better in the Champions League, and whether United are willing to pay significant compensation. Emery likes a 4-2-3-1 but has always had a central striker at his disposal, and United lack someone strong in this department. Very calm but with a ruthless edge when required, he has plenty of silverware to back up his credentials. He is regarded as one of the game’s great pragmatists and is happy to play on the counterattack, which would suit the United squad.

Antonio Conte (unattached)

The Italian, who left Napoli in the summer, knows the Premier League from spells with Chelsea and Tottenham, winning the title with the former in 2017. A fierce competitor and disciplinarian, he would shake up the dressing room with his high standards. His fiery temper can also result in fascinating interactions with the media, including telling a post-match press conference after losing to Burnley that maybe he was not the right man to manage Spurs. His willingness to speak out when it may not necessarily be wise could put United off. His preference for playing three at the back could be problematic considering the personnel at United, as Ruben Amorim found out.

View image in fullscreen Antonio Conte has a record of winning trophies but a combustible style that may not be ideal for an already turbulent Manchester United. Photograph: Dave Thomposon/AP

Kieran McKenna (unattached)

The Northern Irishman worked within the United academy before stepping up to be part of José Mourinho’s backroom staff alongside Carrick. He stayed when Ole Gunnar Solskjær replaced the Portuguese and was credited with having a strong tactical influence as United secured second place. It is often a strength to have a link to a club but considering the struggles Solskjær and Carrick have endured, an external candidate seems more appropriate. He departed to become a head coach at Ipswich and his work there meant he was linked with a return to United to replace Erik ten Hag. McKenna resigned in June after securing promotion to the Premier League for a second time to take time away from the day-to-day grind of managemen. Would he want to end his sabbatical by jumping into a precarious situation after five or so months?

Eddie Howe (unattached)

The English option and a manager with plenty of Premier League experience who took Newcastle to the Champions League. Arguably this makes him the safest pair of hands. A hard worker, Howe was often first in and last out at the Newcastle training ground as he pored over every detail. A lover of wingers and 4-3-3, he would be reliant on a central striker such as Benjamin Sesko to step up. He likes to work closely with his nephew Andy, who held senior roles at Bournemouth and Newcastle, which would create an interesting dynamic if he wanted similar at United. Howe, like others in contention, would not cost anything in compensation – and every penny counts at Old Trafford.

Fabian Hürzeler (Brighton)

The 33-year-old has a growing reputation, with his Brighton team third after scoring 23 goals in seven games. This could explain why he is not particularly keen on leaving at the moment. His team are outperforming United with a squad that looks stronger. The size of United is alluring for many coaches but moving mid-season to a struggling club is not always advantageous because it means stepping into a firefight.

Sports.title: Europa League: Sunderland held in Poznan as Juventus denied comeback win
Sports.content:
Sunderland’s winning start in the Europa League was ended with a 1-1 draw away to Lech Poznan. The point keeps Sunderland unbeaten in Europe this season but ends their winning start, which saw them claim back-to-back victories over AZ Alkmaar and Torreense.

A thrilling opening saw Sunderland go in front early through Timur Tutierov, who was making just his third competitive start since arriving at Sunderland’s academy in 2023.

The visitors had opportunities to extend their lead when Malick Fofana hit the post and Nordi Mukiele forced a strong save from Mateusz Lis, but Lech responded in the 70th minute through the substitute Leo Bengtsson’s low strike.

Régis Le Bris made six changes from Sunday’s Premier League defeat to Bournemouth, including a first start of the season for Habib Diarra following his return from injury.

Sunderland took the lead in the second minute when Nilson Angulo pounced on a tame pass from Lis, and the winger crossed into Tutierov in the middle of the box to comfortably nod home for his first Sunderland goal.

Robin Roefs was called into action at the opposite end with a double save to deny Patrik Wålemark and palm away Antoni Kozubal’s header before Diarra charged up the pitch and fired into the side netting.

The hosts had two good chances to level when Pablo Rodríguez blasted just past the post and Daniel Håkans was played through in a one-on-one with Roefs but flicked his shot wide.

Sunderland enjoyed a good spell of possession which saw the skipper, Granit Xhaka, have a strike parried away by Lis and the rebound fell to Fofana, who rattled the woodwork. Moments later Dayann Méthalie was denied at the near post by Lis as the visitors pushed for a second goal.

Early in the second half, Fofana cut into the box but could only send his effort over and Poznan looked to strike when Wålemark scuffed a shot wide following a good solo run.

Diarra fired wide for and Angulo’s low strike was scooped up by Lis, who moments later made a great save to tip Mukiele’s shot over the bar.

View image in fullscreen Timur Tutierov scores his third goal for Sunderland’s first team since joining the academy in 2023. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty Images

Bengtsson looked to make an instant impact from the bench when his effort from Wålemark’s cross was sent wide. However, the midfielder made no mistake when next presented with an opportunity as a corner rebounded towards him just inside the area and he fired into the bottom corner with 20 minutes to play.

Poznan almost took the lead moments later when Roefs made a brilliant point-blank stop from Michal Gurgul.

Fofana skewed an effort wide as Sunderland looked to restore their advantage and the substitute Chris Rigg’s powerful shot landed on the roof of the net, but the spoils were shared.

Quick Guide Conference League: Salah breaks Hearts and Brighton held by Jablonec Show Injury-hit Hearts produced a spirited display in Turkey but ultimately went down to a 2-0 Conference League defeat at the hands of Mohamed Salah-inspired Trabzonspor. The Scottish side acquitted themselves well amid a hostile atmosphere before going down to Salah’s first-half penalty and a second-half strike from Franculino, laid on by the former Liverpool star (pictured). The defeat leaves Wouter Vrancken’s side with one point from two matches ahead of their trip to Swiss champions Thun in a fortnight. Their visit had started in painful fashion after left-back Harry Milne suffered a suspected anterior cruciate ligament injury during training. Brighton drew a rare blank as they were held to a goalless draw by Czech minnows Jablonec. The Premier League’s top scorers, who have scored 23 goals across their first seven matches, misfired badly in the foothills of the Jizera Mountains in northern Czechia. Brighton head coach Fabian Hürzeler, in his 100th match in charge, made eight changes from that memorable win with only Bart Verbruggen, Olivier Boscagli and Pascal Gross keeping their places. The visitors squandered a host of chances, the best falling to Jack Hinshelwood, Georginio Rutter and Ibrahim Osman, and Jablonec were looking the likelier to score towards the end. Antonín Rusek almost capitalised on a mistake by Joao Costinha before Verbruggen had to make a spectacular fingertip save to prevent Jiri Slama’s drive from hitting the top corner. Press Association Photograph: Hasan Tascan/Anadolu Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Juventus dropped their first points of the Europa League campaign after coming ⁠from behind to draw 2-2 with visitors Rennes.

Zeki Celik gave Juventus a fifth-minute lead, but ⁠the French side ⁠kept their ​composure and were level 10 minutes later when the Jordan international Musa Al-Taamari finished from close range for ⁠his first goal in the competition.

Rennes then stunned the hosts with a Boulaye Dia penalty two minutes before the ⁠break as the Italians struggled to create chances until Nick Woltemade equalised ​from the spot in the 67th ‌minute.

The Germany forward ‌twice went close to scoring again as Luciano Spalletti’s team upped the ‌pressure, and Juve thought they had won it in the 88th minute when Jhon Lucumí found the net from close range, but his effort was ruled out for offside.

View image in fullscreen Nick Woltemade equalises from the spot for Juventus in their 2-2 draw with Rennes. Photograph: sportinfoto/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock

The draw at least spared Juventus a second successive defeat following Sunday’s 3-0 home loss to Lazio ‌in Serie A.

Jonas Hofmann made the most of his surprise start for Bayer Leverkusen, scoring twice in three minutes ​to give the Bundesliga side a 2-0 victory at OFI Crete to go top of the table with their third straight win.

Crete, who stunned Hoffenheim 2-0 in their opening league-phase match, were twice caught napping by Hofmann, ⁠who was added to the side following an injury to ​Martin Terrier. Leverkusen have ​nine points and lead Ferencvaros ​on goal difference after the Hungarian side beat Torreense ​4-1.

Sports.title: Bruno Guimarães had sleepless nights before Newcastle exit but hopes for same ‘love’ at Arsenal
Sports.content:
For Bruno Guimarães, it was a time to show his steeliness, to fix his eyes on the prize – even if he knew it would surely mean them welling up. And then some. It was a tumultuous summer for the Brazil midfielder. A fine World Cup on a personal level was marred by a crucial penalty miss in the last-16 loss against Norway. Now he had the dream move lined up to Arsenal but it could not happen without breaking some hearts at Newcastle.

Guimarães admits he lay awake at night as the emotions swirled. How could he leave Newcastle, the club where he made so many connections and enjoyed so many highs after joining from Lyon in January 2022? There were the Champions League qualifications and, above all, the Carabao Cup triumph in 2025 that ended a 70-year wait for a domestic trophy. On the other hand, how could he resist Arsenal and the prospect of competing regularly for the game’s top honours?

Sometimes, you simply have to take a deep breath and the plunge. Nobody wants to die wondering. Guimarães knew the Newcastle team was breaking up. Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali had gone to Barcelona and Tottenham. The manager, Eddie Howe, was at the end of the line and would also leave. Guimarães went through with the £75m transfer and nobody can say it has not worked out so far.

Arsenal felt he would provide a different element for them, different ways of unlocking defences, plus his trademark work rate and snarl. Guimarães has brought all of that. Already he has made a difference. He even gave a little back to Newcastle when he scored his first Arsenal goal at Sunderland in September, paving the way for a 2-0 victory. Two Premier League games later, he scored the winner at home against Leeds.

Guimarães almost got another vital goal on Wednesday in the Champions League tie at Bayern Munich only for Manuel Neuer to deny him with an outrageous save. That would have put Arsenal 2-1 up. The game finished 2-2, Arsenal fighting until the end and equalising through Declan Rice in the 82nd minute. Still, it has not been easy for Guimarães and he surely has Arsenal’s visit to Newcastle on 21 November circled in his diary. His greatest hope is that he can build the same relationships at his new club.

“It was not just hard to tell Eddie but to tell the owners and my teammates [about deciding to leave Newcastle],” Guimarães says. “But I think the club went to a new rotation; a lot of players left, as well. The gaffer left. It was tough because my connection with the club was unbelievable. I never felt so loved like the way I was at Newcastle. I hope I can have the same love here at Arsenal.

View image in fullscreen Bruno Guimarães says he had sleepless nights contemplating leaving Newcastle for Arsenal. Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/Reuters

“It was hard for me to say bye. I remember when I said bye to the lads, I was crying. They were crying as well because we were a family there. I lost many, many nights of sleep because it was difficult for me, for my family. But sometimes in your life you have to make decisions and in my mind, I needed a new challenge. I wish Newcastle all the best because they were so nice to me. It is just time to move on and I’ve been enjoying my time here at Arsenal, as well.”

Guimarães is enjoying his burgeoning midfield partnership with Rice, not to mention Martin Ødegaard, who tends to be the most advanced of the trio. That said, there is plenty of fluidity between the positions. There is the sense that the manager, Mikel Arteta, is searching for the perfect balance.

“Declan can play – like me – as a No 6, No 8 or No 10,” Guimarães says. “The manager is still trying to get the best version of ourselves. Against Bayern, I played more as a No 6, Declan played more as a No 8. I enjoy playing with him a lot; with Martin, as well. We have been on a good run so far.”

Guimarães’ battles when he was at Newcastle against Rice have been well documented. He said Rice had messaged him as he prepared to sign for Arsenal, saying: “No more fights, now we’re friends.” Guimarães is the player you loathe when he is against you but love when he is in your ranks.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Manuel Neuer keeps out Bruno Guimarães’s header in the Champions League. Photograph: Michael Zemanek/Shutterstock

What was the worst thing Guimarães said to Rice when they were in opposition? “It is difficult to say,” he replies with a smile. “I am like this when I play against teams. When we were playing against each other, I was not nice to him, he was not nice to me! Now we try to help each other on the pitch.”

Guimarães cannot believe how Neuer kept out his close-range header; the 40-year-old goalkeeper clawed the ball up against the crossbar and away. “He pulled off a miracle,” Guimarães says. “I asked him after the game: ‘How did you manage to save that?’ He said: ‘I don’t know. I just saved it!’ He’s unbelievable, one of the best keepers in the world. No matter how old he is, he is top.”

What Guimarães has seen with clarity is the remorselessness of the collective attitude at Arsenal; the insatiable will to win, which comes from Arteta. Next up for them is Everton at home on Saturday. Guimarães knows he is in the right place.

“The mentality of the club has changed a lot and Arteta shows this perfectly,” Guimarães says. “We don’t accept a draw at Bayern. We always want to win. That is the mentality that we go to the training ground with every day. Arteta is always a little bit addicted to videos and the way that he can make us feel better on the pitch. We have a top manager with a top mentality. We want to win everything possible.”

Sports.title: Champions League review: PSG take a hit, Man City’s empty seats and teenage hope for Liverpool
Sports.content:
A big week for …

Paris Saint-Germain beat Barcelona 4-2 on Tuesday, but the reigning champions lost the best player in last season’s tournament, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. This autumn has seen much lobbying for the Ballon d’Or, with the Georgian a popular choice, despite his absence from the World Cup. He is expected to be out for six months, although Rodri’s comeback from serious injury – he was rested by Barcelona on Tuesday until coming off the bench in the 60th minute – shows it can take far longer than that for players to rediscover their highest level.

“Why me?” Kvaratskhelia asked his Instagram followers. The PSG policy of resting players in Ligue 1 to save them for the Champions League failed to protect him. By resting Rodri, Barcelona followed a wider practice among major clubs in European competition of saving stars’ legs for big domestic occasions. Barcelona face Real Madrid this weekend though Lamine Yamal is not being spared; his brilliant goal in Paris made it 10 goals, matched by 10 assists, from 10 matches.

Another heavyweight battle saw Arsenal lose Bukayo Saka to a first-half quad injury in an entertaining 2-2 draw at Bayern Munich. Declan Rice powered in a late equalizer after Harry Kane had put on a show that included a goal and an assist. Does the Ballon d’Or beckon for Kane? The prediction markets suggest so.

Matching Barcelona’s perfect record this season at home and abroad are Manchester City, who continue to thrive amid infamy. A resurgent Phil Foden scored a hat-trick and new signing Allan impressed. The official crowd for their 5-1 defeat of AEK Athens was 40,402, but it looked smaller, and mockery duly descended on the club. There is mitigation for those who stayed away, including high ticket prices for Champions League matches in tough economic times, and a run of five home matches in 17 days. Still, City remain in the crosshairs, and the empty seats raise eyebrows for a club reporting record revenues. Equally, it is fair to point out that Anfield was not full, either, for Liverpool’s 4-3 defeat of Villarreal.

A clean sweep of wins for Serie A, with three of their clubs scoring four goals. Inter let the side down with their 1-0 defeat of Shakhtar Donetsk. Roma defeated Slovan Bratislava 4-0, and Como beat Manchester United 4-1, but the game of the week came in Naples. Scott McTominay scored twice, his first goals since a procedure on a benign heart arrhythmia as Napoli beat Bodø/Glimt 4-3 for their first win of the group stage. “I still need to find my best form, but I am not far away,” said McTominay.

Player of the week

Liverpool were a mess in the first 30 minutes against Villarreal and it was Rio Ngumoha who led the recovery. The 18-year-old played off the right, supplying two assists with his left foot: the long-term replacement for Mohamed Salah may already be at Anfield. Liverpool have nursed Ngumoha along, though this was his fifth start of the season. “Everyone is chipping in but for him to work with Mo [Salah] last year was obviously massive,” Virgil van Dijk said of the teenager.

Club in focus: Como

With traditional Serie A giants Juventus and Milan in the Europa League, Como are enjoying their first season in the Champions League. If Manchester United were dreadful on Wednesday, Como’s rise hit its highest point yet. The club’s success carries echoes of Brighton and Bournemouth’s ascents, although Como’s is even more remarkable. They were a Serie D club in 2008, and the city is now known for something beyond its glorious scenery. Champions League winner Thierry Henry is among the investors in the club as is Como’s coach, Cesc Fàbregas, although the prime financiers are the Indonesian billionaire Hartono brothers.

Jamestown Analytics, the Brighton owner Tony Bloom’s company, has been consulting Como. Arsène Wenger, Pep Guardiola, José Mourinho and Antonio Conte are the elite coaches Fàbregas played under, and he has forged a high-pressing style against Italian orthodoxy. As United labored, they were swarmed by Como’s worker bees. Real Madrid have a buy-back option for Nico Paz, bought by Como in 2024, and the scorer of two fine goals against United. Argentina’s latest Messi replacement is rather beefier than his country’s idol.

As Como deepened Michael Carrick’s plight, thoughts moved to potential replacements. Fàbregas has been mentioned, though United fans will recall the summer of 2013’s unsuccessful chase for him. Had a deal been done, his midfield partner would have been … Carrick.

View image in fullscreen Nico Paz piled misery on Manchester United. Photograph: Kieran McManus/Shutterstock

They said it

Another week, another Manchester United PR crisis. This one involved Carrick hitting back at his players, a rarity in his managerial career. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” Bruno Fernandes said.

Carrick’s riposte: “If you don’t run and you don’t run forward and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”

On CBS, Jamie Carragher weighed, saying of Fernandes: “They all think he’s working hard. He’s not. He’s killing the rest of the team doing it.”

The Amazon All or Nothing documentary series currently in production for United’s season will be appointment viewing.

Looking ahead

After two consecutive weeks of action, we have a fortnight off. Will Carrick still be at United by the time they host Roma on 3 November? Aston Villa, who have three wins from three and are second place in the table, have a glamour trip to Barcelona. Real Madrid, another side on three wins, travel to AEK.

After defeat to Inter, Shakhtar’s adopted home, Stamford Bridge, hosts Sporting Lisbon, who this week were on the wrong end of Lask’s first ever group-stage win.

Sports.title: Harry Kane says wait to learn if he has won Ballon d’Or is stressful for family
Sports.content:
Harry Kane would love to know now whether he has won the Ballon d’Or because the uncertainty and constant questions are driving his family to distraction. But the Bayern Munich and England striker accepts the ­suspense before the big reveal at the London Palladium on Monday night is part of the show.

Kane is the odds-on favourite to win the prestigious individual ­honour after a prolific run of form. The 33-year-old scored 61 goals for Bayern last season and 12 for England. This time out, he has 10 for Bayern and six for England.

He scored from the penalty spot in Wednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw against Arsenal at the Allianz Arena, although his standout moment was the inch-perfect through ball that set up Alphonso Davies to make it 1-1.

Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal is the second-favourite for the Ballon d’Or and Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid is next in the betting.

“I think my wife would prefer to know and my family … it’s very stressful for everyone,” Kane said. “I can see why they don’t tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names, and there will be more people watching it if they don’t know so I can understand why.

“From my point of view, I’d love to know to just kind of see and not have to wait throughout the whole night. But it is their decision, I can’t control that. We’ll have to just enjoy it and try not to stress out too much.

“I try not to think about it. ­Obviously it is hard not to. There are always rumours and stuff flying around so you try to stay away from it.”

Sports.title: Nottingham Forest’s false start places early focus on Glasner and Delap
Sports.content:
Sitting 19th in the Premier League was not the plan for Nottingham Forest after the arrival of a highly acclaimed manager and a £45m striker to fuel their ambitions. The fates of Oliver Glasner and Liam Delap are intertwined and with the stark stats of zero home goals and a solitary point at the City Ground it is not the dream start they were aiming for.

As Delap prepares to return to Ipswich, where his career ignited, on Friday night, Forest are remaining calm. There is a desperation to get away from the short-termism that caused so many problems; 12 months ago, they were on their third head coach of a disappointing season. This summer they were ruthless with the removal of Vítor Pereira, who had done a fine job to escape the drop, because they saw an opportunity to upgrade with Glasner, hoping he could transform Forest like he did Crystal Palace.

It cost plenty to acquire Glasner and Delap, which many fans believe should lead to instant results, but that is rarely the case in an industry as complicated as football. For the coach, it is a case of learning the club inside out while influencing performance through his carefully choreographed methods. For the striker, he needs to rebuild confidence and that comes via goals.

In Glasner’s first full season at Palace, they won one of their first 13 league matches but ended comfortably in mid-table and FA Cup winners. It was similar at Eintracht Frankfurt, getting one victory in 10, but going on to win the Europa League.

Learning the Glasner way is not straightforward. Playing three at the back is rarely the norm and nor is having two No 10s, all with the background of Forest losing their best player in Elliot Anderson.

The recruitment was measured, targeting positions that required strengthening and avoiding needless purchases that dogged the club after promotion. Replacing Anderson became a priority, but Glasner felt James McAtee could adapt to a deeper role in midfield alongside the shrewd free signing Xaver Schlager. Ousmane Diomande was a coup in defence and Glasner convinced Daniel Muñoz to follow him from Selhurst Park.

Behind the obvious figures, there is plenty of underlying encouragement for Forest. Based on chances created and conceded, Glasner has had the best start of any Forest manager in the Premier League era. His team rank seventh, according to Opta, for expected goals (xG), but have scored the fewest – five – and are the biggest xG underperformers at -6.2. It is a huge discrepancy, missing out on almost a goal a game. It includes 62 shots at home that have come to nothing and if Glasner wants buy-in from the fans, that needs to change quickly. If every team had scored and conceded the goals measured by xG, Forest would be fourth.

View image in fullscreen Nottingham Forest, and Liam Delap, are yet to score at the City Ground this season. Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty Images

It is understandable that Delap is yet to find his feet after a disappointing year at Chelsea and the lack of pre-season set him back. Forest tried to sign him before he went to Stamford Bridge and have great faith in him, but he needs to improve his record of one goal every five league appearances. He is the ideal No 9, possessing pace, power and sharp finishing, but unless he is on peak form, turning that into guaranteed output is not straightforward.

Delap has scored once for Forest, but is putting in the effort through being the front line of defence, relentlessly pressing opposition centre-backs. He has shown plenty of quick thinking, demonstrated by his quick throw-in to set up a goal at Anfield, something almost replicated against Arsenal only for Chris Wood to miss the chance.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Forest allowed Arsenal a single shot on target last Sunday – it just happened to be deflected in for a winner. Glasner can also point in that match to the absence of his captain, Morgan Gibbs-White, the team’s attacking fulcrum. “It feels very unfair,” Glasner said of the result. “We have to accept we are missing some bits. But the performance in many parts was very good.”

In two full seasons at Selhurst Park, Glasner won two major trophies for a club that had gone almost 120 years without one. He has two European titles and his own distinctive formation and execution, something he has harnessed over 12 years in coaching, so he knows how long it takes to develop the complexities.

The picture looks clearer after almost four months together. The hope at Forest is that the endeavour is rewarded with greater luck, the missing ingredient among well thought-out recruitment led by the chief football officer, George Syrianos, and his team and clever coaching. Syrianos is Glasner’s biggest advocate and told fans the manager would be given time.

Friday will be Glasner’s eighth Premier League match at Forest, three more than Ange Postecoglou was permitted before being sacked this time last year by the owner, Evangelos Marinakis. Glasner, unlike the Australian, can show progress and will be justifiably confident points will come.

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca says honest talks have revitalised Foden’s Manchester City form
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca has revealed he held heart-to-heart conversations with Phil Foden to help the midfielder back to his best. Foden has struggled over the past two years but has scored four goals in his past two games to give hope he can recapture the form that won him the Professional Footballers’ Association player of the year award in 2023-24.

City travel to Aston Villa on Saturday lunchtime aiming to continue their perfect Premier League start under Maresca, with Erling Haaland fit after sitting on the bench for Wednesday’s Champions League win over AEK Athens.

“Since we started I sat down with Phil two or three times, especially at the beginning,” said Maresca, who knew Foden from a spell as Pep Guardiola’s assistant. “Maybe love is not the right word to use but just to show him how important he is.

“I said many times that I know Phil from years ago so I know how good he is. For different reasons the last few years he was not good enough, but again I think when you have more players like Phil available you are a better team because at the end it’s a matter of improving players. If you improve the players you improve the team, so for me it’s my duty to try to help Phil to be again one of the best players in England. But it’s not just about one game – the season is very long.”

Foden, 26, needs to remain consistent to keep his place in the team, with plenty of competition for the attacking roles, including from Rayan Cherki, who Maresca has described as “one of the best players in Europe”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

City’s only competitive defeat under Maresca came against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League, and they have seven straight wins in the Premier League to sit three points clear at the top. Maresca is waiting to find out whether Matheus Nunes, Mateo Kovacic and Nico O’Reilly are available after missing the AEK game. “The mood is good, we are happy with our start but we are still hungry for more wins,” Maresca said.

Sports.title: Sorry England suffer embarrassing defeat as Sri Lanka complete second-highest ODI run chase in HISTORY in thrilling clash
Sports.content:
England suffered one of the worst defeats in their one-day history as Sri Lanka sensationally knocked off a target of 430 in Rawalpindi after Harry Brook’s record-breaking double-century appeared to have taken the game beyond their reach.

The Sri Lankans completed a two-wicket victory with one ball to spare, thanks to 130 from Pavan Rathnakaye, and 97 apiece from Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka. And with six needed off two balls, Janath Liyanage then completed a stunning turnaround by launching Josh Tongue over long-off.

Only once before have the team batting second made more to win an ODI, when South Africa overhauled Australia’s 434 with one wicket in hand at Johannesburg more than 20 years ago.

And when Sri Lanka found themselves 24 for two, with captain Kusal Mendis run out at the non-striker’s end without facing a ball, they looked doomed.

But Fernando and Rathnayake put on 166, before Shanaka helped Rathnayake add 133, as England disintegrated. Sam Curran’s nine overs went for 103.

England chipped away, and Tongue even found himself on a hat-trick in the final over after bowling Dunith Wellalage and Eshan Malinga in successive deliveries – only for Liyanage to have the final say.

England managed to lose their ODI against Sri Lanka despite setting a score of 429/4

Sri Lanka seemed to have no chance at the halfway stage but battle back remarkably

Earlier, Brook had scored England’s first ODI double-century from just 114 balls, a world record, in his team’s 429 for four. But it wasn’t enough.

'It was an incredible game of cricket,' said Brook. 'Both teams were exceptional. Sri Lanka just outplayed us. We couldn’t hit our straps with the ball and played to their strengths a bit. Fair play to them.

'It was a nice innings. Unfortunately it doesn’t mean anything now. Being on the losing side, it has no value, in my eyes.'

Sports.title: No repeat of late heroics as Sunderland squander lead against the Europa League's WORST team - as free-scoring Brighton misfire in drab draw with Czech minnows
Sports.content:
No repeat of late heroics as Sunderland squander lead against the Europa League's WORST team - as free-scoring Brighton misfire in drab draw with Czech minnows

Goalkeeper Robin Roefs looked to the heavens and shouted 'f***!’ Regis Le Bris stood brooding off stage. Sunderland had conceded, and it had been coming.

In a dismal domestic season for Sunderland, they have been able to count on their European travels for a sprinkle of light relief, however hard-fought. Until now, that is.

There is no papering over the cracks after a troubling night at Lech Poznan, where a strong starting XI that included Granit Xhaka hobbled to a draw against the Europa League’s basement boys.

It had all started so rosily when Timur Tutierov – a Crimean refugee whose very existence is a tribute to his resilience – scored his first goal for the club with a header after just 78 seconds.

But in front of one of central Europe’s more forbidding crowds, Sunderland failed to handle the frenetic, end-to-end pulsations of this game and eventually wilted.

To their credit, the Black Cats were on top for large swathes of the game, having 22 shots, but Nordi Mukiele, Malick Fofana, and Chris Rigg all saw chances go begging and the visitors were punished for their profligacy.

Sunderland drew 1-1 at Lech Poznan in the Europa League despite leading after just 78 seconds

Timor Tutierov had given Sunderland the lead with a header after just 78 seconds

But Leo Begtsson spoiled the party with a deserved equaliser for the hosts in the second half

It is not the end of the world for Sunderland, who sit fifth in the Europa League standings, but it leaves much to be desired after narrow wins over AZ and second-tier Portuguese outfit Torreense.

To put the result in context, Lech Poznan arrived at this game bottom of the Europa League after 4-0 drubbings by Crystal Palace and Bayer Leverkusen. This is not the side who once beat Manchester City.

And for the 2,000 Mackems who made this trip, and filled Poznan’s Old Town with their songs, the performance did little to part the dark clouds which have recently congealed over the Stadium of Light.

Sunderland sit bottom of the Premier League with one point in their last five games and Le Bris, for all his brilliant achievements in the North East, has started to come under pressure.

There are no suggestions of the Frenchman’s position being immediately at threat – and there should not be – but even he has admitted that Sunderland have not been themselves recently.

A side known for their solidity last season have opened this campaign with a comedy of errors and ill discipline. They lead the way for mistakes leading to goals in the league, having already committed five. Mukiele recently accused his own team-mates of 'arrogance'.

This performance was no different, with Kevin Danso error-prone once again, and picking up a booking for dragging down Mikael Ishak while trying to atone for his own miscontrol.

Most worrying was the ping-pong feel of the game, which saw 32 shots, and several gilt-edged chances for the Polish side to snatch a win after Leo Bengtsson's 70th-minute equaliser. Roefs had to make an incredible double save shortly after the goal to hold off the hosts.

In the absence of Brian Brobbey and Wilson Isidor, Sunderland's front four buzzed around with energy, but the wastefulness will worry Le Bris.

Leeds are up next before a trip to Coventry on Halloween, with the chance for things to get hairy if Sunderland flo again.

Jablonec 0-0 Brighton, Press Association

Brighton drew a rare blank as they were held to a goalless draw by Czech minnows Jablonec in the Conference League.

The Premier League’s top scorers, who have scored 23 goals across their first seven matches, misfired badly in the foothills of the Jizera Mountains in northern Czechia.

Jablonec coach Lubos Kozel had said his side would need a “miracle” to get anything from the match.

It turned out they only needed a below-par display from the favourites to lift the trophy to take a point, and in fact they could have had all three.

Around 1,000 Seagulls fans made the trip from the Sussex coast to the homely Stadion Strelnice in the city of Jablonec nad Nisou.

These are heady days for their team, who lie third in the English top flight, fresh from Sunday’s 5-0 thrashing of M23 rivals Crystal Palace.

Brighton, typically so prolific this season, were held to a goalless draw by Czech side Jablonec

Boss Fabian Hurzeler, in his 100th match in charge, made eight changes from that memorable win with only Bart Verbruggen, Olivier Boscagli and the omnipresent Pascal Gross keeping their places.

They pinned the hosts in their own half for the first 20 minutes but Jack Hinshelwood’s shot was saved by Jablonec keeper Jan Hanus while Gross and Ibrahim Osman were off target.

Jablonec eventually got far enough forward to win a corner, which Antonín Rusek headed narrowly wide.

Goalkeeper Verbruggen also had to be alert to smother a cute backheel from Rusek.

But they were rare moments of concern for the Seagulls, although they were frustrated in front of goal in the first half.

Georginio Rutter was cleverly put through by Gross but flashed his shot across the face of goal and wide, and Boscagli fired over from long range.

Early in the second half Rutter’s pass found Osman, but his effort flew wide before Malick Yalcouye tucked the ball into the net, only to be flagged offside.

Then Osman’s reverse pass got Matt O’Riley in behind, but his fizzing ball across the six-yard box could not find Rutter.

Hurzeler had seen enough after Osman blazed another chance high over the crossbar, making four changes with Chema Andres, Luka Vuskovic, Yasin Ayari and Promise David sent on.

However, the changes had little effect and Jablonec were looking the likelier to score towards the end.

Rusek almost capitalised on a mistake by Joao Costinha before Verbruggen had to make a spectacular fingertip save to prevent Jiri Slama’s drive from hitting the top corner.

Rutter, who scored twice in Brighton’s opening 4-0 victory over Kauno Zalgiris, had a chance to win it in stoppage time but his snapshot was beaten away by Hanus.

Sports.title: Newcastle Confidential Q&A with CRAIG HOPE: Tino Livramento's mystery injury revealed, what sources are telling me about Matthias Jaissle's future, Anthony Elanga fitness boost and January transfer plans
Sports.content:
Newcastle United are a club with more questions than answers right now, after a run of three defeats in four matches that leaves them 11th in the Premier League.

Two painful defeats last week, away at Coventry and at home to Aston Villa, have punctured some of the confidence that had built up from the club's strong start to the season.

From Matthias Jaissle's future and tactics to injuries and January transfer plans, there is no shortage of issues to address. And for this week's Newcastle Confidential, we've handed the floor to you.

Here, CRAIG HOPE tackles your biggest questions with insight and information from inside St James' Park…

Section 1: Jaissle's prospects

Q. How much time will Jaissle be given if results don't improve? Is he already under serious pressure? (Kazuyoshi Funaki, Sibierski’s Baldy Heed & Clare Bremner)

As a journalist, it’s our job to stay across the above questions every day, especially when results aren’t good. That does not mean we think the manager should be changed (and I don’t, in this instance) but exploring the notion is valid.

Everything I’ve had back in the past week or so has been in support of Jaissle. So much so, the idea of a ‘vote of confidence’ type message was dismissed even as a suggestion. Ultimately, it is PIF who will decide – and in five years of ownership they have only sacked one manager, Steve Bruce a couple of weeks after the takeover. The message from their side is one of calm and patience.

Everything I’ve had back in the past week or so from sources in and around the club has been in support of head coach Matthias Jaissle

A manager cannot lose every game, of course, and the team entering the bottom three and staying there for a prolonged period would require a serious reconsideration of said patience – which sources have acknowledged this week – but while Newcastle are in a relatively comfortable league position, all of the hierarchy’s energy will go into supporting the head coach.

Q. Will the club reconsider its Vision 2030 ambitions, accept that this is a season of transition and give Jaissle their full backing? (Doddsy)

In terms of Vision 2030, it stands, and no one internally is rowing back on that. Chief executive David Hopkinson sees such ambition as imperative to progress and exuding a message of confidence and bullish intent.

I would not draw direct correlation when it comes to Jaissle’s future and Vision 2030, and we should not take the 2030 date as a literal deadline of ‘best club in the world or heads will roll’. It is more Hopkinson’s way of focusing minds from an off-field perspective.

However, Vision 2030 will be a stick with which to beat the hierarchy if results do not improve – that is the upshot of being so bold. I admire it in many ways, and believe it to be necessary from an internal standpoint, but I’m not sure it will do them too many favours in the short term.

Q. Why did the owners choose Jaissle as manager? (Poolie Mags and MuckeFe111)

Well, it was not, as some have speculated, because they wanted a manager from a PIF-owned club. It took £9million to buy out Jaissle from his Al Ahli contract and talks were far from straightforward. When I suggested Newcastle might return to Al Ahli in an effort to sign young French midfielder Valentin Atangana, said to be a Jaissle favourite, it was dismissed on account of the somewhat frosty relations.

Newcastle’s hierarchy believed – and still do – they were getting a coach who could be an elite-level manager. This summer, I detected an absolute conviction among those who appointed Jaissle that he would succeed.

Sporting director Ross Wilson called Hopkinson after his first meeting with Jaissle and the latter knew immediately that Wilson was sold on the German. So much so, there was one meeting where Newcastle chiefs wanted to walk straight back into the restaurant and offer him the job on the spot.

Other options, such as Kieran McKenna, were explored (and Hopkinson has said 130 candidates came up in their data analysis) but all roads led to Jaissle once they knew it was possible.

Sporting director Ross Wilson (left) called David Hopkinson (right) after his first meeting with Jaissle and the latter knew immediately that Wilson was sold on the German

Former Ipswich manager Kieran McKenna (left) was one of the options Newcastle looked at but they were set on Jaissle

Q. Why do you think a section of our fanbase and media have turned against Jaissle after a handful of weeks and games with barely any pre-season? Teams below us have got less grief in the last week! (G Star)

It’s a fair question, but online reaction is framed through results. Team wins, manager good. Team loses, manager bad. So the extreme reaction we’re seeing to Jaissle among some fans, primarily online, is governed by that, I suspect. If Newcastle beat Crystal Palace, all will be well (for a few days until Everton).

In reality, the truth I feel is somewhere in the middle. There is concern at obvious issues when it comes to game plan and shape, but also understanding that Jaissle inherited a squad with missing parts. The boos after Aston Villa were for a combination of the two: a poor performance coupled with frustration at a diminished playing staff and the likelihood of a difficult season. But yes, online especially, I think a more balanced reaction to results would reflect better on all fanbases, including Newcastle.

As for the media, I don’t think we have turned on Jaissle. We have to report on what have been two alarming performances (and even before the recent defeats, there was reason to urge caution despite decent results) but, on the whole, I believe we accept he needs time. Saying that, there also has to be evidence of progress.

All of the above is also the price on the ticket at a club like Newcastle – the scrutiny and interest will always be there. It will be a worrying day when it is not.

Q. Why are you calling out the current manager’s tactics and results when, in my opinion, you said nothing last season? (Micky B and Magpie Lee)

The criticism of performances and tactics was there (YouTube headlines on my channel from March and April included: ‘Broken: This team is not a team anymore', 'Too Soft', 'One Word: Weak' and 'This Didn’t Work!'). But I believed Eddie Howe was still the right manager to turn things around and that he deserved one below-par season. I stand by that and always will.

Yes, at the time I was fully aware of a want (mainly online) to go after the manager, but I believed from my conversations around the club that Howe retained the support of his players and the hierarchy. I also thought that was right.

I’m not afraid to go after managers (see Steve McClaren and Steve Bruce...) but I’ll do so when I believe it’s fair, not just because a team is going through a difficult spell. My belief remains that Howe was the best manager in the club’s recent history, while also falling short towards the end of last season.

As for Jaissle, I’m analysing his tactics and results, of course, but on the whole I’d say I’ve been supportive of him. I don’t think his team is playing well at all, but there is mitigation.

I don’t think Jaissle's team is playing well at all, but there is mitigation

Q. What would the owners consider a successful season? (Adrian Bromfield and Ben Levey)

There is a hope, and perhaps even an expectation, of European football. Financial forecasts have been drawn for all eventualities, and Newcastle can absorb a finish similar to last season (12th), but returning to continental competition is openly spoken about as an ambition in conversations I’ve had.

How does that tally with patience for the new manager? Well, it doesn’t, does it? And that is the fascination in seeing how this season plays out. Because, for me, qualifying for Europe is probably unlikely.

Section 2: Injuries and young talent

Q. Is there any update on Tino Livramento? (various)

Yes, Confidential can exclusively reveal that Livramento has suffered a knee injury. Given his history of significant knee problems, the club are understandably cautious.

I'm told that the issue, first felt in training last month, was initially thought to be innocuous. However, after tests, it was revealed that Livramento needed a period of rest and recovery. He has avoided serious injury, I understand, and has been doing some light work on the grass the past week or so.

It is too early for a definite return date, but work has now begun in terms of easing him back to full fitness. The England defender was forced to pull out of last month’s international fixtures and he is unlikely to make next month’s internationals either.

Q. Is Matias Fernandez-Pardo injured? When are Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey expected to return? (David McConnell)

Fernandez-Pardo has been suffering from an illness, but I can reveal some good news on Elanga – he has been back with the group this week and is pushing for involvement on Sunday. Palace may come too soon, but all of the noises around him are positive. Ramsey is due back this week, but we’re awaiting an update.

Q. What are Newcastle's plans for young prospects Rory Finneran and Ousmane Diabate? Do either feature in the club's long-term first-team plans? (Geordie Messiah)

Diabate, 19, was a signing we revealed in the summer, and there is definitely excitement around the midfielder's progress back on loan in Turkey. I would expect him to be part of pre-season next summer, and likewise 18-year-old midfielder Finneran, who has shone on loan at Notts County.

Once they’re given that window to train with the senior squad, it’s then up to them. At the very least, the club have two players with sell-on value.

Confidential can exclusively reveal that Tino Livramento has suffered a knee injury. Given his history of significant knee problems, the club are understandably cautious

But it's good news on Anthony Elanga (right), who is pushing to be involved at Crystal Palace on Sunday

Section 3: Tactics and transfers

Q. What exactly is Jaissle's 'vertical football' and could he switch to a 4-3-3? Opponents regularly cut through the team with a single pass, why hasn't Jaissle addressed this obvious weakness? (Craig Forsyth, Cumbrian Mag and Sam)

Vertical football is getting the ball forward quickly and directly. The rule in training where players are penalised for passing backwards is evidence of this tactic.

Clearly, however, there are some issues with its implementation on a matchday. As Craig Forsyth points out, the midfield in a 4-2-3-1 system is too easily bypassed. Jaissle was furious on Saturday when one Villa attack went from their box to Newcastle’s in the space of a few passes and a few seconds, and Joao Gomes hit the post.

So, will he change to a 4-3-3? I can’t tell you what Sunday will bring, but as I reported last week, my information was that he would not deviate from 4-2-3-1 against Villa. They were defending in a 4-4-2 at times, but that still left two exposed midfielders – and that is an issue that needs to be addressed, especially away from home.

Q. Will Newcastle look to sign another striker or No10 in January and is money available? (Sam and OneGuyNUFC)

Q. Newcastle's '2.0' transfer window looks like an enormous gamble. Did the club congratulate itself on the summer business too soon? (Brit Boxing Blog)

There is definitely headroom to spend in January, I’m told, but there is also a belief that the squad has been built for the entire season, not just half of it.

I would not expect a striker to be sought (they have Will Osula, Fernandez-Pardo and Yoane Wissa already) but a No10 feels like an obvious target. I know now of agents who are suggesting players in that position to the club.

Rory Finneran, an 18-year-old defensive midfielder, has shone on loan at Notts County

With the likes of Matias Fernandez-Pardo (right) at the club there is a feeling Newcastle do not need to go and buy another striker

To answer the second question, Newcastle were very satisfied with their summer business come the end of the window, and they remain pleased with how it played out. They’ve stated that on the record.

As ever, though, results dictate how history judges any window, and right now both the manager and hierarchy are in need of an upturn. There is not a feeling of panic as yet, but ask me that question again as January approaches if improvement has not arrived.

Q. If you had been given £500million to spend on rebuilding Newcastle's squad, do you think you could have done better? (Tino’s Fur Coat)

No, I would have spent it all on Cherno Samba.

Sports.title: Widow of Middlesbrough icon Willie Maddren calls for greater protection for footballers over link between headers and fatal MND - which caused Rob Burrow's premature death
Sports.content:
Long before Rob Burrow's brutal illness and premature death launched Sir Kevin Sinfield on his quest to raise millions for research into motor neurone disease (MND) there was Willie Maddren. For Teessiders of a certain age, Maddren needs no introduction. For the benefit of others, he was a local hero at the heart of a glorious era for Middlesbrough, a fearless centre forward converted into a fearless centre half in Jack Charlton's brilliant team promoted as runaway second tier champions in 1974. They rattled the elite on their return to the topflight with an unlikely tilt at the title before a late fade to finish seventh. England recognition came for Maddren at Under-23 level and senior call-ups in the 1974-75 season, but there would be no full cap before knee problems set in and cut short his playing career. At 26, with 351 Boro appearances behind him, he retired. Later, he returned as physio and manager and, at the age of 44, was diagnosed with MND. He died in 2000 at 49. Middlesbrough icon Willie Maddren needs no introduction on Teesside but following his retirement, the centre half received a heartbreaking MND diagnosis After his death at the age of 49, his widow Hilary has become outspoken raising awareness of the connection between the disease and his playing career More than a quarter of a century on, Sinfield is on a mission to beat the disease that killed his teammate Burrow, raising more than £11million to fund much-needed research. There is still no sign of a cure. Precious little is known about the causes but as the list of sports stars with MND extends, Maddren's widow Hilary has become increasingly convinced that their athletic pursuits are central to the problem, whether that be the shuddering contact in rugby or heading the ball in football. 'There's got to be a connection,' Hilary tells Daily Mail Sport from her home in North Yorkshire. 'I follow it all closely and it takes me back with a slight sadness to see it happening to such a huge extent. 'It's quite frightening there's so many of them, that's the problem. I realise that you can't just go around bandying these things about, but it feels strange to me nothing is said. 'We know in football, heading the ball is causing neurodegenerative diseases. Years ago, we found out there was a bigger chance of getting lung cancer if you smoked. Not everybody with lung cancer smoked but now we know it is a contributing factor. 'When you see the percentage of rugby players and footballers, this has got to be the same thing with MND. There's nothing definitive, I know nothing is proven but it's got to be. 'I'm not trying to blame anybody. Willie would not want to blame anybody. I'm not on a witch hunt. I don't want to stop anyone playing the game, but I have nine grandchildren and nearly all of them are football mad. It's about education and being aware of heading the ball.' The Maddrens are one of five families – all connected to Boro – leading a new campaign for clear legal limits to reduce heading in training which they believe will protect future generations from the post-career health problems they have witnessed at close quarters. It is led by the Head Safe charity founded by Judith Gates, whose husband was a friend and teammate of Maddren's. Bill Gates, who retired before he was 30 suffering serious migraines, died three years ago at the age of 79 after living for years with dementia. Others at the forefront of the campaign are families of England World Cup hero Nobby Stiles, Gordon McQueen and Hugh McIlmoyle. Stiles, who died in 2020 aged 78, played for Boro after leaving Manchester United. Scotland legend McQueen, who died in 2023 aged 70, coached at the club for seven years and later worked for them as a scout. McIlmoyle, 86 years old and diagnosed with Alzheimer's eight years ago, spent two seasons at Ayresome Park during his prolific career as a centre-forward in the 60s and 70s. Gary Pallister, a former Boro, Manchester United and England defender, is also backing the cause. When Pallister spoke at the launch of a new petition which the group hopes will force the matter into the House of Commons, he was embarrassed because he could not summon the name of Maddren, the man who had plucked him from the obscurity of non-league Billingham Town. Former Manchester United star Gary Pallister is among the ex-players to throw their support behind the cause Hilary teased him afterwards. 'Oh my God, you've got it already,' she said, although acutely aware that behind this light-hearted exchange between friends lurked a serious point. 'Gary and his contemporaries are into their early 60s. They've played their football and headed all those balls. It must be a little bit worrying when they start forgetting things. 'What's ahead? Are they going to suffer dementia? It feels like a ticking time bomb.' Studies have proved the link between heading the ball and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease which can lead in later life to different forms of dementia. MND is slightly different but nevertheless a neurodegenerative condition which damages the nerves sending messages to the muscles. Over time, they stop working and the muscles weaken. It is terminal and often health deteriorates quickly. Maddren's first sign of the disease was a twitch in a thumb later spreading to an arm, then to the other arm, by which point it had become clear it was not a trapped nerve as he hoped. In search of reason, he wondered if it was to do with stress from the end of his playing career, and the long hours spent on his business running sports shops and managing Boro in crisis when the club he loved was going into liquidation. But there seemed no point wasting time searching for answers he could never expect to find, he was determined to spend what limited time he had trying to enjoy life and make a difference. Middlesbrough held a benefit match and proceeds enabled Maddren to adapt his home and transport to his wheelchair, and he threw himself into raising funds and awareness. He took part in a clinical trial for riluzole, a drug that is now prescribed in treatment. Proceeds from his book 'Extra Time' went to the MND Association and funds continued to be raised long after his death, estimated close to £500,000. His family including four children from two marriages, friends, former colleagues and Boro fans joined forces. His eldest daughter, artist Lucy Pittaway, maintains an active partnership with the charity. 'Willie was convinced if you threw enough money at it, you would find a cause and a cure,' says Hilary, who has continued to campaign tirelessly and worked in volunteer roles for MND charities and others. 'We still don't have a huge amount of hope anybody can be given when they receive the diagnosis. It's not a lot different. 'The incredible amount raised in Rob Burrow's name will make huge inroads.' Leeds Rhinos legend Burrow died in 2024 at the age of 37. Other international stars from the two codes of rugby include Scotland's Doddie Weir who died in 2022 at 52 and Joost van der Westhuizen of South Africa who died in 2017 at 45. Lewis Moody, 48, revealed last year he was living with MND. Earlier this month, former Wallabies hooker Nathan Charles, 37, revealed he too had been diagnosed. The MND Association notes the patterns but notes 'correlation does not prove causation' and that the health benefits of playing sport far outweigh any risks involved. From football, Marcus Stewart and Stephen Darby are living with MND. Former Rangers favourite Fernando Ricksen died in 2019 at the age of 43. Lenny Johnrose, who played for Bury and Burnley among others, died in 2022 at the age of 52. 'Willie loved his life,' says Hilary. 'He thought he'd had an amazing life and was so lucky to have done the things he wanted to do. He played football for a living. He managed his club, albeit that wasn't brilliant, but he was involved in football, he loved it. 'And if you would have said to him, well this might be the cause of what's going to kill you, would he have done any different? Possibly not. And that's how I feel now. Don't blame anybody, let's draw a line, but we need to learn from it. 'Anybody who has seen the slow-motion footage of a clash of heads or a rugby tackle when you see the head thrown back, it's not a good sign, it's not the way our bodies are meant to work and it's got to be doing something. It's just got to be.' To sign the petition, follow the link here.

Sports.title: 'Keep your eyes on the road': Diogo Jota's new wife's text message to husband revealed in her heartbreaking account of how tragic Liverpool star's Lamborghini crash death unfolded
Sports.content:
Diogo Jota's widow Rute Cardoso has revealed she told him 'keep your eyes on the road' in her final message to the Liverpool star, as she gave a heartbreaking account of the night of his death in a new book. In a biography about the late Liverpool forward, Cardoso explained she had exchanged messages with Jota shortly after he had left for the Spanish city Santander with his brother Andre Silva. Jota had planned to travel to the city to drop off a Lamborghini he had rented shortly after the couple's wedding, before taking a ferry back to the UK for pre-season. Cardoso revealed she had told Jota 'keep your eyes on the road' after he had responded to her message following his departure. 'It was a surprise,' Cardoso said in an extract of the book Diogo Jota: Forever In Our Hearts, shared by the Liverpool Echo, regarding his decision to rent a Ferrari then a Lamborghini in the summer of 2025. 'Unlike most players, who like fancy cars, jewellery and watches, Diogo was never into that sort of thing. He was happy with the cars we had. Rute Cardoso has given a heartbreaking account of the night of her husband Diogo Jota's death in a new biography Cardoso explains in the book that she grew increasing concerned after Jota and his brother Andre Silva, left, failed to respond to WhatsApp messages and had not arrived at their hotel 'So perhaps because he'd never been particularly into cars, he took that chance to try driving a Ferrari before our wedding. After that, he would also rent a Lamborghini, which he had to drop off in Santander. 'A few minutes after they'd left, I sent Diogo a message saying, "Safe journey". He replied with an emoji, and I told him to keep his eyes on the road.' Jota and his younger brother died when the Lamborghini Huracan he was driving careered off a motorway in northern Spain. Jota, 28, a father-of-three, was travelling back to Liverpool by road after he was advised by doctors not to fly following surgery, and crashed close to Spain's north-west border with Portugal. He married his childhood sweetheart Cardoso at a church in Porto, Portugal, just 11 days before the devastating collision. Cardoso explained how she had grown increasingly worried after several WhatsApp messages to Jota were left undelivered. The first of which was Cardoso informing Jota she had a video to show him, having just received footage from their wedding day. A subsequent message was also undelivered when she attempted to contact Andre. Cardoso revealed she had requested to visit the location of the crash which killed Jota and his brother as she made her way to collect his belongings She then rang the hotel the brothers had been due to stay at in Benavente to break up their journey. After being informed they had not arrived, Cardoso said she then phoned a hospital and the local police without success. Cardoso then contacted her uncle Vitor, a lorry driver with good contacts in the Spanish transport police. 'Suddenly, my uncle asked me to put Nuno, my brother-in-law, on the line. At that time of night, in the silence, I could make out every word they were saying. I heard my uncle tell him: "The bodies are being taken away". I think he added "to the mortuary", but that's when my mind went blank,' Cardoso said in the book extract. 'Bodies? My brother-in-law froze. My sister took the phone from him and asked my uncle to speak to her. My main concern was to ring Diogo's father and tell him: "You must come here immediately". I rang André's girlfriend and said the same thing: "Paula, come over now".' Cardoso revealed in the biography, written by former footballer Jose Manuel Delgado, that the family was visited by two psychologists to offer support. Her uncle called again and passed Cardoso onto a Spanish police officer, who officially informed her of Jota's death. Cardoso added in the family-authorised biography, which will support the LFC Foundation, that she requested to visit the scene of the accident when en route to mortuary to collect Jota and his brother’s belongings. 'I told the driver I wanted us to take the same route that they had taken,' Cardoso said. 'I imagined that, so many hours on, there would be no traces left, but I wanted to know where it had happened. But when we reached that cursed Kilometre 64, what was left of the car was still there.' Cardoso had attempted to move closer to the scene of the accident but was stopped by a police officer. Former Liverpool bosses Jurgen Klopp and Arne Slot are among those to have contributed to the biography about Jota A funeral was held for both Jota and Silva two days after their devastating deaths in a chapel in Gondomar, a city that overlooks Porto, where both brothers played during their academy careers. Following an investigation, a Spanish court ruled earlier this year that the crash was due to the Lamborghini suffering a blown-out tyre while overtaking a car, before bursting into flames upon hitting a barrier in the middle of the carriageway. The High Court of Justice in the province of Zamora, north-west Spain, has concluded that no criminal action was necessary regarding the deaths of both Jota and Andre, following the review of the entire evidence. Jota turned out 123 times for Liverpool, scoring 47 goals, and played a significant role in their 2024-25 Premier League title-winning season. Former Liverpool bosses Arne Slot and Jurgen Klopp are among those to have contributed to the biography, along with former team-mates. 'This book began as an opportunity to help preserve Diogo’s memory at a moment of profound sadness. My commitment throughout was to tell his story with care, honesty and respect for Diogo, André, and the family and friends who loved them,' said author Delgado. 'What moved me most was the generosity of those closest to them. Family members, teammates, coaches and friends shared their memories to help future generations understand the person Diogo was, and their love for both brothers can be felt on every page. 'While researching the book, I came to understand the unique bond between Diogo and Liverpool FC. Everywhere I went, people spoke not only of his talent, but also his humility, commitment and character. 'My hope is that Forever in our Hearts serves as a fitting tribute to Diogo’s life and legacy, and ensures his story continues to inspire others for years to come.' The Anfield faithful continuously paid their respects to Jota last season, singing his name in the 20th minute of every match, while the club also retired his No20 shirt. A permanent memorial to Jota and Andre was installed at Anfield in July.

Sports.title: Delusional Bruno Fernandes is an insult to the Man United captaincy. Humiliations like Como are when you find out who your real men are, and all he could do is show off his vast ego. Is anything EVER his fault?
Sports.content:
The trouble with being a club in a state of such blind desperation as Manchester United is that the centre no longer holds and individuals can begin imagining themselves untouchable and answerable to no one.

We witnessed this deeply unpleasant process on Wednesday night as the vast ego of the deeply divisive, self-promoting Bruno Fernandes revealed itself.

Bruno is very good on tactics, we’re told. An obsessive student of the game, apparently. And this seemingly made him consider it appropriate to mount a vicious attack on his manager in the aftermath of a scandalously poor performance at Como that resulted in a 4-1 Champions League thumping.

Such nights are the ones when you discover who your real men are – the ones you really want in your trenches – and Bruno, stepping forward with a look of faux solemnity on his face and a vial of poison to dispense, told us plenty about himself.

He is so wrapped up in his own delusion of self-importance that he seemingly imagined that his skewering of Michael Carrick’s tactics would not be seen as the disgraceful act of spite it actually was. He is an insult to the title ‘Manchester United captain’.

But this has become a pattern with him, hasn’t it? The way he throws his arms up on the field week in, week out gives a permanent impression that he considers himself so vastly superior to the lesser mortals around him, when his own positional indiscipline is so often the problem. It never, ever seems to be his fault.

Bruno Fernandes mounted a vicious attack on his manager in the aftermath of a scandalously poor performance at Como that resulted in a 4-1 Champions League thumping

This has become a pattern with him, hasn’t it? He considers himself so vastly superior to the lesser mortals around him, when his own positional indiscipline is so often the problem

As Jamie Carragher put it in his excellent analysis for CBS on Wednesday night: ‘He runs all over the place like a kid in the school yard for the supporters. They all think he's working hard but he is not. He is killing the rest of the team by doing it.’

United’s problems are systemic, of course; rooted in the high and mighty Sir Jim Ratcliffe, a man blind to his own gross incompetence. But if there is one founding principle that has kept this great club together through good times and bad down the years, then it is the collective taking precedence over the individual.

Bruno is not the first United captain to be playing in a side which doesn’t win trophies. Bryan Robson found himself in that same position for years and was in the twilight of his career before a title came. Yet we never heard a word against manager or team from him.

Those principles of discipline and collectivism at United have nearly always been self-policed. The morning after Wayne Rooney publicly challenged Sir Alex Ferguson about the club’s signings, in an infamous press release ahead of a Champions League match against Bursaspor in 2010, Ryan Giggs and Gary Neville told him he was out of order. Rooney apologised and, though Manchester City were sniffing around, signed a new contract the following day.

When Roy Keane lambasted team-mates in an MUTV interview which was subsequently pulped, Ferguson privately decreed that it was over between him and the club.

Ask the real men of central midfield, like Robson and Graeme Souness, how they’d solve a problem like those facing United on Wednesday night and they will tell you: ‘You worked it out yourself, on the pitch.’ Ferguson said the only player he allowed to challenge his tactics and change them on the field was Robson, though others had that ability to problem-solve.

Carrick has extracted far more from Fernandes than the hapless Ruben Amorim, by restoring him to his rightful position. He lifted last season’s PFA Player of the Year award because of it.

But the best for all concerned would have been for United to have taken £100million from Saudi Arabia for him, which is what the club were waiting for last year, in anticipation of using that money to rebuild. Only when he knew United were willing to let him go did he dig his heels in to stay.

Sir Alex Ferguson (right) said the only player he allowed to challenge his tactics and change them on the field was Bryan Robson (left, celebrating winning the 1990 FA Cup)

When Roy Keane lambasted team-mates in an MUTV interview which was subsequently pulped, Ferguson privately decreed that it was over between him and the club

Amid the insurrection, Michael Carrick has conducted himself precisely as Ferguson would have – not giving the outside world the satisfaction by publicly censuring these players

It remains to be seen if United have the appeal or resources to attract Carlo Ancelotti – the manager who, far more than Fabian Hurzeler or Antonio Conte, has the presence to handle the most difficult job in world football and restore a semblance of the old authority and unity.

But whoever arrives, there can certainly be no place at Old Trafford for Fernandes, a symptom of the canker at the heart of the place, just like Lisandro Martinez, another who deemed it appropriate to trash the club in public.

Amid the insurrection of the past two weeks, Carrick has publicly conducted himself precisely as his old boss Ferguson would have – not giving the outside world the satisfaction or the headlines by publicly censuring these players. But there is no doubt that the old man would have no place for them now, whatever their contribution on the field.

‘I placed discipline above all else and it might have cost us several titles,’ Ferguson reflected from retirement. ‘But if I had to repeat things, I’d do precisely the same, because once you bid farewell to discipline, you say goodbye to success and set the stage for anarchy.’

Sports.title: Man United's civil war spills over into the boardroom with chiefs SPLIT over Michael Carrick's replacement: Insiders fear club are 'wasting too much time' as under-fire boss clings on to his job for Bournemouth game
Sports.content:
Manchester United’s problems are piling up with there understood to be growing tensions between director of football Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell. Speaking to a handful of key figures close to the dressing room, each of whom are in regular dialogue with the United hierarchy, Daily Mail Sport has learned that along with disagreements on the pitch between players and manager, there is also growing discontent in the boardroom. Wilcox and Vivell are said to have differing opinions on who should succeed Michael Carrick, should the decision be made to move on to a third manager in 2026. There is some sympathy in the United hierarchy for the position Carrick is in, with nine senior absentees for the Como trip. They too are having to face up to the reality that not enough was done in the summer to strengthen this team to play multiple games a week. Results - which includes just two wins from 11 - are getting worse at an alarming rate and all is not well behind the scenes. Carrick will take charge of United for Sunday’s home match against Bournemouth but potential successors have already been sounded out privately. Michael Carrick is expected to stay in charge of Man United for their match with Bournemouth Director of football Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell are said to have differing opinions on who should succeed Carrick if the decision is made to move him on Vivell is understood to be pushing hard for Julian Nagelsmann to be the leading candidate, with the 39-year-old out of work following a disastrous World Cup in charge of Germany. Chelsea assessed Nagelsmann as a potential manager when Vivell was technical director in west London and his admiration remains. But sources have suggested that Wilcox, who is Vivell’s boss in the chain of command, prefers a Premier League proven manager, with Eddie Howe, Fabian Hurzeler, Unai Emery and Antonio Conte, who have all come up on a shortlist, a tick in that category. Hurzeler does not have a release clause in his Brighton contract and so would require enormous compensation. There is well-placed scepticism as to whether any move would even be remotely possible, regardless of how well liked he is inside Old Trafford. Carrick will face the music when he addresses the media on Friday in his pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday’s game against Bournemouth in which he’ll have to address doubts creeping in from players, tensions upstairs among execs and whether he will be able to keep hold of his job. United are refusing to press the panic button and sack Carrick who is now expected to stay in charge for Sunday’s game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at least. United then face Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa before a two-week international break next month. Vivell is understood to be pushing hard for Julian Nagelsmann to be the leading candidate, with the 39-year-old out of work following a disastrous World Cup in charge of Germany Sources have suggested that Wilcox prefers a Premier League proven manager, with Eddie Howe, Fabian Hurzeler, Unai Emery and Antonio Conte a tick in that category The fact that Carrick will speak to the media again, less than two days after he tried to explain his team’s shocking performance in the Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium, is the strongest signal yet that United are aiming to stand by Carrick for the time being. In-fighting at United is rife right now, not least after captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned the tactics of his manager after the abject 4-1 defeat at the hands of Como. ‘It needs to start at the top,’ one source close to a first team player said. ‘Recruitment guys, manager, the lot need to go.’ Another source said: ‘This needs a strong board to make hard decisions fast. They’ve already wasted too much time.’ United have stressed that Vivell and Wilcox maintain a healthy relationship even in such trying circumstances, but many close to the dressing room are telling a different story. ‘At this club, there’s too much focus on what’s been done in the past, but we’re not those people anymore,’ Fernandes told Sky Italia after the Como defeat. ‘The club and the players need to understand that. Unfortunately for us - especially when it comes to the players - those who join expect to win trophies, win games, and reach the highest level, but unfortunately that's been very difficult at this club in recent years. That's the situation.’
