Sports.title: Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon.

Not, at least, according to those who watched him endure 11 gruelling rounds against Daniel Dubois in Manchester in May. Not according to those who questioned whether his corner should have pulled him out earlier, as his face became increasingly battered and his right eye swelled shut. And certainly not according to those who believe the punishment he absorbed makes a rematch a risk too far.

But Wardley has never been one to follow the script.

When the 31-year-old first faced Dubois, 29, he did so as the WBO heavyweight champion. He dropped his opponent twice in the opening three rounds, threatening to produce one of the biggest victories of his career before Dubois fought his way back into the contest and eventually stopped him in the 11th.

Now, with the WBO title back on the line, Wardley finds himself in more familiar territory in one respect: he is the challenger, the underdog and the man many expect to lose again.

And, as he explains when we sit down ahead of the rematch, he rather likes it that way.

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon but he's never one to follow the script

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

'It's been the staple of my career for as long as I can remember, well, since I started. It has been the main focal point. After the first five or six fights, when I started to step up the level, even incrementally, even slightly, people were saying I was going to lose, that it was a step too far, and all the rest of it. It's all the stuff everyone's heard before,' he says.

'It's a side of the coin I'm very much used to, and the pressure's off. I'm the challenger here. I'm expected to lose and expected to go even quicker, and Daniel's supposed to put on a better performance, and all the rest of it. So there's no pressure on me. There's nothing on my shoulders.'

It is a strikingly relaxed assessment from a fighter preparing to walk back into the ring with the man who inflicted the first defeat of his professional career.

Wardley, however, insists that defeat has done little to change him. He is not pretending that losing a world title is enjoyable, but nor does he regard it as a defining moment in his life.

'Not a lot has changed. I'm not that different. Don't get me wrong, a loss is never fun. It's never nice, it's never enjoyable. But for me, at least, it wasn't soul-crushing or devastating, and it hasn't had any effect on me as a person, my character or anything else.

'The job’s the job, the game’s the game. From the very beginning, I’ve accepted that getting through heavyweight boxing unscathed isn’t guaranteed, especially given the way I compete at the highest level and my desire to take on the biggest challengers out there.

'I think people forget that the first time around, I picked Daniel. I asked for that fight because I looked at the crop of heavyweights and thought, "That's the best one to challenge myself against."

'Knowing that about myself, and knowing that's my angle, was I ever going to get through this undefeated like Floyd Mayweather? Probably not. So, look, it comes how it comes. But as long as I'm happy with myself in terms of the performances, that I've given my all and all the rest of it, I can sleep at night.'

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

Wardley took a lot of punishment in the latter rounds of their first encounter in May (above)

It is that willingness to put himself in the firing line which has made Wardley such a compelling heavyweight. His fights are rarely short on drama, and the first meeting with Dubois was no exception. He started at a blistering pace, dropping DDD in the opening 10 seconds, only for the momentum to swing as the punishment began to accumulate.

By the later rounds, Wardley was absorbing heavy shots and fighting through considerable damage. His condition between rounds prompted questions about whether the contest should have been stopped sooner, with particular scrutiny falling on his corner for allowing him out ahead of the 10th.

Wardley disagrees with the suggestion that his team failed him. He regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

He is equally dismissive of the noise surrounding the timing of the rematch, arguing that those watching from the outside cannot know the full picture of his recovery. His position is that he and his team are best placed to judge the damage he sustained and whether he is ready to fight again.

For Wardley, the prospect of another brutal encounter is not something he has brushed aside or refused to think about. It is a reality he has had to confront with himself, knowing that by stepping back into the ring with Dubois, he is willingly putting himself in a position where he could once again withstand a frightening amount of punishment.

It is a remarkable thought process: to acknowledge the possibility of enduring the same damage all over again, to ask himself whether he is prepared to go through it, and then to make peace with the answer before he has even thrown a punch.

'It's a level of early acceptance. The second I triggered the rematch clause, even before that, I had to have a conversation with myself and ask, "This could go the exact same way. Are you ready for that? Are you OK with that?"

'As long as the answer is yes from me to me, then cool, let's go. But by now, it's nowhere near my brain as a question mark or something I'm having to deal with, battle with or anything else. It's already been ticked off, boxed and put away. It is what it is.'

Wardley was checked by the doctor and spoken to by the referee multiple times in the fight

As a result, Dubois became a two-time heavyweight champion and will now defend his belt

There is little melodrama in his delivery. When the possibility of going through the same ordeal again is put to him, Wardley does not attempt to dress it up as fearlessness or pretend that the risks do not exist.

'It's an acceptance of the game and the sport we got into, and especially the way I fight as well,' he says.

That approach is perhaps best illustrated by what goes through his mind when he is taking punishment in the ring. Wardley is not a heavyweight who is inclined to retreat quietly after being caught cleanly. His instinct is to make sure his opponent knows there will be a response.

'Especially in those moments, it's about getting back at them. All right, you took one… let your hands go. Don't just let them get away with it for free. At least let them know. Let them have it in their brain that if they get off a few shots, I'm not just going to take them, run away and roll over.'

It is a mindset that makes for spectacular viewing, but one which also places enormous demands on a fighter's corner.

Wardley describes those 60 seconds between rounds as almost too precious to waste on anything other than the information he needs to continue. With the clock ticking and another round approaching, he wants tactical instruction rather than an emotional check-in.

'No, I think it's 90 per cent tactical, 10 per cent everything else, because in those moments, compassion doesn't need to come into it. That's not where the compassion needs to be.

'Those 60 seconds are so precious, such a small moment. It feels like a click. It feels like nothing. It feels like it's done and gone so quickly that you're on your stool, you're off your stool and the next round has started.

'In that time, you need to get the information. It's not time for, "Oh, a little rub on the shoulder. Are you doing OK, Fab? Is everything alright? Are you going to be alright, mate? Do you want me to dab your face a bit?" No. Let me know what I need to know. Let's get this going again.'

Wardley knows that the rematch will be gruelling. He knows his durability will continue to be questioned. But he also knows why he wanted the first fight in the first place.

For Wardley, the pursuit of the biggest challenges has always mattered more than protecting an unbeaten record. Defeat by Dubois has not changed that. He is back because in his mind, the possibility of the same ending has already been accepted and because it’s a risk worth taking.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival
Sports.content:
Even the most hardened boxing fans can be taken aback by the depths of brutality which two men are capable of inflicting on each other. Especially the heavyweights.

So it was on the Saturday night this May when Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley battered hell's bells out of each other in Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena. Wardley dropped his world title challenger twice in the first three rounds. Just 28 seconds into the 11th, Dubois had to be pulled off the champion he had reduced to a bleeding and battered but still-standing wreck.

We mere mortals can only ask: How on earth do they do it? ‘We’re fighters,’ says Dubois. ‘Honoured to share a ring with him.’

‘Born to do it,’ says Wardley, who found out that truth of himself when he tried white collar boxing. ‘Love being in with such a great fighter.’

What in heaven goes through their minds at the prospect of doing it again, as they are on Saturday night at the O2? Do they not realise the danger this sledgehammer head-banging presents to their health?

Prepare yourselves, dear gentle readers, for this stunning answer from Dubois: ‘Dementia? If you’re talking about dementia, no point worrying. We’ve probably got it already.’

Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley have both spoken of their love for stepping into the ring with one another ahead of their rematch on Saturday

But as brutal as their meeting in May was, tomorrow night's clash at the O2 has been teased as even bloodier

A chilling insight, this, into the mentality of men who fight not only for a living but for the lust for glory, the thrill of battle, the roar of the crowd, the smell of the greasepaint, the glare of the lights and not least their manly pride.

And on nights like this, for a world championship. This time the WBO belt which Dubois ripped from Wardley’s fairy-tale grasp five months ago.

What, no nerves? ‘I live with the chaos,’ says Dubois. ‘Chaos all day every day and specially on the night. I love the fear. It gives me the power. I hold the chaos in until it’s at its peak when the first bell goes. Then it explodes as I let it out. Which brings power and clarity.’

Wardley comes not only from his different background in commerce but also with an opposite mindset. He says: ‘No one wants to lose a world title but if it has to be, then what really matters is how it happens.

‘I feel more relaxed and confident having proved I can engage a top-level fighter in a great fight, which everyone expected me to lose easily. Calm makes me better.’

That and the lessons he learned in the five months since his gladiatorial — and only — defeat thus far. ‘We’ve studied every critical moment of the first fight,’ he says. ‘And I’ve adapted where necessary. Had to because I have more to work on than Daniel with all his experience.

‘But we’ve not only looked at me. We’ve looked at him. He’s not as adaptable as me. He’s not suddenly going to become light-footed and free moving. I’ll give him something different.’

To which Dubois says: ‘I’ll give him another beating. Bash him up. Smash him worse than before. And quicker. We didn’t know quite what he might do in the first fight. Now I know what to expect.

‘I also know that he’s not good enough to adapt. I’m his daddy now.’ That is clarity, Dubois style. He also discounts those two knock-downs. As a man who has been a slow starter at times — although not when he demolished Anthony Joshua from the get-go — he says: ‘Things happen in boxing. You can get caught. But I also know now that he doesn’t have the power. No real power.’

Wardley, for his part, denies that he was as badly hurt as it appeared in fight one. Their respective trainers have disagreed about the 11th-hour stoppage. Dubois’ coach Don Charles says the towel should have been thrown in earlier.

Wardley supports his man Ben Davison’s assertion that he was still in the fight throwing punches, saying: ‘The optics looked bad, what with the blood and the bruising and the punches. But I trust my team to take care of me. Trust them with my life.

‘A lot of the punches were glancing and in the 10th round I shook him with an uppercut. If the big right that followed had connected cleanly we might have had a different ending.’

This man who escaped office drudgery to chase his dream hopes to go on to meet the December winner of Joshua v Tyson Fury. Dubois fancies some of that big money but is also looking beyond, to unifying all the other world titles vacated by Oleksandr Usyk.

Will the ending on Saturday be different from Wardley v Dubois One? Probably not. Dynamite Dan likely added the more valuable knowledge to his wider experience and has never looked this bullish before a fight.

What we do know for sure is that this pair will give us another thriller.

Sports.title: Following decades of US domination, British heavyweight boxing is on top - after Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley and Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua, there are Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
Following decades of US domination, British heavyweight boxing is on top - after Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley and Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua, there are Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made, writes JEFF POWELL MBE

In the small hours of May 16, 1955 my father woke me in the darkness, lit a candle in the scullery, plugged in his old crystal radio set and told me to listen to a world heavyweight title fight taking place in San Francisco.

Don Cockell of Balham, south London, was challenging Rocky Marciano of Brockton, Massachusetts, for the world heavyweight championship. Most of the sound which came whistling through the static was that of Marciano’s eight-ounce gloves thudding into Cockell’s head and body.

Marciano kept knocking down Cockell, who kept getting up. Until the ninth round, when Rocky nailed him to the canvas for good with a booming right which seemingly connected while he was on his knees.

When the BBC radio commentator put that question to the champ, Marciano replied: ‘Britain can be proud of her boy Don Cockell.’

Jack Powell, whose toughness had carried him through the landings and trenches of the Second World War as well as countless fights inside and outside the ring, slammed his fist on the kitchen table and said: ‘As if keeping beating us ain’t enough, they have to bloody patronise us.’

I was 13. Not until I was 50 – and Marciano had long since become the only heavyweight champ to retire undefeated – would Lennox Lewis end our century-long wait for a successor to Bob Fitzsimmons.

Lennox Lewis (pictured) ended Great Britain's wait for a successor to Bob Fitzsimmons as the United States dominated the heavyweight scene

American stars such as George Foreman (left) and Muhammad Ali (right) dominated the previous era

That eternity was flooded with such revered Americans as Jack Johnson, Jack Dempsey, Joe Louis, Floyd Patterson, Sonny Liston, Muhammad Ali, Joe Frazier, George Foreman, Mike Tyson, Larry Holmes and Evander Holyfield.

The golden age of heavyweight boxing gave us the Fight of the Century and the Thrilla in Manila – both between Ali and Frazier – the Rumble in the Jungle with Ali and Foreman, the Upset of the Century by Buster Douglas over Tyson, Dempsey v Gene Tunney, Louis v both Max Schmeling and Jersey Joe Walcott and Ali’s slaying of the Liston monster. That was the time when the Star Spangled Banner flew over America’s mocking of ‘Britain’s Horizontal Heavyweights.’

Henry Cooper remained perpendicular against The Greatest of them all but there was scant recognition over the water of how he knocked Ali down and almost out with the left hook renowned as ‘Enery’s ‘Ammer’ in the first of two stadium fights he lost to his propensity to suffer cuts.

So, oh, how we gloated when we watched Riddick Bowe dump his WBC belt in a London dustbin rather than fight Lewis, who was thereby elevated to his first title by decree. Rejoiced when Lennox validated his title by beating Oliver McCall in September 1995. Acclaimed Lenny the Lion when he became our only three-time world heavyweight champion.

We breathed a huge sigh of relief when Frank Bruno beat McCall at an emotional Wembley, finally to become world champion. Just as we fretted for him when he genuflected umpteen times on his way to the Las Vegas ring for a second crushing by Tyson and the loss of his crown.

Even so, British heavyweight boxing was transitioning from famine to feast. The US can boast 53 champions all time in the prize-ring’s marquee division. All the way back to the immortal John L Sullivan in the late 1880s. But the UK has accelerated from one active heavyweight champion in 2003 – Lewis when he bloodied and defeated Vitali Kliltschko – to a running total of 11 today if you delete the asterisks against Michael Bent, Herbie Hide and Henry Akinwande who wore the WBO belt before that organisation was fully recognised.

David Haye built on the Lewis legacy when he bamboozled Russia’s 7ft giant Nikolai Valuev and thereby emulated Holyfield’s feat of an undisputed cruiserweight king becoming world heavyweight champion.

The Russo-Ukraine brothers Klitschko broke the US domination but then both Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua followed that Lewis victory over Vitali by vanquishing Wladimir.

British heavyweight boxing was transitioning from famine to feast, which has included the likes of Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right)

Britannia’s Rule was stunningly interrupted by Oleksandr Usyk’s revival of the Kyiv Conspiracy with two dazzling victories apiece over the Gypsy King and AJ, followed by another double over their heir apparent Daniel Dubois.

Oleksandr The Great’s abrupt relinquishing of all the belts opened the gateway to an immediate UK renaissance. One in which it is not Americans but Brits fighting each other for the glittering prizes.

This Saturday at the O2, Dubois and the amazingly reconstructed white-collar boxer Fabio Wardley reprise their blood and thunder war for the now-respected WBO title. This time with Dynamite Daniel as the champion.

The winner is likely to go on to meet in the not-too-distant future whoever prevails in the over-long awaited settlement between Fury and Joshua - which, belatedly though it comes in December, is so full of fascination that it has sold ticket at prices higher than the gross national product of some third-world countries.

By then Moses Itauma should have recovered from the drastic loss of stamina – and a blown IBF title shot against Croatia’s Filip Hrgovic – to resume leadership of the next generation. German WBC champion Agit Kabayel will soon be in all those crosshairs.

With all the above except Joshua in Frank Warren’s stable there are more Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made. With only one big guy of promise, Jared Anderson, to be seen on the western horizon.

And to think Americans used to belittle their last heavyweight champion of note Deontay Wilder as ‘just a puncher’.

The biggest puncher since Iron Mike, as it happens. How they must be wishing over there that Fury had not ended the Bronze Bomber’s five-year run of knockouts in the murderous final act of their epic trilogy.

Daniel Dubois (left) and Fabio Wardley (right) will face off this weekend with more Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made

Throughout America’s glorious boxing history the world heavyweight champion was the symbol of their national manhood. Today they lay no claim to any of the alphabelts.

There are extraneous factors at work. The majority of strapping young American athletes - be they graduating from college or seeking ways out of the projects - are taking to basketball, their version of football and baseball, rather than take a headbashing in the ring on the off-chance of making their fortunes.

US boxing is down to pinning its hopes on a brash young Mexican-American welterweight Ryan Garcia - on the back of his destruction of a humiliated Conor Benn. All while the Blue Riband of the ring is hoisted this side of the pond.

Not so Yankee-Doodle-Dandy now, gentlemen.

Sports.title: 'You cannot keep fighting gung-ho like that': Daniel Dubois' trainer warns Fabio Wardley is risking his boxing future - and says team put his health at risk by letting him battle on in first bout
Sports.content:
'You cannot keep fighting gung-ho like that': Daniel Dubois' trainer warns Fabio Wardley is risking his boxing future - and says team put his health at risk by letting him battle on in first bout

Daniel Dubois' trainer Don Charles believes Fabio Wardley is already feeling the effects of the punishment he absorbed in their brutal first encounter, as he suggested the former heavyweight champion's corner did him a 'disservice' by allowing their fight to continue for so long.

Wardley and Dubois produced a gruelling contest in Manchester last May, with the fight eventually stopped in the 11th round after the former world champion had subjected his opponent to a sustained assault in the latter rounds.

Wardley's remarkable resilience was a defining feature of the contest, but Charles believes the damage he endured could already be catching up with him ahead of their highly anticipated rematch this Saturday.

The veteran trainer also questioned whether Wardley's team should have intervened sooner, suggesting that their hope of seeing the champion produce another fight-changing punch may have come at a cost to his health.

'They let Fabio down a little bit, in my opinion, for his health,' Charles said.

'Being the champion, being a guy who has done it previously and is able to pull out a shot at any point during the fight, whether early or late, he has got that in him.

Daniel Dubois' trainer Don Charles believes Fabio Wardley is already feeling the effects of the punishment he absorbed in their brutal first encounter

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

'So perhaps the team were thinking, 'Maybe he just needs that one punch', because he has done it in the past. But there comes a point where you have to do the sensible thing.

'A couple of days after the fight, I relaxed and watched it back. Oh my God, it was really bad, in my opinion.

'Again, it is their decision. There is the referee there and there are the doctors. But I think they let Fabio down a little bit, in my opinion, for his health.'

Charles stressed that his focus during the fight had been entirely on Dubois, meaning he had not fully appreciated the extent of Wardley's punishment until he watched the contest back afterwards.

His comments come amid renewed scrutiny of the first fight and the decision to allow Wardley to continue into the championship rounds, although the man from Ipswich has defended his corner against suggestions they got it wrong.

Wardley regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

Charles believes the physical demands of Wardley's all-action style could have consequences beyond a single night in the ring, arguing that the damage accumulated in such gruelling contests can gradually take its toll.

'I think he is already noticing the wear and tear, from an observational point of view,' Charles said.

Charles suggested the former heavyweight champion's corner did him a 'disservice' by allowing their fight to continue for so long

Dubois has just signed a six-figure deal brokered by NVA SEG Talent Group to become the global ambassador for British performance and lifestyle brand Resonance Energy Wear

'It is entertaining for the public, granted, but you cannot have a very long career fighting like that. It catches up with you. It really does, and it chips away at you.

'You cannot keep fighting gung-ho like that. It is very entertaining, like I said, but you really have to look at the bigger picture.'

Charles believes Dubois will approach the return bout with greater discipline after being caught off guard in their initial meeting and warns the rematch could end early despite preparing for the possibility of another prolonged battle.

'What you are going to see is a more disciplined display and more alertness,' he said.

'Obviously, we got caught off guard last time, so we have rectified that. This time, it is going to be a more disciplined, more dynamic and more technical performance.

'We have trained as if this were the olden days, when you boxed up to 15 rounds. If this fight has to go 15 rounds to get a victory, 15 rounds it is.

'This fight could end in round one, or it could end in round 12 or 15. It needs to be.'

One of Charles's biggest questions ahead of the rematch concerns how Wardley will respond when Dubois lands cleanly, particularly if DDD can recreate some of the punishing moments from their first encounter.

Charles believes Dubois will approach the return bout with greater discipline after being caught off guard in their initial meeting and warns the rematch could end early

Charles believes the physical demands of Wardley's all-action style could have consequences beyond a single night, arguing that the damage accumulated can gradually take its toll

The expert trainer suggested that the memories of that night could return once Wardley begins absorbing shots again, although he acknowledged the 31-year-old's extraordinary toughness.

'Fabio is made of something else. He is made of steel, that man, the amount of punishment he took and kept taking,' Charles said.

'But it is our duty to recall those entries, to remind him of the pain he felt last May in Manchester.

'As soon as that bell rings, our duty is to recall that pain. If he has forgotten it, Daniel will remind him in that ring: 'This is what you were feeling.'

'He is a human being like you and I. Once he starts feeling that unbearable pain, the rest is up to him and his team, and what they do under the referee's supervision.'

Sports.title: Floyd Mayweather gushes over Donald Trump after President praises boxer's 'good looks' at Republican rally
Sports.content:
Floyd Mayweather gushed over Donald Trump on stage in Arizona - after the President praised the boxer's good looks.

Mayweather flew on Air Force One to Bullhead City, Arizona for a campaign rally held to support Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

The undefeated fighter was the latest sports star to join Trump on the campaign trail and drew high praise as he was introduced.

'One of the greatest fighters in boxing history,' Trump said, calling Mayweather an 'unbelievable defensive fighter.'

'That's why he looks so good,' Trump continued, before adding as he walked up to the stage: 'Look at this guy, he looks so good. Who would believe he's a fighter? He looks so good! He doesn't have a mark!'

And the high praise was reciprocated, as Mayweather declared: 'We couldn't have chosen a better president twice than Donald Trump.'

Donald Trump welcomed boxer Floyd Mayweather to the stage in Bullhead City, Arizona

Trump praised Mayweather's good looks as he welcomed him to the stage at the rally

Mayweather delivered praise of Trump as he called America the 'greatest country in the world'

Mayweather had started his address by telling the crowd: 'America is the greatest country in the world. If I died and came back a million times, I would always choose America.

'It was great to represent this country in the 1996 Olympic Games,' Mayweather said. 'To go out there and represent the red, white, and blue.'

He then turned his praise to Trump before adding: 'So it's all about keeping this country strong, sticking together, and believing in one another. America is the greatest country in the world. Thank you.'

Mayweather, 49, a Vegas native, happens to have strong business ties in Arizona.

Dennis Rodman, Mike Tyson, Jake Paul, Roger Clemens and Jon Gruden have all made appearances at recent rallies in support of Trump.

Mayweather has long been an outspoken supporter of Trump, hailing him the 'best president in US history' last year.

He attended Trump's first inauguration as president and supported him throughout his first term in the Oval Office.

Policy-wise, Mayweather and Trump have been aligned on a few issues, including in the Middle East. Mayweather is a staunch supporter of Israel and donated $1million to the United Hatzalah of Israel in 2024.

Mayweather flew to the event on Air Force One earlier in the day to travel to the event

Mayweather has been aligned with Trump on several issues and been a public supporter

Mayweather is the latest sports star to be brought in by Trump on the midterms campaign trail

Join the discussion What do you think motivates celebrities like Mayweather to publicly align themselves with political figures?

'We had Trump before, we didn't appreciate him,' Mayweather told Fox Business in February of last year. 'I think Trump is a great president, actually he's the best president in my eyes, he's the best president we've ever had. Great business man and that's what it's about.'

'Trump has done an amazing job and a lot of people around America are upset. But no matter who goes into the White House, we're always upset. And I think Trump is the man for the job, he's the best president in my eyes.'

Mayweather's fellow boxing icon Tyson also joined Trump on the Presidential aircraft last week, making the journey from the White House to Syracuse, New York.

During his speech at the rally, Trump spotted Tyson in the crowd and invited the former boxing champion on stage.

'I think we have to call him up, Mike Tyson, will you get up here?' Trump said.

As the President's athletic guest of the day, Tyson praised Trump in front of the Syracuse crowd, thanking him during a brief moment on stage.

'Thank you, thank you very much. I'm just happy to be up here with my president, President Trump. There's no way in the world I would ever be here if it wasn't for a president like Donald Trump,' Tyson said.

Trump was also joined by NBA icon Rodman in Durant, Oklahoma, and former NFL coach Gruden and influencer-turned-boxer Paul in Youngstown, Ohio.

He announced his intention to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to MLB legend Clemens when the former pitcher joined him at a rally in San Antonio, Texas.

Sports.title: Sainz yet to be "convinced" that F1 2026 will finish in the Middle East
Sports.content:
Carlos Sainz has admitted that it's "difficult" to be convinced by Formula 1's chiefs that its final rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi can go ahead as planned despite the ongoing Middle Eastern conflict.

Both F1 management and governing body the FIA have maintained the position that the final two rounds of 2026 in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, scheduled back-to-back at the end of November and first weekend of December, can go ahead as planned.

With no resolution in sight for the ongoing conflict between the US and its ally Israel, and Iran, and new strikes on Saudi Arabia by the Houthi rebels, the situation in the Middle East remains extremely volatile.

The outlook is also likely to be influenced by the US midterm elections on 3 November, with several outlets reporting the US and Israel are preparing for fresh attacks on Iran afterwards.

F1 has been working on a contingency plan with an alternative season finale in Imola, on the weekend of the planned Abu Dhabi race, but all indications from series chiefs are that they are very keen to press ahead with the Middle Eastern double-header based on the current information and assurances they have received from various stakeholders.

But Sainz, who acts as director of the F1 drivers association GPDA, feels it is "difficult" and "premature" to envisage a finish in the region based on the current news cycle.

Abu Dhabi GP 2025 Photo by: Nicolas Economou / NurPhoto via Getty Images

"They seem very convinced that it's going to go ahead," Sainz said on Thursday ahead of this weekend's United States Grand Prix in Austin. "I think on my personal side, and not speaking as a GPDA, it's very difficult to be convinced right now because there's still plenty of things happening in the Middle East.

"And also there is obviously an election that is going to happen in the US and things that are going to happen in the political side of the world that could affect the next month and a half very suddenly. So, I think it's relatively premature to be so convinced."

But Sainz also felt that the drivers have little choice but to put their faith in what series executives decide, as they have more information on what is happening on the ground.

"As it stands, we would go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi and if the FIA and Formula 1 decide that's still safe and a good scenario, I think we as drivers have to go with whatever they say," the Spaniard added.

"It's not like we don't have as much inside information as they have, so we need to follow their lead and trust in their decision making.

"But only as it stands, I think the world can change a lot in the next month and a half. So we need to be [reactive] to whatever happens and not just go because we want to go right now."

Sports.title: When Cadillac will open its F1 engine factory
Sports.content:
Cadillac has revealed its Formula 1 engine factory will open on 18 December.

General Motors was approved by the FIA in 2025 as a power unit supplier from the 2029 season onwards, hence the construction of new F1 engine facilities at the manufacturer’s base in Charlotte, North Carolina.

“We're opening our whole engine factory, if you will, in Charlotte, North Carolina on 18 December,” General Motors president Mark Reuss announced in a conference at Autosport Business Exchange in New York. “So that's coming really well.”

General Motors now has another couple of years to design its own power unit, though the timing may be suboptimal – FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has committed to F1 switching back to V8 engines – potentially running on sustainable fuel with a smaller share of electric power – by 2031. In that case, GM’s powertrain would get two seasons in action at best, potentially just one if the switch is brought forward to 2030.

In the meantime, Cadillac is running customer Ferrari power units, and the team’s maiden season has been tricky thus far. It is the only outfit yet to score a point in 2026, and the MAC-26 has qualified slowest of all at the last four rounds.

General Motors president Mark Reuss presents Cadillac's one-off shakedown F1 livery for Barcelona Photo by: Cadillac Communications

“You know, we’re not here to finish last, so we’ve got to follow through and build this team, build the powertrain and build the car, like we did in GTP,” Reuss said. “That takes a little more time here, because this is a place where we've never raced. You’ve got to get the right people with the right engineers and the right drivers, and we’ve got to get that process really going, and it's logarithmic, it's not linear.”

Veterans Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas have been bringing invaluable experience in that context, but they have also been recording their worst career results.

“You can't win every race – no one can win every race – so when it happens, when they have a day that is unfortunate, or mistakes were made, they move on from that race and perfect their craft – whether it's with the car or themselves, or their physicality, or whatever that is – and they drive for that perfection,” Reuss said.

“Both of these gentlemen in the race for us do that, and they really understand what it takes and the process. I'm very, very happy that they're patient with us, to be honest; that takes a special person.”

Sports.title: Slater set for F1 practice debut with Audi in Mexico
Sports.content:
Audi junior Freddie Slater will make his debut at the wheel of a Formula 1 car with a couple of Free Practice 1 outings in Mexico City and Sao Paulo.

Audi took over the Sauber team ahead of 2026 for the German brand’s maiden F1 season, incidentally launching a new driver academy, which has largely rested on Slater’s shoulders.

Previously an Italian F4 and Formula Regional European champion, Slater has lived up to expectations by taking second place in Formula 3 behind Ugo Ugochukwu – the 18-year-old Briton was the highest-placed rookie in the standings.

Ahead of his step up to Formula 2 with Invicta – following in the footsteps of fellow Trident F3 racers Gabriel Bortoleto, Leonardo Fornaroli and Rafael Camara – Slater will be in action in FP1 at the Mexican and Brazilian grands prix, helping Audi fulfil the rules’ young-driver requirements.

Alpine junior Paul Aron was loaned to Audi on two occasions earlier this season for free practice sessions, and Slater is getting the team’s last two mandatory rookie outings, replacing Nico Hulkenberg and Bortoleto once each.

“Getting behind the wheel of a Formula 1 car at a grand prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I’ve been dreaming of since I was a kid,” Slater said. “I’ve learned a lot this year, and these free practice outings with Audi will be another opportunity to keep gaining on-track experience.

Freddie Slater, TRIDENT Photo by: Dom Gibbons - Formula 1 via Getty Images

“Being part of the Audi Driver Development Programme has already given me some incredible opportunities, and I am grateful for their trust and support. I’m really looking forward to getting out on track: my focus will be on doing the best job I can, helping the team with its programme and taking as many learnings as possible from both sessions.”

Audi racing director Allan McNish added: “We have seen Freddie making great progress throughout recent years, both on and off the track; it is the right time for Freddie to step up.

“These appearances in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development before he steps up to Formula 2 next season.

"We are looking forward to seeing him in the R26 and supporting him through these two important FP1 sessions.”

Colton Herta in at COTA

Earlier, Cadillac test and development driver Colton Herta will be in action at this weekend's United States Grand Prix, driving Sergio Perez’s car. Austin will mark the Californian’s fourth FP1 session of the year, though his latest, in Monza, was cut short by a suspected hydraulic issue.

“Driving the MAC-26 in front of the American fans at COTA is going to be special,” Herta said. “I have great memories at this track – winning my first IndyCar race here back in 2019 was a huge moment in my career, so stepping into an F1 car on this layout feels like coming full circle.

Colton Herta, Cadillac Racing Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I’ve built up a good rhythm with the team through my previous FP1 runs in Barcelona, Budapest, and Monza, so my goal for Friday morning is straightforward: execute the test programme cleanly, help the engineers gather good data on the set-up, and hand the car back to Checo with some useful feedback to support the team for the rest of the weekend.”

Team principal Marcin Budkowski added: “The high-speed sweeping section in sector one [at COTA] and the tight, low-speed turns at the end of the lap are a tricky for car set-up, and the bumps always add an extra dimension.

“We are looking forward to having Colton back in the car for FP1 on Friday, and we also plan to bring some small floor and cooling upgrades for evaluation.

"Colton knows this circuit very well from his IndyCar career, so his feedback will be valuable as we establish our baseline for the weekend.”

Currently a lowly 19th in the F2 standings, Herta told Autosport he was still aiming at F1 by 2028, while his plans for next year remain unclear.

Sports.title: MotoGP "can’t just copy" F1’s Drive to Survive success – Chase Carey
Sports.content:
Liberty Media director Chase Carey believes MotoGP “can’t just copy” Netflix’s Formula 1 docuseries Drive to Survive to gain widespread recognition.

Liberty acquired F1 in January 2017, and one of the major events under the American company was the release of the Netflix show’s opening season two years later, which substantially contributed to the world championship’s increased popularity.

Liberty then bought 84% of Dorna Sports (now known as MotoGP Sports Entertainment Group) in July 2025. The group is seeking to make motorcycle grands prix more diverse – 11 of the top 12 riders in the 2026 MotoGP championship are Spanish or Italian – while increasing its presence in the United States.

“Certainly there are elements of what teams need to do in MotoGP that will have similarities to Formula 1,” Carey said in a conference at Autosport Business Exchange in New York. “Obviously, it is a global franchise.

“In some ways, MotoGP is even crazier. When you look at these guys, they look like they're lying on the pavement riding the motorcycles around. But it is a sport that also has its unique characteristics. And I think you can't just cookie-cutter [the approach].

“It's early days. They're working on it, developing the strategies, the opportunities of how you take that sport and grow it in the way we've tried to with Formula 1.”

Drive to Survive has been credited with introducing F1 to a brand-new audience, boosted by the COVID-19 pandemic’s lockdowns, which first occurred a couple of weeks after season two was released.

“Drive to Survive is probably the most obvious example,” Carey acknowledged. “We recognised we needed to have the personalities that make up the sport, give them a bigger platform and let fans engage.

“The digital world today is a 24/7 world. The premium experience is still that live race, but at the end of the day people are connecting with the race, following the race and clips of the race, clips of what people are doing, things going on behind the scenes.

“They're following that 24/7. So we need to continue to find ways to feed that appetite and that desire to connect with their sport, provide the vehicles that enable fans to connect with the sport in that way.

Liz Claman and Chase Carey Photo by: Bryan Bedder / Getty Images

“Right now the US is the biggest YouTube market for our sport. So it tells you about the connection we're having through [those] vehicles.

“Drive to Survive has become a centerpiece in the digital efforts. A lot of efforts are going on with digital, but that certainly is the centerpiece. It has been an incredibly important, valuable franchise for us.”

Many competitions, in motorsport and beyond, have attempted to emulate this success, but Carey doesn’t believe that would be right for MotoGP.

“You should look for opportunities,” the American insisted. “Realistically, everybody saw Drive to Survive and then everybody tried to do it. Golf tried to do their Full Swing, tennis tried to do Break Point – everybody.

“Usually, you can't just copy something. I think we learned that at Fox with American Idol. American Idol sort of captured the world's imagination, and there were shows that came behind and did well, but there was only one American Idol that really did that.

“I think generally you can't go out and do the same thing. You've got to find ways to use opportunities, use personalities, use digital platforms, develop great partners.

“A partner in Formula 1 like Apple, I think this is where Apple has brought a whole new perspective to how you broadcast and connect with fans. So I think that type of opportunity, you've got to then see what you can do with it, how you develop it.

“They have to follow their own path and find their own opportunities. The Formula 1 movie was a great opportunity for that, but you can't just go out and do a MotoGP movie. That may not be the right opportunity.

“But there may be something else – there will be something else. It's probably not just doing the same things you did, it's finding those opportunities, finding those personalities.”

Sports.title: Horner reveals Red Bull call to thank him for F1 engine project after maiden win
Sports.content:
Christian Horner has revealed Red Bull shareholders called him on the back of the Red Bull Ford Powertrains engine’s maiden Formula 1 victory in Malaysia.

Horner joined the Milton Keynes-based squad as its team principal when the brand acquired the Jaguar outfit ahead of the 2005 season, but was sacked and replaced by Laurent Mekies in July 2025.

Across two decades at the helm of the team, Horner not only led it to eight drivers’ and six constructors’ titles but also oversaw its transition from an engine customer into a power unit manufacturer, following Honda’s exit from F1 at the end of the 2021 season.

Red Bull was able to keep using the Japanese powertrains until last year; its own power unit, designed in collaboration with Ford, debuted in 2026.

The Red Bull engine clinched its first victory at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, courtesy of Max Verstappen, with the Dutchman making it back-to-back wins one week later in Singapore.

“We managed to do it on the chassis side and then the challenge came, could we do it on the engine side?” Horner related in a conference at Autosport Business Exchange in New York.

“You know, we needed to have an engine after Honda announced their withdrawal in 2020. So we created this start-up company, Red Bull Powertrains, with the same philosophy of attracting the talent, giving people a chance, giving people the opportunity, and then empowering them and encouraging them to push the boundaries.

“I've been super proud to see how that engine has developed and delivered this year.”

Christian Horner Photo by: Autosport

Horner’s contribution was acknowledged by the brand itself, as he received the aforementioned phone call from its leaders.

“It was an appreciated gesture, seeing that engine and knowing what went into it, you know, the sweat and tears along the way,” the Briton continued.

“For all the men and women involved, it was an incredible, incredible achievement. And their 16th attempt to win a grand prix, which is very hard at the best of times.

“I was very grateful to both the shareholders who reached out, and [Red Bull CEO] Oliver Mintzlaff who reached out to thank me as well. It was quite a different call than I had from him 15 months earlier.”

Horner is referring to the phone call that led to his dismissal, as his position had become increasingly precarious following Red Bull cofounder Dietrich Mateschitz’s death.

Errol Barnett and Christian Horner Photo by: Bryan Bedder / Getty Images

Horner did not have the Verstappen camp on his side and was losing the support of the Yoovidhya family – Chalerm Yoovidhya is a majority owner of the company – but still describes the news as “pretty abrupt and quite brutal”.

“I felt that things were changing,” he added. “Nothing stays the same forever, and after the founder, Dietrich Mateschitz, sadly passed at the end of ‘22, it was always going to be the case that the company was going to evolve and was going to change.

“Dietrich, he was Red Bull, he was the power behind it, he made all the big decisions. And suddenly, obviously, trying to replace somebody like that is impossible.

“Inevitably, as the group evolved and took on that challenge, it was just different. There was a drive to bring more control back into the head office, and that sat differently from the autonomy that we'd enjoyed at Red Bull Racing and in Milton Keynes.

“It was a different path that essentially what we were on, and you could feel that that was changing. It wasn't that it was right or wrong, it was just different. And I didn't feel, certainly, that it was what had allowed us to achieve so much success over the years.

“So, inevitably, it came to an end.”

Sports.title: FIA set to close F1 cost cap loophole with new rules
Sports.content:
The FIA’s World Motor Sport Council has approved new regulations to prevent teams’ non-F1 staff from working on Formula 1 projects.

F1's governing body has likely intervened because some had managed to take advantage of staff and facilities officially allocated to other activities to bypass the budget cap.

This decision will prevent an imbalance between teams with other activities and those with no other programmes other than grand prix racing, but will also radically alter the way F1 squads operate. Those who are an integral part of automotive giants will have to function entirely independently of their parent companies.

The aim of the five new articles in the 2027 operational regulations is clear: to close a loophole which allows for an already limited transfer of know-how between the F1 team and the company’s other business units, therefore concealing spending within programmes such as product development, WEC, Formula E or sailing.

Until now, it was possible to split an engineer’s expertise between two different activities, declaring which part of his role was dedicated to F1 and which to the other programme, attributing only a percentage to the budget cap.

The FIA is now going much further by genuinely separating F1 from all other activities, with significant restrictions being imposed on the use of technological assets (simulators, wind tunnels, test benches, data centres, IT systems).

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

These new segregation measures mean non-F1 staff will be barred from entering the F1 factory and those working on grand prix activities won’t be allowed to visit colleagues in other divisions.

The transfer of staff from F1 to another sector can no longer be direct, requiring a new contract detailing their new duties; their company badge and email will be disabled. An employee who leaves the team won’t be able to return until at least one year has passed.

If those working on non-F1 programmes are to switch to the F1 squad, they will also have to undergo a three-month gardening period during which they will not be allowed to engage in any company activities.

The new rule is expected to lead to an increase in staff numbers and costs, as those managing non-F1 programmes turn to external candidates and peripheral projects forgo synergies and opportunities for collaboration.

Sports.title: Norris promises to make "better decisions" following fresh talks over Singapore GP clash
Sports.content:
Formula 1 world champion Lando Norris has conceded he needs to make "better decisions" as McLaren aims to draw a line under his clash with team-mate Oscar Piastri in Singapore.

Norris drew the ire of his bosses for colliding into Piastri during their battle for fourth on the final lap of the Marina Bay sprint race, costing eight points and going against McLaren's principles.

Team boss Andrea Stella revealed that the Woking outfit would hold further talks back at HQ and it is understood those talks happened last week.

McLaren is now keen to move on from the incident as Norris, who finished the sprint in eighth with Piastri retiring, apologised for his error of judgement.

“I take responsibility for my mistakes, and I learn from them," Norris was quoted in the team's preview for this weekend's United States Grand Prix.

"This team is my motivation every weekend, and my aim is to repay the hard work everyone puts in by improving, making better decisions, and representing the team in the best possible way.”

Lando Norris, McLaren, Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

The 26-year-old's clash with Piastri added to what had been a tough triple-header for McLaren, who failed to score a podium and had no answer for the upgraded Red Bull.

Red Bull took back-to-back wins via Max Verstappen in Malaysia and Singapore - Mercedes' George Russell won in Azerbaijan - and is now only seven points behind third-placed McLaren with six rounds remaining.

Stella, whose squad has won the last two constructors' titles, said: "After a difficult triple-header, we take the lessons learned from both our performance and execution and put them into action.

"In F1, success is never guaranteed – so our response is to keep building, keep developing, and keep pushing forward together as one team."

McLaren brings latest round of upgrades after performance falls flat

McLaren had brought its own upgrades to the MCL40 too, and while it was left confused by its lack of performance in Malaysia, Singapore further underlined that while its own updates appear to work as intended, it had simply been out-developed by Red Bull.

Second-placed Ferrari, meanwhile, was also extremely strong on the high-downforce Marina Bay Street Circuit, and runaway leader Mercedes has also added performance to its car.

McLaren is now bringing its latest round of relatively minor upgrades this weekend, largely focused on the front of the car, as it hopes Austin will suit the MCL40 better. It has also applied further tweaks to make its drivers feel more confident under braking.

"We’re bringing a modest selection of upgrades for this event, aimed at improving some braking reliability and performance issues," said chief designer Rob Marshall.

"We also have some small floor changes to test. We have all seen how difficult it is to predict the relative performance of the top teams over the last five or six races. Obviously, there are many factors in play here: cars being upgraded, cars suiting and drivers liking certain circuits among other factors.

"The last few races have not been great for us, but I think we’re getting stronger again and Austin is probably a better circuit for our car."

Sports.title: FIA expects F1 races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi to run as planned
Sports.content:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem is confident that the Formula 1 races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead, amid the current tensions in the Middle East.

Due to the conflict between the United States-Israel and Iran, the races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled earlier this year, although the Bahraini organisers effectively moved its postponed grand prix to Malaysia. Ship attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, currently contested by both sides as oil exports have slowed dramatically, have continued.

Further conflict has arisen between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen; a missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport claimed the lives of 13 people. The airport has recently reopened with a limited service following the attacks, and the UK has recently pledged to support Saudi Arabia with fighter jets to defend from further Houthi assaults.

The proximity of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates to the current areas of conflict has meant that the two season-ending races in the Middle East were in doubt, although F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali stated some weeks ago that retaining the races remained the championship's Plan A - with a back-up plan to host the season finale at Imola should tensions continue to escalate.

Talks over the potential cancellation of both races have dwindled in recent weeks, and the championship looks set to retain both Qatar and Abu Dhabi races. In MotoGP, teams have been told that the rescheduled Qatar round will be going ahead in November.

Read Also: MotoGP MotoGP teams told Qatar Grand Prix expected to go ahead in November

Speaking to selected media, including Autosport, Ben Sulayem stated that he feels "secure" about the races for the time being, explaining that he would not leave his family residing in the Emirates if he felt it was unsafe to do so.

"They're fine. One thing I would say, I have my children there - you think I would leave them there, and I'm here now with you?" Ben Sulayem said.

F1 cars lined up at the start of the race Photo by: Nicolas Economou / NurPhoto via Getty Images

"You have to be sensible in this and saying, 'are we going to have an issue?' What you read in the media is actually different than we have there. You know, we read and we see the TV, we don't have that, really. Otherwise, why will I stay there, you know? Why would I leave my family?

"But does this say that there is nothing going to happen? I cannot predict with this. I can only tell you today that there is nothing and the two races are going to happen.

"I am happy [for FIA staff to go there]. Listen, I don't think the FIA staff would be more important to me than myself and my family, you know, but if I am there, it means I feel secure about it.

"But we don't know for the time being. As I said, the Dakar [Rally in Saudi Arabia], if we hear anything from them, we will adjust. When I say them is the Federation of Motorsport in Saudi Arabia, we will adjust to that and we will help.

"Like when we helped with Bahrain, when the request was there to not organise the event in Saudi Arabia, then there was another call from the Crown Prince of Bahrain to move it to Malaysia. The relationship was there and it's sending a message that, like with all of this, we still will have motorsport."

Ben Sulayem added that the FIA had contingency measures in place in case of any travel disruption, such as leaning on local ASNs for any volunteers and officials to help facilitate the running of the events.

He used the example of the Lebanese round of the FIA Middle East Rally Championship, which ultimately rebooted this year's series. This was staffed by officials from Cyprus, Greece, and Jordan - before the Cypriot round concluded this year's championship when the Saudi Arabian round was cancelled.

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, FIA President, Stefano Domenicali, Formula 1 President and CEO Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

"Of course, the FIA is always ready. I told them to have another team ready from the FIA if there was nothing going on. But maybe some of the governments say, you cannot travel - so what do we do?" Ben Sulayem said.

"If everybody is there and then the teams are there and the FOM is running it and suddenly we say, 'oh, we cannot have our race director, we cannot have our stewards.' You have to be ready, and you have to have another team ready in case.

"We have also the common sense here that we will never take our staff or drivers or any officials to a place where we feel it is risky."

Ben Sulayem added that the prospect of the 2027 Dakar Rally was uncertain, but suggested that it could be moved to Morocco if it is unable to host the race in Saudi Arabia.

Sports.title: Verstappen would have won Singapore GP in a Ferrari, says Hadjar: ‘It was the fastest car’ | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen’s Singapore Grand Prix victory would have been even more dominant victory if he had been driving for Ferrari, according to his team mate.

“I don’t think we have the fastest car,” said Isack Hadjar ahead of this weekend’s race in Austin.

His team mate Verstappen has won the last two grands prix in a row. He beat Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc by seven seconds in Singapore.

However Hadjar believes his team mate is getting more from his car than Ferrari’s drivers are from theirs.

“The car is still very hard to drive,” he explained. “In Malaysia it was dominant but I don’t think in Singapore it was the fastest car. That’s what I believe.

“I think if you put Max in the Ferrari he would have won the race with more margin so that’s my opinion. In Singapore I think [the Ferrari] was the fastest car.”

Verstappen beat Charles Leclerc to pole position by five hundredths of a second. Lewis Hamilton, who was quickest in Q1 and Q2, was another seven hundredths of a second behind in the other Ferrari.

Hadjar finished 10th in Singapore after starting from the pit lane due to a penalty for replacing a failed power unit. He is eager to have a more competitive weekend in Austin.

“It was one of those weekends where you get a failure in each session, so you learn from it and we just move on,” he said. “I’m happy to be here in Texas. I like that track and the car’s been, performance-wise, working really well this last couple of weekends.

“We’re confident as a team, but of course we are aware of the upgrades in the other garages so we’re still down to earth. We still know our weaknesses on the car, we’re still working on it.

“So I just want to go out there and have another clean one because the last two weekends have been very frustrating considering the car I have been given.”

Sports.title: FIA’s new Formula 1 Race Operations Centre opens at FOM’s Biggin Hill base | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA is using Formula 1’s base at Biggin Hill in the UK as the site of its new Race Operations Centre.

Biggin Hill is the home of F1’s broadcasting operations, where raw footage from the hundreds of camera operators which cover every session are combined into the video feeds seen by millions of viewers worldwide.

The governing body of motorsport announced the opening of the new facility which will allow its officials to manage events around the world without being present in person.

A key part of the facility’s functions will involve providing support to race control and stewards on decisions during sessions. It will assist in detecting when drivers have jumped the start or lined up incorrectly on the grid, exceeded track limits or committed offences in the pit lane.

The ROC will also use new artificial intelligence systems to automate processes and detect incidents.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem and Formula 1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali were among those who attended the formal inauguration of the new facility.

“As the championship grows globally, it is vital that we continue to invest in the people, technology and infrastructure that underpin world-class race operations,” said Ben Sulayen. “This state-of-the-art facility will strengthen our ability to support accurate, consistent and efficient decision-making, ensuring that our sport continues to operate at the highest possible standards.”

Sports.title: “I’ll probably need to order a new spine” – Verstappen braced for bumpy weekend at COTA | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen expects a rough ride from the notorious bumps at the Circuit of the Americas this weekend.

The track in Austin, Texas has a reputation for being one of the bumpiest on the calendar. The race promoters have attempts to ease the bumps on several occasions and F1’s latest generation of cars are supposed to offer a less harsh ride than the ‘ground effect’ designs used last year.

However after watching footage of the World Endurance Championship round at COTA last month (below), Verstappen expects a tough time this weekend.

“From what I saw in WEC, the track is incredibly bumpy,” he said. “Oh my God, yeah, I’ll probably need to order a new spine, I think, after the weekend. I’ll become like RoboCop. That’s a new challenge for everyone, to deal with those bumps.”

Red Bull go into this weekend’s race as the favourites to win, having performed strongly across the three previous rounds. Verstappen has taken two grand prix wins, one sprint race win and second place in a grand prix over that time.

However he says the different characteristics of the upcoming circuits makes it unclear how competitive they will be.

“I don’t want to say now that I will be in the fight in Austin,” said Verstappen. “The last few weekends have been great.

“But I just take it race by race and once we are in Austin, then we’ll see how it will go there. It’s again a very different track.”

“From there we have to go to Mexico [which is] high altitude, everything will run super-hot,” he added. “We need to see how the engine is going to perform in that altitude, how the car is behaving, because it’s very different.

“So there are so many different things that you can get right or wrong in those races, but we’ll see.”

Sports.title: Formula 1’s move to shorter grands prix in 2027 will not be permanent | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 will reinstate full grand prix distances in 2028 after shortening the races this year, the FIA has confirmed.

The championship announced last month it will cut 15 kilometres from the standard grand prix distance next year as a result of the new fuel flow limits which will come into force. Shortening the grand prix distances will reduce the number of components teams need to redesign next year.

The shortened distance of 290 kilometres will apply for all grands prix except Monaco, which has run to a shorter distance of 260km for many years and will continue to.

However the first edition of the 2027 Formula 1 Sporting Regulations published by the FIA notes the previous distance will apply again from 2028. “The distance of the race [i.e. grand prix], from the start signal referred to in Article B5.7.2 to the end-of-session signal referred to in Article B5.16.1, shall be equal to the least number of complete laps which exceed a distance of 305km,” it states.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Budget cap not to blame for lack of winning teams in F1 | Brief
Sports.content:
This week’s poll asks whether Formula 1 needs to rethink its budget cap as the series’ top four team have pulled further away from their rivals this year.

But reader @Skydiverian suggests it might not be realistic to expect F1 to regularly have more than four race-winning teams:

Four competitive teams has happened before but it’s still not great and the problem is as it always is, money. And I’d like to see more teams in a season have a realistic shot of winning races. It’s unfortunate that the stats are not on my side.

Pretty much since the late 80s the problem has been that the best teams could throw more money at the problem to fix it. Now, teams that are significantly behind can’t throw more money at the problem to catch-up due to the cost cap, rather than simply not having the money in the first place as was common in the 80s. (This season is interesting. It seems that Mercedes blew most of it’s cap early to get and maintain their advantage, whereas Red Bull didn’t and that’s in part why Max has had a better car the last two races. But it’s not like Williams or Aston Martin can fix their problems by spending more money to fix the deficit).

The problem is that ultimately there’s no easy fix, but spending millions to be the so-called best of the rest basically seems pointless if there is a very unlikely chance of a team outside of the top four having a realistic shot at the podium or even a win. And that’s always been a problem going back decades.

Some number crunching by looking at the history books: the 500th race was 1990 Australia, 1,100th being Vegas 2023. In those 600 races I’ve found six that were won by drivers driving for teams who finished outside the top four in the constructors championship.

That’s six of 600 races over 33 years where we had a winner driving for a team who finished outside the top 4 in that years constructors championship, 1% of all races. Seven if you count Johnny Herbert’s win at the Nurburgring which to me was a genuine surprise at the time. To me those stats aren’t good enough.

Whether that’s the fault of teams with no money, teams with too much money or teams with a cash limit so they can’t design their way out is up for debate. But my point is that I’d like to see more teams have a reasonable chance of winning. F1 has never really had that and will continue not to unless something changes (maybe by letting teams further down have a bigger budget the following season rather than just more CFD time).

I’d rather that at least 70% of drivers have a realistic chance of winning, ideally 100% of teams. It’s the reason I preferred IndyCar before Alex Palou showed up, results were unpredictable and smaller teams have a chance of getting a win or two. That’s just so rare in F1 and the current cost cap rules will continue to make unlikely.

@Skydiverian

Sports.title: Early coronation for Antonelli? Five talking points for the United States Grand Prix | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli could win the world championship this weekend in only his second year as a Formula 1 driver. Here are the talking points for the United States Grand Prix.

Will Antonelli clinch the title?

The odds are stacked heavily in favour of Mercedes’ new star clinching the title at some point, but most likely not this weekend. That said it is not beyond the realm of possibility team mate George Russell could have another poor weekend and come away point-less while Antonelli takes his ninth victory of the season, putting him over the line.

The title has been won at this track twice before, and both times it was by a Mercedes driver: Lewis Hamilton won the championship there in 2015 and 2019. But regardless of whether Antonelli does clinch the title this weekend it is clearly a matter of ‘when’ not ‘if’.

Verstappen dominating again?

The driver most likely to delay Antonelli’s championship celebrations is not his team mate but Max Verstappen. Red Bull have made a breakthrough with their RB22 and as well as winning the last two grands prix plus a sprint race, Verstappen could have taken victory in Baku as well with better luck.

He arrives at this weekend’s race looking like the driver to beat, with every indication he could dominate the final rounds of the season, setting himself up for a shot at the title next year.

McLaren’s driver headache

McLaren arrive in Austin in a curiously similar situation to last year: a clash between their drivers at the previous race in Singapore has created an obvious tension. What’s more, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri’s collision during the sprint race in Singapore was more costly than the one they had in the grand prix 12 months ago.

Norris’s radio messages during the grand prix gave the distinct impression he was looking for ways to make amends, having eventually accepted he was the one at fault for their collision. But above all the team will be anxious to avoid a repeat of the first-corner collision which wrecked their sprint race at the circuit 12 months ago. Particularly as a resurgent Red Bull are poised to relegate the reigning constructors’ champions to fourth place in the standings.

US teams’ driver decisions

Of the two teams competing in their home event this weekend, one has settled its driver plans for 2027. Haas has announced Rafael Camara as the replacement for Esteban Ocon, whose Formula 1 future is in serious doubt as few likely alternatives remain for next year.

Could Cadillac be one of them? F1’s new American team is yet to confirm its plans for next year. However its hopes IndyCar star Colton Herta would take Formula 2 by storm and make himself an obvious candidate for promotion have been dashed: he lies 19th in the standings, 181 points behind fellow rookie and championship leader Camara.

Are Colapinto’s die-hards paying attention?

Last week Franco Colapinto spoke out in criticism of the element of his fanbase which has sent vile abuse to his rival drivers, team members and FIA officials since he made his F1 debut this year. The Alpine driver told those attacking others in his name that they are not helping his cause in F1.

Will they take his words on board? We’ll get an indication the next time he is involved in any kind of incident on-track – however slight it may be.

Are you going to the United States Grand Prix?
