Djiby Sow, Senior Researcher, ISS Regional Office for West Africa and the Sahel

World.title: South Africa: Black Market Weight-Loss Drug Sellers Are Moving Fast. South Africa's Regulators Are Struggling To Keep Up
World.content:
Why is South Africa struggling to stop the sellers of illegal weight-loss injections, and how can consumers tell whether the medicines they're buying are safe?

South African regulators have won an important court battle against a pharmacy making its own versions of popular weight-loss injections. But illegal and experimental drugs are still being sold openly, while new rules to crack down on the trade are months away. Why is the country struggling to stop the sellers — and how can consumers tell whether the medicines they're buying are safe?

South African pharmacies are allowed to make up medicines for patients with specific needs. But some are producing weight-loss injections in large quantities without the licences required to manufacture medicines.

In June, the Gauteng High Court ordered Tshwane-based compounding pharmacy iDexis to stop producing medicines containing semaglutide, the substance that makes Ozempic work.

Yet experimental weight-loss drugs such as retatrutide, which are still being studied and haven't been approved for sale anywhere in the world, are still being sold openly in South Africa.

Regulators say clearer rules for pharmacies that make their own medicines are on the way, but these are only expected by February or March 2027. The pharmaceutical industry warns that the delay gives illegal sellers more time to operate.

Australia has banned pharmacy compounding of weight-loss jabs, citing such drugs as "potentially unsafe and dangerous". So why are South African so-called compounding pharmacies still making their own versions of blockbuster weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro , and selling them to the public?

The reality is that such activity is illegal in South Africa as well, at least in instances where the pharmacies make up copycat weight-loss jabs — which dampen appetite and make people feel full for longer — in large quantities, or use unregistered or illegally imported ingredients to make them.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

But as demand has soared, some pharmacies have turned the niche practice of compounding into a lucrative business. In June, the Gauteng High Court ordered iDexis, a compounding pharmacy in Tshwane, to stop producing medicine containing semaglutide — the active ingredient of Ozempic — after large quantities of compounded weight-loss jabs had been confiscated on its premises.

The court order was an important legal victory for the country's regulators, including the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (Sahpra), Stavros Nicolaou , chairperson of the Pharmaceutical Task Group , an umbrella organisation for the pharmaceutical industry in South Africa, said during a panel discussion held in Sandton last week.

But he said the momentum built by the court order could be lost if Sahpra and the South African Pharmacy Council (SAPC) don't follow up on it quickly with clearer guidelines for compounding pharmacies about what they can, and cannot legally do. "You can go and win these court cases, and have people on the back foot, but all of that can unravel because we're just not acting swiftly enough as a country," he said.

Illegal drugs in plain sight

The panel gathered representatives from Sahpra and the SAPC, as well as the police service, border control, revenue service and the pharmaceutical industry, to explain to the public how they are working together to stop the trade in fake drugs.

Sahpra says it has received around 600 complaints so far this financial year relating to illegitimate and fake medicines being sold through informal supply chains, reaching the public via online portals, gyms, or even local hairdressers.

"We are worried that the scourge is getting out of control," said Daphne Fafudi , the body's head of regulatory compliance. And it's the public that can pay the ultimate price, she added. "People do die, and it doesn't even come to our attention," she said.

Some fake or illegitimate drugs are sold covertly. Others are traded in plain sight. One of them is retatrutide , a weight-loss injection that is still being tested in studies and therefore hasn't been licensed for sale by a drug regulatory anywhere in the world. Yet, it is sold "openly and brazenly" around the world, including in South Africa, said Nicolaou.

In the July episode of Bhekisisa 's TV programme, Health Beat, we reported how a Johannesburg woman's doctor sold her retatrutide, telling her it's safe because he "had it tested", while making her sign a waiver to release him of any responsibility for what might go wrong .

Earlier this year, a man reportedly died in the United States after taking injections sold as retatrutide on the black market — although the British Medical Journal said the evidence for the drug causing the fatality was "less clear cut" than media reporting suggested.

Nicolaou urged the police service and the Hawks to make an example of those who sell retatrutide in South Africa, as a deterrent to others. "The public needs to know that our enforcement agencies are actually enforcing the law," he told the meeting last week.

Vincent Tlala , CEO of the SAPC , said revised guidelines for compounding pharmacies were underway, a process Sahpra is leading, with input from the SAPC. However, Tlala said, these were not expected to be ready until February or March next year.

According to Nicolaou, this is too late. "The regulations are taking too long," he says. Regulators in other countries have introduced bans and restrictions on compounding pharmacies specifically for weight-loss jabs, to prevent the kind of products that have flooded South Africa. "Why are we not doing the same thing?"

What South African law says about compounding

Compounding medicines is lawful in South Africa, but only under specific conditions . Compounding requires a healthcare professional's prescription, generally for a formulation that is not available as a registered medicine — for instance, if a patient requires a medication as an oral liquid that is only normally sold as a pill.

As for compounding in bulk, the law says that a pharmacy may prepare stock in advance if they can show that patients regularly need the medicine — such as repeat prescriptions for the same person.

But some pharmacies produce large quantities without that evidence, Sahpra chief executive Boitumelo Semete-Makokotlela told Bhekisisa. This means "you're not compounding, you are manufacturing", which requires a good manufacturing practice licence that compounding pharmacies do not hold.

A good manufacturing practice licence shows that a company has met the safety and quality standards required to manufacture medicines.

A second concern is where ingredients come from. Active pharmaceutical ingredients — the substances in medicines that make them work — must be registered in South Africa and imported by a licensed entity, says Semete-Makokotlela. A pharmacy's operational licence does not authorise it to import unregistered ingredients, she says, yet some have arrived in travellers' luggage.

Another loophole that needs to be closed, Semete-Makokotlela notes, is where people sell experimental drugs (meds still being studied) or medicinal products directly to the public that are authorised for "research purposes" only. This includes some peptide products that are neither registered medicines nor experimental drugs in formal trials (like retatrutide), yet are still widely bought and sold as lifestyle or wellness drugs to do things like lower inflammation and boost energy.

Peptides are short chains of amino acids — small building blocks that the body uses to make proteins. Insulin is a peptide , as is semaglutide , the active ingredient in Ozempic. Both are registered medicines in South Africa.

However, there are other peptides, such as BPC-157 , which are being sold online and in gyms as solutions to specific health problems, such as tissue repair. These peptides aren't technically medicines, nor are they actively being studied in drug trials. Yet, they are sold as healthcare products, without evidence that they are safe or effective at treating humans.

Then there is the battle for public opinion, which is proving to be another hurdle. Semete-Makokotlela admits regulators are "on the back foot" when consumers see people losing weight while official warnings struggle to compete.

Close 

The answer, she believes, includes offering people registered alternatives at different prices — including cheaper generics — and working with healthcare professionals to steer patients towards safe, registered medicines.

South Africa's first generic weight-loss drug, containing semaglutide, hit the shelves in August .

How the public can keep safe

During the panel discussion, South African Revenue Service official Gene Ravele called the lack of coordination between enforcement agencies "the number one problem that organised crime is taking advantage of", and that this is also true for counterfeit and illegitimate drugs.

Border Management Authority head Nakampe Masiapato added that police detectives and prosecutors are often generalists, ill-equipped for specialised pharmaceutical cases. "They have no idea what this is about," he said.

For consumers, the advice from regulators is to use authorised channels and check that medicines are registered. Common signs that a drug is not legitimate is that it has unusual or blank packaging, no printed expiry date on the box or container, or that it doesn't have a normal insert detailing how to take it and the common side effects. Broken or dented packaging is another big 'tell', the Sandton meeting heard last week.

The bottom line is that a product's online availability, or a seller's claim that it is equivalent to a registered medicine, is not proof that it has been assessed or approved, said Fafudi. "If you cannot trust the source, do not trust the medicine."

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 22, 2026
World.content:
Cameroon Train Disaster Survivors Still Await Justice 10 Years Later

Ten years after Cameroon's deadliest rail disaster killed 79 people and injured more than 500, survivors are still dealing with serious injuries, while some victims have not received compensation and legal proceedings remain unresolved. The Camrail train derailed near Eseka on 21 October 2016 while travelling from Yaoundé to Douala. An investigation found that it was travelling at 96km/h in a section with a 40km/h speed limit. Overloading, defective brakes and the addition of extra carriages also contributed to the crash. Survivors continue to suffer from chronic pain and lasting disabilities. In 2018, Camrail and 11 employees were convicted of involuntary manslaughter and causing unintentional injuries. The company's former managing director received a suspended sentence, while other officials were also given suspended sentences. The train driver was sentenced to five years in prison. However, Camrail appealed the ruling, and the appeal has yet to be heard. Victims' lawyers say compensation has been inadequate, with some payments still outstanding.

Burkina Faso Restores Death Penalty Amid Crackdown on Critics

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Burkina Faso's unelected parliament has unanimously adopted a new penal code restoring the death penalty for offences including high treason, terrorism, espionage, parricide and importing expired or prohibited products. The death penalty for ordinary crimes was abolished in 2018. Human Rights Watch warns that reinstating capital punishment could further threaten civil liberties under the military junta, which took power in a 2022 coup. Authorities have restricted media outlets, suspended civil society organisations and unions, and targeted critics through arrests and enforced disappearances. The government said that the measure will help combat terrorism. Rights advocates argue that weaknesses in the justice system increase the risk of wrongful convictions and irreversible injustice.

Nearly 200,000 Zimbabweans Returned From South Africa

Nearly 200,000 Zimbabweans have returned home from South Africa amid anti-migrant protests and attacks targeting foreign nationals, according to the government. Cabinet was told that 197,294 people had returned, including 42,553 repatriated through government assistance and 154,741 who returned independently. The government deployed buses to collect stranded nationals, including those in Cape Town. The protests, involving groups such as Operation Dudula and March and March, have targeted Zimbabweans and other African migrants. Authorities said the number of returnees has declined but are continuing to monitor the situation. Zimbabwe is also screening deportees arriving from South Africa, including 700 people received from the Lindela Repatriation Centre.

Gambia to Compensate Victims With Proceeds From Jammeh's US Mansion

The Gambia's Reparations Commission has received more than US$2.57 million from the sale of a Maryland mansion belonging to former president Yahya Jammeh. The funds will be used to compensate victims of abuses committed during his more than two decades in power. US authorities secured the right to sell the property in 2022, arguing that it had been acquired using criminal proceeds and misappropriated public funds. Jammeh seized power in a 1994 coup and was accused of overseeing torture, forced disappearances, rape and extrajudicial killings. He lost the 2016 election to Adama Barrow but initially refused to step down. He eventually left office in 2017 and went into exile in Equatorial Guinea. A national inquiry found that he had amassed hundreds of properties and misappropriated more than US$300 million.

Latin American Drug Cartels Expand Operations Across Africa

Latin American drug trafficking organizations are expanding into Africa, using the continent as a transshipment point for cocaine and as a new production base for methamphetamine. Global demand is rising, and enforcement efforts are harder to maintain in the Americas, so criminal groups have tried to link up with African networks. Methamphetamine labs have been found in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, and Mozambique. It is still common for cocaine to travel through West Africa on its way to Europe. They generate revenue by engaging in money laundering and drug trafficking. They achieve this by capitalizing on corruption, porous borders, and a scarcity of police officers. Nevertheless, the drug trade is gaining popularity, which is a cause for concern as it undermines government institutions and results in a rise in crime, addiction, and violence. The authorities have increased the number of arrests and seizures. Experts warn that criminal networks will continue to thrive where oversight and law enforcement remain weak.

Close 

Kagame Urges Rwanda's Youth to Put Health Before Ambitions

Rwandan President Paul Kagame has called on the youth to prioritise their health and well-being as they chase their personal and professional aspirations. Speaking at a youth engagement event at BK Arena on October 21, he stressed the importance of developing healthy habits from childhood. Kagame warned against alcohol and drug abuse, saying such behaviours can worsen personal difficulties rather than solve them. He also encouraged young people to exercise, continue learning, work hard and make responsible decisions. He called on them to challenge harmful practices in their communities instead of allowing them to become normalised. Kagame said young people should recognise their potential, distinguish right from wrong and take responsibility for shaping their futures.

World.title: South Africa: Government Investigates Gastrointestinal Illness Cases in the Eastern Cape
World.content:
Government has launched an investigation into reported cases of gastrointestinal illness affecting 111 people at Rhodes University in Makhanda and 23 inmates at St Albans Correctional Centre in Nelson Mandela Bay.

The investigation was announced in a joint statement by the Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS), the Eastern Cape Provincial Government, Makana Local Municipality and Nelson Mandela Bay Metropolitan Municipality.

The investigation follows reports of individuals in the two municipalities receiving treatment at various healthcare facilities for symptoms including severe abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting and dehydration.

The joint statement explained that DWS received a media alert about gastrointestinal illnesses reported by Rhodes University, prompting the activation of a response team involving the provincial Department of Health and the DWS regional offices.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A multi-stakeholder technical team has since been established to investigate the source of the illnesses and contain their spread.

The team comprises the DWS, provincial departments of Health and Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs, Sarah Baartman District Municipality, Makana Local Municipality, Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD), Amatola Water and Rhodes University.

An intergovernmental meeting was held on Wednesday evening, led by Water and Sanitation Minister Pemmy Majodina and Eastern Cape Premier Oscar Mabuyane, alongside Makana Executive Mayor Yandiswa Vara and Nelson Mandela Bay Executive Mayor Babalwa Lobishe.

"The meeting received reports from the technical team covering information on the number and location of gastrointestinal illness cases, the samples taken by the NICD and water quality tests conducted by the DWS as well as additional urgent measures being implemented to protect communities," the statement read.

The technical team collected water samples from various water sources in Makana, including Rhodes University's internal water storage and distribution system, the municipal distribution network and the water treatment works.

At St Albans Correctional Centre, samples were collected from the elevated water storage tower through which the facility receives potable water from the Nelson Mandela Bay municipal supply system.

"Preliminary findings indicate that the spread is currently concentrated within the university and the Saint Albans Prison. Initial test results indicate that the contamination is within the university's water distribution system and within the prison's water distribution system, and not within the municipal water distribution systems.

Close 

"Laboratory test results of all the samples taken are still pending and will be communicated as soon as they become available," the statement said.

Government has urged residents who develop symptoms of gastrointestinal illness to seek medical attention early and report suspected cases to their nearest healthcare facility or local health authority.

"Early reporting protects not only individuals and families but also enables health authorities to respond quickly and prevent further spread."

Communities have also been urged to observe good hygiene practices, including washing hands after using the toilet and before handling food.

Earlier this week, the DWS Minister announced the establishment of a multi-pronged response team after 408 cases of gastrointestinal illness were reported at Bronkhorstspruit in the City of Tshwane (CoT) Municipality.

World.title: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night.

The hourlong showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932.

The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall.

Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate.

SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Debate opens with candidates confronted over personal controversies

The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates.

Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills.

"Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric."

Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse.

Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation.

FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO âNOT THAT INFORMEDâ: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS

"I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part."

Marshall says 'President Trump is not always right'

Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week.

"And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd.

Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda.

"No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump.

Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports.

"Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right."

Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate.

Both candidates say there are 'two genders'

The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are.

"There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls."

"There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded.

TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR

The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports.

Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females.

"I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight."

Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology."

Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people.

Hamilton calls AI an 'existential threat' â but can't name regulations he'd support

Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons.

"We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said.

But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer.

"You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers.

Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement.

Hamilton pushed back sharply.

"This is an existential â potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best."

BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH

Hamilton calls Biden's border policies a 'disaster'

Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle."

The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed.

"The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders."

"I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle."

World.title: Supreme Court Justice Kagan warns some conservative rulings have been 'destructive of our democracy'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan suggested Tuesday that some recent decisions by her conservative colleagues have undermined democracy, while admitting at times they had also pushed back against the Trump administration.

Kagan took part in a discussion on recent U.S. Supreme Court decisions while speaking at Catholic University's Columbus School of Law. She specifically took issue with cases like Louisiana v. Callais, which ruled in a 6-3 decision that race-based gerrymandering of congressional districts was unconstitutional.

In her dissent, Kagan called the decision the "latest chapter in the majority's now-completed demolition of the Voting Rights Act" and she continued to criticize election and campaign finance decisions made by the court.

KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS

"Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said, according to NBC News.

She went on to warn that decisions that undermined voters' ability to choose their candidates were "very destructive of our democracy."

"I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn't work as well as it should," Kagan said.

SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES

She also criticized the conservative view of originalism in the Supreme Court, calling it "misconceived" and "not a very good match with the Constitution we have."

Kagan claimed that these and other decisions have contributed to the country becoming more "polarized," particularly around campaign finance.

"I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they're right," she said.

CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION

However, Kagan stopped short of accusing the court of being beholden to President Donald Trump, pointing out several cases where even conservative justices "definitely pushed back" on his agenda. Trump nominated three of the current justices on the court in Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett.

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Heritage Foundation Senior Legal Fellow of Courts and the Constitution Zack Smith denounced Kagan and what he characterized as far-left politicians' efforts to delegitimize SCOTUS decisions.

"The job of the Court is not to play politics with its decisions. Instead, its job is to faithfully apply the Constitution and other laws as they are written. Justice Kagan has disagreed with the majority of her colleagues in some of those decisions, but that doesn't mean they are illegitimate or even wrongly decided," Smith said.

World.title: RILEY GAINES: Call Her Daddy's advice is a dangerous recipe for lifelong regret
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

In a viral exchange this week, Call Her Daddy host Alex Cooper and actress Sophia Bush offered young women a familiar piece of relationship advice: If you're questioning whether to leave your marriage because you fear you won't find someone better, the answer is always yes.

Bush went further, suggesting that the fear of being too old or unreasonable for wanting more is a product of the patriarchy.

Cooper built her brand largely by celebrating sexual experimentation, including encouraging young women to engage in highly explicit sexual experimentation early in dating. This is the same podcast Kamala Harris joined prior to the 2024 election, but I digress.

RILEY GAINES FIRES BACK AT ALEX COOPER’S GRAPHIC DATING ADVICE: ‘IT IS NOT EMPOWERMENT. IT IS POISON’

Bush is now on her third marriage, with the first one lasting 5 months, the second lasting about a year, and the third to a woman.

These are the voices our culture elevates as influential guides for young women. But enough about the who. Let's examine the what.

The exchange reveals a worldview in which something better is always waiting. That personal and fleeting dissatisfaction is sufficient reason to abandon a commitment, and that the pursuit of more is interchangeable with empowerment.

More what, exactly?

More excitement? More affirmation? More freedom? Another relationship that will inevitably encounter the same imperfections as the last?

At what point do we consider whether the relentless pursuit of more is precisely what leaves us feeling we have less?

AMERICAN WOMEN HAVE BEEN LIED TO ABOUT MOTHERHOOD AND IT’S TIME TO FIX IT

For decades, women have been sold a particular vision of liberation. Prioritize your career. Maximize your independence. Explore your sexuality without consequence. Reject marriage, delay motherhood, and never compromise your ambitions for someone else's needs. Above all, put yourself first.

We were assured that freedom from traditional obligations would produce unprecedented happiness.

TRADITIONAL TWO-PARENT FAMILIES VANISH FROM BIG AMERICAN CITIES AS 'MARRIAGE DESERTS' EXPAND

If that were true, we would certainly see it in society. But instead, what was promised as empowerment has delivered emptiness.

Despite constant technological connectivity, loneliness and social isolation remain pervasive. Anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation are serious concerns, particularly among younger generations. These problems have many causes, and attributing them all to feminism would be intellectually dishonest. But ignoring the possibility that our prevailing philosophy has failed to deliver its promised fulfillment would be equally foolish.

We’ve spent decades dismantling the institutions that tether individuals to one another, only to discover that autonomy is a poor substitute for belonging.

Perhaps most tragically, we’ve taught women to regard sacrifice as oppression rather than an indispensable part of love.

Consider the contradiction.

A woman who sacrifices her time, energy, and health to climb the corporate ladder is celebrated as ambitious. A woman making comparable sacrifices for her husband and children is too often regarded as having surrendered her potential to the patriarchy. Why?

ONE GROUP OF MARRIED AMERICANS IS HAVING MORE SEX — AND HAPPIER MARRIAGES

I am profoundly grateful for the opportunities women have today. I’ve competed as a collegiate athlete, traveled the country, built a career, and achieved things my younger self could never have imagined. But no professional accolade, public recognition, or personal achievement has given me the satisfaction and purpose I’ve found in marriage and motherhood.

They require more of me than anything I've ever done (even a 200-yard butterfly). It's hard. But "hard" and "bad" are not synonymous.

Motherhood fundamentally changed my understanding of success. There's something remarkably clarifying about being needed by someone who has nothing to offer you in return except themselves.

I don't view it as a limitation on my freedom, but instead a revelation of what my freedom is for.

Which brings me back to Cooper, who just welcomed her first child with her husband.

I genuinely congratulate her. But there's irony in continuing to promote perpetual self-prioritization through meaningless hookups and "girl-bossing" while building a life rooted in the very institutions modern feminism so often characterizes as oppressive.

Perhaps motherhood will offer her the same perspective it offered me: that the deepest fulfillment isn't found in putting yourself first, but in loving someone enough to put them first.

Of course, marriage and motherhood aren't the only paths to meaning. Women who are single, childless, or unable to have children are no less valuable. Purpose takes countless forms, but lasting meaning generally requires looking beyond ourselves.

This is hardly a novel insight. Christianity has taught for centuries that a life centered exclusively on the self is ultimately impoverished. Love is not merely a feeling to be pursued while convenient. It is a commitment expressed through action, fidelity, humility, and sacrifice.

Our culture treats these virtues as antiquated burdens, then wonders why so many feel unmoored.

Cooper and Bush's advice is troubling because it reduces marriage to personal optimization. Marriage becomes less a covenant to honor than an arrangement to continually reassess against hypothetical alternatives.

There are legitimate reasons marriages end, including abuse and betrayal. But reflexively encouraging people to search for something better without acknowledging the responsibilities of commitment isn't teaching empowerment like the self-proclaimed feminists like to claim. It teaches disposability.

A generation encouraged to keep every option open may eventually discover that life's most meaningful commitments require closing certain doors.

Choosing a spouse. Raising children. Building a family. Practicing faith. Serving a community. Creating something that will endure long after your own ambitions have faded.

Like everything associated with risk, these commitments impose limits, but I’ve found they also give life its depth.

Women deserve more than the hollow assurance that happiness is perpetually waiting in the next relationship, promotion, or reinvention of themselves. They deserve to know that fulfillment isn't always found in acquiring more and finding someone that validates your every desire. Often, it's found in giving more.

The great lie of modern empowerment isn't that women are capable of extraordinary things. It's that a life devoted primarily to ourselves is the most extraordinary thing we can aspire to.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

We should stop telling women that the ultimate goal is to have everything and start reminding them of the beauty of having something worth giving everything for.

And perhaps the grass isn't always greener on the other side.

It’s greener where you water it.

World.title: Supreme Court justice turns on her own court with dire warning about American democracy
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan made the case that recent rulings from the conservative-majority high court are destabilizing democracy, suggesting that it isn't working "as well as it should."

The remarks from the liberal justice came during a closed discussion before faculty and students at Catholic University's law school in Washington, D.C.

The discussion between Kagan and law professor Joel Alicea Alicia, who previously clerked for Justice Samuel Alito, comes just weeks after the Supreme Court began its new term, during which it's expected to rule in major cases that will determine the scope of gun rights and state election integrity laws, among other issues.

The conversation also comes less than two weeks before the midterm elections as President Donald Trump and Republican state lawmakers have pushed for new congressional maps drawn to favor Republicans and bolster their chances of maintaining control of the House. Democratic-led states have responded by redrawing their own maps, fueling ongoing lawsuits and court battles.

SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE

Kagan pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2019 ruling in Rucho v. Common Cause, in which she dissented, as the beginning of a "race to the bottom." She argued that the decision, which barred federal courts from invalidating maps solely because they unfairly favor one political party, deprived "masses of citizens" of their "rights to voting equality."

Kagan suggested that the influx of gerrymandered maps is "driving people away from the center toward the wings, toward the extremes.

"Making what I think is, unfortunately, a too polarized country even more so," Kagan said.

Kagan also criticized rulings from the previous term, including the court’s decision limiting campaign finance restrictions and its ruling that made it more difficult to draw majority-minority congressional districts under the Voting Rights Act.

"Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said.

"I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should."

DESANTIS SIGNS FLORIDA REDISTRICTING MAP TO POTENTIALLY FLIP 4 HOUSE SEATS RED

Last term, the Supreme Court struck down federal limits on how much state and national political parties could spend in coordination with their candidates.

Meanwhile, Kagan argued in dissent that the limits were necessary to prevent wealthy donors from working around direct contribution caps and that striking them down effectively allowed a political party to become an "alternative checking account" for a candidate.

"The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare," Kagan said. "And they’re right."

Kagan, who was appointed to the court by President Barack Obama in 2010, argued that it was in a much better position when there was greater ideological balance.

"There was a period of time where the court was in a better place, and the country was in a better place because the court was more balanced, and it was unclear whether the court could push through anybody’s program."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"Nobody in America thought that the court was in the pocket of any one group or any one party," she said. "And the court had a kind of legitimacy. When the court has a legitimacy of that kind, it helps to create a stable country."

However, Kagan pushed back against the characterization that the conservative-leaning court simply rubber-stamped Trump's entire agenda. She pointed to previous rulings by the high court rejecting birthright citizenship restrictions, tariffs and Trump's restrictions on mail-in voting.

"It’s why the president sometimes really has not very nice things to say about the court’s decisions and some of my colleagues," Kagan said.

World.title: Ilhan Omar says she lives 'paycheck to paycheck' as DOJ probes financial disclosures
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., described herself as a member of the "working class" who lives "paycheck to paycheck" during an interview with MS NOW host Chris Hayes on Wednesday night.

"I mean, it’s, you know, working — working class, I guess, like paycheck to paycheck still," Omar said. "We’ve got four kids, and we live, I think, like a basic life. I have a Toyota Camry that’s from 2016."

Omar's characterization of her finances comes despite her $174,000 annual congressional salary and scrutiny over financial disclosures that once listed assets tied to her husband as being worth as much as $30 million.

The comments came during Omar’s first public appearance since Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched her Washington, D.C., residence on Oct. 12 as part of an investigation into possible immigration-related offenses.

ILHAN OMAR BELIEVES TRUMP RAID ON HOME WAS MEANT TO 'INTIMIDATE AND SCARE PEOPLE' FROM VOTING

Since the raid, the representative has used the investigation twice as a reason to publicly fundraise.

"That goes a long way as we fight Trump and his administration for trying to intimidate me and so many people right before the midterm elections," Omar said in a video she uploaded to social media on Wednesday. "We know that they’re running scared. We’re not going to be intimidated. We’re not going to be silenced."

The Democratic National Committee has also sent out its own fundraising email based on Omar’s campaign request for money.

"It’s Ilhan Omar — Trump’s DHS agents just carried out a raid and search of my home," the email says. "This is a drastic escalation of the ludicrous, partisan investigation that they launched into my immigration status."

ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME

Omar also acknowledged during the MS NOW interview that the federal agents who searched her home were "polite" and left the property in good condition, even folding some of her clothes.

"When they left, what did you do?" Hayes asked Omar.

"I just went back around the house just trying to make sure everything was put back," Omar replied. "And they did a really good job in putting everything back in its place. They actually even folded some of my clothing that [was] not folded. So it was … a very bizarre [situation]."

The Minnesota Democrat added that she thought the HSI agents who raided her home were "intrusive, but polite."

"And yeah, they, they left the house, I think, you know, in good shape," she told MS NOW.

Omar claimed during the interview that the federal agents were searching her house for four to five hours. She added that they left the raid with more than a dozen items, including notebooks and a children’s Somali-language phrasebook.

"[That] was why I was surprised when they handed me the receipt for the items that they take in, to do that long of a search and to walk away with 17 items, of like 10 that were just notebooks and, like, old phones. Was such a bizarre, bizarre thing," Omar said.

A separate Justice Department investigation is examining Omar’s financial disclosures, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said during an appearance on Fox News’ "America Reports."

The disclosures previously showed that the reported value of two businesses tied to Omar’s husband, Tim Mynett, rose from as much as $51,000 in 2023 to as much as $30 million in 2024, according to House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky.

Omar later amended the filing, saying the original figures were the result of an accounting error. The amended disclosure listed the couple’s assets at between $18,004 and $95,000. Omar has denied wrongdoing, and no criminal charges have been filed against her in connection with the disclosures.

Mynett’s businesses include eStCru, a winery, and Rose Lake Capital, an investment firm. The winery has reportedly shut down.

ILHAN OMAR RAID SPARKS OMINOUS PREDICTION FROM WATCHDOG: 'THEY PROBABLY GOT THE GOODS'

On Fox News’ "Sunday Night in America," Comer told host Trey Gowdy that his committee’s initial review of Omar’s disclosures identified multiple issues that could justify further investigative steps.

"First of all, not only was there a huge discrepancy in the financial disclosure form, there was the winery that was the big base of her $25 million listing on her financial disclosure form," Comer said. "That winery has, according to the press, been shut down because of fraud."

In a February letter to Mynett, Comer noted that Omar’s 2023 disclosure listed her stake in eStCru as being worth between $15,001 and $50,000.

"The following year, her financial disclosure form listed a stake in eStCru ‘worth between $1,000,001 and $5,000,000,’" Comer wrote. "There are serious public concerns about how your businesses increased so dramatically in value only a year after reporting very limited assets."

World.title: Blanche won’t rule out DOJ post-election action in a ‘doomsday’ scenario
World.content:
NORFOLK, Va. — Attorney General Todd Blanche on Thursday left open the possibility that the Justice Department could seek to block states from certifying votes in the midterm elections, though Blanche insisted it wasn’t his intention to “improperly interfere with elections.”

NBC News reported this week that the Justice Department is weighing more election-related litigation against states, following a lawsuit against California to compel state officials to review 18,000 registered voters the DOJ suspected could be noncitizens seeking to cast fraudulent ballots. California has an all-mail election and sends out ballots automatically.

Seven other states and Washington, D.C., do, too: Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington state. Mail voting has frequently been a target for President Donald Trump’s voter fraud claims, which have escalated ahead of the 2026 midterms, even as he uses the voting method to cast his ballot in Florida.

The legal threats come amid a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what voting experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizens.

The Justice Department’s role in U.S. elections is limited by law, chiefly allowing it to safeguard civil rights and prosecute individuals who violate election law.

While private citizens and candidates can sue to challenge ballots or election results, there are no U.S. laws that say the Justice Department can challenge ballots or delay certification. U.S. elections are run by state and local officials, who are charged with certifying results.

On Thursday, Blanche was asked whether he could rule out any action by the Justice Department that could seek to delay the counting of ballots.

“It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process,” he told reporters before he boarded a plane.

Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel traveled to Norfolk for a press conference Thursday to announce racketeering charges against an 82-year-old Virginia state senator.

Blanche said there could be some “doomsday” scenario in which the Justice Department would seek to get involved in state and local election officials’ certification process.

“To say that there’s no circumstances that we would ever do that .... of course, I’m not going to say that,” he said. “But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not.”

Asked about the Justice Department’s litigation against states at the press conference earlier in the day, Blanche said the Justice Department was “not trying to create chaos” but that they were trying to alert officials to potential issues.

“I’m not trying to not have an election certified. Of course not,” Blanche said. “What we’re trying to do is guarantee to the American people that the only people that are voting are people that are eligible to vote.”

Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-New York, reacted to Blanche’s comments, saying Senate Democrats “have been preparing for this for months and will be ready for whatever” the Trump administration tries.

“As Trump and his cronies attempt to steal this election, we are fighting them at every turn,” Schumer posted on X. “Our elections must always belong to the voters — not Donald Trump.”

World.title: On Main Street, Goldman Sachs makes a big bet on AI
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is already a huge business for Wall Street. But how is it playing on Main Street?

Goldman Sachs, as part of a philanthropic effort, is spending big in an attempt to help ensure smaller employers get in on it. The bank announced Thursday that it has launched the Small Business AI Institute as part of a $500 million expansion of its 10,000 Small Businesses, a program geared toward educating and supporting entrepreneurs. It said it would partner with Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta to provide AI training and tools to small businesses.

“You’ve got to embrace new technology always, because if you’re not embracing it, trying to figure out how it can make your businesses better, there’s a real chance that you can fall behind,” Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said in an exclusive interview for NBC News’ Business in America series.

It’s a pivotal moment for the AI wave and its financial backers, including Goldman. The technology is broadly available to consumers, and U.S. economic growth increasingly depends on the buildup of data centers.

“We believe AI will create the greatest boom in entrepreneurship and small businesses that the world has ever seen,” Sam Altman, CEO and co-founder of OpenAI, said in an announcement from Goldman Sachs. “This is an incredible moment for anyone with an idea for a new endeavor because the gap between imagining it and bringing it to life is getting much smaller.”

Yet the growth that AI is already driving has also helped push up prices for inflation-weary Americans. Anger at data centers is a rare point of bipartisan agreement among voters, and the midterm elections are days away.

In the finance world, critics say AI is an investment bubble that could burst and potentially wipe out companies and jobs. Cracks are forming in the AI trade in markets after Big Tech firms drove much of stocks’ recent surge to record highs.

Goldman Sachs, like much of Wall Street, is in the thick of it all.

The bank’s share price has approximately tripled over the past three years while AI-related companies pushed the stock market to record highs. Goldman helped lead the much-ballyhooed, record-breaking initial public offering for Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which counts xAI and Grok among its core businesses. Goldman is also reportedly working on the IPO of Anthropic, the startup behind the AI chatbot Claude.

“There is going to be a lot of financing to do,” Solomon said last week on an earnings call, “and we’re going to be in the middle of that.”

Goldman and other big firms are counting on small businesses, which make up more than 90% of all U.S. companies and drive most of America’s job growth, to buy in. It won’t be easy getting everyone on board, though.

A recent NBC News poll found that 79% of respondents believe the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI use. Sixty-seven percent disapprove of how President Donald Trump is handling the technology. Trump has said he favors lax AI regulation from the government.

Meanwhile, some small businesses that already embraced AI have faced backlash from the public, including restaurants that used AI-generated images of food that critics denounced as “slop.”

Still, according to Goldman, entrepreneurs are adopting the technology at a fast clip. A survey this year of more than 2,400 graduates of the company’s small business program found that 86% of respondents were using AI in their businesses, up from just 56% in 2024.

Rechelle Balanzat, founder of the laundry services app Juliette and an alumna of the 10,000 Small Businesses program, told NBC News she sees AI as a tool to help her gin up more business with limited resources.

Rechelle Balanzat, founder of the laundry services app Juliette. Kayla Steinberg / NBC News

“I really treat my AI as my consigliere,” Balanzat said. “They are not there to replace your accountant and lawyer. They are not there to replace humans. However, it does help prep me to have much more meaningful questions when I am meeting with my accountant and with my lawyer.”

Despite the widespread use of AI among the Goldman program alumni, just 15% of them said they had fully integrated AI into their core operations, according to Goldman.

Mike DiMarino, who heads Linda Tool in Brooklyn, New York, was part of the inaugural class of Goldman’s program in 2010. The company makes precision machine components for the military and aerospace industries, and DiMarino thinks AI can help with planning, management and processes.

“I’m sure there’s a lot more it can do that I don’t know yet,” he said.

But DiMarino is also cautious about how Linda Tool uses the technology, especially given how much sensitive information the company handles for its work in defense, aerospace and manufacturing.

Mike DiMarino heads Linda Tool. Kayla Steinberg / NBC News

His concerns mirror broader cybersecurity fears about AI. In July, a swarm of about 700 AI agents created by OpenAI hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face. Last month, Google said Chinese hackers are using AI to automate their attacks.

In addition to the security risks, company leaders are also increasingly raising concerns about the cost of AI, especially relative to its concrete impact on the bottom line. After spending on AI tokens exploded in the past year, companies from Uber to Microsoft to Meta have all taken steps to limit or re-evaluate how their employees use AI compute power.

Americans are also concerned about what AI will do to the job market. A recent Gallup Poll found that a growing number of workers are worried that technology will make their jobs obsolete. Small businesses employ fewer people than large firms, which makes their workforces especially vulnerable to potential losses.

Balanzat and DiMarino told NBC News they want to use AI to support employees at their businesses, not replace them.

“Machines are expensive,” DiMarino said. “People are priceless.”

World.title: Despite security concerns, NFL plans to stage Paris game amid French protests
World.content:
As nationwide protests continue across France, raising security concerns, the NFL says its first regular-season game in Paris on Sunday is still planning to be staged.

When the New Orleans Saints arrived in France following their win Sunday against the New York Giants, and the Pittsburgh Steelers arrived Thursday, they came to a country that has been roiled by protests since early October over high cost of living and deteriorating conditions in the country’s schools. French officials have said the unrest has led to thousands of arrests. The French government estimated that some 550,000 people took part in demonstrations last Saturday and a curfew has been put in place in some parts of Paris. Though much of the protests have been peaceful, some have turned violent as masked looters clashed with riot police.

In one instance the mayor of the Parisian suburb Saint-Denis, the site of Stade de France where the Steelers-Saints game will be held, stood between police officers and protestors. A league spokesman wrote Wednesday that “preparations continue as scheduled.”

The security and events team the league uses to host events such as the Super Bowl are also staging this international game inside Stade de France, the spokesman added, and that “there’s been no disruption or impact at league sites.”

The NFL has moved the locations of some games due to natural disasters, such as a Los Angeles Rams game in January 2025, as wildfires raged across Southern California. Peter O’Reilly, the NFL’s executive vice president of club business, international and league events, told reporters after league owners’ meetings Tuesday that no such discussions had taken place in this case.

“We have never been close to that point,” O’Reilly said. “We’ve always got contingency plans for every game, every single one of them. But no, we were not at that point at any point in the conversation.”

O’Reilly said that officials from the league including Cathy Lanier, the NFL Chief Security Officer who used to run Washington D.C.’s Metropolitan Police, had been in Paris for several days to oversee operation plans.

The protests have altered at least one event surrounding the game, however. The Steelers said Thursday that they were canceling plans to host a “Steelers House” for fans “following recent events in the Bastille neighborhood, and after careful consideration.”

Asked about his comfort level regarding security around the game, NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said Wednesday that “very high is my comfort level.” Goodell said he had spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and that the league was “involved at the highest levels, both in France on a global basis, with our officials here in the United States.”

“We’ve made all the preparations,” Goodell said. “We’ve been in touch with the appropriate authorities. Protests are not unusual in France, as you know. And that’s something that we will be aware of and make sure that the appropriate arrangements are made.”

Goodell said he was looking forward to attending the game.

01:03 Paris officials prep for NFL game amid civil unrest 00:00 00:00

“We’re guests in the country, we’re going to be good guests, and we’re going to do our thing, and I’m confident they’re going to do theirs,” Goodell said.

Amid the unrest in France, Paris has already hosted one major sporting event this week without incident. On Tuesday, the two-time reigning European champion soccer club Paris Saint-Germain hosted Barcelona in a Champions League match that was attended by some Saints players.

“NFL does feel comfortable in sending us over,” Steelers defensive lineman Cam Heyward said Wednesday on The Rich Eisen Show. “That’s the trust we have to believe in. Hopefully we’re not going into a firestorm, but for us, we have to be smart about what we’re doing out there. No traveling alone, make sure we stay in groups and don’t wander off too far.”

“The NFL likes money,” Heyward added, “so we’re not missing that opportunity.”

World.title: Top adviser to Kennedy resigns from Trump administration
World.content:
Calley Means, a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and central advocate for the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, has resigned from the Trump administration.

“I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and RFK — two historic figures who are committed to confronting a corrupt DC bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo,” Means said in a statement to NBC News. He posted a similar one on X.

Means was an adviser on Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign and a key architect of his MAHA agenda. He joined the White House early last year as a special government employee. He transitioned to a full-time role as senior adviser to the Health and Human Services Department after divesting from his wellness company, Truemed.

A person familiar with Means’ decision to resign said Means had been growing increasingly frustrated as he realized how little he could get done in Washington to advance his MAHA priorities.

The final straw, the source said, was the lack of progress on rolling out a federal definition of ultra-processed foods — one of Means’ biggest priorities. The administration teased a definition in August but has yet to release it.

The source also mentioned Trump’s executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S. (glyphosate is the key ingredient in Roundup), as well as some actions at the Environmental Protection Agency that have clashed with Kennedy’s agenda.

The Trump administration’s EPA has, for example, weakened mercury emissions standards and rolled back drinking water limits for certain PFAS chemicals — actions the MAHA movement has largely opposed.

Frustrations over a lack of progress on MAHA goals have reverberated throughout the movement. Earlier this month, some supporters — including former members of Kennedy’s presidential campaign — accused the Trump administration of breaking nearly every promise made to them on food, agriculture and environmental health.

One of the MAHA movement’s central beliefs is that corporations hold too much influence over the food supply and healthcare system. Many of its supporters, including Means, had hoped to see a greater crackdown on pesticides and artificial dyes, as well as more significant changes to vaccine policy that emphasize what some describe as “medical freedom” over universal recommendations.

On pesticides, one particular setback for the MAHA cause came in June, when the Supreme Court ruled that Bayer, the manufacturer of Roundup, didn’t need to warn consumers about a potential cancer risk associated with its product. The Trump administration had backed Bayer in the case.

Means’ resignation came less than a month after he spoke at a MAHA summit in Washington, D.C. At the time, he said he was inspired by the way federal agencies had collaborated to advance the MAHA agenda but acknowledged roadblocks, as well.

“D.C. is a tough place. It’s a toxic place, and there’s a lot of complaints you can make about D.C.,” Means said. “But I am more optimistic today than I’ve ever been about what I feel is my life’s work of evangelizing the chronic disease crisis and empowering Americans who want to be healthy to address the root cause of disease.”

In his statement on Thursday, Means highlighted several policy wins for the MAHA movement during his tenure, including restricting soda purchases through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), fast-tracking research and review of psychedelics, urging food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and overhauling the federal dietary guidelines to recommend less ultra-processed food and more protein.

“More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history,” he said.

World.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer ask guests to clean dishes or make beds
World.content:
Airbnb hosts can only set “reasonable” housecleaning duties for guests, according to new guidelines rolled out by the tech giant, with tasks such as dishwashing and bed stripping now the sole responsibility of homeowners.

While Airbnb bookings have always included a cleaning fee, there hadn’t been universal policies on what hosts can ask their renters to complete.

But now, starting with rentals on Nov. 20, Airbnb will limit these guest responsibilities in order to “set clear expectations” for hosts whose house rules must be “reasonable and comply with” these new requirements.

Hosts cannot ask “guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes,” Airbnb said.

The new guidelines come after years of customer complaints, travel industry expert Clint Henderson told NBC News.

“So this is pretty major for consumers,” said Henderson, managing editor and spokesperson for travel industry website The Points Guy.

“The complaints have been really ramping up lately with owners asking guests to do the most ridiculous things, like stripping beds, washing dishes, doing all the laundry and taking the trash out,” Henderson said.

“It’s just gotten really out of hand,” he said. “And from a consumer’s perspective, it’s like, ‘Why am I going to stay at Airbnb when I have to do chores?’”

While Airbnb host Gabriel Valk, in Greenville, South Carolina, believes small tasks like dishwashing and bed stripping should be “common courtesy” performed by guests, he understands why Airbnb would institute these more clear guidelines.

“But I do understand the pushback,” Valk said, citing the service fees that are supposed to cover cleaning costs.

“OK, you guys are paying, whatever, $100 for the cleaning. ‘We shouldn’t have to do anything,’” he imagined the guests saying. “So totally makes sense to me.”

Airbnb had to give guests a break or risk consumers flocking back to traditional hotels, according to Henderson.

“Why (stay at an Airbnb) when I can stay at a hotel and not have to do all that busy work?” he said. “And these days, Airbnb is as expensive, with all the fees and everything, as a hotel is. So I think Airbnb has lost some of its competitive edge over the years.”

World.title: What to know about the PHP bug affecting 70% of world's websites
World.content:
Hackers could exploit weaknesses in a widely used programming language for websites, online platforms and other technology services to steal users' information and cause other problems, cybersecurity researchers warn.

The programming language PHP, short for "Personal Home Page," powers up to 70% of the world's websites and web applications, including those used by government agencies, social media platforms such as Facebook and sites including Wikipedia.

The bug, dubbed PHP2Shell, can target two security flaws in PHP, according to Voldemaras Kadys, head of security at Mediatech. Those weaknesses could enable cybercriminals to seize control of unprotected website servers, install malware, pilfer customer data and even take sites down completely.

"The potential impact of these vulnerabilities may be huge, as most websites run on PHP," he said in an email.

The flaws in PHP were discovered when security researchers used an OpenAI artificial intelligence model to identify the problem, Wall Street Journal reporter Robert McMillan, who first reported on the PHP security issue, told CBS News.

"There are a lot of sites that I don't think even know that they have a problem, and they may find out the hard way."

What should consumers know?

Consumers' personal information could be vulnerable if they have an account with an online store or booking platform whose site uses PHP and is exposed to the bug.

"For regular internet users, simply visiting a PHP website doesn't necessarily mean their device will be compromised," Kadys explained. "The risk is that attackers may exploit a website that holds their personal information. For example, if a user has an account with an online shop, attackers may be able to hack that website through this PHP vulnerability and extract the information the user has stored there, such as their email address, physical address, name and date of birth."

But just because a site is vulnerable doesn't guarantee that a breach has occurred or will occur.

"There's no reason to stop browsing or shopping online, but users should still be extra cautious about suspicious messages because we don't know what kind of data hackers may have stolen through this vulnerability, and from which websites," he added.

Racing hackers

Andrés Guerrero-Saade, vice president of intelligence and security research at SentinelOne, told CBS News that the incident illustrates "how AI is accelerating the ability of vulnerability researchers" while also boosting bad actors' capacity to exploit security flaws.

The time between a vulnerability being detected and a fix being released is crucial for cybersecurity experts, he added. Yet that vital window of time has been shortened by AI, allowing cybercriminals to move much faster today than in the past.

"That whole gap between the patch being available and attackers getting to exploit that before anybody patches, that's the whole game essentially," Guerrero-Saade said.

In a post on X, the FBI's cyber threat division encouraged any organization that can't immediately patch its sites to temporarily take them offline.

The PHP Foundation, which includes tech developers who work on securing the programming language, said on Wednesday that it had released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems.

"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now. The announcement on php.net contains and references technical details on the vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and instructions on how to update on which systems," the group said.

The discovery of the flaws highlights the battle between security professionals and hackers in using AI to spot potential holes in organizations' technology systems. In this case, security researchers were the first to uncover the bug, which had existed for at least a decade, McMillan noted.

"People knew something weird was going on. But no one could really find a way to write an exploit — of turning a bug that might cause a computer to crash into something really bad that would allow somebody to run software that they weren't supposed to be able to run on a computer," he said.

World.title: Tom Skerritt, known for roles in "Alien," "Picket Fences," dies at 93
World.content:
Tom Skerritt, the actor known for his roles in "Alien," "Top Gun" and TV's "Picket Fences," has died, his publicist confirmed to CBS News on Thursday. He was 93.

Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement.

"We are heartbroken by his loss," the family said. "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives."

World.title: GOP officials divided over Ramaswamy ad with Acton's mom
World.content:
Ohio's GOP Gov. Mike DeWine said Thursday that Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee to replace him, should take down an ad that features Democratic opponent Amy Acton's estranged mother calling her a liar.

DeWine's comments come one day after Vice President JD Vance told Republicans to "stop whining" about the ad.

"It's wrong to run this ad," DeWine told reporters. "I would urge Ramaswamy's campaign to take this down."

DeWine, who is term-limited, called the ad "on its face, deeply, deeply troubling" but said when one knows the backstory of allegations of abuse and neglect, "it makes it even more wrong."

DeWine refused to say if he had spoken with the Ramaswamy campaign, but said he was not rescinding his endorsement of Ramaswamy.

In response to DeWine's comments, Ramaswamy campaign spokesperson Connie Luck doubled down in defense of the ad, saying "the first and only candidate to attack the mother of her opponent in this race was Amy Acton."

"Acton's mother is speaking out about her clear pattern of lying — not abuse — and it should be covered as such, not just with the Acton campaign spin," Luck said.

The ad first circulated Monday night on social media with unclear origins, before Ramaswamy confirmed Tuesday it was "an ad from our campaign."

In it, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, whose husband was accused of raping Acton when she was a child, says, "It's not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy was a serious problem. She is a liar; she lies about her past."

Acton, who served as the state's public health commissioner under DeWine during the pandemic, has previously talked about being abused by her now-deceased stepfather. According to documents provided by the campaign, in 1978, Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton, when she was between 10 and 12 years old. He entered a not guilty plea and left the area while out on bond; the case never went to trial.

Acton has not been in touch with her mother since a court date after her stepfather was arrested. The court records also show that the family lived in a tent, which Arthur disputed in the ad.

Ramaswamy on Tuesday defended the content of the ad, saying, "Every person who appears to know her the best … have told voters not to vote for her but to vote for me instead."

Acton said Thursday on CNN that she had hoped Ramaswamy "wouldn't sink this low, but of course he did."

She said some Republicans "just don't have the courage" to speak out about an ad she said crossed "everyone's boundary that has ever been done before."

But Vance, who represented Ohio in the Senate before becoming vice president and was campaigning in the state on Wednesday, had a different reaction, telling reporters that "whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern."

"Politics is a tough business," Vance said. "And my message to my fellow elected Republicans is, if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an  and go win the race in 13 days."

DeWine is not the only Republican to speak out against the ad. Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, who is in a tough reelection battle against Democrat Sherrod Brown, said Wednesday in a statement to The Associated Press that he would not have run it.

Former Republican Rep. Jim Renacci posted on social media that "any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well."

When asked about the ad on Wednesday, President Trump said, "I know nothing about it." He added, "It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much, but I don't think that has anything to do with Vivek."

Former U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley, who was subjected to personal and family attacks by Ramasway in the 2020 GOP presidential primary campaign, responded to the ad in a social media post saying that she's "just seeing what we tried to tell everyone back then. He's a bad guy. It's a shame he continues to get away with it."

World.title: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, opts for shorter-term ban
World.content:
In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, failed to pass a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city, which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.

Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days.

Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi.

Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution.

SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but on Monday, a Mississippi federal judge rejected that bid.

Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary.

The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations.

The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development.

Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations.

FILE -- Construction on a SpaceXAI data center on Riverport Road in Memphis, Tennessee, on April 25, 2025. Photo by Brandon Dill/The Washington Post via Getty Images

The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting.

Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country.

Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact.

"It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said.

Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month.

A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

World.title: Hegseth bans use of nonpublic info for bets on U.S. military ops
World.content:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has banned Defense Department personnel from using nonpublic information to bet on U.S. military operations, according to a memorandum obtained by CBS News.

In the Oct. 20 message to senior Pentagon leadership and combatant commanders, Hegseth said the prohibition would apply to classified and unclassified information and specifically includes prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi, which are named in the memo.

The defense secretary warned that financial transactions on prediction markets could expose sensitive military movements to foreign adversaries and endanger American troops.

"Make no mistake why this matters. Our enemies watch movements in these markets," Hegseth wrote. "When an American Service member, intelligence professional, or other Department civilian engages in a financial transaction on a military outcome, they create a signal."

Hegseth warned that foreign intelligence services could analyze betting activity to anticipate American military movements, targets and timing of an operation. The memorandum said violations could result in administrative disciplinary or criminal action under federal law or the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the laws and regulations governing the U.S. military.

The directive follows growing scrutiny of service members participating in military-related prediction markets. In April, a U.S. Special Forces soldier involved in the military operation that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro was arrested after allegedly betting on Maduro's removal from office before news of the raid was made public.

Federal investigators believe U.S. Army Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke made bets of more than $33,000 on the prediction market Polymarket within hours of President Trump's announcement in January that Maduro had been captured. The bets resulted in winnings of more than $409,000.

The soldier entered a not guilty plea in New York federal court.
