World.title: Crackdown on delinquents
World.content:
SAMUDA... says customers making occasional payments, should not assume they will escape actionNaphtali Junior

THE National Water Commission (NWC) says it is aggressively pursuing registered customers who can afford to settle their overdue bills but refuse to pay, with thousands already disconnected and placed on repayment programmes.

Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda said customers making occasional payments should not assume they will escape action as the utility moves to recover outstanding revenue.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s St Andrew headquarters on Wednesday, Samuda said the commission has traditionally given customers room to address their arrears once they were making payments. However, he said, enforcement has intensified since its debt amnesty.

“Over the last year, I’d say post the amnesty, those who didn’t come forward and say they have these issues, we’ve had thousands who have been disconnected and been put on a six-month programme to clear their space,” he said.

The NWC had implemented general and micro small and medium enterprises (MSME) amnesty programmes ending on May 31, 2025 and December 31, 2025, respectively.

The general amnesty provided write-offs of up to 100 per cent for vulnerable groups pensioners, Programme of Advancement Through Health and Education (PATH) beneficiaries, disabled individuals and graduated discounts for residential accounts. Additionally, MSMEs benefited from a 50 per cent waiver on qualified arrears and reconnection fee write-offs for eligible establishments.

The water minister pointed to the amnesty’s success as an effort to help customers resolve long-standing liabilities and return to regular payment. He said approximately 14,000 customers had been brought back into the formal system, while the commission was working through issues involving another 16,000.

Against that backdrop, the water minister argued that there was a stark difference between those who simply cannot afford to pay the fees charged and those who refuse to pay, even while capable of doing so.

“So we’ve tried the first route, which is to be nice for those who did not engage during that process because we’re still going through approximately 16,000 persons to resolve some of these long-standing issues,” he said.

“If we detect theft in an area and at a facility based on consumption that obviously could pay for it, I assure you we’ll enforce, we’ll enforce hard,” warned Samuda.

Adding to the conversation, NWC Board Chairman Michael Shaw said the commission has teams actively pursuing outstanding payments, even if those efforts are not widely publicised.

“Maybe it is because we’re not putting the persons on the front page of the paper or on social media, but we have a team out there aggressively going to collect our funds because we need it for our cash flow,” Shaw said.

He disclosed that they had been seriously pursuing delinquents, noting that the NWC’s revenue collection rate moved from 2.4 to 3.5 per cent monthly.

“There’s no, for the most part, new water supply systems. It was people who were avoiding paying it and we had a strategic plan to go after those — particularly condominiums, commercial customers, and so on — to make sure that they were paying their portion,” he clarified.

He acknowledged, however, that the essential nature of water influences how the commission deals with customers.

“We’re probably not as aggressive in actually treating with customers because of this commodity, water. You have to treat it a little differently. But I think we are probably being strategic about it,” he explained.

The crackdown on registered customers who continue to avoid payments comes as the NWC is navigating a revenue position that has deteriorated over time, particularly in relation to customer payments.

Appearing before Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee on Tuesday, the utility’s chief financial officer, Fabian Christie, acknowledged that the utility has undertaken several initiatives to recover outstanding payments and bring indebted customers back into the formal system.

Alongside those collection efforts, the commission is seeking regulatory approval for a 51 per cent increase in water and sewerage rates to help finance operations and critical investments over the next five years. It is also pursuing an islandwide programme to reduce water losses, which remain a significant drain on its finances.

World.title: Another blow
World.content:
.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Hoteliers are warning that a proposed 51 per cent increase in water and sewerage rates could deepen the financial strain on Jamaica’s tourism industry, with smaller independent properties facing the risk of further hardship.

The National Water Commission (NWC) is seeking prompting concern among tourism stakeholders about the potential impact on an industry still struggling to recover from successive shocks.

Richard Wallace, operator of Boardwalk Village Hotel in Negril, said water was already one of the sector’s highest expenses, warning that the proposed increase could prove devastating for hotels, particularly those already burdened by substantial sewerage charges.

“In the resort area of Negril, we pay not just for water, we [also] pay for sewerage,” Wallace explained, noting that sewerage charges effectively double the water bill.

“So if we pay $100 for water, we pay another $100 for sewerage,” he said, describing the arrangement as a major expense for hotels in the resort town.

Wallace also warned that unexpected leaks could leave smaller properties facing crippling bills, citing cases in which hotels had accumulated water charges running into hundreds of thousands of dollars, with one reported case exceeding $1 million.

“So it’s very frightening. It’s very scary in terms of what potentially can happen if that is granted,” he said of the proposed increase.

Meanwhile, Jamaica Inn Managing Director Kyle Mais described the prospect of higher water rates as another blow to an industry that has yet to fully recover from the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, Hurricane Beryl, and Hurricane Melissa.

Speaking both as a hotelier and a citizen, Mais said the proposed increase was particularly troubling given the pressure households were already experiencing from high inflation.

“For us, as citizens, we’re already facing extremely high inflation, and this is just going to put more pressure on us,” he said.

Mais said smaller, independent and family-owned hotels, which account for a large proportion of the country’s properties, were especially vulnerable because many had borrowed heavily during the pandemic to keep their businesses operating and retain staff.

Their balance sheets, he said, remained heavily burdened by debt even as they tried to rebuild following subsequent disruptions.

“We’re on the road to recovery, but we haven’t recovered. We’re still struggling,” Mais said, adding that the summer had been disappointing for visitor arrivals, with expensive airfares making it more difficult for travellers to afford trips to Jamaica.

He also pointed to the proposed 50 per cent increase in General Consumption Tax (GCT) affecting the industry, warning that the combination of additional tax and higher water rates could push some businesses closer to the brink.

“That could be a nail in the coffin for many of us,” Mais said of the tax proposal, adding that the proposed NWC increase could represent another.

While acknowledging that the 51 per cent water and sewerage rate increase had not been approved, Mais said he was concerned about the implications for businesses, their employees and the wider population.

The Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA), meanwhile, acknowledged the importance of reliable water supply and the NWC’s need to invest in infrastructure and maintain financially sustainable operations, but said more clarity was needed on the proposed adjustment.

JHTA President O’Brian Heron said a 51 per cent increase was significant and raised questions about how the new rates would affect the different categories of customers served by the NWC, particularly hotels and attractions, which rank among its larger commercial users.

“The NWC serves several classes of customers at different rates, and we need to understand how the proposed increase would apply across those classes, including what improvements customers could expect in return, particularly in service reliability, water quality and the reduction of system losses, and how soon those improvements would materialise.

“The JHTA is aware of the presentation made by the NWC to the Public Accounts Committee. We look forward to meaningful consultation with the NWC,” Heron said.

World.title: Trucker blockades in southern Italy ramp up pressure on Meloni
World.content:
Regarding the decree, she said her government would not be “blackmailed by those who use violence as an instrument of pressure.” But she cushioned that blow by acknowledging that financial relief measures were needed to offer "immediate responses, especially to workers, to people who are in difficulty, to families."

With elections expected in spring next year, the truckers’ protests threaten to shift the political debate from immigration and crime to whether Italians can afford to keep their businesses running.

Gaetano Amato, a lawmaker from Naples for the populist left 5Star Movement, accused the government of offering security measures instead of answers to the economic grievances driving the protests.

“The government has done nothing and is continuing to do nothing, because it is basing everything on security decrees,” he told POLITICO.

Stefano Orlacchio, president of the opposition center-left Democratic Party’s youth wing in the southern region of Campania, also slammed the government’s response as “an anti-southern attitude.”

“The protests in the south aren’t being taken into consideration at all,” he told POLITICO.

World.title: Farage plays down his Trump friendship in Britain — and talks it up to MAGA
World.content:
“Donald’s been a friend for many, many years. I’m a regular at Mar-a-Lago,” Farage boasted on the Benny Show. “I get on with many of his family. We have a laugh together — I mean, he’s a proper bloke.”

In Britain, Farage has publicly dampened his closeness to Trump as he tries to position himself as a contender for U.K. prime minister, particularly since the war with Iran.

“I haven’t really been in touch with Trump for many months,” Farage said in an interview with Times Radio in April, as the U.S. and Israel got bogged down in a price-spiking conflict with Tehran.

A spokesperson for Farage told POLITICO: “Nigel has never hidden his relationship with the President. However, he has been a critical friend over Canada, Greenland, Ukraine and various other issues.”

Farage, whose right-wing Reform insurgency has been a disruptive force to traditional British politics, had to correct his initial support for the war, which has been perceived negatively in U.K. from the off.

Initially Farage said that Britain should “do all we can” to support the U.S.-Israeli action in the Middle East. He’d later go on to say “let’s not get ourselves involved in another foreign war.”

World.title: First known human case of Shamonda virus confirmed in France
World.content:
They added that this is “an exceptional case in a highly immunocompromized patient,” and that there is “no health risk for the general population.”

Health authorities have highlighted the potential of zoonotic spillover — or the jump of diseases from animals to humans — being behind the next pandemic. Currently, over 60% of emerging infectious disease threats are of zoonotic origin, including Covid-19 and Ebola. As diseases adapt and jump from wild animals to pets to humans, their potential for pandemic threats evolves too. For this reason, scientists have been on high alert for the bird flu.

The Shamonda virus, which spreads between animals through bites from infected midges, was detected in European farm animals for the first time this year. It had previously been found only in countries outside Europe, predominantly in Africa. It is mainly observed in cattle, but there have been cases of infections in horses, sheep, goats and an alpaca.

Since the summer, the virus has been detected in farm animals in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said. In cattle, its symptoms include fever, diarrhea, lethargy, reduced milk production and mild respiratory signs.

It's still not clear whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired, the ECDC said. French authorities said they believe the patient might have been infected by a midge bite while in eastern France, an area where the virus has been circulating in animals since the spring.

The ECDC said it is “carefully monitoring the situation” and is in touch with French authorities and European partners to “investigate the potential public health implications of this first human infection.”

World.title: Macron tells local authorities to ban non-union protests on Saturday
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets, while incidents of vandalism and looting affected thousands of businesses and public buildings on the sidelines of the protests.

Calls for a fresh round of protests have already begun to emerge online, raising the possibility of a protest movement that becomes a weekly occurrence, as was the case during the 2018-2019 Yellow Vest movement.

“The president believes that six months before a presidential election, debate should take place more in TV studios, in newspapers, and ultimately by the choice at the ballot box,” a person close to the French president said.

Trade unions usually hold talks with local authorities ahead of planned demonstrations. For Saturday, authorities may offer “alternative routes” to ensure maximum security, Macron announced.

He added that he will chair a defense council Friday and announce “new decisions” afterward.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said elite tactical police units and a military unit normally deployed on French soil for counterterrorism operations would also be mobilized this weekend.

World.title: Brussels proposes delaying tuition fee demand till after UK-EU summit
World.content:
The diplomats — all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely about ongoing talks — said the proposal would involve asking the U.K. to commit to finalizing an agreement on tuition fees within six months. The proposal was first reported by the Financial Times.

The EU is pushing for European students to pay the domestic rate for tuition fees when studying at British universities, as they did before Brexit.

But one of the diplomats highlighted that the tuition fee demand was still part of a wider “package” linked to the other three agreements slated for the summit, and that the agreements would not enter into force until there was agreement on all areas.

In addition, the diplomats confirmed that both sides were considering a joint summit statement on economic security, amid mounting U.K. concerns about the EU’s Made in Europe proposals.

Meanwhile, negotiations on a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal — which would see the U.K. and EU align on agri-food standards — are close to completion, two of the diplomats said. The deal would include temporary arrangements for gene-edited plants and novel foods, such as lab-grown meat.

For gene-edited plants, the U.K. wants to keep its own rules until equivalent EU rules come into force, and has pledged not to change them in the meantime.

For novel foods, the U.K. would follow EU decisions to approve or reject products, but could set its own rules for products the EU has not yet assessed. In both cases, the products would be sold only in Great Britain and would not have access to the EU single market.

Dan Bloom contributed to this report

World.title: EU-Parlament will Methan-Vorschriften um drei Jahre verschieben
World.content:
Dies geschah nach einer monatelangen Kampagne von Öl- und Gasunternehmen. Sie machten geltend, dass wesentliche Elemente der Vorschriften, die sie zur Überwachung und Nachverfolgung von Leckagen des starken Treibhausgases verpflichten, unklar seien. Das berge die Gefahr von Verstößen, was dazu führen könnte, dass wichtige Lieferungen Europa nicht erreichen.

Mit seiner Haltung schließt sich das Parlament der Forderung der Industrie nach einer dreijährigen Verschiebung an. Die Abgeordneten schlossen sich den Bedenken der Branche hinsichtlich des Risikos von Versorgungsengpässen an, die mit einer übereilten Umsetzung der Vorschriften verbunden wären.

„Die Verschiebung der Anforderungen an Öl- und Gasimporteure im Rahmen der Methanverordnung ist eine Frage der politischen Verantwortung … Wir brauchen rechtssichere Vorschriften …, um die Energieversorgung und die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit Europas zu sichern“, erklärten die Europaabgeordneten Andrea Wechlser und Christian Ehler, beide von der EVP, in einer Stellungnahme gegenüber POLITICO.

„Die Krise im Nahen Osten übt bereits enormen Druck auf die Energiemärkte aus – etwa 20 Prozent des weltweiten LNG-Handels werden über die Straße von Hormus abgewickelt“, fügten sie hinzu.

Der Standpunkt des Parlaments könnte den nationalen Delegationen Rückenwind geben, die auf eine längere Frist drängen. Zuvor hatten sie sich am Mittwoch nach Widerstand seitens Deutschlands, Italiens und Polens nicht auf einen gemeinsamen Standpunkt einigen können. Die Mitgliedstaaten hoffen, am kommenden Mittwoch einen Kompromiss zu finden, nachdem sie daran zu Wochenbeginn gescheitert waren.

Dieser Artikel ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

World.title: Von der Leyen’s coalition fractures over need for AI liability rules
World.content:
Thursday’s plenary debate, in which discussions centered on a global framework to regulate AI, showed strong tensions inside Europe between the centrist coalition backing von der Leyen. While the center-left pushed for new rules to address a series of AI-fueled hacking incidents, the center-right doubled down on simplification to ensure European companies can compete in the global AI race.

Socialist and Green lawmakers called for a new AI Liability Act in a bid to hold AI companies liable for harm done by their models, as with more traditional manufacturers’ products.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman floated a similar idea for a new liability framework for companies whose models are capable of autonomous cyberattacks in the wake of this summer’s hack by autonomous OpenAI agents into another AI platform, Hugging Face.

“If a phone charger explodes in your house, we never call it innovative. We call it cheap, dangerous junk, and we hold the manufacturer liable for damages,” said Dutch Green European Parliament lawmaker Kim van Sparrentak.

She urged the Commission to “stop scrapping rules to please [U.S. President Donald] Trump” and come up with a “strong new liability act that covers the testing and the development of AI.”

The debate quickly descended into a fierce back-and-forth between key AI-focused lawmakers from von der Leyen’s centrist coalition.

World.title: EPP teams up with far right to win Parliament vote delaying EU methane law
World.content:
The requirements were due to come into force in 2027, but the Commission last week proposed delaying implementation by a year following intense lobbying from the oil and gas lobby and the U.S. government.

The EPP proposed going further, calling for a three-year delay. The amendment passed by 326 votes to 244, with the support of far-right groups Patriots for Europe, the group of Marine Le Pen's National Rally; and Europe of Sovereign Nations, the group of the German far-right party the AfD. Giorgia Meloni's European Conservatives and Reformists also backed the proposal.

Most lawmakers from other centrist and center-left groups, including Renew Europe, Socialists and Democrats and the Greens, opposed the three-year delay.

The right-wing majority also voted for an amendment that would force the Commission to review the law and propose any necessary changes by mid-2029.

It comes a year after the EPP — the group of Commission President Ursula von der Leyen — set a new precedent when it sided with the far right to vote to weaken environmental reporting rules for companies, breaching the so-called cordon sanitaire. Since 2024, right wing groups have made up a majority in Parliament.

Thursday's vote, if adopted by other EU institutions, would move the deadline for implementation of rules to 2030 — well beyond the Commission’s proposed delay to 2028.

World.title: Portuguese and Spanish unions in talks over 'Iberian general strike'
World.content:
Portuguese and Spanish trade unions are in contact with a view to organising a possible "Iberian general strike", Unai Sordo, secretary-general of CCOO (Comisiones Obreras), said on Thursday in an interview with the programme "Los Desayunos" (source in Portuguese) produced by Spanish broadcaster RTVE and the EFE news agency.

 

According to the Spanish union leader, Portuguese unions are considering calling a general strike on 11 November. A similar stoppage has already been scheduled in the neighbouring country for that date, bringing together, among others, Spain's two main trade union confederations, CCOO and UGT (General Workers' Union).

The aim, Sordo explained, is thus to give shape to an "Iberian general strike". However, he stressed that this will depend on the decision to be taken by trade union organisations in Portugal. "It is up to the Portuguese to decide whether, in the end, we join forces in a mobilisation across the Iberian Peninsula that would also be historic", the CCOO secretary-general said.

Jokingly, he also referred to the only Portuguese writer to have won the Nobel Prize in Literature, José Saramago, who not only spent almost two decades of his life living in Lanzarote, in the Canary Islands, but also maintained an inseparable link with the progressive movements of his time. "If they hold [the strike] in Portugal, we are going to call it the Saramago strike", Sordo concluded.

The general strike in Spain on 11 November has been a foregone conclusion for several weeks, having been scheduled for 18 days before the snap elections called by the country's prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after parliament rejected measures proposed by the national government to tackle the housing crisis.

Both countries have, in fact, seen various initiatives to defend that right and to oppose the rising cost of living. Taking inspiration from the protests that began, at the end of September, in Puerta del Sol, one of the most famous squares in the Spanish capital, Madrid, thousands of demonstrators spent several nights camping out in the centres of Portuguese cities such as Porto and Lisbon.

The demands in both cases are the same: protesters are calling for decent housing at affordable prices, with many complaining that having a job is no longer enough to be able to rent a flat in the major urban centres.

World.title: Women protest across Poland over stalled abortion law reforms
World.content:
Women in Poland are demonstrating in more than 20 cities and towns on Thursday to protest against restrictions on access to free and legal abortion.

 

Protesters accuse Prime Minister Donald Tusk's liberal government of failing to deliver on its promise to ease the country's strict abortion laws, despite parliament passing two bills on Tuesday aimed at relaxing the rules. Both measures are expected to face a veto from conservative President Karol Nawrocki.

Zofia Marcinek of the Warsaw-based reproductive rights group Abortion Dream Team described the legislation as a series of "token gestures" rather than a genuine attempt at reform, arguing that the government was aware the bills were unlikely to survive a presidential veto.

She accused the government of trying to win back women's support ahead of next year's parliamentary election by appearing to take action on abortion rights.

What the two abortion bills propose

Poland's parliament voted on Tuesday to ease the country's strict abortion laws, which are among the most restrictive in the European Union.

The first bill, proposed by Tusk's Civic Coalition (KO) and the Left, would partially decriminalise abortion and remove criminal penalties for assisting someone in obtaining one, an offence currently punishable by up to three years in prison.

The second bill, introduced by the more conservative coalition partners Poland 2050 and the Polish Peasants' Party (PSL), would overturn the effects of a 2020 Constitutional Tribunal ruling that banned abortion in cases of severe foetal abnormalities.

The first bill passed with 217 votes in favour, 213 against and three abstentions, while the second was approved by 233 votes to 203, with one abstention.

Where the protests are taking place

Alongside full decriminalisation, protesters are demanding access to legal abortion up to the 12th week of pregnancy, full access to the "morning-after" pill, and action by local authorities to disperse illegal protests held outside hospitals in Warsaw and Gdańsk and the AboTak clinic in Warsaw.

Demonstrations are planned in 26 Polish cities as well as in London.

World.title: Judge orders Trump to sit for a deposition in his BBC defamation lawsuit by December 11
World.content:
A federal judge on Thursday ordered US President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by 11 December in his $10 billion (€8.6 billion) defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

 

The order by US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came after the BBC's lawyers accused Trump of delaying his appearance.

Trump could face sanctions, including the possible dismissal of his lawsuit, if he fails to comply, unless the discovery period is extended beyond 18 December.

Charles Tobin, an attorney representing the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”

Tobin said Trump had initially agreed to be deposed on 16 October but cancelled, citing a “matter of national importance.” However, the president was campaigning in Georgia that day, according to the lawyer.

“He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.

US President Donald Trump listens to Senate candidate Mike Collins at a campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, on 16 October 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Trump filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December 2025, accusing the British broadcaster of defamation and deceptive and unfair trade practices over a documentary titled “Trump: A Second Chance.”

The 33-page lawsuit accused the broadcaster of presenting a “false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump,” describing it as “a brazen attempt to interfere in and influence” the 2024 US presidential election.

The BBC admitted to editing together parts of Trump's 6 January 2021 speech, making it appear he had encouraged violence at the US Capitol. The broadcaster apologised, and two senior executives resigned, but it denied defamation.

World.title: MEPs call for Yemen's Houthis to be added to EU terrorist list
World.content:
The European Parliament on Thursday approved a resolution calling for Yemen's Houthis to be added to the EU’s list of terrorist organisations.

 

The call follows an escalation in recent weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Iran-backed group, which prompted the UK to pledge defensive missions to protect Riyadh, while the EU struggles to increase its naval presence in the Red Sea to shield commercial vessels from possible attacks.

The non-binding text, adopted by a large majority of MEPs in a show of hands, urged the freezing of all funds and economic resources belonging to the Houthis and their facilitators.

Inclusion on the EU terrorist list mainly entails financial restrictions — freezing all bank accounts and property held in EU countries, and banning EU individuals and companies from financing the listed group.

The final decision rests with the EU member states, which must approve any new listing unanimously.

The European Parliament justified its request by condemning the Houthi naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and their attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb strait, which are severely disrupting maritime traffic and driving up energy prices in the region.

The resolution describes the attacks as flagrant violations of international law, stressing that many Yemeni civilians have been killed and displaced, and that the country’s humanitarian crisis has deepened since the latest attacks.

The group formally known as Ansar Allah, which has been at war with the internationally recognised government of Yemen since 2014, launched a blitz offensive along the Red Sea coast in July to take control of the vital waterway crucial to the world's energy and cargo shipping.

A counteroffensive by the Saudi-led coalition saw much of the gains made by the Houthis reversed, but the group still poses a threat to international vessels traversing the strait that links Europe and Asia.

The Houthis have pledged safe passage to all ships bar those linked to Saudi Arabia, while continuing their attacks against energy infrastructure and airports across the neighbouring kingdom.

MEPs also stressed the crucial role of Aspides, the EU naval mission in the Red Sea, and urged member states to provide additional naval and air assets.

The mission currently has three ships from Italy and Greece, with two more pledged by Belgium and the Netherlands. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has said at least 10 are needed.

World.title: How migration is reshaping the political debate in Spain's Ceuta
World.content:
More than two months after over 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco on July 30 and 31, the crisis continues to shape political debate in the Spanish enclave ahead of next month's election.

 

Some residents say the government's response has influenced their voting intentions, while others are calling for a tougher stance on migration. Esperanza Ansede, a teacher who previously voted for Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialists, says she now plans to vote for the centre-right Popular Party. Gema Miralles, a beautician who identifies with the right, says she wants right-wing parties to take a tougher stance on migration, particularly in Ceuta.

Meanwhile, community leader Ahmed Enfed-Dal warns that right-wing rhetoric has become more radicalised and urges left-wing parties to unite against the far right.

Watch the video to hear from Ceuta residents.

World.title: France: Artists and collectors gather at Art Basel Paris despite unrest
World.content:
The fair’s fifth edition gathers 211 galleries from 41 countries, with public days running from Friday 23 to Sunday 25 October. Visitors explored works by artists including Yayoi Kusama, Julian Schnabel and Matthew Wong, alongside new paintings by American artist Drake Carr.

 

The fair’s Emergence section also showcased more experimental installations, with 16 solo booths dedicated to emerging practices. Artist Yann Stéphane Bisso highlighted the opportunity to present work beyond conventional commercial formats.

The event is taking place under heightened security following violent protests in the French capital. Anti-ram barriers and security guards surround the Grand Palais, while organisers are coordinating with Paris police over possible adjustments.

Art Basel Paris director Karim Crippa said a comprehensive security plan had been prepared and activated, adding that the safety of exhibitors, staff, visitors and artworks was the priority. Indian collector Saloni Doshi described witnessing fires, protesters and scenes of panic on her arrival in Paris, leaving her concerned about fellow visitors travelling from abroad.

Despite the tense atmosphere outside, the fair continued to welcome collectors and art enthusiasts, with works also displayed in public spaces around the Grand Palais.

World.title: Germany: Humanoid robots and AI supercomputers take centre stage in Berlin
World.content:
At Nvidia’s GTC conference, visitors can explore a range of live demonstrations, from robotic arms sorting objects and fruit into boxes to facial recognition systems identifying people in real time. Other exhibits showcase humanoid robots, interactive safety technology and Nvidia’s latest AI computing hardware.

 

The company’s Vera Rubin NVL72 supercomputer rack is attracting attention alongside its RTX Spark devices, illustrating the growing range of applications for AI technology. Nvidia has also unveiled the Vera Rubin DSK Pod, a modular, container-sized AI data centre designed to cut deployment times from months to days.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang addressed about 3,000 developers, analysts and journalists, showcasing the company’s push to bring AI beyond software and into factories, vehicles and robots.

During his keynote, Huang demonstrated small robots and outlined the company’s ambitions for AI across European industries. “There’s no question everybody will become an AI company, and we’re going to have a thriving AI economy here in Europe,” he told the audience.

The event, which runs until 22 October, highlights how AI is moving beyond software into robotics, industrial automation and increasingly powerful computing systems. But as governments and businesses explore these opportunities, researchers are also emphasising the importance of developing technology that remains safe, reliable and useful to people.

World.title: Albania's student protests are only getting bigger
World.content:
As police try to suppress anti-corruption protests by young Albanians, Prime Minister Edi Rama is claiming that "antifa" is behind the unrest. Few are buying that explanation.

The fallout from the October 13 protests was still visible when students and faculty from the University of Tirana gathered outside the Education Ministry in Albania's capital on Tuesday to express their continued discontent. Smashed windows have yet to be replaced; the walls are still black with soot from fires that broke out during the protests.

Albania has seen nearly five months of peaceful anti-government protests, sparked initially when plans were made public that Jared Kushner — a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump — and associates intended to build a luxury hotel complex within a nature reserve.

Since then, anti-government and anti-corruption protests have escalated. Now, college and high school students clash with police forces almost daily, with the fiercest clashes so far occurring last week.

Why Albania's political crisis is deepening To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Protesters denounce corruption, mismanaged universities and the rising cost of education in Albania — and call for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in office since 2013.

Wearing a black hooded jacket and a scarf across her face to conceal her identity, a woman who asked to be called Sara because she fears repercussions for speaking to the press told DW that protesters "communicate via text messages — that's the only way."

She cut the interview short as some protesters began flinging stones at the Education Ministry. Police pushed demonstrators and journalists out of the way, using water cannons to disperse the crowd.

"Social media is the most important public space today — more so than physical spaces," Besmir Semanaj, a prominent Albanian cybersecurity advocate told DW. "Young Albanians no longer organize through traditional structures such as political parties, associations or public appeals. Instead, they organize themselves where they spend much of their daily lives: on their cellphones."

"The most important communication channels include Instagram, WhatsApp groups for academic-year cohorts, departments and dormitories, Telegram channels for general announcements, and TikTok for sharing videos," Semanaj said. He added that people who are especially concerned with security use the Signal messaging app.

"This is a horizontal organizational structure, without individual 'leaders' and without a central command structure," Semanaj said. "That is exactly why the government is having such a hard time understanding and controlling the situation."

Semanaj said the Telegram messenger app had proven particularly useful for protesters. "Telegram channels allow you to reach tens of thousands of people at once," he said. "Notifications are sent out within seconds, and external control is more difficult to establish than on traditional platforms."

Anti-corruption protester "Sara" says communication occurs online Image: Kristi Çavo/DW

Rama: 'Hybrid war'

Rama has called the youth uprising a "hybrid war." He said protesters thought they could "make Albania a better country through TikTok and without even being able to string together more than seven coherent words." Though not all are terrorists, he said, he believes that "they are hostages to a certain mindset, a new ideology that has only one goal: to destroy, to turn everything upside down, to raze everything to the ground."

Over nearly five months, Rama has accused various "true" masterminds of organizing the anti-government and anti-corruption protests. He has alleged that the governments of Greece, Russia and Iran are stirring up dissent.

Most recently, Rama said it was "antifa" — or a decentralized movement of global antifascists — that had stoked anti-government and anti-corruption sentiments in Albania. "These are young people who have been radicalized and ideologically indoctrinated and who are acting under the pressure or influence of a new, dark force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, a force that the President of the United States has designated as a terrorist organization: Antifa," Rama claimed.

A protester hurls back a tear gas canister fired at students by police Image: Florion Goga/REUTERS

Redion Qirjazi, a security affairs researcher who focuses on violence prevention and conflict resolution, told DW that Rama's claim was not likely to prove true. "That is a serious accusation — one that requires equally compelling evidence," Qirjazi said. "To date, no verifiable evidence has been presented to prove the existence of an organized Antifa structure in Albania, let alone its involvement in coordinating the protests."

Qirjazi said Rama's reference to Trump's calling antifa a terror group was problematic. "Antifa is not a unified international organization with a centralized structure or leadership," he said, "but rather an umbrella term for various movements and groups united by the fact that they are, at their core, anti-fascist."

Sara said she rejected the "terrorist" label that Rama had attempted to slap on her and her fellow protesters. "There are groups that are willing to use violence — that's true — but I have nothing to do with them," she said. "As soon as I see violence, I walk away; I'm against it."

Is Rama deflecting?

Arlind Qori, the chairman of the Together Movement, a social-democratic opposition party with just one seat in Albania's parliament, said youths had taken to the streets out of dissatisfaction with the status quo rather than any particular ideology. "Young Albanians are outraged by the current socioeconomic conditions: the poverty, the fact that many of their parents have emigrated because they couldn't support their families, the decline of the education system, the lack of postgraduation prospects," Qori said. The students' central demand is for Rama to resign, he added "not a socialist revolution."

Arlind Qori says the protesters are voicing legitimate demands Image: Kristi Çavo/DW

"People aren't demanding anything radical," Qori said. "They merely want a corrupt head of government to resign — that's a fundamental and moderate demand. But Edi Rama continues to meet this demand with police violence and arrogance."

Qirjazi said Rama's allegations of foreign interference could be a strategy. "When a government faces protests and public discontent, linking demonstrators to extremism and foreign influence may serve to divert attention away from the actual causes and toward a national security narrative," he said.

"This can serve several political purposes: to delegitimize the protesters, to weaken their support among the public, and to justify a tougher crackdown in the name of law and order," Qirjazi said.

Semanaj said this was a common pattern in governments' efforts to dismiss dissent. "Protests are portrayed as acts of violence," he said. "Young people are cast as manipulated, and their legitimate concerns — conditions at universities, tuition fees, corruption and a lack of prospects — vanish from the news agenda."

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Lina Attalah: Mada Masr journalist sent for trial in Egypt
World.content:
Lina Attalah, who is accused of managing a website without a license, will go to court next week. Mada Masr has published reporting critical of Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.

Egypt's Supreme State Security Prosecution sent Mada Masr journalist Lina Attalah to stand for trial, the independent Egyptian news website said Thursday.

One of Madr Masar's co-founders, Attalah serves as the site's editor-in-chief. The website, which publishes in both Arabic and English, frequently features critical reporting related to Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.

What do we know so far?

Prosecutors questioned Attalah for six hours on Wednesday in New Cairo, Mada Masr said.

She is accused of running a website without a license and the publication of false news "with the aim of disturbing public peace." Under questioning, the latter allegation was dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.

The trial has been referred to a New Cairo misdemeanors court and is slated to begin on October 27.

Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr's legal counsel, said there was "haste" in the trial referral and said the trial beginning next week signals "unjustified urgency."

Al-Azhari said Attalah could face a financial penalty of between 1 million to 3 million Egyptian pounds (around €16,000 to €48,000; $18,000 to $54,000) if convicted.

Mada Masr said the organization has sought a license from the Egyptian government to run its news website since 2018 — the same year Egypt passed and ratified a law to regulate the press.

Egyptian authorities have been unresponsive over the past years to Mada Masr's attempts to procure a license, with Mada Masr later finding out in 2022 that its request was rejected. The site filed a lawsuit in 2022 and found out in 2023 that the rejection was due to missing documents.

The proceedings against Attalah come after Egyptian authorities arrested six journalists last month for independent fact-checking and investigative website Matsadaash (Egyptian Arabic for "don't believe").

Press freedom groups condemn actions against Attalah

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) expressed alarm about Attalah's referral to trial.

"Egypt is weaponizing its media law to punish independent journalism and intensify one of its worst crackdowns in years, which began with the arrest of the six Matsdaash journalists," the CPJ's director for Middle East and North Africa Sara Qudah said. "It is long past time for Egypt to end this campaign and allow independent media to report freely."

Reporters without Borders (RSF) had earlier said it was alarmed by prosecutors' questioning of Attalah.

According to RSF's World Press Freedom Index , Egypt ranks 169 out of 180 countries, with many of the country's biggest news outlets either state-owned or controlled by wealthy businessmen who submit to the will of the government.

Egyptian President el-Sissi came to power in a 2013 military coup against Islamist President Mohamed Morsi. Since then, el-Sissi has cracked down and blocked websites such as Qatar's Al Jazeera and The New Arab on allegations of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood.

World.title: 96% of world's coral reefs face critical risk of collapse, IUCN warns
World.content:
Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs are at risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change the biggest threat. A new study found that 96% of reef systems are critically endangered.

Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change being the greatest threat, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Thursday.

In the first systematic survey of the world's 127 tropical and subtropical coral reef systems, the IUCN said 96% were critically endangered, which is its highest risk category.

Shallow-water reefs are colorful coral ecosystems found at depths of up to around 40 meters (131 feet), and are home to a high level of biodiversity.

Among the reefs affected are Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Reef System and the reefs in the Red Sea.

"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said when it presented the study at the United Nations' COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.

Coral reefs are home to a high level of biodiversity Image: Yuddy Cahya Budiman/REUTERS

What are the threats to the reefs?

Worldwide, shallow-water reefs cover around 188,000 square kilometers(73,000 square miles).

Their corals are highly sensitive to temperature changes. This means when the water gets too warm, the corals expel the tiny algae living in their tissues, which provide much of their nourishment.

This then leads to coral bleaching and can ultimately lead to their death.

Overfishing is another major threat. In particular, the overfishing of parrotfish and groupers affects reef ecosystems since these fish help maintain ecological balance.

Coastal development, pollution, tourism and increasingly severe storms also contribute to reef degradation.

When hard corals disappear, their structures are often replaced by algae, rubble and sponges, leaving less diverse ecosystems that do not sustain as many species. Affected animals include reef fish, mussels, sea turtles, and sharks.

Sea turtles are among the animals that depend on coral reefs Image: Great Barrier Reef Foundation/dpa/picture alliance

Can the reefs still be saved?

"The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems," according to Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

The study uses a climate scenario developed by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which expects global warming of around 2.7 degrees Celsius (4.86 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

Despite the bleak outlook, the IUCN said most reefs had not yet been lost. Without projections of future climate change and based on the changes over the past 50 years, only 24% would qualify as critically endangered.

"This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring," Gudka explained.

"The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people," he added.

IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar said it was "not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover."

"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," she said.

World.title: Canada's Mark Carney visits Turkey to boost trade ties
World.content:
It's the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey. Canada and Turkey upgraded their relations to a "strategic partnership" as Canada seeks to diversify trade beyond the US.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Turkey on Thursday to kick off a two-day visit to the Mediterranean country.

During the visit, Carney met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the Turkish presidential palace in Ankara.

Erdogan: A 'new era' in Turkey-Canada relations

The two leaders announced that the Canadian-Turkish relationship would be upgraded to a "strategic partnership," covering areas such as trade, energy and people-to-people ties.

"We've planted the seeds of something new: a strategic partnership that will create new opportunities for our workers and businesses, and greater security and prosperity for both of our peoples. With care and commitment, it will grow for generations to come," Carney said alongside Erdogan.

Erdogan said we "are starting a new era between Turkey and Canada," while hailing Carney as a leader with "common-sense and acumen." The Turkish leader said negotiations on a free trade agreement with Canada will begin before the end of 2026.

"We hope to increase our trade volume, which is currently around $3 billion (€2.6 billion), to $5 billion and then $10 billion. We will approximately double direct flights between our countries," Erdogan continued.

Turkey has a bigger military than Canada and is a global leader in drone production Image: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/PA Images/picture alliance

Canada and Turkey, both members of the NATO military alliance, agreed to deepen their defense relationship during the visit.

Canada seeks to diversify trade relationships amid Trump tariff onslaught

The Canadian prime minister, a former central banker, is expected to meet with Turkish business leaders on Friday in Istanbul.

Carney's visit comes as Canada seeks to broaden its trade relationships with other countries beyond its southern neighbor. Nearly 70% of Canadian exports go to the United States.

Since reentering office in 2025, US President Donald Trump escalated a trade war against Canada and imposed tariffs on many Canadian goods, leading Canada to wean itself off the US.

Turkey has a population of over 86 million people and the world's 16th-largest nominal GDP as of 2026. Canada, meanwhile, has a population of over 41 million people and the 11th-largest GDP.

Amnesty tells Canada: Emphasize human rights in negotiations with Turkey

Carney's visit to Turkey also comes as Erdogan and his conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP) crack down on the opposition and critical media. In addition, the Turkish government has targeted the LGBTQ+ community with mass arrests.

LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ruhat Sena Aksenir, the Turkey director of human rights watchdog Amnesty International, said: "Canada must not treat human rights as secondary in the negotiations."

"Sustainable partnerships depend on accountability and respect for the rule of law," she continued.

The AKP has ruled Turkey since 2002, with the party, and particularly Erdogan, consolidating power.

According to human rights organization Freedom House , Turkey is "not free" and scores low in the areas of political rights and civil liberties. Reporters without Borders ranks Turkey 163 out of 180 on its World Press Freedom Index .

World.title: France's Macron says 'illegitimate' protests will be banned in coming days
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to ban unauthorized protests after France was rocked by violence and looting. As anger over public services and the cost of living grows, authorities are bracing for more protests.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that demonstrations organized by groups without legitimate authority would be banned in the coming days.

Over the past weekend, protests over the education system and the cost of living escalated into violence and looting, which the government blamed on ultra-left groups.

"Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic," Macron said after a special security meeting at the Elysee Palace with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers.

"The general recommendation is not to hold demonstrations in the coming days," he explained. "We want calm to return."

French business owners share harrowing accounts of violent protests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Macron said the ban on protests aimed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.

"Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law, but alternative routes will be proposed," he added.

Fresh demonstration in Paris

In the wake of the past weekend’s violence, several cities had already implemented curfews for certain parts of town. Protests planned Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were banned from going ahead.

Authorities say a massive security operation was planned for the coming weekend to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence.

The historic city hall in Limoges was set on fire and partly collapsed on October 17 Image: Elise Cabane/PHOTOPQR/Populaire du Centre/MAXPPP/IMAGO

Student and university groups as well as unions have said they would continue to mobilize and hold protests. On Thursday, thousands gathered in Paris when a local court was said to have overturned the day's demonstration ban.

France's main student union, UNEF, has called for rallies on Saturday, while the Yellow Vest movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook the country in 2018 and 2019, has filed plans for a march through central Paris.

France: Why students are taking to the streets To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What are the protests about?

The protests started in September at a school near Paris over lack of funding for the education system.

The demonstrations then spread to other Paris suburbs and eventually to other French cities. They have since widened to also address the soaring cost of living and deteriorating public services.

On October 17, the protests escalated into the worst urban unrest in years when masked rioters clashed with police, looted shops and set cars and buildings on fire.

Two people have been arrested over an arson attack on the 19th-century Limoges city hall, French media reported.

Across France, there were around 2,700 arrests last weekend and hundreds of protesters, police and firefighters were injured.

French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said courts jailed 217 people in fast-track trials linked to rioting over the weekend, adding "this figure is continuing to rise a lot."

Macron on Thursday said talks between authorities, student groups, unions, and employers would take place on Monday. He stressed that dialogue over protesters' legitimate demands should continue.

The unrest comes just months before next year's presidential election, in which voters will choose Macron's successor.

World.title: Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
World.content:
As protests continue in France, the French police are under scrutiny after new allegations of police brutality. The force has a bigger arsenal than most in Europe.

Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.

The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups , not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.

France's protests grow

More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.

Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.

The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.

More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.

Some tools used by the French police are banned or rarely used in other countries Image: Manon Cruz/REUTERS

Weapons made for war?

The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.

Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.

"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."

Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.

What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.

"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.

Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material ."

France: Why students are taking to the streets To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

French police: the 'most brutal' in the EU?

The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.

"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Roche.

He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.

"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."

Confrontation vs. de-escalation

Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.

Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.

"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."

Police arrested protesters in the German town of Lützerath, but with less force than at similar protests in France Image: Federico Gambarini/dpa/picture alliance

When can police officers use force?

According to international standards set by the United Nations , use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.

French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.

However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."

The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.

DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.

"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."

Experts are critical of the police's actions.

"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."

Less oversight than in the UK and Denmark

The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.

Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.

"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
World.content:
Iranian officials say the goal is to keep the regime in power and threaten enough regional costs to make a prolonged campaign unattractive. US media reports indicate that Trump is considering strikes after the midterms.

Officials in Tehran are preparing for renewed strikes

following media reports that the United States and Israel have been examining new options for escalating their war against Iran.

The US midterm elections on November 3 and Israel's October 27 election have injected a political factor into how both countries are approaching the conflict, which they launched in late February.

Polls show that high energy prices brought on by the Iran war are hurting Donald Trump's Republican Party. On October 8, the president posted on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, citing "productive discussions" with Tehran. The United States last launched strikes on Iran in early September.

After the elections are over, however, Trump may feel less politically constrained.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Iran.

Analysts say Iran's regime is preparing to clamp down on unrest unleashed by possible US strikes [FILE: 2022] Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Report: Plans in place for 'short' US-Israeli operation

Citing senior US officials the New York Times reported on Wednesday that the United States and Israel have "developed specific plans" for a "short but intensive operation" in Iran that would include targets such as nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure, and the country's arsenal of missiles and drones.

One official told the newspaper that the goal would be to force Iran into making "diplomatic concessions" by further weakening its economy, as negotiations to end the conflict have gone nowhere. The United States has also maintained a blockade of Iranian oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz that has sapped Tehran's oil revenues.

Other outlets have reported similar plans in recent weeks. In early October, Axios reported that the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command "to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran."

There are currently two US aircraft carrier strike groups in the Arabian Sea, with a third expected to arrive by late November.

On October 15, Trump told the right-wing broadcaster Newsmax that he was considering a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, where US officials say Iran may have moved sensitive nuclear-related material underground.

A day later, CNN reported that Trump is considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb on Iranian targets. As the MOAB creates a humungous blast wave above ground, its effectiveness in targeting underground facilities such as Pickaxe would be limited.

Has Iran learned from earlier attacks?

Iranian officials say they are prepared for another attack, with a broad response that would include strikes on US bases and energy facilities in the Gulf.

Ali Asghar Shafieian, a media adviser to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, told DW that, although the United States retains a significant technological and military advantage, Tehran's strategy is based on preserving the regime's hold on the country rather than matching US strength.

"The United States has the upper hand in military power and technology, but Iran's strength is in how it deals with a crisis," Shafieian said.

Shafieian pointed to the rapid replacement of senior officials killed in previous attacks as an example of how Tehran has tried to make its political structure more resilient. Iran has also been rebuilding missile and drone capabilities that were hit during the massive wave of strikes during the first weeks of the war.

Citing Iranian officials, the Reuters news agency reported this week that Iran is "preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," adding that Tehran was prolonging negotiations to try to weaken Trump ahead of the midterms.

Iran has told regional governments that US military bases and critical infrastructure could become targets if neighboring countries assist another US or Israeli operation.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that participation or cooperation by regional states would result in a "decisive and proportionate response."

"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," Araghchi posted on X Wednesday. "But, if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."

US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How Iran prepares for new strikes?

Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based political analyst, told DW that Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security.

That includes confronting armed opposition groups, preparing for possible protests and developing plans to prevent external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.

Another conflict, he said, could bring renewed internet restrictions and a stronger mobilization of government supporters in public spaces.

"In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible," Ghahremanpour said.

Ghahremanpour added that some factions within Iran have supported returning to a negotiated agreement. But he believes that Washington's demands are now considered so extensive that even Iranian officials who favor compromise struggle to build domestic support for them.

"For now, we are facing a deadlock," Ghahremanpour said. "Iranian officials do not appear optimistic about reaching an agreement."

Talks continue to snag on Iran's nuclear program, which US officials say must top the agenda.

Iran's latest proposal to the United States, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control, in exchange for the US's lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending military actions.

Citing data from the ship tracker Kpler, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers and shipping companies are more willing to take risks for a bigger payoff. This raises questions about whether Iran's leverage over oil flows might be weakening.

Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal is reached To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fear of war inside Iran

An escalation in the confrontation would come at a moment of severe economic pressure and growing political polarization for Iranians.

A doctor in Tehran told DW that she fears what would happen should fighting resumed. Speaking with the media in Iran remains very dangerous, and she spoke under condition of anonymity.

"The economic situation has become extremely bad," she said. "Even if you have a good income yourself, you don't feel good living among so many people struggling with poverty," she added.

She expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes.

A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of confrontations on the streets.

Asked about possible attacks on underground nuclear sites, she said the issue felt increasingly detached from her everyday problems.

"What do the nuclear sites have to do with us?" she said. "They are inside mountains."

Iran's regime: inside the system protecting its rulers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited: Emmy Sasipornkarn

World.title: Is EU putting profits over human rights in Vietnam?
World.content:
The EU and Vietnam are deepening economic and diplomatic ties, but closer cooperation raises concerns about whether Brussels is doing enough to address Hanoi's human rights record, labor standards and trade imbalances.

Vietnam's Communist Party chief and president, To Lam, arrived in Brussels on Wednesday for an official visit to the European Union (EU) and Belgium in another sign that relations continue to expand.

The visit comes just days after Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

Trade ties between Vietnam and Europe have deepened in recent years. The EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), which took effect in August 2020, substantially expanded Vietnam's commercial ties with most European states.

Amid global tariff wars, the EU-Vietnam relationship "is a welcome  for keeping markets open," Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW.

"This is a win-win for both sides," he said. "Vietnam offers Europe an established manufacturing base and another foothold in Asian supply chains. Europe offers Vietnam capital, technology and a large market, helping Hanoi reduce its exposure to American demand and Chinese industrial inputs."

Vietnam-EU ties deepen

Vietnam is now the EU's largest goods-trading partner in Southeast Asia and its 14th-largest globally. The EU is Vietnam's fourth-largest trading partner and a major source of foreign investment.

Noneconomic relations are also advancing. In January, both sides upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership — the first such agreement between the EU and a Southeast Asian country.

Vietnam has become a key strategic partner for the EU in the Indo-Pacific, Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW.

"The cooperation is crucial for advancing the EU's economic security agenda and its strategy of de-risking from China," he said, referring to the European Union's efforts to diversify its supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing.

Several EU states have signed defense agreements with Vietnam. Bloc foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas held talks with Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung on Wednesday to discuss ways to improve security cooperation, including in the South China Sea, where Hanoi is locked in territorial disputes with China.

Concerns over Vietnam's human rights record

The relationship has also faced difficulties. Questions remain over whether European companies are benefiting sufficiently from Vietnam's economic boom and whether Brussels is overlooking Hanoi's worsening human rights record.

Vietnam remains a one-party communist state that severely restricts political opposition, independent journalism and civil society. Rights organizations say repression has intensified under To Lam, who previously headed the country's powerful public security ministry.

In an open letter sent this week to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa, 12 international human rights organizations raised "grave concerns over the Vietnamese government's intensifying repression" and urged EU leaders to demand meaningful reforms.

When negotiating the EVFTA and the accompanying political agreements, Hanoi agreed to obligations on human rights, labor protections and environmental standards.

These included commitments to reform labor legislation to permit independent worker organizations and align domestic regulations more closely with International Labour Organization (ILO) standards.

Rights groups say Hanoi has failed to deliver. Vietnam has still not ratified the ILO convention on freedom of association, and independent trade unions remain prohibited.

"The EU has taken no action in response to Vietnam's repeated breaches of its EVFTA-related obligations and pledges; instead, in January it upgraded bilateral relations," the joint letter read.

Vietnam signed a free-trade agreement with four European countries — Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein — in Hanoi, on October, 18, 2026 Image: Hoang Thong Nhat/Vietnam News Agency/AP Photo/picture alliance

Benefits 'distributed unevenly'

There are also questions about which Vietnamese companies have benefited most from the EU's trade liberalization.

Large foreign-invested manufacturers and established exporters have been better placed to exploit tariff reductions than smaller domestic businesses, which often lack the resources to navigate Europe's complex import requirements.

Vietnamese exporters also face growing demands from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and its deforestation regulations, which require businesses in affected sectors to provide more detailed information about their production processes and supply chains.

"It is quite clear that the EVFTA's benefits have been distributed unevenly across sectors, firms and social groups, while political, regulatory, and economic challenges may complicate the next phase of the relationship," Hai Thiem Bui, a researcher at the Stockholm Center for Global Asia, Stockholm University, told DW.

"The next phase of EU-Vietnam trade relations is likely to depend less on tariff liberalization and more on whether Vietnam can adapt to increasingly demanding EU standards concerning labor rights, sustainability, and regulatory governance," he added.

Better for EU?

Another challenge concerns how much European businesses are gaining from Vietnam's expanding export economy.

Although the EVFTA has considerably strengthened bilateral commerce, it has been far more successful at increasing Vietnamese exports to Europe than EU sales to Vietnam.

The EU's goods-trade deficit with Vietnam reached €51.7 billion ($57.9 billion) in 2025 — up from roughly €24 billion in 2019.

This imbalance is becoming more conspicuous as Brussels seeks greater economic security and new export opportunities for EU industries.

Is Vietnam set to replace China as the world's factory? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Another obstacle is the EU-Vietnam Investment Protection Agreement , signed in 2019, which has still not entered into force.

"We have also seen an uptick in investments by European businesses in Vietnam, despite the lack of an Investment Protection Agreement being in place," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.

Germany ratified it in February and Poland followed in April, but France, the Netherlands and several other member states have yet to complete ratification.

The agreement will strengthen legal protections for investors and establish a permanent mechanism for resolving investment disputes, potentially encouraging greater EU investment in Vietnam.

"With a new government in Vietnam pursuing an ambitious legislative program but with an overall target of maintaining Vietnam's extraordinary growth path, we would expect trade to continue to flourish," Humphrey said.

"That said, many European businesses are looking carefully at what the legislative program may bring in terms of reform," he added.

For Brussels, the next phase of relations is about ensuring that EU businesses benefit from that growth, while demonstrating that its commitments to human rights and sustainable trade are more than diplomatic promises.
