World.title: Prague’s Indian Community to Celebrate Navratri With Music and Dance
World.content:
The Indian community in Prague will gather for an evening of traditional music, dancing and food on Saturday, October 24, as Navratri 2026 returns to Top Hotel Prague.

Organized by Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj, the event will celebrate the cultural traditions of Gujarat, a state in western India known for its distinctive music, colourful clothing and energetic folk dances.

The programme will start at 5 pm and is open to people interested in Indian culture and traditions.



The celebration will feature Garba and Dandiya Raas, two traditional dances closely associated with Navratri festivities in Gujarat.

Visitors will also have an opportunity to enjoy Indian food, see traditional clothing and learn more about Gujarati culture.

Garba will be one of the main attractions of the event. The traditional Gujarati folk dance is performed in circles, with participants moving rhythmically to music and following a series of coordinated steps. The dance is closely associated with Navratri, a Hindu festival celebrated over nine nights in honour of the goddess Durga and the feminine divine.

Dandiya Raas is another traditional dance associated with the festival. Participants dance in pairs or groups while striking decorated wooden sticks together in time with the music. The movements, rhythms and colourful outfits make it one of the most recognisable features of Gujarati Navratri celebrations.

Beyond the dancing, the event will offer visitors an opportunity to explore different aspects of Gujarati culture, including traditional clothing and Indian food.

Traditional clothing is also an important part of the festivities. Women often wear colourful chaniya cholis, while men may dress in traditional kediyu outfits. Embroidery, decorative patterns and bright colours are common features of clothing worn for Garba and Dandiya Raas.

Tickets and further information are available on the Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj website.

World.title: Czech Constitutional Court Rules Sex Workers Must Pay Taxes
World.content:
The Czech Constitutional Court has ruled that income from voluntary sex work is subject to taxation, placing it on the same footing as earnings from other self-employed professions.

The decision clarifies that collecting taxes from sex workers does not amount to state approval of the activity.

The case concerned a woman who was ordered to pay more than CZK 900,000 in back taxes for income earned from paid sexual services in 2013 and 2014.



She challenged the assessment in court, but lower courts upheld the decision of the Czech Financial Administration. She subsequently appealed to the Constitutional Court, Novinky reported.

The woman argued that taxing prostitution effectively turned the state into a pimp, pointing to the distinction in Czech law between providing sexual services voluntarily for payment and acting as an intermediary in such activities.

While the former is not a criminal offense, procuring or facilitating prostitution in certain circumstances can be punishable under the Criminal Code.

The Constitutional Court rejected her argument, ruling that taxation serves a different purpose. According to the judges, the state is not profiting from another person’s labor but ensuring that taxpayers contribute fairly to public finances.

The court added that taxation should not be interpreted as moral approval of sex work or as official state recognition of the activity.

Under the ruling, income from prostitution falls into the category of earnings from independent professions.

The same broad category includes income earned by entertainers, coaches, athletes and models, as well as people who publish sexually explicit material on subscription platforms such as OnlyFans.

The court warned that exempting income from sex work would undermine the fair distribution of the tax burden and discriminate against other taxpayers.

The ruling does not legalize every activity associated with prostitution. Instead, it establishes that income earned through voluntary sex work must be declared and taxed under the same general principles that apply to other forms of self-employment.

World.title: Prague’s First Film Screening Took Place 130 Years Ago
World.content:
Prague’s first public film screening took place on October 18, 1896, at the Hotel U Černého koně on Na Příkopě Street.

Organized by the French branch of Thomas Edison’s company, the presentation introduced audiences to moving pictures, a technology that would soon transform entertainment across Bohemia.

The screening marked another milestone in a period of rapid technological change that had begun five years earlier.

In 1891, Prague hosted the Jubilee Provincial Exhibition, celebrating a century of industrial progress. The event helped reshape the city, leaving behind landmarks including the Industrial Palace, Petřín Lookout Tower and mirror maze.



The Hotel That Brought New Technology to Prague

The Hotel U Černého koně, or At the Black Horse, was among Prague’s most luxurious establishments in the late 19th century. Its owners, brothers Jindřich and Karel Cífka, were quick to recognize the commercial potential of new inventions.

Later in 1896, the hotel introduced another technological novelty, the X-ray machine. The device had been developed by German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who announced his discovery in December 1895.

Initially presented as an attraction, the machine soon acquired medical significance. In January 1897, physician Rudolf Jedlička used it to examine a patient suspected of having swallowed a foreign object. The image revealed a nail lodged in the man’s stomach.

Edison and the Lumière Brothers Compete for Audiences

The first film screening was organized by Adolf Oppenheimer, an optician and mechanic who operated a cinematograph supplied by Edison’s French company.

According to a contemporary invitation reproduced by Czech Radio, screenings took place daily, beginning at 4 p.m. and continuing hourly until 8 p.m. Additional shows were held on Sundays and public holidays. Admission cost 40 kreutzers, with discounts for schools.

Competition arrived almost immediately. Just five days after the Edison presentation, the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph was shown at the Hotel U Saského dvora on Hybernská Street.

Both companies promoted their technology as the genuine article. Their s emphasized the quality of their moving pictures and their international reputations, reflecting the intense competition surrounding the new medium.

Czech filmmakers soon began producing their own material. In June 1898, Národní listy reported on a cinematograph pavilion at the Prague Exhibition Grounds where two young architects presented original films, including scenes from everyday life in Prague.

Viktor Ponrepo Opens a Permanent Cinema

For several years, traveling cinematographs brought films to audiences around the country. A permanent venue eventually followed.

In September 1907, Dismas Šlambor, better known as Viktor Ponrepo, opened what is widely regarded as the first permanent cinema in the Czech lands. It was located in the U Modré štiky building on Karlova Street.

Originally a magician and illusionist, Ponrepo had become interested in image-recording technology after encountering Edison’s phonograph at the 1891 exhibition. He later toured the country with a traveling cinema before establishing his Prague venue.

Ponrepo became famous for greeting audiences with a bow before every screening. He eventually filmed the gesture and projected it before his shows, turning it into his personal signature.

By then, moving pictures had evolved from a technological curiosity into a new form of mass entertainment, with Prague among the cities embracing the change.

World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: Prague Expands Tram Network With Five Projects Underway
World.content:
Prague is expanding its tram network, with five projects now under construction across the capital.

Two new projects began in October 2026, extending the network from Malovanka to Strahov and from Libuš to Nové Dvory.

Work is also progressing on the tram line across Wenceslas Square, where the tracks have been connected between Vinohradská Street and the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.



The projects aim to improve public transport connections to developing residential areas and strengthen links with other transport services, including the future Metro Line D.

New tram line to connect Malovanka with Strahov

Construction of the new tram line from Malovanka to Strahov began on October 5, following preparatory work. The tracks will run along Vaníčkova Street, starting at Bělohorská Street and continuing toward Strahov Stadium.

The Malovanka stop will also be modified and moved to a position before the intersection, allowing it to serve trams heading toward Strahov.

The existing Stadion Strahov stop, currently used for passengers to disembark, will be renamed Strahov.

Tram extension to Nové Dvory will complement Metro Line D

Construction of the second new line, extending the tram network from Modřany through Libuš to Nové Dvory, began on October 7, 2026.

The extension will introduce two stops, Přírodní and Nové Dvory. At Nové Dvory, the line will end in a loop using Durychova, Libušská and Chýnovská streets.

The new connection is being developed alongside plans for Metro Line D and the wider expansion of the surrounding residential area. It will provide a direct tram connection to central Prague, including the Palackého náměstí area, with a future connection toward Smíchov also planned.

The extension will change operations on tram line 17. Once the project is completed, the temporary dead-end terminus in Libuš will be removed, allowing single-ended trams to return to longer routes. A second tram line is also planned for the new tracks after Metro Line D opens.

Hodkovičky gains a new tram stop

The new Hodkovičky stop, located between Belárie and Černý kůň, is another addition to Prague’s tram infrastructure in the south of the city.

The stop is intended to improve access to public transport for residents of the growing residential developments nearby. Further housing construction is also expected in Nové Dvory, where the planned tram extension will provide additional transport capacity.

Tram tracks connected across Wenceslas Square

Work on restoring tram services across Wenceslas Square is also progressing. In early autumn, construction crews connected the tracks running from Vinohradská Street, past the National Museum, across the square and toward the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.

The track infrastructure in this section is complete. Remaining work includes finishing the surrounding surfaces and installing overhead power lines.

Once these works are finished, the new line will restore tram services across Wenceslas Square, strengthening public transport connections in central Prague.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: PM Magyar: In 1956, demonstrators became free Hungarian citizens
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar paid tribute to the demonstrators of 1956 and their yearning for freedom in an address at a ceremonial wreath-laying on Bem Square in Budapest on Thursday, held to mark the 70th anniversary of the Revolution and Freedom Fight. Magyar also announced the establishment of a museum commemorating the heroes and victims of the 1956 uprising.

The prime minister said that when the university students setting out from the Technical University, and the Budapest residents who joined them gathered, they did not yet know that they were revolutionaries; they became so only hours later, when the first shots were fired at the Hungarian Radio building. But they already knew something of themselves, he said: that with their silent march and their dignified procession they had become free Hungarian citizens, “and this could never again be taken from them.”

“No later retribution could take it from them, nor the tramping of Soviet boots, nor the prison years, nor the decades spent under oppression,” he said.

“Nor could they take away that strength which also fills us whenever we grow weary, whenever we lose faith in Hungary for even a moment — that strength which also carries us forward. For nothing is stronger than the will of free Hungarians and the courageous stand of free Hungarians,” the prime minister said.

Photo: MTI

The prime minister said that it was a matter of “shame and pain” that in seventy years, and even since the change of regime, the nation had failed to discharge one of its greatest debts: there was no single, worthy place dedicated in its entirety to the memory of the heroes and victims of 1956.

He said that, in homage to the heroes of the Revolution and Freedom Fight, the government undertook to create in the coming years a “worthy shrine of Hungarian freedom”, establishing a museum of 1956 that pays tribute to the victims, to those who fought, and to the nameless heroes.

Magyar said the martyrs of the revolution would never be forgotten: the innocents led to the gallows, the martyrs buried in unmarked graves, the courage of “the Pest lads and the Pest girls”, the thousands tortured in prisons and the hundreds of thousands driven from their homeland, the innocent victims of the firing squads, and the pain of Hungarian families torn apart.

“Their names and their sacrifice live forever in our hearts and in the memory of the Hungarian nation,” he added.

Photo: MTI

He said the proof of their victory was that Hungarians could celebrate with cheerfulness, pride and a sense of liberation. That cheerfulness, he said, proved that the Hungarian people had not been broken and had not bowed their heads, and that people could still look one another in the eye today, backs straight, proudly, with a smile.

“We know that the sacrifice was not in vain: the homeland is free, and we have a common future,” the prime minister said.

Magyar called the flag with a hole, born when the Rakosi coat of arms was cut out of the national colours, a world-famous symbol of the 1956 Revolution. Everyone understood it, he said, because it said the same thing in every language: this is our country, and we want to decide its fate. That is why it is still raised high with pride today, he said, because the hole in the middle of the flag is an everlasting symbol of Hungarian freedom.

Magyar described presenting awards to former ’56 university students as one of the most uplifting experiences of his life. Those who stood up for the homeland seventy years ago “are still among us”, he added.

Photo: MTI

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

The prime minister also declared that dividing the nation “is a sin”. He said there were still some who failed to understand that there were minutes and hours when “we are Hungarians only, without qualifiers, without regard to origin or political sympathy”; they could still decide whether bowing their heads to 1956 or their day-to-day political interests mattered more to them, he said.

Anyone arriving with respect and good will would be embraced as a friend, he said, “but we will not yield an ounce of our freedom.” The nation had grown into its own history and looked forward to its independent future “with heads held high and unshakeable faith”, he added.

Paying homage to every hero of 1956, the prime minister closed his address with the words: “Long live the free, truly independent Hungary.”

Most of those attending the ceremony arrived at Bem Square with a torchlight procession setting out from the Technical University, part of the Gloria Victis 1956 memorial series organised by the Rákóczi Association. The march commemorated the student assembly held at the Technical University on October 22, remembered as one of the defining events of the revolution, at which the students set out their demands point by point and decided that, in a gesture of solidarity with the Polish people, they would march to Bem Square the following day, October 23. Many of the marchers waved national flags and the pierced flags symbolising the revolution.

Photo: MTI

The Rakoczi Association wrote on its website that 15,000 secondary school and university students were taking part in its commemorative programmes. Some 3,500 of them, from 170 schools in Hungary and abroad, were arriving in Budapest between October 21 and 23 for the memorial events.

After the ceremony on Bem Square, the participants marched to Imre Nagy Square, where the prime minister lit the flame of the revolution.

World.title: Hungary to build a dedicated 1956 revolution museum, Magyar announces
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has pledged to establish a museum dedicated to the heroes and victims of Hungary’s 1956 Revolution, saying the country has failed to honour this historic debt for 70 years.

Hungary will establish a dedicated museum commemorating the 1956 Revolution and its heroes, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced in a speech in Budapest on 23 October, marking the uprising’s 70th anniversary.

Speaking at Bem József Square, Magyar said it was both shameful and painful that Hungary had not yet created a worthy national memorial devoted entirely to those who fought against Soviet-backed rule and those who lost their lives.

“We undertake to create, in the coming years, a worthy sanctuary of Hungarian freedom. We will establish a genuine museum of 1956 that pays tribute to the victims, the fighters and the anonymous heroes,” the prime minister said.

A museum to honour the heroes of 1956

Magyar stressed that, seven decades after the revolution, Hungary still lacked a dedicated place where the memory of the uprising could be preserved in its entirety.

He described the proposed institution as a long-overdue tribute to those who risked their lives for the country’s freedom, including the many ordinary people whose names never became widely known.

The prime minister arrived at Bem Square after walking along the Bem embankment from Budapest University of Technology and Economics. It was from the university that students began marching towards the city centre on 23 October 1956, helping set the Budapest uprising in motion.

“There is no force stronger than the determination of free Hungarian young people,” Magyar said, praising the students who took a leading role in the revolution.

‘Thirteen days that shook the world’

Reflecting on the events of October 1956, Magyar described the uprising as a historic turning point that shook the foundations of tyranny and left an enduring mark on world history.

The revolution began on 23 October and developed into 13 days of resistance against Soviet domination and Hungary’s communist regime. Although the uprising was crushed by Soviet military intervention, Magyar argued that it had made Hungarians free citizens in a way that subsequent repression could never entirely undo.

He also highlighted the courage required of those who joined the movement, noting that individuals had to decide for themselves what they were willing to risk for their country.

“Someone had to say that it was time to set off. Someone had to take the lead, and everyone had to decide individually what they would do for their homeland in its hour of need,” he said, expressing gratitude to the students and all the heroes of 1956.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Magyar praises Polish-Hungarian solidarity

The prime minister also paid tribute to the longstanding friendship between Hungary and Poland, explaining that the choice of Bem József Square was particularly fitting because the square is named after a Polish-born general who became a hero of the Hungarian Revolution of 1848–49.

Magyar recalled how workers in the Polish city of Poznań had given Hungarians hope during protests in the summer of 1956. In the autumn, he said, the Hungarian uprising in turn inspired and encouraged the Polish people.

“Thus, in those days, the friendship between the two nations became courageous solidarity, active cooperation and life-saving assistance,” he said. He also paid tribute to the heroes of both nations.

A call to remember the victims and overcome divisions

Magyar called the 1956 Revolution an enduring symbol of Hungarian freedom, while stressing that celebrating the country’s spirit did not mean forgetting the tragedy that followed the uprising’s defeat.

He urged Hungarians to remember those who were executed or persecuted, the young revolutionaries known as the Pesti srácok (‘the boys of Pest’) and the girls who also took part, the innocent victims of the shootings, and families torn apart by repression.

Their memory, he said, demonstrated that the Hungarian people had not been broken and could still look one another in the eye with pride.

Magyar also used his speech to call for national unity, arguing that there are moments when Hungarians should put aside political loyalties and other divisions.

“Dividing this homeland is a sin,” he said, adding that people still had a choice between paying tribute to the heroes of 1956 and prioritising their immediate political interests.

He concluded by calling for a free and genuinely independent Hungary. The prime minister also invited the public to attend the anniversary celebrations at Kossuth Square, in front of Parliament, later that day.

World.title: Macron, Meloni and Merz won’t attend Budapest’s 1956 anniversary: Who is coming instead?
World.content:
Hungary’s Prime Minister Péter Magyar invited dozens of foreign leaders to Budapest for the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution, but several prominent European leaders will be absent. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Moldovan President Maia Sandu are among the high-profile guests expected at Friday’s commemorations.

Several of Europe’s most prominent political leaders will not attend Budapest’s commemorations marking the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 Revolution on 23 October. French President Emmanuel Macron, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will all be absent in person, despite invitations from Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

Instead, most foreign delegations will be led by ministers, parliamentary speakers and state secretaries. However, some of the European Union’s top officials and a number of national leaders are expected to attend the events.

The Hungarian government has not yet published a complete guest list. Hungarian news outlet Telex contacted European embassies, foreign ministries and presidential and prime ministerial offices to establish who had accepted Magyar’s invitations.

Which foreign leaders are coming to Budapest?

The most prominent guests confirmed so far include:

Ursula von der Leyen , President of the European Commission, who is also expected to deliver a speech.

, President of the European Commission, who is also expected to deliver a speech. António Costa , President of the European Council, whose official schedule includes the Budapest commemorations.

, President of the European Council, whose official schedule includes the Budapest commemorations. Maia Sandu , President of Moldova.

, President of Moldova. Đuro Macut , Prime Minister of Serbia.

, Prime Minister of Serbia. Jens Stoltenberg, former NATO Secretary General and Norway’s current finance minister.

Several European countries will also send senior parliamentary representatives and government ministers.

Czech Senate President Miloš Vystrčil, Slovenian National Assembly President Zoran Stevanović and Swiss Council of States President Stefan Engler are among those expected to attend.

Austria will be represented by Federal Council President Christine Schwarz-Fuchs and former Chancellor and Foreign Minister Alexander Schallenberg. Belgium’s delegation will include Deputy Prime Minister Vincent Van Peteghem, while the country’s King Philippe has sent a message to Hungarian President András Baka marking the anniversary.

The Netherlands will send former Prime Minister Jan Peter Balkenende, who holds the honorary title of Minister of State.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Who will represent France, Germany and Italy?

Despite earlier expectations, some of the most prominent European leaders will not personally attend the celebrations.

The French Embassy in Budapest confirmed to Telex that Emmanuel Macron will not be coming. It also clarified that the French side had never officially confirmed a possible visit, despite Magyar previously suggesting that the French president would attend.

Germany will send two official delegations. Federal Transport Minister Steffen Bilger will lead the delegation representing Chancellor Friedrich Merz, while Hamburg Mayor Peter Tschentscher will lead a second delegation.

Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni will also be absent. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto will represent the country instead. According to the Italian Embassy, his attendance reflects the strong relationship between the two countries and Italy’s solidarity with the Hungarian people during the 1956 Revolution.

Norway’s Jens Stoltenberg will attend in his current capacity as finance minister rather than as a former NATO chief.

Several invited leaders have declined

A number of other European heads of state and government have also confirmed that they will not attend.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen received an invitation from Hungarian President András Baka during a meeting in Slovenia last week. However, his office said other commitments would prevent him from travelling to Budapest, adding that he looked forward to his next visit to Hungary.

The following leaders have also declined their invitations:

Kristen Michal , Prime Minister of Estonia, who will instead be represented by Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta.

, Prime Minister of Estonia, who will instead be represented by Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta. Micheál Martin , Prime Minister of Ireland, whose country will send European Affairs Minister Thomas Byrne.

, Prime Minister of Ireland, whose country will send European Affairs Minister Thomas Byrne. Finland’s President and Prime Minister , who have other previously scheduled commitments.

, who have other previously scheduled commitments. The Prime Ministers of Lithuania and Latvia, who are also unable to attend because of prior engagements.

Hungary invited a broad range of foreign leaders, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy recently said he would not rule out travelling to Budapest, but Magyar has indicated that he does not expect the Ukrainian president to attend.

Magyar previously said that everyone had been invited except Russian President Vladimir Putin, estimating that the number of invitations could be between 100 and 150.

Magyar had hoped for a larger gathering of world leaders

Magyar began inviting foreign leaders to the anniversary celebrations shortly after winning Hungary’s parliamentary election in April. At a press conference on 13 April, he expressed hope that even the US Secretary of State, Vice President or President might attend.

He subsequently extended invitations to leaders who congratulated him on his election victory, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. During his first international trips as prime minister, he also invited leaders from Poland, Austria, Germany and France to visit Budapest for the occasion.

In an interview with Hungarian outlet Partizán last week, Magyar described the celebrations as a multi-day series of events rather than a conventional national holiday programme.

The planned events include a ceremonial session in Parliament, a large gathering at Kossuth Lajos Square and a gala performance at the Hungarian State Opera. Magyar also plans to host arriving heads of state, heads of government, parliamentary speakers and other international guests at the Museum of Fine Arts.

The government has not yet responded to Telex’s questions about the final guest list. As several foreign ministries and diplomatic missions have also not replied, the confirmed list may grow.

World.title: Budapest’s Buda Castle could ban Airbnb rentals completely from 2028
World.content:
Budapest’s District I council has proposed a complete ban on short-term accommodation rentals in the Buda Castle district from 2028, following a local survey in which two-thirds of respondents from the historic neighbourhood backed the measure. Stricter rules, substantial fines and new powers to temporarily close accommodation providers are also on the table.

Airbnb-style short-term rentals could disappear entirely from Budapest’s Buda Castle district from 1 January 2028 under new proposals put forward by the District I Municipality. The plans are part of a wider effort to protect the residential character of the historic area and the peace and quiet of its residents.

The municipality announced on its official Facebook page that a draft regulation had been prepared based on residents’ feedback. The proposal has now been opened for public consultation.

A survey conducted in September attracted 4,503 district residents. Of those who responded, 58.6% supported a complete ban on short-term rentals across the district, while support for the measure reached 66% among respondents living in Buda Castle itself.

What would change for Airbnb hosts in Budapest?

The proposed regulation would introduce different rules for Buda Castle and the rest of District I.

Buda Castle: Short-term accommodation rentals could be completely prohibited from 1 January 2028.

Short-term accommodation rentals could be completely prohibited from 1 January 2028. The rest of District I: Existing accommodation providers operating in apartment buildings would need the building community’s consent to continue their activities from 2028.

Existing accommodation providers operating in apartment buildings would need the building community’s consent to continue their activities from 2028. Stricter enforcement: Authorities would carry out tighter checks, with substantial fines and temporary closures possible for violations.

The plans are not yet final. The municipality is inviting residents and other interested parties to submit comments and suggestions over a 15-day consultation period. Feedback can be sent to airbnb@budavar.hu, and the local council is expected to decide on the final regulation in November.

Don’t miss this: New EU housing rules could pave the way for tighter Airbnb restrictions in Budapest

Existing rentals would have a transition period

Owners of short-term accommodation properties in Buda Castle would not necessarily have to stop operating immediately if the proposal is adopted. Under the draft rules published on the municipality’s website, accommodation providers already registered by 31 December 2026 in the protected World Heritage area could continue operating until the end of 2027.

This would give owners a one-year transition period to prepare for the proposed ban, the municipality said.

District I says the main objective is to protect Buda Castle’s role as a place to live and safeguard the long-term interests of people who call the area home.

Photo: Anadolu/İlkin Eskipehlivan

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Fines of up to HUF 2 million and temporary closures proposed

The draft regulation would also introduce tougher penalties for accommodation providers that fail to comply with the rules.

The district clerk would be responsible for checking compliance. In the event of a violation, the authority could impose a fine and order the accommodation to close temporarily for 45 days.

The proposed fines would be charged for each inspection:

HUF 200,000 (approximately EUR 546): For private individuals and sole traders.

For private individuals and sole traders. HUF 2 million (approximately EUR 5,464): For legal entities and other organisations.

The measures are still proposals, and their final form will depend on the outcome of the public consultation and the council’s decision, expected in November.

World.title: Budapest braces for major traffic chaos on 23 October: Roads closed, metro changes and tram disruptions
World.content:
Budapest is preparing for significant traffic restrictions on 22 and 23 October as Hungary marks the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution. Road closures, commemorations, torchlight marches and visiting high-level delegations will disrupt traffic across the city centre, with several public transport services running on altered routes.

Residents, commuters and visitors to Budapest should plan their journeys carefully on Thursday and Friday, as major roads and sections of the Danube embankments will close for events marking Hungary’s national holiday.

According to the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK), the restrictions will affect both motorists and public transport passengers, particularly around the city centre, the Buda embankment, Kossuth Lajos Square and Andrássy Avenue.

The BKK recommends using the metro network and trams 4 and 6 for journeys through central Budapest. Metro line M2 and tram 2 will run more frequently than usual to accommodate passengers.

Real-time updates and planned changes are available on the BKK’s official national holiday transport information page.

Thursday, 22 October: Torchlight procession to disrupt Buda traffic

The Műegyetem Embankment will be closed from approximately 8 am to 8 pm on Thursday. A commemorative ceremony and wreath-laying event will take place near the Budapest University of Technology and Economics between 2 pm and 4 pm, followed by a traditional torchlight procession starting at 4 pm.

The march will travel along the Műegyetem Embankment, Szent Gellért Square, Szent Gellért Embankment, Döbrentei Square, Várkert Embankment, Ybl Miklós Square, Lánchíd Street, Clark Ádám Square, Fő Street, Jégverem Street, Bem Embankment, Csalogány Street, Nagy Imre Square and Fő Street before reaching Bem József Square.

The procession will cause temporary disruptions to several bus and tram services, particularly between 4 pm and 6.30 pm.

Friday, 23 October: Major closures around Parliament and Heroes’ Square

Friday will bring further restrictions as Hungary marks the anniversary of the 1956 Revolution. The official flag-raising ceremony will take place at Kossuth Lajos Square in the morning, with events continuing throughout the day.

What this means for travellers

Anyone planning to visit central Budapest on 22 or 23 October should allow extra time for their journey and check their route before setting off. World.title: Hungary’s 23 October long weekend is here: When shops and pharmacies will be open
World.content:
Most shops in Hungary will close on Friday, 23 October, for the national public holiday, but normal Saturday opening hours will resume the following day. Here is what residents, expats and visitors need to know about shopping, pharmacies, post offices and rubbish collection over the three-day weekend.

Hungary is heading into a three-day long weekend as 23 October, the national holiday commemorating the 1956 Revolution, falls on a Friday this year. While most shops will shut for the public holiday, many services will return to their usual schedules on Saturday.

If you need to buy groceries or pick up medication, it is worth planning ahead to avoid finding closed doors.

Are shops open on 23 October?

According to 24.hu, under the general rules, shops will be closed on Friday, 23 October. Normal Saturday opening hours will apply on 24 October, while shops are expected to operate as usual on Sunday.

There are some exceptions for those who need to shop on the public holiday. Petrol stations and their shops may remain open, as may certain 24-hour convenience stores and smaller shops where the owner personally serves customers.

Other businesses that may open on the national holiday include:

Standalone florists

Newsagents

Sweet shops

Restaurants, cafés, bars and entertainment venues

Most shops inside shopping centres are expected to close on Friday. However, cinemas, restaurants and other leisure facilities within malls may still operate, depending on the venue.

Market opening hours will vary. Some markets have announced that they will close, while others plan to welcome customers, so check with your local market before setting off.

Photo: Daily News Hungary

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Where can you find an open pharmacy?

Pharmacies will operate according to the holiday duty rota over the long weekend, the National Public Health and Pharmacy Centre (NNGYK) has announced.

On Friday, 23 October, medicine supplies in most towns and cities will be provided by 24-hour pharmacies, pharmacies that remain open on public holidays, and those operating an on-call or emergency service.

You can find the addresses and telephone numbers of pharmacies that are open or on duty through the official pharmacy search database. The information is also available in Hungary’s EgészségAblak health app.

On Saturday, pharmacies that normally open on rest days will generally be available until noon rather than following their usual Saturday schedule. After that, on-call or emergency pharmacy services will be available.

The NNGYK advises people to make sure they have enough of their regular medication before the holiday. Families with children should check that they have suitable fever and pain relief medicines, while adults may also want to stock up on remedies for cold symptoms, coughs and sore throats. Older people and those taking regular medication should pay particular attention to having sufficient supplies.

Will post offices and rubbish collection services operate?

Post offices will be closed on Friday, 23 October, according to the Hungarian Post’s published holiday opening arrangements. If you need to send or collect something, check the opening hours of your local branch for the rest of the weekend.

Rubbish collection, however, will continue according to the usual schedule. If your bin is normally collected on Fridays, it should still be emptied on 23 October.

Schools will also close for the autumn break

The autumn school holiday begins on Friday, 23 October, and runs until Sunday, 1 November. Thursday, 22 October, is the final school day before the break, and classes resume on Monday, 2 November.

The holiday period includes not only the 23 October national holiday but also All Saints’ Day on 1 November.

Tip: If you plan to visit a shop, market, pharmacy or other service on Friday, check its opening hours online beforehand. Holiday schedules can vary, particularly for smaller businesses and local markets.

World.title: Budapest’s newest metro line could be extended to two suburbs by 2035!
World.content:
A major proposal backed by Budapest’s District XV could extend Metro Line 4 in both directions, reaching Budaörs in the west and the Fót Auchan area in the north-east. The ambitious plan would also include large park-and-ride facilities, but it still needs detailed studies and support from the government and the capital.

Budapest’s Metro Line 4 could become the backbone of a much larger suburban transport connection under a proposal approved by the District XV council. The concept would extend the line westwards towards the Auchan shopping centre in Budaörs and eastwards through Zugló and Újpalota towards another Auchan site near Fót.

According to Portfolio, the proposed deadline is ambitious: the entire extended line would enter service by 31 December 2035 at the latest. However, the council’s decision is a request to begin preparing the project, not a commitment that construction will go ahead.

Park-and-ride facilities would help keep cars out of Budapest

A key element of the proposal is the construction of large park-and-ride (P+R) and bike-and-ride (B+R) facilities at both ends of the extended line, near the Auchan sites in Budaörs and Fót. The aim is to persuade commuters travelling towards Budapest from the M1/M7 and M3/M2 motorway corridors to switch to public transport before reaching the capital’s busiest roads.

According to the proposal, this could help reduce congestion, air pollution and through-traffic in inner Budapest, while easing pressure on roads in District XV and other residential areas. The extended line would also create stronger links between suburban railways, the metro, trams and buses, potentially making journeys across the wider metropolitan area easier.

If you missed it: Budapest’s busiest M3 metro to be extended after EU funding secured!

Zugló and Újpalota could gain new connections

The eastern extension would provide a high-capacity, step-free connection through areas including Zugló, Thököly Road, Bosnyák Square and Újpalota. The exact route has not yet been settled.

The proposal calls for detailed professional assessments before a final route is selected. These would include passenger-demand modelling, urban planning studies, cost-benefit analysis, environmental assessments and public consultation.

Two possible routes are being considered for the section from the Szentmihályi stop towards Fót. The District XV proposal favours option B, citing the need to protect green spaces.

The council also stresses that the section near Újpalota and the Pólus Centre must be planned and built with strict environmental safeguards. These would include protecting existing natural areas and local ecosystems, as well as restoring affected land and landscaping after construction.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

The proposed timetable runs until 2035

The proposal sets out a demanding schedule for preparing and delivering the extension.

By 30 June 2027: Complete a preliminary feasibility study covering route options, passenger forecasts, network connections, station and depot requirements, technical needs, environmental impacts, costs, risks and potential funding sources.

Complete a preliminary feasibility study covering route options, passenger forecasts, network connections, station and depot requirements, technical needs, environmental impacts, costs, risks and potential funding sources. By 31 December 2028: Complete the permitting documentation for the selected option and begin the necessary regulatory, environmental, construction and railway-authority procedures.

Complete the permitting documentation for the selected option and begin the necessary regulatory, environmental, construction and railway-authority procedures. In 2029: Conclude implementation and financing agreements between the government, Budapest Municipality and the relevant district and local councils.

Conclude implementation and financing agreements between the government, Budapest Municipality and the relevant district and local councils. By the end of 2035: Aim to bring the entire extended line, from the Budaörs Auchan area to the Fót Auchan area, into service.

The document acknowledges that these dates are political targets and cannot override statutory procedures or technical safety requirements.

The M4 metro line. Photo: BKK

The district cannot decide on the metro alone

Although District XV has approved the proposal, the district council does not have the authority to plan, permit and deliver a metro extension independently. It is asking the government and Budapest Municipality to launch the preparatory work, involving organisations including the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK), Budapest Transport Company (BKV), the Ministry of Construction and Transport, and the local authorities concerned.

The council’s decision does not create an immediate construction obligation or commit the district to a specific level of spending. The project’s cost and financing requirements would only become clearer after the feasibility study and cost estimates are completed.

The district mayor has been asked to send the decision to the prime minister, the construction and transport minister, Budapest’s mayor, the heads of BKK and BKV, and the mayors of Budaörs, Fót, Törökbálint and the relevant Budapest districts. The mayor must also coordinate with the other local authorities and report back to the council within 60 days on responses and progress.

Could European Union funding help pay for it?

The proposal fits with the broader emphasis on rail-based transport and reducing commuter car traffic associated with Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy’s portfolio. However, financing remains one of the biggest unanswered questions.

Vitézy said in September that EU funds made available to Hungary could support several major transport projects by 2029, including HÉV suburban railway upgrades, an extension of Metro Line 3, suburban rail developments and improvements to regional railway lines.

World.title: Reuters: Hungary could drop Russia’s Rosatom from Paks nuclear project
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government is considering replacing Russian state-owned Rosatom as the main contractor for the Paks II nuclear expansion, according to Reuters. A final decision is expected later this year or in early 2027, as the government reviews the project’s costs, viability and potential alternatives.

Hungary is considering a major change to its flagship nuclear power project, with the government reportedly sounding out alternative suppliers to replace Russia’s Rosatom at the Paks nuclear power plant expansion.

Two sources familiar with the review told Reuters that all options remain on the table, including changing the main contractor. The government is examining the legal, technical and financial implications of such a move, as well as its potential impact on the project’s timetable and overall viability.

A source close to the administration said the government was leaning towards the conclusion that the expansion itself was necessary, but that Rosatom should not be involved.

Decision expected by early 2027

The government of Prime Minister Péter Magyar is expected to make a final decision on the Paks II project later this year or early next year, according to Reuters.

The expansion was originally estimated to cost EUR 12.5 billion. By the time the first concrete was poured in February 2026, Hungary had already spent more than EUR 2 billion on the project.

The contract was awarded to Rosatom without a public tender in 2014, under former prime minister Viktor Orbán. It has since been amended five times, while a sixth amendment has reportedly been prepared but not signed.

Replacing the Russian company would not be straightforward. According to Reuters, Hungary could have to absorb the EUR 1.1 billion already paid to Rosatom, as well as potential penalties for terminating the contract. No alternative supplier has been publicly identified.

If you missed it: Hungary could lose EUR billions in compensation if Paks II project is cancelled, expert warns

Rosatom says it has received no termination notice

Rosatom told Reuters that it was continuing work according to the schedule agreed with the Hungarian state. The company also said production of the main equipment for the future reactor units was under way.

“We have received no formal notification from the customer of any intention to terminate the contract, nor do we see any legally justified grounds for such a decision,” a company spokesperson said.

The statement suggests that no formal termination process has been communicated to Rosatom, despite the reported review and discussions about alternative suppliers.

A European supplier could make the project easier to manage in terms of foreign policy and sanctions, one source told Reuters. However, changing the contractor would not eliminate the project’s technical and management challenges.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

EU court ruling adds to Paks II uncertainty

The project has already faced legal and regulatory complications. In September 2025, the Court of Justice of the European Union annulled the European Commission’s 2017 approval of state aid for Paks II, adding another obstacle to the expansion.

The project is also politically sensitive because of Hungary’s close nuclear cooperation with Russia following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. While EU countries have reduced their reliance on Russian oil and gas, Rosatom has so far avoided EU-wide sanctions.

Paks II is Rosatom’s most prominent nuclear power project within the European Union. Finland cancelled its contract with the Russian company in May 2022, and the two sides have since been involved in legal disputes.

Hungary still plans to rely on nuclear energy

Despite the possible change of contractor, the Magyar government remains committed to nuclear power, Reuters reported. Nuclear energy provides large amounts of low-carbon electricity around the clock, helping balance renewable sources whose output varies with the weather.

Hungary expects electricity demand to rise, making nuclear generation an important part of its future energy mix. Zsuzsa Beres, deputy state secretary for nuclear energy and international relations at the Ministry of Economy and Energy, recently said nuclear energy and its supply chain offered significant potential to strengthen Europe’s own capabilities.

As a possible interim measure while the future of Paks II is reviewed, the government is also exploring a 20-year extension of the operating licences for the four existing Russian-built reactors at Paks. Their current licences expire between 2032 and 2037.

World.title: Merz Sees Montenegro in EU by 2028 as Berlin Process Summit Opens
World.content:
At the Berlin Process summit in Milocer, Montenegro, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that Montenegro could realistically become the European Union’s 28th member by 2028. He urged Western Balkan countries to accelerate reforms and regional cooperation.

Speaking at the opening of the summit, Merz said that EU and regional leaders had made progress since last meeting in Tivat in June focused on the EU integration of the Western Balkans.

“Since we’ve met in Tivat in June, we have managed to get the enlargement process back on track, and you all know how difficult it used to be. But now we are on a positive path,” Merz said.

At a joint news conference with Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic later the same day, Merz offered a concrete timeline for Montenegro’s EU accession, by 2028.

“We believe that is realistic,” he said.

Merz stressed that the current push for gradual integration into the bloc must remain merit-based.

The idea of gradual EU integration is being pushed most prominently by France and Germany. It would give candidate countries some benefits of integration before full membership such as potentially including greater access to the EU single market, research and education programmes, and observer participation in some EU meetings, without voting rights.

Access would depend on progress with reforms and could be withdrawn if a country backtracked.

“Let me be clear – gradual integration is also merit-based. We as the EU have delivered, but the reforms and the political will must come from you,” he said at the summit’s opening.

Merz also urged Western Balkan countries to strengthen regional cooperation, arguing that economic integration would make the region more attractive to investors and prepare it for the EU single market.

“You will succeed in the EU only if you work together, and you are doing that,” he said. “Eight million people in one market are simply more interesting for investors than in six small ones.”

Commenting on efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, Merz stressed the importance of European involvement in negotiations.

“We all believe that lasting peace cannot be achieved without Europe. And every negotiating format that contributes to this goal is welcome,” he said.

Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic said enlargement was central to Europe’s security and unity, reaffirming Montenegro’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

“Europe must bring the same clarity of purpose to enlargement,” Spajic said, describing it as “a reunification of our continent” that would extend freedom, security and opportunity to Europeans still outside the bloc.

World.title: Match-Fixing Probe Rocks Greek Basketball Federation
World.content:
Hellenic Basketball Federation President Vangelis Liolios is pictured at the EOK headquarters in Marousi, 03 October 2023. Photo: EPA/ALEXANDROS VLACHOS.

Greek police said on Thursday that six people have been arrested in an investigation into alleged attempts to manipulate basketball matches linked to domestic and international betting rings.

Greek media report that among the arrested is Vangelis Liolios, president of the Hellenic Basketball Federation, whose lawyer has denied the allegations.

The arrests followed a coordinated operation on Wednesday across the Attica region, Achaia and Katerini, led by the police directorate responsible for combating organised crime. Five suspects were arrested during the operation, while a sixth voluntarily reported to the police and was subsequently arrested.

According to a police statement, the arrest warrants concern alleged offences including “soliciting or accepting gifts and other benefits, offering advantages to referees or sports officials, and illicitly interfering with basketball matches to influence their progress, nature or outcome.”

Apart from Liolios, suspects also include current and former referees and other figures connected to the sport, according to Greek media reports.

Liolios has denied wrongdoing. His lawyer, Panagiotis Papaioannou, spoke outside the courthouse and described the case as a “poorly concocted scheme”, arguing that those making accusations against his client had themselves previously been reported by Liolios and asked to be investigated.

The searches yielded 14 mobile phones, six laptops, 22 USB storage devices, two tablets, memory cards, a hard drive, team shirts and memorabilia, police said. Additionally, 931,463 euros in cash and other electronic devices were seized from their homes.

In a statement issued on October 21, the Hellenic Basketball Federation said its board had met to brief members on the ongoing legal proceedings concerning Greek basketball. The federation said it would “continue to monitor” the case through official announcements and formal procedures.

The six suspects have been referred to the competent prosecutorial authorities as the investigation continues.

World.title: Dzimi’s Diggers: Big Contract Follows Show of Loyalty to Serbia’s Ruling Party
World.content:
One March morning last year, before the sun was up, a convoy of tractors and diggers snaked through downtown Belgrade and parked, in a line, around the Serbian presidency building and the park in front of it.

Days later, a protest was due, staged by a student-led movement calling for accountability for the deaths of 16 people when a concrete canopy at a newly renovated railway station in northern Serbia collapsed in November 2024.

Serbia’s then president, Aleksandar Vucic, warned of plans by the protesters to incite “major violence”.

The heavy machinery was there as a buffer between the protesters and Vucic’s supporters.

Among them were diggers of a company called Dzimi Commerce, diggers that Serbia’s NIS oil company – majority-owned by Russian Gazprom – and provincial authorities in the northern province of Vojvodina had hired for years. Until August this year, Dzimi Commerce was co-owned by 63-year-old Mile Samardzija, a close backer of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, before he transferred his 50 per cent share to his daughter. Samardzija remains a director.

In the end, there was no “major violence”. The tractors and diggers had their tyres slashed and windows broken, but this was a small price to pay for Samaradzija.

In January this year, his company received its most lucrative public contract yet, worth 1.1 million euros, with NIS subsidiary Naftagas, BIRN can reveal. Though Gazprom holds a majority stake in NIS, just under 30 per cent is still in Serbian state hands.

Experts say the case highlights the cosy, mutually beneficial relationship between the SNS and certain Serbian businesses, which put their resources at the ruling party’s disposal in return for financial rewards.

“Driven by the interest of profit, many are ready to enter into a pact with the authorities,” said Bozo Draskovic, a former board member of Serbia’s Anti-Corruption Agency.

“And in the service of that business, they put all their resources at their disposal – equipment, machines, means of transport, even workers.”

The collaboration appears to go even further in the case of Dzimi Commerce.

According to police case files seen by BIRN, the company’s co-owner of Dzimi Commerce, Ljiljana Teslic, reported Samardzija to the police last year for allegedly threatening her.

Teslic’s lawyer said Samardzija had been trying to push her out of the firm – with the help of “SNS representatives”.

BIRN contacted Samardzija, Dzimi Commerce, Naftagas, and the SNS for comment but none of them responded. Teslic declined to comment.

Close ties to Vucic regime

World.title: Berlin Process Needs to Level the Playing Field in Bilateral Disputes
World.content:
On October 22, Montenegro will host the Berlin Process Leaders’ Summit while itself dealing with a neighbouring EU member state’s power to halt its EU accession progress.

The country is widely considered a frontrunner for EU membership and has provisionally closed 21 of 33 negotiating chapters. Yet neighbouring Croatia is holding up progress over unresolved bilateral issues ranging from war crimes and missing persons to state property claims, maritime borders and the Jadran sailing ship.

Few would question the importance of investigating war crimes or settling state borders, which are legitimate matters that should not be pushed aside for the sake of enlargement. The real question is: is it acceptable for an EU member state to make the accession process conditional on its own demands without any scrutiny of the demands’ relevance, proportionality or prospects for resolution? When bilateral disagreements become EU accession vetoes, they cease to be a problem for just the two countries involved.

This issue has repeatedly arisen across the Western Balkans. In May 2024, Albania’s relations with Greece became strained after Albania imprisoned Fredis Beleris, the ethnic Greek mayor-elect of Himara, who was convicted of vote buying. Greece warned that the affair could affect Albania’s EU ambitions.
