World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 23, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 27-th day of the second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev shared a publication on Twitter about the liberation of Zilanli, Kurd Mahrizli, Muganli and Alagurshag villages of Gubadli district.

- President Ilham Aliyev shared a publication on Twitter about the liberation of Dolanar and Bunyadli villages of Khojavend district, Dag Tumas, Nusus, Xelefli, Minbashili and Veyselli villages of Jabrayil district, Venedli and Mirzehasanli villages of Zengilan district.

- President Ilham Aliyev had a phone conversation with the father of the National Hero Shukur Hamidov, who became a martyr.

- The Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense disseminated information about the latest situation at the front. Important territories and heights were liberated. The Armenian armed forces, leaving the positions, deserted.

- Territories of Tartar, Aghdam and Aghjabadi districts were subjected to intensive shelling, and four UAVs of Armenian armed forces were neutralized.

- Video of the destruction of Armenian personnel and armored vehicles was published.

- Video from the Minbashili village of Jabrayil district, liberated from the Armenian occupation, was published.

- Video of the destruction of Armenian volunteer detachments in the Khojavend and Fuzuli directions published.

- Video of the destruction of artillery units and the command post of the Armenian armed forces as a result of air strikes was published.

World.title: Turkish MP condemns statements directed against Azerbaijan (VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Turkish-Azerbaijani relations are too deep and ancient to be used as a tool for day-to-day politics.

This was stated today by Şamil Ayrım, a Member of Parliament and head of the Türkiye-Azerbaijan Inter-Parliamentary Friendship Group, during his address to the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye (GNAT).

He noted that these relations go far beyond the standard ties between two sovereign states.

"I strongly condemn the statements directed against Azerbaijan. Criticism is one thing; demeaning rhetoric is quite another. The position of the Justice and Development Party and our government is firm. We do not accept any approach that goes beyond the parameters set by the President of Türkiye, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

Türkiye is strong, and Azerbaijan is strong. One nation, two states—together, we are stronger," said Şamil Ayrım.

World.title: Azerbaijan raises issue of landmine threat at UN
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. During the UNGA81 First Committee thematic discussions on conventionalweapons, Azerbaijan informed the Committee that for nearly three decades, parts of its territory that were under occupation served as a “grey zone”, creating conditions conducive to illicit activity, including the trafficking of conventional arms, ammunition and related material. It was emphasised that, following the restoration of its sovereignty, Azerbaijan strengthened border controls in these areas, thereby reducing the risk of such illicit trafficking.

This is stated on the X page of the Permanent Mission of Azerbaijan to the United Nations.

"Particular attention was drawn to the landmine threat in Azerbaijan. Over the past three decades, more than 3,500 people have fallen victim to landmines and explosive remnants of war. Since November 2020 alone, 443 Azerbaijani citizens, including women and children, have been killed or injured, with the number continuing to rise.

The statement underscored that, beyond the immediate threat to human life, extensive landmine contamination continues to impede reconstruction and rehabilitation efforts, restrict the use of agricultural land, and hinder the safe and dignified return of internally displaced persons to their places of origin.

Addressing the persistent landmine threat in Azerbaijan requires sustained international solidarity, stronger partnerships and enhanced assistance for humanitarian mine action," the statement said.

World.title: Media and Broadcasting Council condemns disinformation about alleged mass arrests over hijab in Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Unfounded reports by some Turkish media outlets and social media accounts alleging mass arrests over hijab in Azerbaijan and claiming that people are leaving the country as a result are a clear example of disinformation designed to exploit religious sensitivities, manipulate public opinion and misrepresent Azerbaijan, the Media and Broadcasting Council of the Republic of Azerbaijan said in a statement.

The statement stressed that the participation of certain political and public figures in spreading fabricated information and presenting baseless claims in offensive terms violates their public responsibilities and constitutes an unacceptable abuse of their influence.

The Media and Broadcasting Council strongly condemns the dissemination of false information about Azerbaijan, calling on media representatives and political and public figures to act responsibly and urging the public to critically assess such posts, check information against reliable sources and refrain from spreading disinformation.

World.title: Moody’s: Azerbaijan’s banking assets grow 11% annually since 2021
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Since 2021, total assets of Azerbaijan’s banking system have increased at a compound annual growth rate of 11%, says Moody’s.

“As of 29 September 2026, the Azerbaijan banking system consisted of 21 banks. As of 31 August 2026, Azerbaijan's banking system reported total assets of AZN62.5 billion. Since 2021, total assets have increased at a compound annual growth rate of 11%,” reads the latest report on the International Bank of Azerbaijan issued by the rating agency.

Moody’s recalls that as of 31 August 2026, Azerbaijan's banking system reported total loans of 34.9 billion manat and net loans to customers of 30.8 billion manat.

“Customer deposits was the largest source of banking system funds, representing 67% of total liabilities and equity, as of the same date,” the report said.

According to the Central Bank of Azerbaijan, banking assets amounted to 46.7% of GDP, a measure of banking sector depth.

The balance sheet grew mainly on the back of an increase in household term deposits, supporting loan portfolio growth.

Earlier, Moody’s said that Azerbaijani banks are the least exposed to geopolitical risks among the Central Asian and South Caucasus countries.

“This reflects the country’s limited economic and financial linkages with Russia, the resilience provided by hydrocarbon revenues that benefit from higher oil prices and the stability afforded by the manat’s peg to the U.S. dollar,” said the rating agency.

World.title: Wallaroos great inspired by mantra 'you can't be what you can't see'
World.content:
As Emily Chancellor runs out for her final Test, she will know she has fulfilled one of her ambitions as a Wallaroos representative.

Upon making her Test debut in 2018, Chancellor wanted to help increase the visibility of the Wallaroos among young fans.

Even though she followed rugby growing up, the Wallaroos were not on her radar as the women's game lacked adequate support and promotion.

Chancellor only began playing as a 21-year-old university student, admitting earlier this week "rugby wasn't an option" during her childhood.

At Canberra Stadium this evening, there will be young girls among the spectators eagerly watching the Wallaroos play Scotland.

They will be cheering on their heroes and dreaming of playing for the national women's rugby team, proving Chancellor has taken giant steps in accomplishing her mission.

Inspiring young fans has been at the forefront of Emily Chancellor's mind. (Getty Images: Robbie Stephenson)

"You can't be what you can't see," Chancellor told ABC Sport on the eve of her Test farewell.

"I feel like that is something that has driven me so hard; to want to keep playing and pushing the image of the Wallaroos to a wider audience.

"I feel like I've had a positive impact on that over the last eight years. I love seeing the kids in the crowd, with their parents, excited.

"What excites me is that there has been so much growth when I look back over the last eight years, considering where I was when I was a kid and the visibility of the game in the women's world [at the time].

"It's come so far. I'm really proud of where we've got to and how many young girls are turning up to games."

Tight bond

After 42 Tests, Chancellor will leave the game as a Wallaroos great.

The 35-year-old appeared in two World Cups and captained the team during the 2025 season.

A stellar domestic career with the NSW Waratahs and stints playing club rugby in the UK and Japan are also among her most cherished experiences.

Emily Chancellor captained the Wallaroos in 2025. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Aside from her on-field achievements, nothing means more to Chancellor than the tight bond she enjoys with her Wallaroos teammates.

She describes the close-knit squad as a "sisterhood".

"We're all struggling or thriving with the challenges rugby faces, particularly in the women's space," said Chancellor, who will start at openside flanker against Scotland.

"Be it pay, the lack of professionalism, or the striving for both of those things, I think that bonds you together massively."

'Limitless' future

The Wallaroos's semi-professional status has made it difficult for the squad to compete with the likes of England and New Zealand, both of which benefit from having full-time programs.

The Wallaroos are in the process of becoming full-time in the build-up to the 2029 World Cup, which will be hosted by Australia.

Emily Chancellor made her Test debut against New Zealand in 2018. (Getty Images)

Chancellor believes the team's opportunities will be "limitless" when this is finally achieved.

"You see how much natural ability the girls have, how much we do with so little in terms of game time at the moment," she said.

"I get excited by what Rugby Australia did with the Aussie women's sevens team when they went full-time.

"A bit more hard work and time together … wow, I think it will be exciting."

Chancellor will be enjoying retirement once the next World Cup rolls around, but her commitment to the Wallaroos's cause shows no signs of diminishing.

The drive to increase visibility of the Wallaroos and women's rugby will remain.

"We've still got a long way to go, and I don't plan on letting up on that goal of making it as visible as possible when I step away from playing," she said.

World.title: Images are all this community has left of their ancestral villages
World.content:
Between rows of leaves and soil, Saber Serhan's father's hands overflow with vegetables.

"That's my father picking me'ta," he said.

"Me'ta's in the same family as the cucumber but longer and lighter in colour, and they'd go down there and there'd be fresh tomatoes, fresh me'ta."

He has been flicking through photographs of farmers, rooftops and fields, captured on a trip to his ancestral village of Kfar Kila in southern Lebanon in 2000.

Today, many of those scenes lie in rubble.

Saber Serhan captured photographs of farmers, rooftops and fields. (Supplied: Saber Serhan)

He has brought the images to an event in Parramatta, in Sydney's west, called The Villages We Carry.

People with southern Lebanese heritage were invited to bring photographs and videos of their ancestral villages, many of which have been damaged or destroyed by the Israeli military over the past six months.

A recent analysis by The New York Times found that 48 out of the 60 villages in occupied areas of southern Lebanon had been mostly levelled, including schools, mosques and businesses.

Many of the villages in southern Lebanon have been destroyed. (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

The Israeli Defense Forces said they had been dismantling infrastructure used by the militant group Hezbollah to launch rockets towards northern Israel.

"In light of what's happening, I see that what I captured at the time with my film camera was a moment in time, and it's been preserved," Mr Serhan said.

Photographs 'help us reconnect'

The one-off event was part of the City of Parramatta's Western Terrace series of workshops in the PHIVE community space.

Zeinab Mahfoud is curator of The Villages We Carry project. (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

Its curator, Zeinab Mahfoud, is working to create a digital archive of southern Lebanese communities which have been shattered by war and displacement.

"Since mass migration from southern Lebanon, we've lost that connection," Ms Mahfoud said.

"We've lost the connection to families, we've lost the connection to the land, and so these photographs not only take us there, but they help us reconnect."

Ms Mahfoud says the photos "help us reconnect". (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

Amani Haydar has brought a photo of her uncle Hussam standing in front of his shop in the village of Aitaroun.

"I thought it would be a good one to bring around because it kind of captures a moment in time, and you can see him standing proudly in front of his shop, which unfortunately he's since lost," Ms Haydar said.

A photo of Amani Haydar's uncle, Hussam, in the village of Aitaroun. (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

Little remains of that shop, except for her now-treasured photograph.

"Those places that we hold dear, those places that represent generations of memories, those places that we call home, are gone," she said.

" The most powerful thing that we can do right now is to hold on to that memory, to affirm that connection to those places and to tell the stories. "

Like many Australians with southern Lebanese heritage, Ms Haydar has grieved the loss of loved ones from afar.

"This is about more than just nostalgia, it's about really honouring those losses, that deep sense of grief," she said.

"That's an important part of our healing as a community, and it's an important part of keeping what we do have for the next generation so that they can learn about it too."

Ms Haydar says the photos are about "honouring those losses". (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

She said she had not lost hope that she could return to rebuild her community, and her uncle Hussam's shop.

"There is a great sense of hope that we will be able to return to our homelands at some point, and keeping that hope alive is really important."

World.title: Quick hits: Bavuma hides from Smith implosion as Boland outgrits batters
World.content:
Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while nightwatchman Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha.

Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Head passes 100 but can't go on

Travis Head began day five needing 13 runs for a gritty, fighting century.

And after a two-hour rain delay, the punchy southpaw reached three figures with relative ease, bringing up the milestone with two leg-side boundaries against South African destroyer Marco Jansen in the sixth over of the day.

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

His celebrations were understandably muted given the state of the game, with his helmet staying in place as he raised his bat and a grin not even threatening to peek through his grill.

It was just Head's second overseas ton after his effort in the 2023 World Test Championship final at the Oval against India, and first against a team on its home patch.

But Head was unable to set up for the long haul his team so craved, with the Australian departing just after the first drinks break, chopping on while attempting a cut shot that was never there.

Head was out for 121 and Australia was 5-209.

2. Boland shows batters how it's done

By now, Australian cricket fans should know better than to doubt Scott Boland.

But even the most optimistic of those watching back home surely wouldn't have expected the nightwatchman to outlast both Head and Steve Smith, take his innings deep into the day and soak up a staggering 166 deliveries.

Boland found the middle of the bat more often than not during his heroic vigil. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

There were a couple of streaky moments, sure, but Boland made his luck more than he rode it, defending with the kind of authority and simplicity his more celebrated batting teammates were so desperately lacking throughout the Test.

He even played a few memorable shots, including an immaculate straight drive back past South Africa spearhead Kagiso Rabada.

But finally, in the second over after tea, Boland's marathon vigil was over, with Wiaan Mulder producing a jagging peach to have the brave nightwatchman bowled through the gate for a new Test best of 40.

3. Bavuma can't watch as Smith throws it away

It was the moment — and didn't Temba Bavuma know it.

The South Africa captain just couldn't watch as Steve Smith top-edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer high into the blue Gqeberha sky, turning his back completely as Matthew Breetzke raced back and settled under the ball.

Bavuma couldn't watch as Breetzke took a dramatic juggling catch. (Fox Cricket)

It was a rash, ugly shot from Smith, and certainly not one befitting of a man tasked with saving a Test match.

But for a moment, it looked like he was going to get away with it.

Having just-about settled underneath the ball, Breetzke juggled once and then twice before securing the wicket that was destined to end the Australian resistance.

Smith, perhaps still struggling with his neck issue from day four, was out for 3 and Australia was 6-255.

4. Mulder does damage after tea

With four wickets still in reserve, Australia reached tea still with a sniff of pulling off one of the great escapes.

But in removing Australia's best two batters, the Proteas had already done the hard part, and there would have been no panic as they readied themselves for the game's final stanza.

And in the opening exchanges of what was being sold as a marathon, 44-over evening session, all-rounder Mulder struck not once, but twice.

First, he ended Boland with that divine off-cutter; then he produced something similarly inspired to send the newly-arrived Pat Cummins packing for 4.

At 8-262, it was all beginning to unravel.

There was only one thing that could save the Aussies now ...

5. South Africa beats descending gloom

All of a sudden, things were beginning to darken in Gqeberha.

With ominous clouds gathering on the outskirts of the oval and ground staff poised to pounce at the boundary rope, the South Africans were in a race with the elements.

Clouds were gathering ominously with the Proteas in search of their final two wickets. (Fox Cricket)

Two wickets were needed.

Well aware of the descending gloom, Bavuma threw the ball to his premier spearhead.

And Rabada delivered in the first over of his spell, bowling Mitchell Starc with the tailender attempting an ugly and wholly unnecessary slog.

But with the skies continuing to intimidate, we were treated to surely one of the most farcical drinks breaks in Test history.

Those five lost minutes, however, were not enough to save the Australians.

The heavens never did open, and number 11 Josh Hazlewood was promptly caught behind the wicket, confirming a chastening innings and 31-run defeat for Australia and a richly deserved series-levelling triumph for the South Africans.

World.title: New Sydney airport honours trailblazing pilot as first passengers welcomed
World.content:
When she was a little girl, Nancy Bird would say "I'm an eppy-plane" as she leapt off fences with her arms outstretched.

It seems the first Australian woman to hold a commercial pilot's licence always wanted to fly.

On Sunday, Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport (WSI) opens to passengers, who will see a large artistic tribute to the pioneer above the domestic departure gates.

Claire Healy and Sean Cordeiro's My God! It's a Woman!! depicts a deconstructed version of Nancy Bird's Gipsy Moth. (Supplied)

"I think being able to see the artworks and her presence there at the airport is a real permanent reminder — not just to me, but to my kids and all the family — that she was a special woman," Nancy's grandson Baron Walton said.

"I think one of her greatest impacts is being a visual example, to women in Australia, of what was possible."

WSI chief executive Simon Hickey said the tribute would be a permanent fixture at the airport.

"Nancy-Bird Walton's story is one of courage, curiosity, and determination, and one that continues to inspire all Australians to this day," he said.

Nancy was born in Kew, NSW, in 1915. She left school at 13 to work in her dad's shop at Mount George and that year, 1928, she took a joy flight at a country show in Wingham and her passion for flying was ignited.

'That's a woman in the air'

In 1933 Nancy started attending Charles Kingsford Smith's flying school in Sydney.

"The social norms was that it was not a place for a woman and Kingsford Smith even said that himself, although his actions showed that he was willing to teach them how to fly," Mr Walton said.

"She just did what no-one thought a young girl would do."

Nancy gained her commercial licence when she was 19 and bought her first plane, a Gipsy Moth she named Vincere. The word "woman" was emblazoned across the underside of the biplane's lower wing.

Loading...

"She used to fly over those hangars quite low so that everyone could see the young girl that they [had told]: 'You'll never fly, you'll never be a pilot — it's not your place," Mr Walton said.

"It was also a way of showing that that's a woman in the air and everybody knew who it was at the time."

In 1935, Nancy began "barnstorming" — offering joy flights — at country shows for 10 shillings a pop.

"Little Bird" Nancy with her barnstorming partner, Peggy McKillop. (Supplied: State Library of NSW/Sam Hood)

She did this with pilot Peggy McKillop and they became known as "Little Bird" and "Big Bird". But Nancy would become better known by the name she was given on her next adventure.

'Angel of the Outback'

During the barnstorming tour in 1935, Nancy was recruited to the Royal Far West Children's Health Scheme by the Reverend Stanley Drummond.

From her base in Bourke, she began delivering medical assistance — including emergency services and maternity care — to people in isolated areas.

It was during that time that Nancy heard the phrase that would become the title of her 1990 memoir, courtesy of a patient who could not contain his disbelief when he clapped eyes on the "Angel of the Outback".

Nancy-Bird Walton defied plenty of expectations. (Supplied: National Library of Australia - Russell Roberts)

"A farmer was in trouble and needed medical assistance urgently," Mr Walton said.

"And when the plane landed to take him to the doctor, this tiny little woman hopped out of the plane and he just said, 'My God! It's a woman' — so that's the name of her book."

That was not the only surprise Nancy delivered during her time in Bourke. Aided by nurses sweltering under red coats and false beards, she also brought Christmas presents to children far from Santa's usual flight path.

Nancy Bird meeting Elgar Thane of Shell Oil. Baron Walton says his nan was as at ease speaking to royalty as she was graziers. (Supplied: National Library of Australia)

'She wasn't just a pilot'

In 1937 Nancy embarked on a world tour to promote an airline and met Charles Walton when she was on her way back home.

Nancy Bird was the first Australian woman licensed to fly passengers. (Supplied: National Library of Australia/Harold Cazneaux)

The Englishman referred to the 24-year-old as "Nancy-Bird" and she adopted the name, along with his surname, when they married in 1939.

During World War II Nancy-Bird recruited and trained female support staff for the Royal Australian Air Force. In 1950 she founded the Australian Women Pilots' Association.

Baron Walton said his nan, who supported charities and received a number of accolades throughout her life, was "was a social reformer".

"She was really passionate about what it meant to be Australian and about helping people that really needed it," he said.

"I've had lots of conversations with the kids about Nan, around the notion that you determine your own destiny — not a person, a group of people, or society."

The tribute to Nancy-Bird Walton AO, OBE, DStJ will greet the first passengers to fly from the airport named for her. (ABC News: Kerrin Binnie)

In 2008 Qantas named its first Airbus A380 in her honour.

"Nan loved the party, even at 92," Mr Walton said.

"She really hung out for it and made a joking comment at the christening of the aircraft: 'I said I'd stick around, and I'm here.'"

Nancy-Bird died at the age of 93 on January 13, 2009, but she continues to inspire successive generations.

Maysa Walton says her great-grandmother is a role model. (Supplied: Baron Walton)

"The amazing thing about Nancy was she wasn't just a pilot, she was a daring person, who moved women in that time," Baron's daughter Maysa Walton said.

"She would always say, "If you're doing something that you know is right and it's annoying other people, that's usually a good sign.'"

A model of Nancy Bird's first plane. (ABC Mid North Coast: Wiriya Sati)

On Saturday Nancy-Bird Walton will be honoured at the Camden Haven Show in Kendall, which will feature a flyover from a Tiger Moth, weather permitting.

The first passenger flight from Western Sydney International Airport will depart for the Gold Coast on Sunday.

World.title: People power in the suburbs exposes the fragility of the AI boom
World.content:
A small data centre operator with three sites being briefly valued at $44 billion, more than Woolworths.

A neighbourhood dispute over power poles that wipes $3 billion off a listed company's value in a single day.

And trillion-dollar global infrastructure build-out getting a wake-up call from the suburbs.

The fragility of the AI boom has been on full display in recent weeks.

An industry that has ignored the concept of "social licence" is colliding with people committed to their communities. And investors are feeling the financial consequences.

Australia ringing the alarm on AI valuations

It's a long way from West Footscray to Wall Street.

But as information has come to move in milliseconds, the titans behind trillion-dollar deals in our AI-boom economy may have spent time looking up "WeFo" on Google Maps, reading about plans for Tasmanian data centres, and wondering: is this where it started to unravel?

Let's step back.

Shares in data centre operator NEXTDC fell 42 per cent in a single day after the company revealed that delays in getting power to a proposed expansion of its massive complex in inner-west Melbourne meant its future earnings would be cut by a third.

The site of the NextDC data centre in West Footscray. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

A neighbourhood dispute and an act of civil disobedience, residents parking their cars in the street to deny trucks access, had stopped the march of industrial-scale power poles that would provide the juice for the next stage of the data centre.

Residents protest giant power poles for data centres Electricity distributor Jemena has been replacing 7-metre wooden power poles with 15-metre industrial poles rated to carry up to 66,000 volts, but there's been one consistent complaint among the residents where this is happening.

Firmus hit a similar hurdle.

The AI data centre company wanted to list on the stock exchange with an initial public offering (IPO) that would have valued it at about $44 billion.

It would have been one of the five biggest floats in the world this year, the biggest in Australia since Telstra went from being government-owned to listed on the markets.

But it fell apart. For one reason, and then a lot of them.

The key reason was that large investors didn't think the company was worth what it thought it was. They refused to buy it at $11 a share, which would have made it one of Australia's 20 largest firms, more valuable than toll road operator Transurban and supermarket giant Coles.

But the others are important, too: growing community opposition to power and water-hungry data centres and the transmission lines needed to feed them; fears about the job-killing nature of artificial intelligence; the collision of election cycles in the US and Australia with voter unhappiness about economic instability and uncertainty.

Craig Scroggie, chair of Data Centres Australia and chief executive and managing director of NEXTDC, speaks during September's AI Summit Australia in Melbourne. (AAP: James Ross)

AI not dead, but hitting resistance

The idea of social licence is that it's the ongoing acceptance and approval of an organisation's activities by people affected by them and society at large.

Whaling has lost its social licence. Very few countries now kill whales.

AI and data centre companies, spawned from the "move fast, break things" ethos of the tech sector, rapidly evolved from medium-sized warehouses in industrial areas to massive facilities closer to homes.

They became the physical manifestation of people's fears about AI. At the end of their street.

Standing outside NEXTDC's massive facility, the behemoth is undeniably dystopian. Devoid of any visible staff, the entirely black box rises vastly above the single-story brick and weatherboard houses on the other side of the street.

The global fight against data centres heats up Last year in the US alone, projects collectively worth $200 billion were scuppered or delayed as communities protested the construction of new data centres promised to deliver the AI of the future.

Protests in Europe and the US tuned leaders to the bad vibes coming from constituents. They didn't see the benefits of facilities that drove up power bills, drained precious water resources, and seemed to be in the business of making masses of people unemployed. The number of jobs in data centres, post-construction, is minimal.

But don't expect the sector to go away. As analysts at Morningstar detail, NEXTDC's assets, "both current and planned, are still in great demand". In addition, community concerns over the centres may increase costs and force new ones further away from built-up areas:

" However, this will affect all developers, will likely be factored into new contracts, and will likely make existing data centres even more valuable. "

A single-street power pole dispute that costs $3 billion

There's a reason NEXTDC's difficulties are getting attention. It exposes the fragility of the AI boom, already unfolding on a scale the world has rarely seen.

Filip Tortevski, senior analyst at Wealth Within, calls it the "first serious warning shot" as investors weigh if this is an isolated incident or the beginning of something much bigger.

"What's concerning isn't simply the $140 million in revenue affected by electricity delays," they write.

"It's the potential chain reaction nobody was pricing in. NEXTDC has acknowledged that delayed customer billing could affect its ability to draw on $6.7 billion in available debt facilities. It has also warned that the delays could affect property valuations, with the financial impact still unknown.

" Think about that. A delay in connecting electricity can potentially affect revenue, financing flexibility and asset values simultaneously. "

The new poles erected in Melbourne are more than twice the height of the 7-metre wooden poles they replaced. (ABC News)

UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce helps manage $175 billion in assets.

Before the Firmus float was pulled, he wished the company well and explained why the fund wouldn't invest a cent in it.

"It all comes down to valuation. We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation. At the current valuation, it's priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation."

Priced to perfection. The amount the company is valued at requires every single plan to run perfectly, in every element.

Many of our large AI and data centre companies appear to rest on the same belief.

This is a world of storms and natural disasters. Of electricity pole installation. Of technologies from labs we hadn't heard of three months ago. Of changes in government. Of residents who don't feel heard. Of shipping delays. Of construction challenges.

Our world is a lot of things. Perfect it is not.

World.title: In occupied Ukraine, Russia is trying to indoctrinate the children it stole
World.content:
Anastasiia's ordeal with Russian authorities in occupied Ukraine is nothing short of terrifying.

Aged 15 at the time, she was living in a foster home in the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson when Russian tanks rolled across the border to start a full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Frightened of the shelling near her home, she and a friend decided to leave, but their plan unravelled when they encountered Russian soldiers.

"We were stopped at a checkpoint," she said, adding the soldiers told them "we were dangerous to their state".

After that, Anastasiia was enrolled in a college, where she says she was exposed to Russian re-education and indoctrination.

At one point, Russia's children's rights commissioner, Maria Lvova Belova, even toured the school and offered study opportunities near Moscow or the chance to join the country's young army cadets.

Race to save Ukrainian kids from war machine Tens of thousands of Ukrainian kids are believed to have been taken by Russia. We joined a rescue mission to bring four home.

During this time, Anastasiia, who is now 19, says she was shunted between Russian foster families in occupied Ukraine.

The ABC has chosen not to publish Anastasiia's full name, in order to protect her identity.

At the second home she stayed in, she says she was physically harmed.

"They beat me there. They humiliated me and told me my mother wouldn't take me back from occupied territory," she said.

Getting a glimpse of what life is like inside Russian-occupied Ukraine is virtually impossible.

People are terrified to speak out, fearing retribution from Russian authorities.

Kherson was captured by Russian troops in March 2022, early in the full-scale invasion. Ukraine liberated it again about seven months later, but many children had already been taken further behind the front lines by Russian authorities.

Anastasiia has been able to share her story because she's now safely in Ukraine's capital after a daring escape.

But there are plenty more stories just like hers. About 1.6 million Ukrainian children are estimated to be growing up under occupation, where newly installed Russian occupation authorities have rolled out indoctrination programs and military training.

The United Nations concluded in 2025 that Russia is committing crimes against humanity in occupied regions of Ukraine in a widespread and systematic manner against the civilian population.

Loading...

Russia trying 'to destroy Ukraine as sovereign state'

Prominent Ukrainian human rights lawyer Kateryna Rashevska is gathering evidence of war crimes and crimes against humanity from those who have lived under Russian control.

Her team then takes the cases to the International Criminal Court (ICC), which has already issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ms Lvova Belova over the illegal deportation of Ukrainian children.

Ms Rashevska has dozens of cases on the go, but the one she chooses to share reveals the extent of Russia's plan.

The mother of a young boy in Kherson was told her parental rights would be taken away if her son didn't participate in Russian military training for children.

"So, this family was persecuted just because he was not loyal at this very young age to the occupying power," Ms Rashevska said.

"This is discrimination. Also, many different violations of the rights of the child," she said.

Kateryna Rashevska is working to make sure Russia one day answers for its crimes. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

The indoctrination and military training started soon after Russia's invasion when the boy was just eight.

But Ms Rashevska said that, since Moscow installed its own authorities in these regions, such activities now started in kindergarten.

"They would like to have young adults prepared physically and mentally to serve to the new motherland, to Russia," she said.

"The fact that we have hundreds or even thousands of the same cases in occupation, we will be able to prove a crime against humanity … [this is] the policy of the Russian Federation."

Ms Rashevska said given the "scale" and "organised nature" of Moscow's intentions to eradicate Ukrainian culture, she believed the crimes could amount to genocide.

"The main goal … is to destroy Ukraine as a sovereign state and to subjugate everything remaining from the Ukrainian nation to Russian influence and control," she said.

A man surveys the damage to his apartment in Kherson. (Reuters: Anna Voitenko)

Earlier this week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News the front lines should be frozen where they are as part of an immediate ceasefire.

Then, he said, more substantial peace negotiations could take place.

As part of its demands to end the war, Russia has consistently demanded Ukraine give it territory it has been unable to capture since its full-scale invasion.

Kyiv, meanwhile, has consistently refused to entertain any peace process that would see it cede land to Moscow.

'We dropped everything and left'

In July 2022, just months after the war started, Dmytro Lubinets was appointed Ukraine's ombudsman for human rights.

Much of his workday is now dedicated to efforts to return Ukrainian children taken by Russia, and gathering evidence to prosecute the cases.

He said, from the evidence they're gathering from witness testimony, life under occupation is repressive.

"Every child now must have … Russian documents, passports, certificate of birth, educational documents, medical documents, everything," he told the ABC.

"Every Ukrainian child must … identify themselves as the Russians.

"And everyone who [is] against this position, according to Russian position, must be killed … including Ukrainian children."

Escaping occupation can be risky and in some cases deadly for those who try.

Ukrainians must pass through myriad checkpoints, with the risk of being stopped and interrogated or arrested at any one of them.

Ludmilla, a foster mother in the Kherson region, made the dangerous decision to flee. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

In some cases, people have disappeared. For two years, foster mother Ludmilla made plans to leave her village near the front line in the occupied Kherson region.

She described living in a constant state of fear as drones flew overhead, and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire made her head feel like it was "caving in".

But she only took the risk to escape when her teenage foster sons received pre-conscription letters at school.

"They were given questionnaires at school. From there, they took them to the military enlistment office. Maybe they would have held them if they were 18, but they aren't yet.

"We dropped everything and left. We decided to leave so that they wouldn't take the children," she said.

It's not safe for Ludmilla to reveal her identity because she still has family living under Russian occupation.

Behind his strongman image, Putin's world is shrinking To his supporters Vladimir Putin restored Russia's pride. His opponents describe a strategist, strongman, gangster and mafia godfather who is living in an increasingly shrinking world.

Ludmilla ends her interview by describing the beauty of her hometown and remains fully intent on returning once the war is over.

But in reality, the future of Ukraine's occupied territories remains a significant point of contention and whether Kyiv ever gets them back is a big unknown.

Ms Rashevska knows she can't control the future of Ukraine's occupied territories but she's working to make sure children trapped there know someone's fighting for their future.

"To abduct children, it is … a way to tell that: 'You don't exist and you will never exist. We are abducting your future'," Ms Rashevska said.

"What we are fighting for is for the absence of war for these children, for the chance for them not to fight in future," she said.

World.title: Children in care at high risk of suicide but national data is patchy
World.content:
Experts say data gaps on suicides in out-of-home care mean prevention efforts are falling short, despite children in care being at higher risk.

Young people are more than three times as likely to attempt suicide compared to children who are not in the care system, according to an Australian Catholic University (ACU) review.

But the lack of readily available public data and insights into these suicides — including whether the child was in kinship care, residential care or foster care — has researchers concerned they are being left in the dark about risk factors.

Experts say we know little about what types of out-of-home care have greater suicide risks. (ABC News: Jessica Hayes)

Sue-Anne Hunter, National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People, said data collection was "fragmented" across states and territories.

"We don't have the full picture, and it restricts the ability to make sure that the right areas receive urgent attention because it leads to blind spots," she said.

"So there's insufficient funding and missed opportunities for early support, and they actually compound the trauma for the children living with the consequences."

While some states do publish data on suicides of children known to child protection departments, they do not all specify whether these children were in out-of-home care.

Profound data gaps do not paint a full picture on suicides in children cared for by the state. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

Professor Daryl Higgins, director of ACU's Institute of Child Protection Studies, said it meant researchers could not design targeted prevention strategies.

"We don't have good data on firstly, the prevalence and secondly, the characteristics, the locations, other factors that might tell us where within the out-of-home care system might children and young people be at greater risk," he said.

"We're not going to get increased investment in … new interventions that support this vulnerable population if in fact we don't have better data."

He suggested the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, which tracks a range of child protection data, could collect and publish suicide data, but it would require "high-level agreement" from all states and territories.

Patchy data

The ABC attempted to gather data from child protection departments on how many children had died by suicide while in the care system.

New South Wales revealed eight children died by suicide in out-of-home care between 2012 and 2022. Five were Indigenous.

Queensland said between 2014 and 2025, 12 children who were under a child protection order died by suicide. Three of those children were First Nations, but it could not provide a breakdown of placements due to the risk of identifying families.

Tasmania, the ACT and South Australia would not provide the data, saying that because the numbers were small, disclosing the information could lead to identification.

Do you know more? Contact Brooke Fryer at: fryer.brooke@abc.net.au

Some states will not provide information on children who have died by suicide while in their care. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Western Australia said every death of a child in care goes to a coronial investigation and directed the ABC to the National Coronial Inquest System (NCIS).

The NCIS, which charges fees to release data, advised it tracks coronial findings and causes of death, but not placement history.

The Northern Territory government referred the ABC to 11 coronial inquests into young people who died by suicide between 2014 and 2023. It said three were in out-of-home care and all three were First Nations. The youngest was nine years old.

Victoria's Commission for Children and Young People (CCYP) revealed there had been 45 deaths by suicide of children known to child protection since July 2017, including six who were Aboriginal children.

The commission's annual report also revealed there were 800 self-harm incidents and 115 suicide attempts among children in care in the last financial year.

Sue-Anne Hunter says addressing suicides in care requires action across government departments. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Ms Hunter said the high number of children attempting suicide in care in Victoria was "horrific".

"We need to remember that every number is a child," she said.

"The state is the parent and so this shouldn't be happening."

Last year, the CCYP found Victoria had made no progress on its 2019 recommendation that it develop a suicide prevention strategy for children in out-of-home care.

Victoria's Department of Families, Fairness and Housing did not respond to the ABC's question about progress on this strategy.

Indigenous children at higher risk

First Nations children are over-represented in the out-of-home-care system and face higher risks of suicide.

Aunty Muriel Bamblett, CEO of the Victorian Aboriginal Child and Community Agency, called for faster screening of children's mental health upon their entry into the care system.

She said in Victoria, the screening took between three and six months.

"These children have gone through huge amounts of abuse and neglect, often being exposed to huge amounts of trauma," she said.

Muriel Bambett says Indigenous service providers help children feel connected to culture while navigating out-of-home care. (Supplied)

Ms Bambett said her organisation had been frustrated to learn of a suicide in out-of-home care of a First Nations young person who had not been referred to VACCA.

"I don't think systems understand really the importance of connection to the Aboriginal community," she said.

Sue-Anne Hunter said "we lose our children" far too often to suicide and preventing it required a whole-of-government approach.

"If a child is removed, are we using a whole-of-system approach to make sure they're safe?" she asked.

"Because we call it child protection, and we put them into care, but if a child's suiciding, it's actually not care and they're not protected."

World.title: Federal Court accused of 'obfuscation' as data breach crisis deepens
World.content:
An integrity crisis in Australia's court system has deepened, prompting calls from the Coalition and the Greens for the Attorney-General to step in and set up an independent audit.

Revelations that highly sensitive court data was accessed in India on at least two occasions has sparked national security fears.

Now, internal court emails have revealed the Federal Court CEO was notified in 2016 of the first data breach — an incident for which no action was taken.

However, a spokesperson for the Federal Court said its CEO, Sia Lagos, had no recollection of having been notified of the data breach by the then-deputy principal registrar.

Security concerns were first raised in 2014 by former Auscript national manager, Paul Cutbush, who made Public Interest Disclosures (PID) to both the family court and the Federal Court as well as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) about the offshoring of sensitive data.

In an email from then-Deputy Principal Registrar of the Federal Court John Mathieson to Mr Cutbush in 2016 he stated:

"I have notified Ms Sia Lagos, who is Acting Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar of the Federal Court, in Mr Soden's absence, as I am required to do so, of the decisions and determinations I have made under the [Public Interest Disclosure] Act."

Paul Cutbush, former Auscript national manager, says the courts and the AFP ignored his disclosures in 2014. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

A spokesperson for the Federal Court of Australia said it was "not accepted that there has been a failure to act" in either the data breach earlier this year or the historical incident.

"Ms Lagos did not have any recollection of a procedural notification she had received almost 10 years earlier concerning the Family Court of Australia and matters pre-dating the present administrative entity," the spokesperson said.

Court dismissed concerns over data breach A whistleblower who raised concerns about Australian court data being accessed in India more than a decade ago says the latest data breach is a "slap in the face".

"Beyond that single notification, Ms Lagos had no involvement in the management of this matter."

Neither the Federal Court, nor the family court acted on the disclosures made to them by Mr Cutbush in 2014. The family court responded two years after the disclosures were made, classifying the breach as "minor and inconsequential" in emails seen by the ABC.

The family court has denied any current executives had knowledge of the first breach despite Mr Cutbush's disclosures.

Last week, Mr Cutbush said the most recent data breach was a "slap in the face" after his concerns were ignored in 2014.

Auscript was responsible for court transcription services in 2014 before VIQ Solutions took over around 2020.

A second data breach occurred earlier this year when VIQ was managing transcription services and the company was shutdown shortly after.

Revelations that sensitive family court data was accessed in India has led to fears of a national security risk. (ABC News: Nour Haydar)

Cases heard in the Federal Court include critical human rights matters, industrial relations cases, taxation law and matters involving multi-million-dollar corporations while the Federal Circuit and Family Court hears migration cases, and matters involving child sexual abuse, domestic violence and property settlements.

It is unclear how many files were accessed in India during either of the offshoring incidents.

'Warning signs ignored by court leadership': Greens

A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said the courts were "responsible for their own operation and management" — a position ridiculed by the Opposition.

Shadow Attorney-General Michaelia Cash said the latest developments strengthened the need for a full independent audit coordinated by the Attorney-General.

Off the record Obtaining court transcripts is expensive and the documents can contain errors, frustrating legal practitioners who say the flaws impede justice.

"I again call on the Attorney-General to take control of this matter and organise a whole-of-government response," she said.

"We need to know what has occurred and how widespread this issue is. It is not good enough for the Attorney-General to keep her head in the sand."

Greens Leader Senator David Shoebridge took aim at the court's leadership.

Senator Shoebridge says the offshoring of data is "deeply disturbing". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"It's almost impossible to believe that we are now facing another round of obfuscation from the Federal Court," he said.

"These data breach issues date back to 2014 and it appears that at least some senior staff members of the court have known this.

"This requires a prompt and public explanation from the court.

"Family court transcripts hold some of the most private and painful moments in people's lives, and twice now that material has gone offshore while the warning signs were ignored by the leadership of the court.

Call for urgent action on VIQ scandal Thirteen government agencies are now embroiled in an expanding scandal involving potential data breaches prompting calls for an urgent audit amid concerns over national security.

"The Attorney-General keeps saying the responsibility is solely with the court, but the fact is the listed entity is under her administrative authority so she also has a clear role here.

"The Attorney-General should order a forensic audit across every agency in her portfolio that used Auscript and VIQ transcription services to provide people with real certainty about what on earth happened with their sensitive court data."

The Federal Court said it was currently reviewing a report by CyberCX into the latest data breach.

A privacy complaint has also been passed on to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) regarding the offshoring of Australian citizen's data.

The Federal Court said it had provided information to the OAIC and the family court said it would "fully cooperate" with the OAIC or any other government inquiry.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Save the Children fundraiser for Helen Haines surpasses $600,000 as the MP remains critical; Canavan set to announce move to lower house, reports say
World.content:
Politicians would receive bolstered police protection and security for homes and offices under options being weighed by Labor to address mounting safety concerns after the attack on Helen Haines.

Parliament will hold a dedicated session of tributes for Haines on Monday, according to sources in the Albanese government, but Labor will still push forward its legislative agenda on taxing trusts, the digital duty of care, and keeping gas onshore.

MPs have privately noted an increase in erratic behaviour at electorate offices since the Haines attack, though it is not clear if this is due to increased reporting.

Loading

Monday’s four-wheel-drive attack on the independent MP has exposed long-running tensions between federal parliamentarians and the authorities responsible for protecting them.

Elected officials claim security agencies are too reactive and need to modernise their communication with MPs to ensure politicians and their staff feel safe. But authorities have also expressed frustration with MPs who fail to follow protocol when flagging high-risk events or reporting incidents.

The solutions currently being contemplated would probably have done little to stop what authorities believe was an opportunistic, rather than planned, attack on Haines.

World.title: I spent thousands on a ‘potentially dangerous’ marathon. I’d do it again
World.content:
BusinessThe economyCars Opinion I spent thousands on a ‘potentially dangerous’ marathon. I’d do it again Millie Muroi Economics Writer October 23, 2026 — 6:00am

October 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I went to the Chicago Marathon with a goal to run 42km in less than four hours … and a budget. I failed on both accounts. For a long time, I swore myself off running. I didn’t understand why people voluntarily spent hundreds – or thousands – of dollars to put themselves through pain, and I couldn’t believe they actually enjoyed it. Running might seem like a free sport, and it can be, but for most people, it’s far from it. Fast-forward two years, and I’ve become that insufferable friend and colleague whose favourite topics include the trials and triumphs of training for, and running in, marathons (it’s rather unfortunate for anyone who asks me what I did on the weekend or what my travel plans are). A few weeks ago, I travelled to the US to run a marathon: my second one after finishing the Sydney Marathon last year. While the temperature took a toll on many runners, including me (24 degrees might sound perfect, but it’s much higher than the ideal marathon temperature range of 4 to 10 degrees), the financial cost of the marathon was possibly more painful.



There’s no doubt the exchange rate – at less than US70¢ for an Australian dollar at the time – worsened the blow to my hip pocket. Related Article Opinion

Competition I’m training for a marathon. It’s about as fun (and pain-free) as fixing the economy Millie Muroi Economics Writer Running, and running events such as marathons, are becoming increasingly large drivers of economic activity, especially as the sport’s popularity has boomed. For a long time, running has been seen as a sport with low barriers to entry. That is, it’s an activity you can participate in with minimal costs or requirements: you don’t need a team, and you don’t need to pay for access to special venues or equipment. All you strictly need is the ability (and willingness) to run, and maybe a decent pair of shoes. But as more people have taken to the sport, businesses have realised there are huge opportunities to cash in.



Shoe companies such as Asics, Nike and Adidas constantly pump out new and improved running gear – including carbon-plated shoes aimed at helping athletes run faster and more efficiently – at eye-boggling price points. Most newer versions cost about $300 to $400, and both the men and women’s marathon world records were broken by athletes wearing a carbon-plated shoe retailing at about $750. Not all recreational runners will spend a fortune on shoes, but if you’re like me, you end up dropping cash on a large collection of running shoes to cater for different situations and needs – including a carbon-plate shoe you hope will help shave a few minutes off your marathon time. Ethiopian runner Tigst Assefa set the women’s marathon world record wearing carbon-plated shoes last year. Getty Then, there’s spending on running clothes, gels (which are consumed on longer runs to keep you fuelled) and technology such as running watches which provide an increasing array of data to inform your training or help you stay on pace during a marathon.



The rise of social media and run clubs has also encouraged spending on running gear and races: a multibillion-dollar industry. Younger generations such as Gen Z, which tend to be especially health conscious, seem to be among the fastest growing demographics for spending on athleisure as well as participating in running more broadly. But perhaps one of the biggest boosts comes from big running events which not only encourage people to spend money (which they might otherwise have saved) but also draw spending from people who otherwise wouldn’t have splashed cash in a specific city or country. That is, they add a significant amount to the total spending in a place. Related Article Sydney Marathon Marathon, not a sprint: Why Sydney’s beast of a course rewards power over pace For example, while I’ve spent a lot of money in Australia on all sorts of running gear and events, a lot of that spending might have otherwise gone towards other leisure activities or goods, meaning the overall effect on total spending in the country is negligible. But as an Australian runner travelling to Chicago, I – along with tens of thousands of international participants – would have added significantly to the total amount of spending in the city during October.



That money largely boosts the earnings of locals working at restaurants, hotels and tourist attractions in the area, and helps increase economic growth (although higher demand can, at least temporarily, lead to some unfavourable price surges too). It’s why cities generally like to hold big events. And big marathons in particular can be especially lucrative. Take the Sydney Marathon, for example. Especially after gaining “major” status (making it one of eight of the world’s most prestigious marathons), it’s become a bucket-list marathon for many runners, receiving 123,000 applications from people across 162 countries this year. About 35,000 people were accepted and ran the Sydney Marathon last year, contributing $100 million in visitor spending to the local economy. Meanwhile, estimates of visitor spending stimulated by the Chicago Marathon last year sit at closer to $1 billion.



Part of the difference probably comes down to how these amounts were measured, but it can also be explained by several factors. First, the Chicago Marathon field was notably larger than Sydney’s, with 55,000 runners last year compared to 35,000. Second, the Chicago Marathon is more established, and with more runners, it drew a far bigger crowd of spectators (about 1.7 million people compared to about 300,000 for Sydney). While Sydney had a bigger share of international runners in 2025, at about half compared to one-third for Chicago, about three-quarters of Chicago’s runners travelled from outside the state of Illinois (there is no state breakdown for Sydney). It’s possible that the share (and almost certainly the number) of out-of-state runners was higher for Chicago, leading to higher spending on expensive services such as accommodation. The Sydney Marathon last year helped bring about $100 million in visitor spending to the NSW economy. Getty Images My spending in Chicago, for instance, was largely dominated by accommodation, coming in at $2000 for three nights. While on most occasions I would have booked a shared room in a cheaper hostel, my willingness to pay for a solid hotel close to the start line was higher knowing that being well rested would be crucial to tackle the marathon.



Then there’s merchandise. Often, clothing and souvenirs from these events are crazily overpriced. For the Chicago Marathon, for example, I spent close to $500, including $170 on a single jacket. But businesses know that marathons are often a significant personal achievement, experience or memory that runners want to remember, show off and have a keepsake for. This means that prices which customers might usually be unwilling to pay for a jacket, shirt or keyring, are unlikely to deter them. Related Article Opinion

Employment Unemployment probably does need to climb … for now Millie Muroi Economics Writer Spending on food can also be substantial, as marathoners look to scoff down copious quantities of carbs in the days leading up to the race – and then celebrate or refuel afterwards. And while extensive walking and sightseeing is generally discouraged before a marathon (and physically difficult after it), plenty of non-local visitors take the opportunity of being in a new city to enjoy shows, sights, and other attractions.



All of this is on top of the $370 entry fee for international participants in the Chicago Marathon and $330 fee for international runners in the Sydney Marathon. While I managed to walk away from the marathon relatively injury-free, it’s also an event that undoubtedly leads to a pick-up in demand for health services, whether that’s hospitals or physiotherapists: another expense (although one people hope to avoid). I missed my time goal by two minutes, which my ego blames partially on the heat (race organisers issued a “red” weather warning halfway through the race, signalling “potentially dangerous conditions”). And while both my body and bank account will take a while to recover, I like to think my running-related spending, wherever it is in the world, is giving the economy legs. And somehow, I can’t wait to do it all again. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.
