World.title: Everyone is making ’90s alt-rock again. Why?
World.content:
Alt-rock is back and, somehow, it’s cool. How did we get here?

A new generation, including chart-topper Olivia Rodrigo, is tapping into the sound and spirit of ’90s guitar music.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s happened often lately. I’m listening to the week’s buzzy new albums, and all of a sudden – amid chiming guitars, singsong harmonies and crunchy distortion – I’m transported back to my teenage bedroom, listening to Siamese Dream and watching Daria in the orange after-school glow. The sound and spirit of ’90s guitar music – from the melodic jangle of R.E.M. and Sugar, to the lush distortion of Sonic Youth and My Bloody Valentine – is suddenly everywhere. Earlier this year, Olivia Rodrigo – a noted ’90s lover who took The Breeders on tour and recently revived Lilith Fair for a new generation – even sent the sound to the top of the pop charts with her album You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, and its jangly highlight, U + Me = <3. Slow Pulp: the band’s new album Melodie adds Cars-inflected ’80s power-pop to their alt-’90s underpinnings. Emily Massey, lead singer of US indie darlings Slow Pulp – whose new album Melodie builds inventively on their signature alt-’90s foundations – says the era holds an untarnished mystique for Millennials and Zoomers raised in its wake. “We were little kids in the ’90s, so there’s a sense of longing for a time you have some sense of but don’t have fully formed memories of,” she says. Slow Pulp formed in Madison, Wisconsin, the city where Butch Vig famously produced the likes of Nirvana and The Smashing Pumpkins at his Smart Studios. “Growing up, there was something in the air, this feeling of, oh, that’s what’s cool,” says Henry Stoehr, the band’s songwriter and guitarist. Over a decade removed from the last dregs of blokey landfill-indie, and with pop’s top stars offering diminished returns, rock music and fuzzy guitars – so central to youth culture in the ’90s – are cool again.



Charli XCX, a couple of years removed from “Brat Summer”, this year declared “the dance floor is dead” and pivoted to rock music on her new album. Alt-rockers like Phoebe Bridgers and Cameron Winter (along with his band Geese) have become surprise chart phenomenons, and bands like Turnstile, Fontaines D.C., Wednesday and This Is Lorelei are critical darlings and festival favourites. Stoehr understands why the ’90s and its sonics has captivated a generation who came of age amid COVID lockdowns. “I feel like post-2020, there was this pent-up feeling of wanting to get out and enjoy yourself and just ‘vibe’, that psychologically lent itself towards club culture and party culture, just because people were deprived of that for longer than was ideal. “We loved that stuff, too!” he adds. “But you reach a point where it’s like, ‘I’m kind of done partying and I want something that is packed with meaning, something that’s gonna hit me in the gut.’ And I feel like that’s the purpose that rock music has always served, and people are craving that.” Adelaide indie-rockers Swapmeet: the band’s members bonded over their love of Sonic Youth and Pavement. Swapmeet, a buzzy Adelaide band whose members are all 23, bonded over a shared love of ’90s acts like Sonic Youth and Pavement. Their new album Mount Zero touches on Swirlies-style noise and Flying Nun-inflected jangle-pop, while their last EP featured the reverb-drenched atmospherics of Mazzy Star. Guitarist Maxwell Elphick says he got into grunge via Guitar Hero and the CDs his uncle gave him as a teen. The ’90s era’s scrappy DIY looseness immediately appealed to him. “It feels like weird music became cool and popular then, like you didn’t have to be a great vocalist to be in a good band. It was very much just if you could write songs, you could do it, which was really cool. That’s why I gravitated towards it,” he says.



“We’d be making this kind of music anyway, but it’s great that people think rock music is cool again. Because I feel like everyone thought it was a little cringe for a bit.” Of course, amid a critical discourse that favours innovation and “forward-thinking music” over repeating the sounds of yore, looking back can mean being overlooked. “There’s not much originality left in music in terms of what hasn’t been done, and that’s not what we’re trying to do anyway, and I’m sure a lot of music heads would have something to say about that,” says Nina Pitchkites, vocalist/guitarist of US band Wishy, with an era-appropriate eye roll. Nature’s Pill, the new album from US band Wishy, revives ’90s twee and power-pop. Rian Archer Kevin Krauter, the band’s guitarist, says while the new wave of ’90s revivalists aren’t reinventing the wheel, they’re tapping into the way music has functioned since the dawn of time. “Think about blues music,” he says, “they’re all just playing these standards, but what makes someone stand out and special is the unique style and personality they bring to it.” For Wishy, whose fantastic new album Nature’s Pill revives ’90s power-pop and twee – a particular strain of sweet, fuzzy, melodic alt-rock laden with boy-girl harmonies and inspired by cult ’90s indie-rockers like Velocity Girl and Tiger Trap – the current era’s cultural conditions have set an intriguing proposition. In the ’90s in the US, twee and riot grrrl – mostly on Pacific Northwest record labels like K Records and Kill Rock Stars – were driven by feminist politics and anti-macho sensibilities. So, has the age of Donald Trump and the manosphere set the stage for a ’90s-twee revival?



On a couch in his parents’ home in Carmel, Indiana, Krauter ponders the question. “You saw the same thing in the Bush-era of the early 2000s, and we got a lot of effeminate emo music coming out of that, guys wearing really skinny jeans and guyliner, sort of throwing a big middle finger to the macho stereotype that was the dominant structure of the state and culture at the time,” he says. When chauvinism and toxic masculinity is the prevailing culture, it seems natural that artists would want to subvert it. Suddenly, it’s more transgressive to be gentle and sincere – or, as three-inch badges in the ’90s put it, “twee as f—.” There’s already evidence in the burgeoning nu-twee movement featuring (admittedly less guitar-centric) cult bands like ear and Worldpeace DMT and The Femcels. “You think about the Obama-era when we had Burger Records and garage rock, that whole scene was so macho,” Krauter adds as a contrast, citing the hipster hub of trash-rock bands like Black Lips. Burger Records folded in 2020 amid sexual assault accusations over its roster. “I remember being in high school and going to DIY shows and the whole attitude of that scene was very ‘whatever, f— it’. But then, around 2016 when Trump was elected, you started to see more of this ‘softboi’ vibe enter the culture. And so it makes sense that people would rediscover twee attitudes and aesthetics right now”. Although they’re an indie act, signed to the label Winspear, the wild success of bands like Geese points to breakout potential they never imagined a couple of years ago when Wishy released their debut, Triple Seven. “I mean, hopefully all this will result in some kind of favour for us, that’d be nice,” Krauter deadpans. “Like, suddenly rock music is super lucrative again? That would be convenient.”

World.title: Australia’s patched-up batting has reached boiling point. It must change for Cape Town
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Australia’s patched-up batting has reached boiling point. It must change for Cape Town Daniel Brettig October 23, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Gqeberha: “It’s not that hard!” At tea on day five, Jason Gillespie exclaimed these words while admiring the way Scott Boland had held up South Africa for three hours with a straight bat, the occasional cut shot, and a heap of determination. Twenty-nine years ago, Gillespie had played an underrated role in what is still Australia’s most recent Test victory at St George’s Park, taking eight wickets then surviving a critical over from Jacques Kallis. Ian Healy sealed the epic, by a two-wicket margin, with a mighty six over square leg the following over. End of the resistance: Scott Boland is bowled by South Africa’s Wiaan Mulder. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Gillespie’s statement was also tinged with the same exasperation felt by Australian cricket followers both here and back home. The rush of wickets that led to this innings defeat is a sign of bigger problems with Australia’s ageing and patched-up batting order. Coach Andrew McDonald took the view that the day four loss of 13 wickets was not representative of the team he has mentored since early 2022. However, skipper Pat Cummins was a little more forthcoming at game’s end.



He did not have much choice. To suggest that Australia does not have significant problems in the batting order, issues that have attempted to be band-aided by the selection of seasoned domestic role players like Beau Webster and Nic Maddinson, while Marnus Labuschagne has been persisted with through thin and thin, would have been foolish. Cummins is no fool. So it was that he spoke, perhaps with a little of the underlying indignation that bowlers like him – Boland and Gillespie – sometimes feel about malfunctioning batsmen, with a fair sense of perspective about how Durban’s opener, while handsome on the surface, had been somewhat deceiving. Loading “Even last week, [Matt] Renshaw had an amazing game, but I still think we weren’t at our best, particularly in batting,” he said. “Looking around the change room, how good our batters are, and the standards they all hold themselves to, I think we’re probably a little bit shorter in runs of where we’d like to. So it is that balance. “It’s what do we look like at our best? We’re still finding ways to win. We make it hard for ourselves sometimes, but we’ve got three or four days to get it right for Cape Town. There’ll be lots of conversations.



“I think a loss can sometimes kick yourself into gear. I know there’s paper over the cracks sometimes in a win, whereas I think in a loss, it makes you ask questions as a player of yourself. What could I have done differently to try and win?” The views from Australia after day four had been blunt and uncomplimentary. And as much as this team has made great strides through remaining calm and level, the tendency to favour older players is becoming increasingly hard to stomach. That’s true not only of many figures around the states, who are constantly trying to graduate young talent to the next level, but also those serving as custodians of Cricket Australia. Matt Renshaw was out twice on day four. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe McDonald and selection chair George Bailey have been adept at managing up to CA’s senior management and board, most recently in frank discussions with chief executive Todd Greenberg in Durban. But regeneration of the team will become unavoidable, even during the current 12-month glut of Test cricket, if this week’s scenes come even close to being repeated. Perhaps the most significant name in this context right now is not Cameron Green or Josh Inglis, the two players most likely to come back into the side should change be made for Newlands.



Instead, it is the young left-hander Cooper Connolly, adept against pace, who may be the bellwether for further change. In 2024, Bailey and McDonald had made a calculated gamble on Sam Konstas and been rewarded by turning a 1-1 series ledger with India into a 3-1 Border-Gavaskar trophy haul. Konstas’ inclusion didn’t just surprise India. It also served as a shot of adrenaline to the team. Labuschagne, for one, played arguably his best Test innings since 2023 in the teenager’s slipstream. There is cause to look at Connolly in a similar vein for Cape Town. Cummins acknowledged that his men needed something to spark them, certainly in terms of partnerships. Related Article Australian cricket Player ratings: From Boland’s steely defiance to the captain’s shocker “It’s the little moments that, at the end of the game, you look back, and they’re the things that really add up,” Cummins said. “I just think there’s a lot of moments this game where we just weren’t good enough. Whereas last week we weren’t at our best, but those little moments we won. And again, the game becomes a little bit easier once you get through those little moments. “So a couple of key partnerships, you know, look pretty solid, and if you have another go at them, maybe extend them a little bit longer, and suddenly you’re away, and you’re into the game. So that’s all part of the conversation. As batters, could we have played some better shots at different times? Could we have hung in with a batter and extended that 99 into 150 or something?



“As a bowling group, we didn’t take 20 wickets, so I don’t think we’re out of the woods either this game. So as a team effort, you’re always looking at that.” Australia’s longest innings this series 397 balls – Matt Renshaw (190)

190 balls – Travis Head (121)

166 balls – Scott Boland (40)

99 balls – Matt Renshaw (82)

98 balls – Pat Cummins (43)

98 balls – Marnus Labuschagne (39)

92 balls – Nathan Lyon (27) A common accusation levelled at this team following Justin Langer’s exit four-and-a-half years ago is that it has become a club run by the bowlers. While that is an exaggeration, there is undoubtedly a closeness to the senior group – both players and staff – that will be challenged by more bad results. And in terms of what Australia need to win at Newlands, nothing matters more than partnerships – between batsmen, between bowlers, and between players of whatever generation are chosen. In 1997, at their moment of glory, Healy was 32 and Gillespie 21. It’s not that hard. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ASX set to slide as Wall Street falls; oil at highest since May
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide as Wall Street falls; oil at highest since May Stan Choe October 23, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging markets down worldwide, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran. The S&P 500 sank 1.3 per cent with the Nasdaq composite down 2.4 per cent, but stocks outside of tech did better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down a more modest 0.1 per cent. Wall Street again came under pressure from weakness in AI-related stocks. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures at 4.55am AEDT pointing to a loss of 19 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US70.19¢. AI-related stocks on Wall Street have been shaky on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that stock prices simply shot too high in their years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.



Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.1 per cent. It gave a range for its forecast for profit this quarter whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4 per cent surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the already healthy gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment. Related Article Opinion

Elon Musk Sky’s not the limit: $5 trillion sci-fi deal could bring Musk closer to Mars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Other big tech stocks were unsettled following their own quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7.4 per cent after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.



Tesla slipped 2.1 per cent after flipping between gains and losses in the morning. It reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast. The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.3 per cent. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total value, the chip giant was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 9.6 per cent, though it’s swung between wide gains and losses of roughly 4 per cent within each of the last two days. The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7 per cent. Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.9 per cent to $US111.99 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s at the high end of the $US97 to $US112 range it’s been yo-yoing through in October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4 per cent. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds. Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt. Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns have pushed yields in the US bond market to their highest levels in decades, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors. But US yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.



Related Article Renewables ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98 per cent from 5.13 per cent late Wednesday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country. That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks. Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.



CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 6.3 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: The NSW regional towns where house prices defied the downturn
World.content:
PropertyNewsNSW residential property The NSW regional towns where house prices defied the downturn Elizabeth Redman October 23, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. House prices are higher than a year ago in most parts of regional NSW, despite edging down in recent months as rising interest rates and the cost of living take a toll. The median house price for regional NSW slipped 1.2 per cent to $820,000 in the September quarter, the latest Domain House Price report, released on Thursday, shows. The typical regional house in NSW still costs 2.6 per cent more than a year ago, but in some areas the past year’s rise has been steeper. In Dungog shire in the Hunter region, the median house costs $907,500 after rising 26.9 per cent in 12 months. Inverell, north of Tamworth, jumped 23.4 per cent to a more affordable median of $475,000, while in the state’s west, Broken Hill rose 22.7 per cent to just $270,000. There were also rises of at least 20 per cent in Armidale, Liverpool Plains and Edward River.



Investors looking for affordable properties have pushed up prices in some towns where homes cost far less than Sydney. Those buyers have thinned out recently after the federal budget’s changes to investor taxes and the ongoing high cost of mortgages. Experts say price moves can be volatile in smaller towns with few homes for sale. Related Article Sydney house prices ‘The downturn’s broadened’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.66m Domain senior residential economist David Cannington said regional markets had not experienced as sharp a drop-off in sentiment as capital cities. Sydney house prices fell 4.7 per cent in the quarter. “The regional market’s probably driven more so by the underlying market fundamentals, so the supply and demand balance,” he said. “Higher mortgage rates, the higher cost of living, they’re factors that are impacting the major capital cities and the regions.” Regions offering strong employment opportunities and population growth may have jumped in price, as well as their affordability benefits, compared to Sydney, Cannington said.



“That’s creating that draw for housing demand which is, of course, going to drive some strong price growth,” he said, noting regional markets would be more resilient amid a wider property price slowdown. Herron Todd White chief economist Cameron Kusher said rate hikes and poor sentiment for housing had translated into a lack of buyer willingness. Inverell house prices have jumped. Ray White At the same time, sellers in regional areas were having to reduce their expectations, although many were likely to come out ahead. “Most of the people selling in these areas have still made a significant amount of money over the past few years,” he said.



“A lot of investors were active in the market right up until the federal budget … That rush of investor buying has pushed up prices.” Related Article Renting The regional NSW towns that boomed most over the past year Kusher said city dwellers had been moving to some of the towns where prices had risen, drawn to jobs in agriculture, mining, healthcare or education, but growth had moved away from coastal markets that previously boomed. The Byron shire rose just 2.7 per cent in 12 months to a median house price of $1.51 million, not far below Sydney, while Kiama rose 1.7 per cent to $1,475,000. “It’s [Byron] become out of reach for people who want to buy there but can’t afford it,” he said.



In Dungog, Dillon & Sons principal Tavis Chivers said there were not a large number of homes for sale, which underpinned price growth. “We just don’t have the oversupply. We only sell on average 30 residential houses a year, whether things are good or bad,” he said. “If you come up and say ‘I want a brand-new house’ or ‘I want a weatherboard’ … We’ve got plenty for sale, but nothing that suits you.” Chivers added that there had been some upper-end sales, which had also contributed to the higher median price.



“You can buy something absolutely amazing and beautiful for $1 million. We’ve had quite a few transactions in that bracket,” he said. “I think Dungog is a beautiful place to raise a family. I think Dungog is a beautiful place to retire to.” In Inverell, Annabelle Gleeson of Annabelle’s Inverell had been fielding demand from investors – until recently. “The last 12 months we’ve been inundated by buyer’s agents coming to town like investors from Sydney and Melbourne, buying anything up to the $550,000 mark,” she said.



“But since the last two months, eight weeks, it’s really slowed up, so whether that’s the cost-of-living crisis and everything, it has slowed down. But we still have people moving here,” she said. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Point Piper mansion Akuna hits the market for more than $55 million She said investors were drawn to properties up to about the $550,000 mark, and could get a good rental return. The market for more expensive properties was a little slower, she said, although buyers are still arriving from the city. “It is a beautiful town, beautiful country town,” she said. “And very safe and healthy to live in with jobs and good country schools, new police station, new hospital.” Property alerts are now available in the SMH app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.

Capital Gain The last of the Melbourne pubs embroiled in the spectacular collapse of Jon Adgemis’ Public Hospitality Group is up for grabs with expectations of around $4 million. The Vine Hotel, 59 Wellington Street, Collingwood. The Vine Hotel, on the corner of Derby Street, at 59 Wellington Street was reportedly earmarked for a George Calombaris restaurant before the Adgemis empire crumbled, owing $1.8 billion. The sell-down of the 22-hotel portfolio has so far yielded about $80 million. While the Vine is currently vacant and covered in graffiti, the Art Nouveau-style pub is in the fast-gentrifying southern regions of Collingwood and ripe for revival.



The location is A1. It’s on 417-square-metres of land with three street frontages, next door to Gurner’s huge Victoria & Vine apartment project and across the road from The Commons office building. Records show an Adgemis company, The Vine at Collingwood, paid $4.75 million in November in 2021 but plans for its glow-up never got off the ground. The Saint Hotel, St Kilda. Adgemis, also busy with the burgeoning Sydney stable, was lining up big name restaurateurs for the other two Melbourne venues. Guy Grossi’s Osteria went into The Clifton in Kew and Karen Martini took over the Saint Hotel on Fitzroy Street, St Kilda. The south side pub sold last December to the Kokoda Group for $8.4 million and negotiations are well-advanced for the sale of the Clifton. HTL’s Scott Callow and George Iliopulos have the listing.



In other hotel news, the strata-titled Hotel Lincoln at 91 Cardigan Street, Carlton, sold for $2.5 million through CVA’s Jarrod Moran and Matt Knox. The Clifton Hotel in Kew Junction. Luis Enrique CBD leasing Not every renovation is a success story and the 2021 ‘de-furbishment’ at the Centreway Arcade left many people baffled, including potential tenants. However, the arcade at 259 Collins Street is now fully leased with the opening of a luxury-focused Cash Converters in a 30 sqm space and Bami Station which also signed up for 30 sqm. An escape room, Escape This, has leased 750 sqm in the building’s upper floors.



The interior of the seven-level building, constructed in 1917, was remodelled in 1987 by architects Cocks Carmichael and Whitford and won several awards. Frankly, it was one of the city’s few successful post-modern architectural statements. However, the building’s newish owner, sushi queen Anna Kasman, ripped out the fixtures in 2021 and had the whole arcade painted a stark white. Centreway Arcade in 2018 before its renovation. Michael Clayton-Jones After the pandemic and the sterile renovation, tenants were slow to return to the building Kasman had bought for $40 million in 2014. In good news, however, Ainsworth Property’s Zelman Ainsworth has got the building leased up along with a string of other deals. Down at the rebuilt Melbourne Walk arcade, Sydney Cigars has leased 50 sqm and Boston Clothing a further 117 sqm. Akubra Hats is also moving into the Walk.



Meanwhile, local accessories maker Bellroy is opening its first brick-and-mortar shop, leasing 118 sqm at 271 Little Collins Street. The local bag maker is also opening in Sydney, New York, London and Kuala Lumpur next year. Bellroy is opening its first shop at 271 Little Collins Street. Eamon Gallagher Retail leasing demand was consistent across the board, Ainsworth said. “We’re seeing retailers willing to commit to long-term leases at full market rents, provided landlords take a collaborative approach to structuring deals,” he said. In other deals, former NSW credit union, IMB Bank, is opening a branch in a 200 sqm shop in the newly refurbished 114 William Street. At the other end of town, Bupa Dental has taken out 357 sqm at Collins Place where Truefitt & Hill are also opening up in a 31 sqm shop.



CBD office Editor's pick Commercial real estate Property sells for lucky number: $4,888,888 Hexa Group, a once active Chinese-capital backed property player, is selling a pair of CBD office buildings in the legal district. Hexa bought 369-375 Lonsdale Street in 2023, paying the auspicious price of $18.888 million – the number 8 is believed to bring luck in Chinese culture. However, the current price quoted for the buildings is around $25 million. The 1002 sqm three-storey building at 369-371 Lonsdale was previously occupied by Dean’s Art at the street level and is on 580 sqm of land. Its neighbour, a 600 sqm two-storey property rented to IDP Education, is on 337 sqm of land. Cushman & Wakefield’s Daniel Wolman, Oliver Hay and Leon Ma have the listing.



The building next door at 365 Lonsdale Street, which is on 417 sqm of land, last sold in 2023 to a Vietnamese investor for $10 million. Hexa Group has been relatively quiet since 2020 when it developed the 31-level Panorama tower in Box Hill. Strata Meanwhile, another floor of Golden Age’s 27-floor 130 Little Collins Street tower has sold and just two whole levels remain. The upper levels of Golden Age’s 130 Little Collins Street tower. The tower, dominated by luxury watch sellers, restaurateur Chris Lucas and Golden Age’s corporate offices, replaced a modest brown brick building owned by the Uniting Church.



The 351 sqm level 21 sold last week and levels 20 and 17 remain, as well as a few smaller spaces on other floors. The tower’s upper levels have spectacular views of the CBD. Cushman & Wakefield’s Jack Cooper and Angus Parnham are handling enquiries but declined to comment on the price. The building is now 80 per cent sold and has achieved rates of more than $20,000 per square metre which puts the likely price of the recently sold floor at around $7 million. A couple of blocks away, not-for-profit health insurer Latrobe Health Services is selling its level 12 penthouse office at 343 Little Collins Street in Equitable House. The boardroom at level 12, 343 Little Collins Street. Records show the Gippsland-based insurer paid more than $1.43 million for the 340 square metre offices in 2006, shortly after the 11,910 sqm 12-storey building was strata-titled. CBRE’s Alex Brierly and Nathan Mufale are handling the campaign and quoting between $2-$2.2 million for the vacant property.



Industrial Editor's pick Hotels After a decade of drama, Corkman pub’s concrete clone is complete A Derrimut industrial property, leased to blue-chip tenants SunRice and Asahi, is up for sale through its mortgagee with price expectations of around $40 million. The companies which own 10-16 Fulton Drive – Fulton Road Properties and Fulton Properties Over – are run by the Kutlesovski family. Records show Stefce Kutlesovski, one of the developers who knocked down the Corkman Irish pub in Carlton, owned the companies until 2021, after which they were transferred to Lube Kutlesovski. The corporate database also shows KordaMentha took control of the companies in late September and gained possession of the property on October 6.



Built in 2020, the two warehouses cover 20,031 sqm. They’re in the Gilbertson Industrial Estate on a large 37,940 sqm land holding. They have a relatively short lease average of just under eight months with Asahi set to move to a purpose-built facility in Ravenhall. Current rent is approximately $2.5 million but the leasing rate of $125 per square metre is less than the market average of $150 in the area. Capital Gain The Catholic Archdiocese of Sydney (CAS) is hoping to raise more than $20 million in the sale of its landmark property in Sydney’s inner west which it has owned and occupied since 1992. The property is currently occupied by the Catholic Institute Sydney (CIS). The heritage site at 95-103 Albert Road, Strathfield, was constructed in the 1890s, was extended in 1911 and had a library added in 1996. According to records, the CAS bought it in 1992 for about $2.1 million, and it now comprises a freehold land area of 6635 square metres with 30 bedrooms, 13 bathrooms and 45 car spaces.



The property is currently occupied by the Catholic Institute Sydney (CIS), which intends to relocate closer to the University of Notre Dame Australia and its Broadway Campus. It plans to grow strategic and educational ties between university students and seminarians. Editor's pick Commercial real estate Collingwood’s The Vine Hotel looking for new owner in $4m sale It originally served the NSW Home Lending Society for the Blind, the Industrial Home for Blind Women, and the Retreat for Aged Female Blind, and was closed and sold in 1897. In 1911, it was extended by the Bedford Collegiate School for Girls, adding a barrack for WWII women. When CAS purchased the site, it had most recently been used by Australia Post. Michael Murphy from McGrath Strathfield and Knight Frank’s Anthony Pirrottina are the agents on the sale.



Foxy move The popular and highly sought-after White Fox boutique online fashion brand has thrown down the gauntlet to traditional high street retailers by buying a large-scale warehouse in Sydney’s south to cater for demand. 19 O’Riordan Street, Alexandria. Proving that online shopping is the growth sector of the retail industry, while shop front-based stores are closing, the business, run by Daniel and Georgia Contos, paid $87 million for the site at 19 O’Riordan Street, Alexandria which is a 10,238 square metre industrial facility on a 13,140 sqm freehold site. The new warehouse was purpose-built by the vendor, and former owner-occupier, True Alliance which is controlled by the Hendler brothers. The facility comprises high-clearance warehousing, a 1,219 sqm mezzanine, three levels of office accommodation and 102 car spaces and has capacity to extend the site to 32,850 sqm.



The Alexandria site will improve order fulfilment for the brand’s high-volume weekly product drops, moving the company from a tenant to a property owner for its logistics network. It will add to White Fox’s $70 million acquisition of a five-storey boutique commercial office on Dunning Avenue in nearby Rosebery in May. That site is the group’s headquarters and boasts a bar, podcast studio, wellness space, gym, its very own pink slide, a café, a library, a ‘treats space’, a vending machine offering tan products, basketball court, a Pilates studio, therapy room, lunchroom, sauna, studios and an auditorium. Colliers agents Michael Crombie and Trent Gallagher advised on the sale. Centennial expands The busy private Sydney-based fund manager, Centennial Property has extended its portfolio with its first regional industrial landholding at Ballina in northern NSW in a deal worth $22 million.



The deal is a major pivot from its usual metro infill stomping grounds after teaming up with Brisbane’s Direct Commercial Property (DCP) to secure the 8.3 hectare site at 45-65 Smith Drive, West Ballina. Centennial is run by chairman Jonathan Wolf and chief executive Paul Ford, with a portfolio of 63 assets and over $2.8 billion under management across the industrial and logistics, office, retail and boutique residential sectors. The 8.3 hectare site at 45-65 Smith Drive, West Ballina. As Ballina’s largest contiguous industrial landholding, with direct exposure to the M1 Pacific Motorway, the joint venture partners will develop it into an 18-lot subdivision for selling down to capitalise on the scarcity of industrial sites in the Ballina-Byron Shires. The development will have an end value around $70 million. JLL and North Coast Commercial Real Estate were the agents on the sale.



Billbergia retail Private developer Billbergia has sold all the retail and commercial section of its Arncliffe Central project for $37 million, in a single deal to a private equity fund. Billbergia’s Arncliffe Central project. The sale covers 4,000 square metres of shops at 161-173 Princes Highway, Arncliffe, which includes a supermarket, smaller stores and a childcare centre. The retail space in Sydney’s south sits beneath 806 apartments across four towers, all of which have sold. Consistent with the strategy of Billbergia to create communities, the development also includes a 1,634 sqm library and community centre, a 4,000 sqm public park, new pedestrian links and customer parking.



The sale was brokered by RWC Sydney City Fringe’s Kamal Silwal. carolynannecummins@gmail.com The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.content:
Politicians would receive bolstered police protection and security for homes and offices under options being weighed by Labor to address mounting safety concerns after the attack on Helen Haines.

Parliament will hold a dedicated session of tributes for Haines on Monday, according to sources in the Albanese government, but Labor will still push forward its legislative agenda on taxing trusts, the digital duty of care, and keeping gas onshore.

MPs have privately noted an increase in erratic behaviour at electorate offices since the Haines attack, though it is not clear if this is due to increased reporting.

Loading

Monday’s four-wheel-drive attack on the independent MP has exposed long-running tensions between federal parliamentarians and the authorities responsible for protecting them.

Elected officials claim security agencies are too reactive and need to modernise their communication with MPs to ensure politicians and their staff feel safe. But authorities have also expressed frustration with MPs who fail to follow protocol when flagging high-risk events or reporting incidents.

The solutions currently being contemplated would probably have done little to stop what authorities believe was an opportunistic, rather than planned, attack on Haines.

World.title: I spent thousands on a ‘potentially dangerous’ marathon. I’d do it again
World.content:
BusinessThe economyCars Opinion I spent thousands on a ‘potentially dangerous’ marathon. I’d do it again Millie Muroi Economics Writer October 23, 2026 — 6:00am

October 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I went to the Chicago Marathon with a goal to run 42km in less than four hours … and a budget. I failed on both accounts. For a long time, I swore myself off running. I didn’t understand why people voluntarily spent hundreds – or thousands – of dollars to put themselves through pain, and I couldn’t believe they actually enjoyed it. Running might seem like a free sport, and it can be, but for most people, it’s far from it. Fast-forward two years, and I’ve become that insufferable friend and colleague whose favourite topics include the trials and triumphs of training for, and running in, marathons (it’s rather unfortunate for anyone who asks me what I did on the weekend or what my travel plans are). A few weeks ago, I travelled to the US to run a marathon: my second one after finishing the Sydney Marathon last year. While the temperature took a toll on many runners, including me (24 degrees might sound perfect, but it’s much higher than the ideal marathon temperature range of 4 to 10 degrees), the financial cost of the marathon was possibly more painful.



There’s no doubt the exchange rate – at less than US70¢ for an Australian dollar at the time – worsened the blow to my hip pocket. Related Article Opinion

Competition I’m training for a marathon. It’s about as fun (and pain-free) as fixing the economy Millie Muroi Economics Writer Running, and running events such as marathons, are becoming increasingly large drivers of economic activity, especially as the sport’s popularity has boomed. For a long time, running has been seen as a sport with low barriers to entry. That is, it’s an activity you can participate in with minimal costs or requirements: you don’t need a team, and you don’t need to pay for access to special venues or equipment. All you strictly need is the ability (and willingness) to run, and maybe a decent pair of shoes. But as more people have taken to the sport, businesses have realised there are huge opportunities to cash in.



Shoe companies such as Asics, Nike and Adidas constantly pump out new and improved running gear – including carbon-plated shoes aimed at helping athletes run faster and more efficiently – at eye-boggling price points. Most newer versions cost about $300 to $400, and both the men and women’s marathon world records were broken by athletes wearing a carbon-plated shoe retailing at about $750. Not all recreational runners will spend a fortune on shoes, but if you’re like me, you end up dropping cash on a large collection of running shoes to cater for different situations and needs – including a carbon-plate shoe you hope will help shave a few minutes off your marathon time. Ethiopian runner Tigst Assefa set the women’s marathon world record wearing carbon-plated shoes last year. Getty Then, there’s spending on running clothes, gels (which are consumed on longer runs to keep you fuelled) and technology such as running watches which provide an increasing array of data to inform your training or help you stay on pace during a marathon.



The rise of social media and run clubs has also encouraged spending on running gear and races: a multibillion-dollar industry. Younger generations such as Gen Z, which tend to be especially health conscious, seem to be among the fastest growing demographics for spending on athleisure as well as participating in running more broadly. But perhaps one of the biggest boosts comes from big running events which not only encourage people to spend money (which they might otherwise have saved) but also draw spending from people who otherwise wouldn’t have splashed cash in a specific city or country. That is, they add a significant amount to the total spending in a place. Related Article Sydney Marathon Marathon, not a sprint: Why Sydney’s beast of a course rewards power over pace For example, while I’ve spent a lot of money in Australia on all sorts of running gear and events, a lot of that spending might have otherwise gone towards other leisure activities or goods, meaning the overall effect on total spending in the country is negligible. But as an Australian runner travelling to Chicago, I – along with tens of thousands of international participants – would have added significantly to the total amount of spending in the city during October.



That money largely boosts the earnings of locals working at restaurants, hotels and tourist attractions in the area, and helps increase economic growth (although higher demand can, at least temporarily, lead to some unfavourable price surges too). It’s why cities generally like to hold big events. And big marathons in particular can be especially lucrative. Take the Sydney Marathon, for example. Especially after gaining “major” status (making it one of eight of the world’s most prestigious marathons), it’s become a bucket-list marathon for many runners, receiving 123,000 applications from people across 162 countries this year. About 35,000 people were accepted and ran the Sydney Marathon last year, contributing $100 million in visitor spending to the local economy. Meanwhile, estimates of visitor spending stimulated by the Chicago Marathon last year sit at closer to $1 billion.



Part of the difference probably comes down to how these amounts were measured, but it can also be explained by several factors. First, the Chicago Marathon field was notably larger than Sydney’s, with 55,000 runners last year compared to 35,000. Second, the Chicago Marathon is more established, and with more runners, it drew a far bigger crowd of spectators (about 1.7 million people compared to about 300,000 for Sydney). While Sydney had a bigger share of international runners in 2025, at about half compared to one-third for Chicago, about three-quarters of Chicago’s runners travelled from outside the state of Illinois (there is no state breakdown for Sydney). It’s possible that the share (and almost certainly the number) of out-of-state runners was higher for Chicago, leading to higher spending on expensive services such as accommodation. The Sydney Marathon last year helped bring about $100 million in visitor spending to the NSW economy. Getty Images My spending in Chicago, for instance, was largely dominated by accommodation, coming in at $2000 for three nights. While on most occasions I would have booked a shared room in a cheaper hostel, my willingness to pay for a solid hotel close to the start line was higher knowing that being well rested would be crucial to tackle the marathon.



Then there’s merchandise. Often, clothing and souvenirs from these events are crazily overpriced. For the Chicago Marathon, for example, I spent close to $500, including $170 on a single jacket. But businesses know that marathons are often a significant personal achievement, experience or memory that runners want to remember, show off and have a keepsake for. This means that prices which customers might usually be unwilling to pay for a jacket, shirt or keyring, are unlikely to deter them. Related Article Opinion

Employment Unemployment probably does need to climb … for now Millie Muroi Economics Writer Spending on food can also be substantial, as marathoners look to scoff down copious quantities of carbs in the days leading up to the race – and then celebrate or refuel afterwards. And while extensive walking and sightseeing is generally discouraged before a marathon (and physically difficult after it), plenty of non-local visitors take the opportunity of being in a new city to enjoy shows, sights, and other attractions.



All of this is on top of the $370 entry fee for international participants in the Chicago Marathon and $330 fee for international runners in the Sydney Marathon. While I managed to walk away from the marathon relatively injury-free, it’s also an event that undoubtedly leads to a pick-up in demand for health services, whether that’s hospitals or physiotherapists: another expense (although one people hope to avoid). I missed my time goal by two minutes, which my ego blames partially on the heat (race organisers issued a “red” weather warning halfway through the race, signalling “potentially dangerous conditions”). And while both my body and bank account will take a while to recover, I like to think my running-related spending, wherever it is in the world, is giving the economy legs. And somehow, I can’t wait to do it all again. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Everyone is making ’90s alt-rock again. Why?
World.content:
Alt-rock is back and, somehow, it’s cool. How did we get here?

A new generation, including chart-topper Olivia Rodrigo, is tapping into the sound and spirit of ’90s guitar music.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s happened often lately. I’m listening to the week’s buzzy new albums, and all of a sudden – amid chiming guitars, singsong harmonies and crunchy distortion – I’m transported back to my teenage bedroom, listening to Siamese Dream and watching Daria in the orange after-school glow. The sound and spirit of ’90s guitar music – from the melodic jangle of R.E.M. and Sugar, to the lush distortion of Sonic Youth and My Bloody Valentine – is suddenly everywhere. Earlier this year, Olivia Rodrigo – a noted ’90s lover who took The Breeders on tour and recently revived Lilith Fair for a new generation – even sent the sound to the top of the pop charts with her album You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, and its jangly highlight, U + Me = <3. Slow Pulp: the band’s new album Melodie adds Cars-inflected ’80s power-pop to their alt-’90s underpinnings. Emily Massey, lead singer of US indie darlings Slow Pulp – whose new album Melodie builds inventively on their signature alt-’90s foundations – says the era holds an untarnished mystique for Millennials and Zoomers raised in its wake. “We were little kids in the ’90s, so there’s a sense of longing for a time you have some sense of but don’t have fully formed memories of,” she says. Slow Pulp formed in Madison, Wisconsin, the city where Butch Vig famously produced the likes of Nirvana and The Smashing Pumpkins at his Smart Studios. “Growing up, there was something in the air, this feeling of, oh, that’s what’s cool,” says Henry Stoehr, the band’s songwriter and guitarist. Over a decade removed from the last dregs of blokey landfill-indie, and with pop’s top stars offering diminished returns, rock music and fuzzy guitars – so central to youth culture in the ’90s – are cool again.



Charli XCX, a couple of years removed from “Brat Summer”, this year declared “the dance floor is dead” and pivoted to rock music on her new album. Alt-rockers like Phoebe Bridgers and Cameron Winter (along with his band Geese) have become surprise chart phenomenons, and bands like Turnstile, Fontaines D.C., Wednesday and This Is Lorelei are critical darlings and festival favourites. Stoehr understands why the ’90s and its sonics has captivated a generation who came of age amid COVID lockdowns. “I feel like post-2020, there was this pent-up feeling of wanting to get out and enjoy yourself and just ‘vibe’, that psychologically lent itself towards club culture and party culture, just because people were deprived of that for longer than was ideal. “We loved that stuff, too!” he adds. “But you reach a point where it’s like, ‘I’m kind of done partying and I want something that is packed with meaning, something that’s gonna hit me in the gut.’ And I feel like that’s the purpose that rock music has always served, and people are craving that.” Adelaide indie-rockers Swapmeet: the band’s members bonded over their love of Sonic Youth and Pavement. Swapmeet, a buzzy Adelaide band whose members are all 23, bonded over a shared love of ’90s acts like Sonic Youth and Pavement. Their new album Mount Zero touches on Swirlies-style noise and Flying Nun-inflected jangle-pop, while their last EP featured the reverb-drenched atmospherics of Mazzy Star. Guitarist Maxwell Elphick says he got into grunge via Guitar Hero and the CDs his uncle gave him as a teen. The ’90s era’s scrappy DIY looseness immediately appealed to him. “It feels like weird music became cool and popular then, like you didn’t have to be a great vocalist to be in a good band. It was very much just if you could write songs, you could do it, which was really cool. That’s why I gravitated towards it,” he says.



“We’d be making this kind of music anyway, but it’s great that people think rock music is cool again. Because I feel like everyone thought it was a little cringe for a bit.” Of course, amid a critical discourse that favours innovation and “forward-thinking music” over repeating the sounds of yore, looking back can mean being overlooked. “There’s not much originality left in music in terms of what hasn’t been done, and that’s not what we’re trying to do anyway, and I’m sure a lot of music heads would have something to say about that,” says Nina Pitchkites, vocalist/guitarist of US band Wishy, with an era-appropriate eye roll. Nature’s Pill, the new album from US band Wishy, revives ’90s twee and power-pop. Rian Archer Kevin Krauter, the band’s guitarist, says while the new wave of ’90s revivalists aren’t reinventing the wheel, they’re tapping into the way music has functioned since the dawn of time. “Think about blues music,” he says, “they’re all just playing these standards, but what makes someone stand out and special is the unique style and personality they bring to it.” For Wishy, whose fantastic new album Nature’s Pill revives ’90s power-pop and twee – a particular strain of sweet, fuzzy, melodic alt-rock laden with boy-girl harmonies and inspired by cult ’90s indie-rockers like Velocity Girl and Tiger Trap – the current era’s cultural conditions have set an intriguing proposition. In the ’90s in the US, twee and riot grrrl – mostly on Pacific Northwest record labels like K Records and Kill Rock Stars – were driven by feminist politics and anti-macho sensibilities. So, has the age of Donald Trump and the manosphere set the stage for a ’90s-twee revival?



On a couch in his parents’ home in Carmel, Indiana, Krauter ponders the question. “You saw the same thing in the Bush-era of the early 2000s, and we got a lot of effeminate emo music coming out of that, guys wearing really skinny jeans and guyliner, sort of throwing a big middle finger to the macho stereotype that was the dominant structure of the state and culture at the time,” he says. When chauvinism and toxic masculinity is the prevailing culture, it seems natural that artists would want to subvert it. Suddenly, it’s more transgressive to be gentle and sincere – or, as three-inch badges in the ’90s put it, “twee as f—.” There’s already evidence in the burgeoning nu-twee movement featuring (admittedly less guitar-centric) cult bands like ear and Worldpeace DMT and The Femcels. “You think about the Obama-era when we had Burger Records and garage rock, that whole scene was so macho,” Krauter adds as a contrast, citing the hipster hub of trash-rock bands like Black Lips. Burger Records folded in 2020 amid sexual assault accusations over its roster. “I remember being in high school and going to DIY shows and the whole attitude of that scene was very ‘whatever, f— it’. But then, around 2016 when Trump was elected, you started to see more of this ‘softboi’ vibe enter the culture. And so it makes sense that people would rediscover twee attitudes and aesthetics right now”. Although they’re an indie act, signed to the label Winspear, the wild success of bands like Geese points to breakout potential they never imagined a couple of years ago when Wishy released their debut, Triple Seven. “I mean, hopefully all this will result in some kind of favour for us, that’d be nice,” Krauter deadpans. “Like, suddenly rock music is super lucrative again? That would be convenient.”

World.title: Australia’s patched-up batting has reached boiling point. It must change for Cape Town
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Australia’s patched-up batting has reached boiling point. It must change for Cape Town Daniel Brettig October 23, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Gqeberha: “It’s not that hard!” At tea on day five, Jason Gillespie exclaimed these words while admiring the way Scott Boland had held up South Africa for three hours with a straight bat, the occasional cut shot, and a heap of determination. Twenty-nine years ago, Gillespie had played an underrated role in what is still Australia’s most recent Test victory at St George’s Park, taking eight wickets then surviving a critical over from Jacques Kallis. Ian Healy sealed the epic, by a two-wicket margin, with a mighty six over square leg the following over. End of the resistance: Scott Boland is bowled by South Africa’s Wiaan Mulder. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Gillespie’s statement was also tinged with the same exasperation felt by Australian cricket followers both here and back home. The rush of wickets that led to this innings defeat is a sign of bigger problems with Australia’s ageing and patched-up batting order. Coach Andrew McDonald took the view that the day four loss of 13 wickets was not representative of the team he has mentored since early 2022. However, skipper Pat Cummins was a little more forthcoming at game’s end.



He did not have much choice. To suggest that Australia does not have significant problems in the batting order, issues that have attempted to be band-aided by the selection of seasoned domestic role players like Beau Webster and Nic Maddinson, while Marnus Labuschagne has been persisted with through thin and thin, would have been foolish. Cummins is no fool. So it was that he spoke, perhaps with a little of the underlying indignation that bowlers like him – Boland and Gillespie – sometimes feel about malfunctioning batsmen, with a fair sense of perspective about how Durban’s opener, while handsome on the surface, had been somewhat deceiving. Loading “Even last week, [Matt] Renshaw had an amazing game, but I still think we weren’t at our best, particularly in batting,” he said. “Looking around the change room, how good our batters are, and the standards they all hold themselves to, I think we’re probably a little bit shorter in runs of where we’d like to. So it is that balance. “It’s what do we look like at our best? We’re still finding ways to win. We make it hard for ourselves sometimes, but we’ve got three or four days to get it right for Cape Town. There’ll be lots of conversations.



“I think a loss can sometimes kick yourself into gear. I know there’s paper over the cracks sometimes in a win, whereas I think in a loss, it makes you ask questions as a player of yourself. What could I have done differently to try and win?” The views from Australia after day four had been blunt and uncomplimentary. And as much as this team has made great strides through remaining calm and level, the tendency to favour older players is becoming increasingly hard to stomach. That’s true not only of many figures around the states, who are constantly trying to graduate young talent to the next level, but also those serving as custodians of Cricket Australia. Matt Renshaw was out twice on day four. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe McDonald and selection chair George Bailey have been adept at managing up to CA’s senior management and board, most recently in frank discussions with chief executive Todd Greenberg in Durban. But regeneration of the team will become unavoidable, even during the current 12-month glut of Test cricket, if this week’s scenes come even close to being repeated. Perhaps the most significant name in this context right now is not Cameron Green or Josh Inglis, the two players most likely to come back into the side should change be made for Newlands.



Instead, it is the young left-hander Cooper Connolly, adept against pace, who may be the bellwether for further change. In 2024, Bailey and McDonald had made a calculated gamble on Sam Konstas and been rewarded by turning a 1-1 series ledger with India into a 3-1 Border-Gavaskar trophy haul. Konstas’ inclusion didn’t just surprise India. It also served as a shot of adrenaline to the team. Labuschagne, for one, played arguably his best Test innings since 2023 in the teenager’s slipstream. There is cause to look at Connolly in a similar vein for Cape Town. Cummins acknowledged that his men needed something to spark them, certainly in terms of partnerships. Related Article Australian cricket Player ratings: From Boland’s steely defiance to the captain’s shocker “It’s the little moments that, at the end of the game, you look back, and they’re the things that really add up,” Cummins said. “I just think there’s a lot of moments this game where we just weren’t good enough. Whereas last week we weren’t at our best, but those little moments we won. And again, the game becomes a little bit easier once you get through those little moments. “So a couple of key partnerships, you know, look pretty solid, and if you have another go at them, maybe extend them a little bit longer, and suddenly you’re away, and you’re into the game. So that’s all part of the conversation. As batters, could we have played some better shots at different times? Could we have hung in with a batter and extended that 99 into 150 or something?



“As a bowling group, we didn’t take 20 wickets, so I don’t think we’re out of the woods either this game. So as a team effort, you’re always looking at that.” Australia’s longest innings this series 397 balls – Matt Renshaw (190)

190 balls – Travis Head (121)

166 balls – Scott Boland (40)

99 balls – Matt Renshaw (82)

98 balls – Pat Cummins (43)

98 balls – Marnus Labuschagne (39)

92 balls – Nathan Lyon (27) A common accusation levelled at this team following Justin Langer’s exit four-and-a-half years ago is that it has become a club run by the bowlers. While that is an exaggeration, there is undoubtedly a closeness to the senior group – both players and staff – that will be challenged by more bad results. And in terms of what Australia need to win at Newlands, nothing matters more than partnerships – between batsmen, between bowlers, and between players of whatever generation are chosen. In 1997, at their moment of glory, Healy was 32 and Gillespie 21. It’s not that hard. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ASX set to slide as Wall Street falls; oil at highest since May
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide as Wall Street falls; oil at highest since May Stan Choe October 23, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging markets down worldwide, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran. The S&P 500 sank 1.3 per cent with the Nasdaq composite down 2.4 per cent, but stocks outside of tech did better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down a more modest 0.1 per cent. Wall Street again came under pressure from weakness in AI-related stocks. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures at 4.55am AEDT pointing to a loss of 19 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US70.19¢. AI-related stocks on Wall Street have been shaky on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that stock prices simply shot too high in their years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.



Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.1 per cent. It gave a range for its forecast for profit this quarter whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4 per cent surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the already healthy gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment. Related Article Opinion

Elon Musk Sky’s not the limit: $5 trillion sci-fi deal could bring Musk closer to Mars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Other big tech stocks were unsettled following their own quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7.4 per cent after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.



Tesla slipped 2.1 per cent after flipping between gains and losses in the morning. It reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast. The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.3 per cent. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total value, the chip giant was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 9.6 per cent, though it’s swung between wide gains and losses of roughly 4 per cent within each of the last two days. The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7 per cent. Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.9 per cent to $US111.99 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s at the high end of the $US97 to $US112 range it’s been yo-yoing through in October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4 per cent. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds. Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt. Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns have pushed yields in the US bond market to their highest levels in decades, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors. But US yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.



Related Article Renewables ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98 per cent from 5.13 per cent late Wednesday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country. That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks. Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.



CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 6.3 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: The NSW regional towns where house prices defied the downturn
World.content:
PropertyNewsNSW residential property The NSW regional towns where house prices defied the downturn Elizabeth Redman October 23, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. House prices are higher than a year ago in most parts of regional NSW, despite edging down in recent months as rising interest rates and the cost of living take a toll. The median house price for regional NSW slipped 1.2 per cent to $820,000 in the September quarter, the latest Domain House Price report, released on Thursday, shows. The typical regional house in NSW still costs 2.6 per cent more than a year ago, but in some areas the past year’s rise has been steeper. In Dungog shire in the Hunter region, the median house costs $907,500 after rising 26.9 per cent in 12 months. Inverell, north of Tamworth, jumped 23.4 per cent to a more affordable median of $475,000, while in the state’s west, Broken Hill rose 22.7 per cent to just $270,000. There were also rises of at least 20 per cent in Armidale, Liverpool Plains and Edward River.



Investors looking for affordable properties have pushed up prices in some towns where homes cost far less than Sydney. Those buyers have thinned out recently after the federal budget’s changes to investor taxes and the ongoing high cost of mortgages. Experts say price moves can be volatile in smaller towns with few homes for sale. Related Article Sydney house prices ‘The downturn’s broadened’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.66m Domain senior residential economist David Cannington said regional markets had not experienced as sharp a drop-off in sentiment as capital cities. Sydney house prices fell 4.7 per cent in the quarter. “The regional market’s probably driven more so by the underlying market fundamentals, so the supply and demand balance,” he said. “Higher mortgage rates, the higher cost of living, they’re factors that are impacting the major capital cities and the regions.” Regions offering strong employment opportunities and population growth may have jumped in price, as well as their affordability benefits, compared to Sydney, Cannington said.



“That’s creating that draw for housing demand which is, of course, going to drive some strong price growth,” he said, noting regional markets would be more resilient amid a wider property price slowdown. Herron Todd White chief economist Cameron Kusher said rate hikes and poor sentiment for housing had translated into a lack of buyer willingness. Inverell house prices have jumped. Ray White At the same time, sellers in regional areas were having to reduce their expectations, although many were likely to come out ahead. “Most of the people selling in these areas have still made a significant amount of money over the past few years,” he said.



“A lot of investors were active in the market right up until the federal budget … That rush of investor buying has pushed up prices.” Related Article Renting The regional NSW towns that boomed most over the past year Kusher said city dwellers had been moving to some of the towns where prices had risen, drawn to jobs in agriculture, mining, healthcare or education, but growth had moved away from coastal markets that previously boomed. The Byron shire rose just 2.7 per cent in 12 months to a median house price of $1.51 million, not far below Sydney, while Kiama rose 1.7 per cent to $1,475,000. “It’s [Byron] become out of reach for people who want to buy there but can’t afford it,” he said.



In Dungog, Dillon & Sons principal Tavis Chivers said there were not a large number of homes for sale, which underpinned price growth. “We just don’t have the oversupply. We only sell on average 30 residential houses a year, whether things are good or bad,” he said. “If you come up and say ‘I want a brand-new house’ or ‘I want a weatherboard’ … We’ve got plenty for sale, but nothing that suits you.” Chivers added that there had been some upper-end sales, which had also contributed to the higher median price.



“You can buy something absolutely amazing and beautiful for $1 million. We’ve had quite a few transactions in that bracket,” he said. “I think Dungog is a beautiful place to raise a family. I think Dungog is a beautiful place to retire to.” In Inverell, Annabelle Gleeson of Annabelle’s Inverell had been fielding demand from investors – until recently. “The last 12 months we’ve been inundated by buyer’s agents coming to town like investors from Sydney and Melbourne, buying anything up to the $550,000 mark,” she said.



“But since the last two months, eight weeks, it’s really slowed up, so whether that’s the cost-of-living crisis and everything, it has slowed down. But we still have people moving here,” she said. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Point Piper mansion Akuna hits the market for more than $55 million She said investors were drawn to properties up to about the $550,000 mark, and could get a good rental return. The market for more expensive properties was a little slower, she said, although buyers are still arriving from the city. “It is a beautiful town, beautiful country town,” she said. “And very safe and healthy to live in with jobs and good country schools, new police station, new hospital.” Property alerts are now available in the SMH app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.
