Capital Gain The last of the Melbourne pubs embroiled in the spectacular collapse of Jon Adgemis’ Public Hospitality Group is up for grabs with expectations of around $4 million. The Vine Hotel, 59 Wellington Street, Collingwood. The Vine Hotel, on the corner of Derby Street, at 59 Wellington Street was reportedly earmarked for a George Calombaris restaurant before the Adgemis empire crumbled, owing $1.8 billion. The sell-down of the 22-hotel portfolio has so far yielded about $80 million. While the Vine is currently vacant and covered in graffiti, the Art Nouveau-style pub is in the fast-gentrifying southern regions of Collingwood and ripe for revival.



The location is A1. It’s on 417-square-metres of land with three street frontages, next door to Gurner’s huge Victoria & Vine apartment project and across the road from The Commons office building. Records show an Adgemis company, The Vine at Collingwood, paid $4.75 million in November in 2021 but plans for its glow-up never got off the ground. The Saint Hotel, St Kilda. Adgemis, also busy with the burgeoning Sydney stable, was lining up big name restaurateurs for the other two Melbourne venues. Guy Grossi’s Osteria went into The Clifton in Kew and Karen Martini took over the Saint Hotel on Fitzroy Street, St Kilda. The south side pub sold last December to the Kokoda Group for $8.4 million and negotiations are well-advanced for the sale of the Clifton. HTL’s Scott Callow and George Iliopulos have the listing.



In other hotel news, the strata-titled Hotel Lincoln at 91 Cardigan Street, Carlton, sold for $2.5 million through CVA’s Jarrod Moran and Matt Knox. The Clifton Hotel in Kew Junction. Luis Enrique CBD leasing Not every renovation is a success story and the 2021 ‘de-furbishment’ at the Centreway Arcade left many people baffled, including potential tenants. However, the arcade at 259 Collins Street is now fully leased with the opening of a luxury-focused Cash Converters in a 30 sqm space and Bami Station which also signed up for 30 sqm. An escape room, Escape This, has leased 750 sqm in the building’s upper floors.



The interior of the seven-level building, constructed in 1917, was remodelled in 1987 by architects Cocks Carmichael and Whitford and won several awards. Frankly, it was one of the city’s few successful post-modern architectural statements. However, the building’s newish owner, sushi queen Anna Kasman, ripped out the fixtures in 2021 and had the whole arcade painted a stark white. Centreway Arcade in 2018 before its renovation. Michael Clayton-Jones After the pandemic and the sterile renovation, tenants were slow to return to the building Kasman had bought for $40 million in 2014. In good news, however, Ainsworth Property’s Zelman Ainsworth has got the building leased up along with a string of other deals. Down at the rebuilt Melbourne Walk arcade, Sydney Cigars has leased 50 sqm and Boston Clothing a further 117 sqm. Akubra Hats is also moving into the Walk.



Meanwhile, local accessories maker Bellroy is opening its first brick-and-mortar shop, leasing 118 sqm at 271 Little Collins Street. The local bag maker is also opening in Sydney, New York, London and Kuala Lumpur next year. Bellroy is opening its first shop at 271 Little Collins Street. Eamon Gallagher Retail leasing demand was consistent across the board, Ainsworth said. “We’re seeing retailers willing to commit to long-term leases at full market rents, provided landlords take a collaborative approach to structuring deals,” he said. In other deals, former NSW credit union, IMB Bank, is opening a branch in a 200 sqm shop in the newly refurbished 114 William Street. At the other end of town, Bupa Dental has taken out 357 sqm at Collins Place where Truefitt & Hill are also opening up in a 31 sqm shop.



CBD office Editor's pick Commercial real estate Property sells for lucky number: $4,888,888 Hexa Group, a once active Chinese-capital backed property player, is selling a pair of CBD office buildings in the legal district. Hexa bought 369-375 Lonsdale Street in 2023, paying the auspicious price of $18.888 million – the number 8 is believed to bring luck in Chinese culture. However, the current price quoted for the buildings is around $25 million. The 1002 sqm three-storey building at 369-371 Lonsdale was previously occupied by Dean’s Art at the street level and is on 580 sqm of land. Its neighbour, a 600 sqm two-storey property rented to IDP Education, is on 337 sqm of land. Cushman & Wakefield’s Daniel Wolman, Oliver Hay and Leon Ma have the listing.



The building next door at 365 Lonsdale Street, which is on 417 sqm of land, last sold in 2023 to a Vietnamese investor for $10 million. Hexa Group has been relatively quiet since 2020 when it developed the 31-level Panorama tower in Box Hill. Strata Meanwhile, another floor of Golden Age’s 27-floor 130 Little Collins Street tower has sold and just two whole levels remain. The upper levels of Golden Age’s 130 Little Collins Street tower. The tower, dominated by luxury watch sellers, restaurateur Chris Lucas and Golden Age’s corporate offices, replaced a modest brown brick building owned by the Uniting Church.



The 351 sqm level 21 sold last week and levels 20 and 17 remain, as well as a few smaller spaces on other floors. The tower’s upper levels have spectacular views of the CBD. Cushman & Wakefield’s Jack Cooper and Angus Parnham are handling enquiries but declined to comment on the price. The building is now 80 per cent sold and has achieved rates of more than $20,000 per square metre which puts the likely price of the recently sold floor at around $7 million. A couple of blocks away, not-for-profit health insurer Latrobe Health Services is selling its level 12 penthouse office at 343 Little Collins Street in Equitable House. The boardroom at level 12, 343 Little Collins Street. Records show the Gippsland-based insurer paid more than $1.43 million for the 340 square metre offices in 2006, shortly after the 11,910 sqm 12-storey building was strata-titled. CBRE’s Alex Brierly and Nathan Mufale are handling the campaign and quoting between $2-$2.2 million for the vacant property.



Industrial Editor's pick Hotels After a decade of drama, Corkman pub’s concrete clone is complete A Derrimut industrial property, leased to blue-chip tenants SunRice and Asahi, is up for sale through its mortgagee with price expectations of around $40 million. The companies which own 10-16 Fulton Drive – Fulton Road Properties and Fulton Properties Over – are run by the Kutlesovski family. Records show Stefce Kutlesovski, one of the developers who knocked down the Corkman Irish pub in Carlton, owned the companies until 2021, after which they were transferred to Lube Kutlesovski. The corporate database also shows KordaMentha took control of the companies in late September and gained possession of the property on October 6.



Built in 2020, the two warehouses cover 20,031 sqm. They’re in the Gilbertson Industrial Estate on a large 37,940 sqm land holding. They have a relatively short lease average of just under eight months with Asahi set to move to a purpose-built facility in Ravenhall. Current rent is approximately $2.5 million but the leasing rate of $125 per square metre is less than the market average of $150 in the area. Cushman & Wakefield’s Charlie Holmes and Chris Jones are running the campaign. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Capital Gain The Catholic Archdiocese of Sydney (CAS) is hoping to raise more than $20 million in the sale of its landmark property in Sydney’s inner west which it has owned and occupied since 1992. The property is currently occupied by the Catholic Institute Sydney (CIS). The heritage site at 95-103 Albert Road, Strathfield, was constructed in the 1890s, was extended in 1911 and had a library added in 1996. According to records, the CAS bought it in 1992 for about $2.1 million, and it now comprises a freehold land area of 6635 square metres with 30 bedrooms, 13 bathrooms and 45 car spaces.



The property is currently occupied by the Catholic Institute Sydney (CIS), which intends to relocate closer to the University of Notre Dame Australia and its Broadway Campus. It plans to grow strategic and educational ties between university students and seminarians. Editor's pick Commercial real estate Collingwood’s The Vine Hotel looking for new owner in $4m sale It originally served the NSW Home Lending Society for the Blind, the Industrial Home for Blind Women, and the Retreat for Aged Female Blind, and was closed and sold in 1897. In 1911, it was extended by the Bedford Collegiate School for Girls, adding a barrack for WWII women. When CAS purchased the site, it had most recently been used by Australia Post. Michael Murphy from McGrath Strathfield and Knight Frank’s Anthony Pirrottina are the agents on the sale.



Foxy move The popular and highly sought-after White Fox boutique online fashion brand has thrown down the gauntlet to traditional high street retailers by buying a large-scale warehouse in Sydney’s south to cater for demand. 19 O’Riordan Street, Alexandria. Proving that online shopping is the growth sector of the retail industry, while shop front-based stores are closing, the business, run by Daniel and Georgia Contos, paid $87 million for the site at 19 O’Riordan Street, Alexandria which is a 10,238 square metre industrial facility on a 13,140 sqm freehold site. The new warehouse was purpose-built by the vendor, and former owner-occupier, True Alliance which is controlled by the Hendler brothers. The facility comprises high-clearance warehousing, a 1,219 sqm mezzanine, three levels of office accommodation and 102 car spaces and has capacity to extend the site to 32,850 sqm.



The Alexandria site will improve order fulfilment for the brand’s high-volume weekly product drops, moving the company from a tenant to a property owner for its logistics network. It will add to White Fox’s $70 million acquisition of a five-storey boutique commercial office on Dunning Avenue in nearby Rosebery in May. That site is the group’s headquarters and boasts a bar, podcast studio, wellness space, gym, its very own pink slide, a café, a library, a ‘treats space’, a vending machine offering tan products, basketball court, a Pilates studio, therapy room, lunchroom, sauna, studios and an auditorium. Colliers agents Michael Crombie and Trent Gallagher advised on the sale. Centennial expands The busy private Sydney-based fund manager, Centennial Property has extended its portfolio with its first regional industrial landholding at Ballina in northern NSW in a deal worth $22 million.



The deal is a major pivot from its usual metro infill stomping grounds after teaming up with Brisbane’s Direct Commercial Property (DCP) to secure the 8.3 hectare site at 45-65 Smith Drive, West Ballina. Centennial is run by chairman Jonathan Wolf and chief executive Paul Ford, with a portfolio of 63 assets and over $2.8 billion under management across the industrial and logistics, office, retail and boutique residential sectors. The 8.3 hectare site at 45-65 Smith Drive, West Ballina. As Ballina’s largest contiguous industrial landholding, with direct exposure to the M1 Pacific Motorway, the joint venture partners will develop it into an 18-lot subdivision for selling down to capitalise on the scarcity of industrial sites in the Ballina-Byron Shires. The development will have an end value around $70 million. JLL and North Coast Commercial Real Estate were the agents on the sale.



Billbergia retail Private developer Billbergia has sold all the retail and commercial section of its Arncliffe Central project for $37 million, in a single deal to a private equity fund. Billbergia’s Arncliffe Central project. The sale covers 4,000 square metres of shops at 161-173 Princes Highway, Arncliffe, which includes a supermarket, smaller stores and a childcare centre. The retail space in Sydney’s south sits beneath 806 apartments across four towers, all of which have sold. Consistent with the strategy of Billbergia to create communities, the development also includes a 1,634 sqm library and community centre, a 4,000 sqm public park, new pedestrian links and customer parking.



The sale was brokered by RWC Sydney City Fringe’s Kamal Silwal. carolynannecummins@gmail.com The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: How All Blacks captain Ardie Savea is breaking new ground in rugby's battle for engagement
World.content:
Ardie Savea is sitting in a Wellington café in a Blues jersey, answering questions from thousands of people watching him live on YouTube.

The comments keep coming - questions about his new club, speculation about his future, jokes, declarations of support and the occasional insult.

Savea reads them all from his phone and, every so often, answers one directly.

The All Blacks captain has announced where he will play Super Rugby next year. There is no press conference, no wall of sponsors' logos and no scrum of reporters.

Instead, Savea is doing it his way, on his own ASAV YouTube channel, which has 31,000 subscribers.

At one point, Savea remarks that he has never had such interest in one of his livestreams. By the time it is over, 13,000 have watched live, many joining the conversation as it unfolds.

The interest probably should not be surprising for he is the All Blacks captain announcing where he will playSuper Rugby next year - almost certainly his final season in the competition.

For New Zealand rugby, this is an unusual way for its biggest star to announce his next move. For Savea, it is part of something bigger - a willingness to bypass the traditional media set-piece, invite fans into his world and build a personal brand on his own terms.

It is after 4pm on Friday, 2 October. The café, owned by friend Tait Burge, with whom Savea interacts, is closed.

He is being filmed by friend Matt Manukia, a former 1News sports reporter who worked closely with Savea during his time as the All Blacks media manager under former coach Ian Foster and who continued afterwards in a similar role at Moana Pasifika.

The livestream has already taken in a flat white-making lesson and a series of costume changes, with Savea trying on the jerseys of potential Super Rugby destinations, teasing moves to the Highlanders, Chiefs, Blues and Crusaders.

Savea takes questions on his YouTube livestream. Ardie Savea YouTube

Earlier, Savea tells his audience before the big reveal: "I wanted to do something different... obviously we've done a lot of announcements and it's always been the same and whatnot.

"Me being injured, it's given me time to 'rip and feel' on the creative flow.

"I just wanted to do something fun, something different and test it out, and pretty much go directly to go you guys and not through anyone else.

"There's been a lot of speculation, so let me know where you want me to go, where you think I'm going to go and I'll be announcing it very soon.

"After I announce [destination], my press conference is going to be right on here in the chat, so you guys ask me anything... I want to give back to you guys and let you guys have a say."

As for his jersey changes, Savea says: "How does it look? You've got to try before you buy, you know?"

At one point, Savea sees a comment that says: "tough watch".

He replies: "Hey, some people are gonna love you and some people are gonna hate you. You can't please everyone."

Savea scores one of his two tries for the All Blacks before leaving the field injured during his team's second test defeat to the Springboks in Johannesburg in September. Muzi Ntombela / BackpagePix / PHOTOSPORT

A star the Blues can build around

Savea, a 33-year-old who has played 112 tests, was officially announced as All Blacks captain in June by new head coach Dave Rennie.

The loose forward, recognised as the world's best player in 2023 and who has maintained his excellence for a decade after making his test debut in 2016, always promised to be a different type of All Blacks skipper.

Savea has his own clothing range and is active in promoting Asics, a direct competitor of adidas, a major sponsor of New Zealand Rugby and the All Blacks.

He is the busiest of the All Blacks on social media. An orthodox captain in the form of Richie McCaw, Kieran Read, Sam Cane or Scott Barrett he is not.

He was given the go-ahead for his do-it-yourself Blues announcement by franchise chief executive Karl Budge, a man who has been in the role for almost exactly 12 months and is also keen to do things differently.

Budge agreed to talk to RNZ a couple of hours before Savea's announcement on the proviso we didn't publish anything until the man himself confirmed it.

During our conversation, Budge said of Savea's signing: "It's going to be transformational for us and it probably epitomises the change we're trying to go through at the Blues."

He went on to talk about the style of rugby the Blues wanted to play under new coach Jason Holland, a former Hurricanes head coach and All Blacks assistant, alongside Savea.

Budge continues: "Equally important, I think he's going to help us connect with fans that we've not been able to do before.

"He is rugby's biggest star and I think we can really leverage that connection and embrace it, and let him really push us into being a modern fan-first organisation."

The embracing of it could be seen later that night, when Auckland's Sky Tower was lit up in blue, and featured Savea's portrait and the message: "Ardie for the 09".

Ardie Savea's portrait and welcome to the Blues lights up Auckland's Sky Tower. Blues Rugby Instagram

Nearly three weeks after Savea's livestream, a hugely successful announcement on every metric for the Blues, Budge told RNZ of the Sky Tower illumination: "The idea was that we very much wanted to celebrate this with our city."

There is no doubt that the Blues are leveraging a new signing like never before and that's fine by Savea.

Talking of his dealings with the Blues and Budge, the question comes up on the livestream.

"They've been amazing. From the very first, he's shown love, care and interest.

"You can't doubt the man. He came to Kobe to catch up with me when I was in Japan and the first time I met him, we sat for five hours just chatting about content, creative ideas, how he sees the Blues... the five hours felt like 30 minutes."

Budge said later he was staggered by the splash Savea's announcement made.

"Compared with the piece of content we shared when we won the title in '24 - across reach, engagement, likes and shares - he got over 100 times more than that," he said.

"It's the modern way of interacting now and it's what new fans are looking for. They want to know the personality, not just the announcement.

"Ardie showed that - it was authentically Ardie.

"We peaked at about 13,000 people live at one point - commenting and interacting. Probably not many of those 13,000 would tune into my [media] stand-ups, it's fair to say.

"We want to be a modern sports entertainment franchise... we want to be open and interact with our fans.

"It's all the stuff that is modern in today's sport around the world, but it's something we don't have too much here in New Zealand."

Borrowing from the American playbook

Beyond the sense that Savea's announcement is so different to what for years has been considered a normal media set-piece for such a reveal - a press release, followed by a press conference at the club's headquarters - there is also a sense that the occasion feels borrowed from the United States and in particular the NBA.

LeBron James, left, pictured during the NBA playoffs in 2015 after his return to the Cleveland Cavaliers. Curtis Compton/PHOTOSPORT

In 2010, LeBron James, a free agent after playing six seasons for Cleveland Cavaliers, agreed to a live announcement on ESPN, titled 'The Decision', were he revealed he was joining Miami Heat. More than 10 million people watched it.

Furthermore, and closer to home, Savea said on his livestream that his season with the Blues would be called 'The Last Dance'.

It is difficult to miss the similarities with the great Michael Jordan's final season with the Chicago Bulls in 1997/98. Jordan's hunt for a sixth successive title was themed in the same way and remembered in spectacular fashion by the 2020 Netflix documentary, overseen by Jordan, entitled The Last Dance.

Why call it that, asked Manukia off screen.

"Because it's going to be my last Super Rugby team that I'm going to play for in New Zealand," replied Savea.

"Moana obviously are not in the comp and shout out to my brothers at Moana... but I'm really blessed to have the Blues beside me. I can't wait."

Savea's platform of choice could be seen to be at odds with his first interview as All Blacks skipper.

In a chat with Sky Sports outside Feilding Yellows Rugby Club back in June, he said: "I'm a man of few words, I try to lead through actions.

"A lot of the leaders that impacted me didn't say much, but really, really led through actions through the training week and the game."

A few months later, he's hosting a 70-minute livestream in which he barely pauses for breath.

However, a little later in the same interview, he said: "We're at the stage now in New Zealand rugby where we need to start being pioneers."

Ardie Savea was announced as All Blacks captain at the Feilding Yellows Rugby Club in June. Marty Melville/Photosport

He is that through the groundbreaking (in New Zealand rugby terms) access he provides his followers (on his own terms).

For example, a seven-minute video of Savea meeting a young man at a Cape Town shopping mall promotion, and which progressed to a meeting with his family and getting a haircut from his mother at the family home on the eve of the second test in August has been viewed more than 142,000 times.

It was filmed by Manukia. Neither Manukia nor Savea responded to several invitations to comment for this piece, but in terms of his broader attitude towards the mainstream media, the seeds were sown six years ago.

In a social media post in 2020, Savea wrote: "Maybe it's that players want to control their own news and bring it out the way they want to, not through a media scrum where you have journos tryna get clickbait.

"The new wave is coming and players are realising they have control over their story through their own channels."

It should be noted that Savea has always been courteous and accommodating to the mainstream media.

Within New Zealand Rugby, there will be an awareness of Savea's power to mould the opinions of many in the player group, especially the younger members, and his growing personal brand.

Many at the organisation will be aware, too, that Savea is conscious that some within the high-performance group of New Zealand Rugby did not want him moving from the Hurricanes to Moana Pasifika, where he spent one hugely inspirational season, because they did not think the environment would be conducive to his development as a top All Black.

Ardie Savea accepts his 2025 Super Rugby Pacific Player of the Year award, after Moana Pasifika's loss to his former team the Hurricanes in Wellington. Elias Rodriguez / www.photosport.nz

There is a theory that his consistently high-class performances in a historic season that featured first-ever victories over the Crusaders and Blues were a result of him wanting to prove people wrong - a theme, apparently, when it comes to Savea.

Back on the livestream and someone comments that the "Blues get another Canes player at the twilight of their career".

Savea replies: "I wouldn't say twilight... but yes, I'd love for you guys to keep doubting - doubting the Blues, doubting myself."

There is no escaping the fact that Savea is catering for a younger, more tech-savvy generation that New Zealand Rugby want to attract. Budge at the Blues has already made that plain.

It was noticeable during the week of the recent Bledisloe Cup test at Eden Park, won 50-19 by the All Blacks, that the proverbial red carpet was rolled out to various social media 'influencers', some of whom were invited to the team-naming press conference at the team's hotel in Auckland's Viaduct and shot various videos with players afterwards.

Many were also sideline during and after the victory over the Wallabies, which featured a sensational five-try second-half finish by the All Blacks, but no Savea - still in rehabilitation mode after the shoulder surgery on his injury in South Africa.

RNZ put several questions to NZ Rugby, including: "What is NZR's overall view of what could be described as Savea's 'brand-building' and livestreaming, rather than going down traditional media avenues", whether there "was a concern an older generation of All Blacks fans was potentially missing out" and whether "the organisation was deliberately targeting social media to capture a younger audience".

In reply, chief communications officer Paul Stevens said: "How fans engage with rugby has accelerated over the last few years.

"Traditional media and content creators now co-exist, and they support each other. Journalists and broadcasters bring depth, analysis and storytelling, and they remain central to how New Zealanders follow rugby.

"Many content creators build their storylines on journalists' work and they add an immediacy that lets fans feel closer to the team in real time. You'll now commonly see influencers and content creators attending media opportunities with the Black Ferns and All Blacks."

He added: "We're really supportive of players connecting directly with fans.

"A player's brand is built through many things working together - social media, traditional media, broadcast, and what they do on and off the field. We're supporting our athletes to make the most of all of that and to build their own star power."

Budge said he hadn't forgotten the traditional media either and was aware that was where most rugby fans still got their news.

"The traditional is important for us," he said. "There's no question that our traditional rugby viewer still tunes into the 6 o'clock news... but if we don't start engaging with the teenagers up [in age], we're going to have problems down the line.

"I see no reason why it can't be both. If I look at how Ardie's announcement rolled out over the week - it built through traditional media and... then it went into that announcement and it still made the TV news that night, it still made the written press the following day."

Patrick Tuipulotu celebrates the Blues' Super Rugby Pacific grand final victory over the Chiefs at Eden Park in 2024. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

The cost of going direct

No doubt some among the mainstream media are annoyed at the developments - indeed some made their feelings known recently to New Zealand Rugby about not getting access to Savea after his Blues announcement - but are there really any downsides?

Potentially, yes, says Dr Sarah Wymer, a senior lecturer in the Sport Leadership and Management team at Auckland's University of Technology, but they can be managed.

Wymer, who specialises in social media in sport, tells RNZ: "You do have to have a thick skin. When it's live and you've got 13,000 comments coming in... it's harder to moderate a live chat."

However, she says the influence of Savea's livestream cannot be underestimated.

"It could easily have been an Instagram graphic and a couple of lines, but it was so much more. Iit took 40 minutes [into the livestream] to get to that announcement and it was focused on that two-way communication.

"Social media is often placed as a media for two-way communication, but often athletes using it are very one way.

"Fans got to spend time with him and they could see his personality. They got to be involved in the conversation, which brought so much more value."

Dr Wymer adds: "Rugby in New Zealand needs more athletes with personalities. I think that's why rugby league has become so big and popular.

"It's because it has athletes that people feel an association with and feel close to. A lot of people now follow the athlete first and then the team."

Back to Savea's livestream.

Ardie Savea and brother Julian - pictured after a match for Moana Pasifika at North Harbour Stadium last year. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

What's your club team in Auckland?

"Mahurangi Rugby Club [in Warkworth, coached by brother Julian]," Savea says before adding: "Shout out to the head coach. Not."

What's your relationship with Jason Holland like?

"I've worked with Jase quite a bit and to see the way he's coaching. I think he did awesome at the Canes last year.

"That was a real testament to him and it was something that excites me to keep my game fresh."

Former All Blacks assistant coach Jason Holland will take charge of the Blues for the 2027 season. Alan Lee / www.photosport.nz

Will you move full-time to Auckland?

"Yes, but my family [wife Saskia and three children Kobe, Keeon and Kove] will stay in Wellington and commute, due to school."

Was the NRL an option?

"(laughs) Nah, NRL wasn't an option."

What do you want to achieve at the Blues?

"Obviously, we want to win games and want to win the [championship], but I want to experience a different culture. I want to add and grow, and help the boys win games on the field and win off the field too."

Was the beef between Moana and the Blues ever real, and did it factor into your decision?

"I think there was, but that's sport and that's why you play. You build a knot in your gut against another team.

"Yeah, it was real, but you move on and get past that. Moana's not here, so now there's only one team in the 09."

What are you doing in 2028?

"I'm not too sure. I can't tell you now, but I will tell you guys probably in a similar way."

Was a return to the Hurricanes (for whom he played 131 games) ever an option?

"This was something that I wasn't sure I wanted to talk about, because I didn't want to disrespect anyone or flame any fires, but the honest truth is that, bless the Blues, they were the only option. They came to the table, showed me love and showed me care.

"I didn't get anything from anyone else."

Why only one year?

"Because my contract with New Zealand Rugby finishes in 2027 and I don't know what I'm going to do post that."

Former All Blacks wing Joe Rokocoko in try-scoring mode in a Bledisloe Cup test in 2003. Andrew Cornaga/Photosport

Who were your favourite players growing up?

"Joe Rokocoko and Ma'a Nonu. Hence why I do a dive when I score a try - I always mimic Joe Roks.

"Obviously Ma'a was at the Blues too [after a similarly long stint at Hurricanes]."

Say what you like about the format for Savea's announcement, but his answers were probably more revealing than had he been sitting behind a table in front of a wall of cameras and microphones.

The platform highlights his personality - which clearly does not lack complexity or self-awareness.

Savea is about to finish.

"I appreciate the Blues for allowing us to do this. They've been open-hearted around my creative mind and the creative people I have around me.

World.title: 'Responsibility to protect': Kāwhia trust blocks vehicle access to beach
World.content:
Audio player for " Kāwhia trust moves to stop vehicles driving on beach " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/environment/2091198%2Fresponsibility-to-protect-kawhia-trust-blocks-vehicle-access-to-beach

Kāwhia trust moves to stop vehicles driving on beach Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A trust is installing a line of poles to block vehicle access to the beach in a Waikato coastal settlement because it's "sick and tired" of people driving over pipi beds, fish spawning grounds, and seabird nests.

Onepū Charitable Trust is installing a wooden pole barrier at Kāwhia Beach near Maketū marae that it says will permanently block vehicle access from the Saturday of Labour Weekend.

"We used to go and gather about a dozen sacks of pipi for the marae, and they're no longer there. They are dying," Merv Ranga said.

The poles with a temporary gap. Supplied / Onepū Charitable Trust

The 74-year-old was born and bred in Kāwhia and had been catching and collecting kaimoana there all his life.

He said they used to catch butterfish, which had also disappeared. The oysters? Also gone, as was the flounder.

It used to take about 30 minutes to get two litres of whitebait. They've also gone.

"You can't do that now. There's nothing."

Tyre marks on the shellfish bed. Supplied / Onepū Charitable Trust

The Onepū Charitable Trust kaumatua said the pātaka kai was their inheritance and if they didn't do anything about it, they'd lose it for ever.

Stopping vehicles driving to Ocean Beach's Te Puia Hot Springs directly over seafood beds was why chair Horahaere Daisy Scott said the trust was installing the poles.

Scott said it was working with local landowners to put the two-metre poles at the end of the Maketū marae seawall down towards the low-tide mark on the beach.

Half the poles were in already, but a gap had been left for cars. From Saturday, that gap would close.

Tyre marks on the dunes. Supplied / Onepū Charitable Trust

"The vehicles and motorbikes have ruined our kaimoana beds. I was born and bred at Maketū marae and the lagoon at Te Ārai o Te Wiwini was our pātaka kai, our food basket. Our kōkota and tuatua were huge. Our seafood stock thrived because our kaumātua and kuia protected the habitat."

Scott said the closure was not about keeping people away from Ocean Beach, it's about protecting the environment.

"Our kaimoana beds are almost destroyed. We have no choice but to close vehicle access travelling over our land to the lagoon.

"We've had enough of being treated as though our local knowledge doesn't matter. This is a very sensitive coastal environment. Shorebirds nest in and around the dunes at the lagoon, and it is also a vital fish spawning ground, especially for flounder.

"Our pātaka kai has sustained generations of our people. We have a responsibility to protect it for the generations coming after us."

Lunchtime for the workers. Supplied / Onepū Charitable Trust

The trust put a petition to the council last year, signed by 600 people, asking for an alternative route to Ocean Beach, in efforts to protect the vulnerable areas.

But it was still waiting.

"That is more or less the idea of why we're putting the poles and putting in this stopping of motorised vehicles, is to hurry them up and find an alternative accessway.

"Otherwise this situation will be going on in my great grandchildren's time. So hopefully we'll have this all sorted before then."

A vehicle submerged by the marae. Supplied / Onepū Charitable Trust

She said drivers were also not taking note of the tides and getting stuck in the mud or incoming water and vehicles ripped up the sand dunes that buffered the harbour's edge from waves and erosion.

Scott said the lagoon would remain open to walkers and horses, and a new sign would mark the barrier to remind drivers the route was now closed.

"We are just waiting for the backlash."

A vehicle on its side. Supplied / Onepū Charitable Trust

Local environmental group Te Taiao o Kāwhia Moana member Rod Barnett said scientists had warned the only way for the kaimoana to recover was by letting it be.

"Kāwhia has been a kai basket for hundreds of years, a kai basket for locals and just about everybody you speak to here who's been living here for say 30, 40, 50 years has talked about how all the kai, the kaimoana has diminished since the place was opened up.

"We've got a real depletion of the local resource for the local people. And not only them but also as the other fishing spots around the country get overfished, more and more people are coming to the west coast because it hasn't been overfished, but now we're getting that too."

The first poles being installed. Supplied / Onepū Charitable Trust

He said there also used to be a big dotterel population, but now there was only about one or two birds

"It's really upsetting. That's why we put the posts up because they're sick and tired."

Ōtorohanga District Council's regulatory and growth group manager Tony Quickfall said private landowners whose title extended into the foreshore could only lawfully stop vehicle access above high tide.

He said the posts situated below the tideline were therefore in breach of Ōtorohanga District Council's Traffic Management Bylaw.

Quickfall said it would work with landowners to remove those barriers below high tide, where vehicles were restricted to 20kph.

World.title: Oil prices surge on reports US again considering Iran strikes
World.content:
Global oil prices have hit their highest level since May on fears of a resumption of fighting between the US and Iran in the Middle East.

At one point during trading on Friday the global benchmark Brent crude was up 4 percent at just over US$113 (NZ$198) a barrel.

West Texas Intermediate, which was more closely linked to the US market, was up 3 percent to just under US$100 a barrel.

The spike follows reports in the New York Times that the Trump Administration has drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's US midterm election.

In addition, the US has reportedly ordered some non-emergency government staff to leave Saudi Arabia.

That comes as Iran-backed Houthi rebels continue to target Saudi Arabia with missile strikes.

Global oil prices peaked this year at US$126 a barrel in April, in the wake of the US-Iran war.

Petrol prices in New Zealand tend to lag global oil price moves by a week or two.

According to fuel monitoring website Gaspy, the average price of 91 unleaded is around $3.55 per litre, down slightly on where it was earlier this month.

World.title: Glenn Phillips flair not enough in record T20 opener against India
World.content:
Black Caps allrounder Glenn Phillips is encouraged by their performance despite coming out on the wrong side of a record-breaking T20 game against India.

New Zealand scored 225 for four after being asked to bat first in the opening international in Christchurch. It was their highest total against India at home.

India then completed a record successful run chase, getting home with two balls to spare to score a four-wicket victory.

The tourists chase got off to a flyer with Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma putting on 93 for the first wicket in 5.5 overs.

Glenn Phillips of the Black Caps © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

"The boys actually pulled it back really well, considering that they basically hit us for 96 in six overs," Phillips said after the game.

"To take it down to the last over with a side like that, that bats to nine, is a fantastic effort to at least show the character to bring it back. To show that we're still in the game the whole time."

New Zealand also got off to a good start in their innings with Tim Seifert [24] and Finn Allen [45] putting on 49 in the first five overs.

"The way the 'Bash brothers' go up at the top of the order is fantastic. They always get us off to a flyer. I think the way that we strung partnerships together throughout the innings was good," Phillips said.

All of the Black Caps batters had a strike rate over a hundred, but it was Philips' knock of 82 off 40 balls that gave them some much needed momentum. His innings included eight fours and three sixes and he switched to bat left handed for the last ball of the innings and still managed to find the boundary.

Black Caps wicketkeeper Tim Seifert © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

"I've definitely been practising a lot [batting left handed] and I thought, you know what, this is probably something worth experimenting with. Boovy [Bhuvneshwar Kumar] wasn't missing as well, so the last ball, why not give it a go."

Overall Phillips is confident they can continue to push India on the rest of the tour.

"The way that the boys still fought, still held on in the middle, still took wickets, that's the fight that we're after. We do just have to go out there and give it our best and obviously India did better than us today."

World.title: Trains cancelled and delayed after ventilation problems in CRL tunnel
World.content:
Delays and cancellations across the train network are continuing as City Rail Link stations reopens.

In a statement, Auckland Transport said a ventilation system issue was identified during pre-service tests on Friday.

As of 7.15am, it has been resolved.

"Trains were initially unable to operate through the CRL stations and Te Waihorotiu and Karanga-a-Hape stations were closed. These stations have now been reopened.

"There will be some delays and cancellations on the East West, South City and Onehunga West lines due to the earlier closure."

AT said buses would accept train tickets.

"Customers are encouraged to check the AT Mobile app or digital screens at stations for the latest information and travel options.

"We apologise for the disruption and appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore normal services as quickly and safely as possible."

World.title: Growing quinoa 'very real, new option' for struggling arable farmers
World.content:
It's been a tough time for arable farmers, but growing demand for quinoa and new export opportunities could offer a solution to some of their struggles.

The closure of McCain and Watties vegetable processing factories is understood to have affected 220 growers in Canterbury and another 100 in Hawke's Bay.

It's seen the sector's morale plummet. Federated Farmers' most recent confidence survey back in September found one-in-four arable farmers were making a loss.

It's precisely this reason why Dan Cottrell of Kiwi Quinoa is encouraging arable farmers to think about growing the dried seed crop to help meet demand from overseas.

The sheep and beef farmer has been growing quinoa for over a decade near Taihape - expanding out to 17 contract growers across both the North and South Island after they ran out of room on his farm.

Cottrell said there was also increased demand here and he wanted to see more Kiwis eating quinoa too. Supplied

Kiwi Quinoa is the licensee partner growing Dutch quinoa - a saponin-free variant developed in the Netherlands by Wageningen University - for European growing companies.

It's also now secured a export contract with a partner in Canada and is looking for more growers to come on board.

Cottrell said it was helping overseas growers whose production and supply chains were under pressure.

"Essentially we're growing in their off season to supplement their production due to a variety of reasons - primarily increased demand for them and certainly climatic pressure and with the likes of what's happening in Europe because they've had some really tough seasons.

"It's not just one season, it's two, three in a row, and 18 months of no rain and then flooding in the south of Spain."

Kiwi Quinoa is the licensee partner growing Dutch quinoa - a saponin-free variant developed in the Netherlands by Wageningen University - for European growing companies. Supplied

Cottrell said there was also increased demand here and he wanted to see more Kiwis eating quinoa too.

"It's a very real new option. We've got long term contracts and the demand is increasing.

"And look, I'm not going to sugarcoat it. It has been challenging within the quinoa industry for the last few years, but I think the demand is certainly taking off."

Quinoa being harvested. Supplied

A field of quinoa. Supplied

For growers, he said New Zealand produces some of the highest yields in the world and he sees it as a good opportunity for those impacted by the closures - it's a "short rotation and low input" crop with a "healthy gross margin".

"Our average yield is three and a half tonne clean and [...] we have reached five tonne this last season.

"[It's] low input, like very similar, or I would say lower fertilizer inputs than, for example, cereals, and there's no sprays on the crop - so no sort of fungicides or herbicides or anything like that."

Cottrell said crops can be planted anytime from now until late December even, with an April harvest - some growers had reported success with double cropping, planting after harvesting processed peas.

He's ideally looking for Canterbury growers - as they have a processing facility here - but he said he was open to anyone and they also have a North Island processing facility.

"This crop [...] it's got an exciting future and we've got growth. The main thing is it grows really well in New Zealand."

World.title: Australia falls to defeat in final session, South Africa levels series
World.content:
Australia's has fallen to defeat by an innings and 31 runs against South Africa in the second Test at St George's Park in Gqeberha.

Brave innings from Travis Head (121) and night watchman Scott Boland (40) were not enough for Australia, as the Proteas levelled the series at 1-1.

"We were a long way away from our best," Pat Cummins said at the presentation.

"Across the board just not enough of us contributed.

"Ideally we'd be scoring more runs. The pitch was pretty good out there."

The two teams will now head to Newlands in Cape Town for the final Test on Tuesday with the series on the line.

The hosts came into the final day needing just six wickets for victory, but were made to wait to get on the field after the first session was washed out by rain.

The persistent drizzle, interspersed by heavier squalls, may have given Australia hope that they may be able to orchestrate a great escape.

Even once play eventually resumed, every over that Head and Boland successfully negotiated raised hopes even further.

Head's 13th Test century was the first by an Australian batter in a follow-on innings since the 1980s and added to the pressure South Africa must have been feeling, with Anrich Nortje's injury leaving the Proteas a bowler down.

"I thought there was some good fight today," Cummins said.

"Scotty Boland and Trav [Head] both played their roles really well, but it was a fair way to come back from and it wasn't quite enough."

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Once Head chopped on to Wiaan Mulder just before the second new ball was due, the writing may have been on the wall.

Steve Smith, batting at seven after being hampered by a sore neck on day four, initially looked sprightly, before he top edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer to Matthew Breetzke when on 3.

Boland's brave, 166-ball vigil came to an end soon after, a brilliant off cutter from Mulder taking the top of his off stump.

Pat Cummins followed in the same way for just 4 to leave South Africa just two wickets from victory.

Still, Australia had hope as clouds gathered and threatened yet more rain to rescue an unlikely draw.

But then Rabada returned, bowling Mitch Starc for 11, before Marco Jansen extracted an edge from Josh Hazlewood for a duck.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Schutt banned for two matches after prescription medication failure
World.content:
Australian women's fast bowler Megan Schutt has been banned for two matches for failing to meet guidelines on the use of prescription medication.

Cricket Australia confirmed Schutt's suspension in a release on Thursday afternoon.

"The breach was a failure to adhere to requirements under the Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication," Cricket Australia said.



"This relates to a single incidence which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance-enhancing purposes."



The two-match ban applies to all international and domestic cricket.

Schutt starred in the recent three-match ODI series against Bangladesh. She had series figures of 10-71.

She has not played in a three-match T20 international series against New Zealand, which wraps up tonight at North Sydney.

Schutt released a statement acknowledging the breach and accepting the penalty.

"I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me," Schutt said in her statement.

"I'm sorry for the attention this has caused and appreciate the support I've received.

"While this occurred out of competition and was not performance related, I understand that I am responsible for following the Sports Science and Sports Medicine Guidelines, which players receive regular education on, and I should have adhered to these guidelines."



Cricket Australia said it would continue to provide "appropriate support" to Schutt and to reinforce standards and responsibilities expected of all involved in the game.

World.title: Aussie Borlase on winning side as Atlanta Dream leads WNBA Finals
World.content:
Angel Reese recorded 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream secure a 97-71 home victory over the Golden State Valkyries, giving the Dream a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals after Game 3.

Rhyne Howard added 16 points, and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who also host Game 4 on Sunday (AEDT).

Australian guard Izzy Borlase played a solid role for the Dream on Wednesday night, local time. She played 26 minutes, finishing with 12 points, including one three-pointer, plus five rebounds, two assists and a block.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

The Dream highlighted one of Borlase's drives to the basket on its social media.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for its first-ever victory in the Finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the Finals.

"It feels good when you're in the finals. It's a long season, and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the off-season is for," Reese said.

"I put the work in for this moment, and I'm just happy I could lead the team to a win. We're feeling good going into Saturday."

With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes's lay-up, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter, scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who got fouled.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points, and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.

"Protect home court," Howard said of the team's focus. "Giving our fans a show. We fought for this arena so we had to protect it. It's big. We went and stole one, but we can't let them come in and do the same thing."

The game was moved from the Dream's home Gateway Center Arena to the NBA's Atlanta Hawks home arena. Wednesday night's game was sold out, with more than 17,000 fans attending, as is Game 4 on Saturday at the same venue.

The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed its first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket with 4:39 left.

They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive 3-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.

Atlanta built its lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State was able to hang around and only trailed 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48 per cent) from behind the arc.

That was more completed 3-pointers in the first 20 minutes than in either Game 1 or Game 2.

Game 1 and 2 had huge ratings, with the opener on NBC averaging 2.1 million, the most ever for a first game of the Finals. Game 2, which was broadcast on USA Network, averaged 1.33 million viewers.

AP/ABC

World.title: Amid the hunt for World Cup glory one of Tonga's greats is not done yet
World.content:
As Tonga's World Cup campaign prepares to hit fever pitch, Tui Lolohea cannot stop smiling even when the young bulls give him stick.

After a training session in the lead-up to Friday's match against Lebanon it is rising prop Demetric Vaimauga, who is the kind of guy you hear before you see, that gees Lolohea up.

"Awwww yeah, it's Mr I Ain't Done Yet!" Vaimauga crows as he grabs Lolohea by the shoulders.

That's what they called Lolohea in an Instagram post after he came off the bench for an injured Latu Fainu to set up a try in Tonga's 30-12 win over England last week and he's been copping it ever since.

It was a cameo Lolohea, at 31 and with Tonga enjoying more depth and talent in the halves than ever before, thought would never come.

But once it did it added to an already sterling legacy in the red jersey, tacking an extra chapter on a story that, against all odds, is still being written.

Lolohea has already played for Tonga more times than any other player in history and against the Cedars he'll extend his own record with his 23rd cap.

Along with Jason Taumalolo, Lolohea is the only player to have appeared in each of Tonga's five wins over Tier 1 nations, making them the only two constant faces in every image of Tonga's greatest days.

Loading Instagram content

Lolohea has been wearing these colours when those days were still just a dream. When he debuted for Tonga back in 2015, Fainu, the man he replaced last week and will partner in the halves on Friday, was only nine years old.

Vaimauga himself had just turned 11 and as the giant youngster runs away cackling, Lolohea fires back in Tongan through a grin and shakes his head.

"I knew I'd get stick for this. Mr I Ain't Done Yet — they're always taking the piss out of me," Lolohea said.

"I hope he gets banged next time he goes off the back fence, so I can go laugh at him.

"They joke around, but I am one of the oldest in the team and it's good to show you can run around with the young bucks."

Jason Taumalolo and Tui Lolohea have played in every one of Tonga's wins over Tier 1 nations. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yueng)

Lolohea and Taumalolo are the elders this time around as the two longest-serving players in the team by a mile and while Taumalolo dragged Tonga into a new world, Lolohea is very much a product of the old.

Watching his debut from 11 years ago against Samoa on the Gold Coast is a measure of how far things have come.

When the two meet again next week it will be in front of a sold-out crowd at Parramatta Stadium, which they probably could have filled twice over, and both sides will boast some of the best players in the world.

Back on Lolohea's first day, a little over 12,000 came through the gates and both nations had to choose between grey beards, who wanted to give back to their community, journeymen who knew this would be as good as it got, or youngsters before their big futures came for them.

International rugby league has come a long way since Tui Lolohea's Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Lolohea was one of the latter and at the time he was counted as one of rugby league's brightest prospects, with feet so fast tackling him was like trying to grab a handful of smoke.

So much has transformed since those times but according to Lolohea, the most important things have stayed the same.

"Why you're doing it, what you're representing, that never changes," Lolohea said.

"We're a little dot on the map and there's always talk about financial stuff but the pride of our island nation, the proud culture we put out to the people, we've built that over the years and the support from the people is massive.

Why Jason Taumalolo is still more than just a man for Tonga In the NRL, we only talk about what Jason Taumalolo can't do anymore. But when he pulls on the red of Tonga it's a reminder of what he still is and always will be for the island nation and for Test rugby league.

"That's what we want to represent, our people and our family names, where we come from.

"I was just a little kid back then. I remember the passion, for Tonga and Samoa, and we're on the big stage now but the passion is still there even though it was a long time ago."

Plenty of familiar faces from that night are still around. Kristian Woolf is still the coach, Sika Manu, Lolohea's first captain, is in camp as an assistant and Konrad Hurrell is the team's media manager.

But only Lolohea is still playing, making him the last son of the olden days before the heroes came back home.

He remembers frantically messaging Taumalolo in 2017, asking if he really was going to come back to Tonga and marvelling at what followed.

He cannot forget his intercept try in the win over New Zealand, head cocked back and laughing as he went over, or his late score in the semi-final against England that gave Tonga hope of a miracle, or of the trip back to the islands that followed, where the team was given medals of honour at the royal palace.

Amid a good NRL career for the Warriors and Wests Tigers before a lengthy stint in Super League, where he's spent the last eight seasons, including the last five with Huddersfield, Lolohea might never have fulfilled the club expectations he carried into his Tongan debut.

Instead, his finest hours have come for Tonga itself, for whom he is both pioneer and icon.

They've never won a big game without him and his reward has been honours that are usually bestowed on heroes of ancient wars.

His people have named trophies after him and he has been granted lands outside the family village of Lapaha by King Tupou VI.

The team's official nickname is Mate Ma' Tonga, which translates to "die for Tonga" but the memories Lolohea has helped create for his nation are immortal, like the win over Great Britain in 2019 or the breakthrough victory over Australia the following week.

Tui Lolohea has carved out a fine legacy in Tongan red. (Getty Images: Kai Schwoerer)

On the back of those glories a whole new generation of stars chose Tonga and players like Isaiya Katoa, Robert Toia, Leka Halasima and Tolu Koula have not just become part of the cause, they have taken it further.

They beat New Zealand again in the Pacific Championships two years ago and pushed Australia to the limit in the final. Lolohea, of course, played in both and set up a try in the latter.

Tonga are not here to compete anymore, they are here to win — against Australia, New Zealand, England, Samoa or anybody else who wants some.

Taking the World Cup itself back to Nuku'alofa is not an idle fantasy. It's a dream Tonga can hammer into reality as part of a new world order Lolohea and his generation helped create and somehow, he is still part of it.

Apart from Taumalolo, his only fellow survivor from 2017, the other legends from the old days are done.

Tui Lolohea has played in England for close to a decade now. (Getty Images via PA Images: Martin Rickett)

Between Katoa, Fainu and Junior Amone, Tonga have more class and options in the halves and the nation had every right to move on from Lolohea years ago.

But Lolohea himself is still here, refusing to be swept away, a lot older and a bit slower but as he showed against England, still capable of making a difference for the better.

"To still be here after all this time, I'm fortunate to be here again and running around with the young guys and some of the superstars of our game," Lolohea said.

"It's an honour, every time.

Rugby League World Cup quick hits From Kalyn Ponga's magnificent Test debut to a mighty Tongan victory years in the making here are the quick hits from week one of the Rugby League World Cup.

"It's crazy to think, because I watch these guys every week and now I'm playing alongside them and I remember when we didn't really have any halfbacks at all.

"The depth we have now, it's such a big positive not just for now but for the years to come."

Lolohea knows this World Cup might be his last. He's finished up at Huddersfield and is still sorting out where he'll play next.

He is expected to drop back to the extended bench for next week's clash against Samoa and barring injury, it will be the same for the knockout stages.

This game against Lebanon could be it, the last time the legend of Tui Lolohea as a Tongan hero happens in front of us and not in our memories and that makes it worth savouring.

Tui Lolohea is hoping to build on his cameo appearance against England. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

He played rugby league for Tonga more times than any other person who has ever lived but it is still a privilege to him, a prize beyond what he can ever say.

Even after all these years it still makes his father, Paul, smile and get as emotional as he ever does.

Growing up it was just the two of them. Lolohea's mother died when he was just one year old due a heart condition and if Friday is the end, father and son will be together for it.

But there might be a truth in the jokes the young fellas tell: Lolohea isn't done yet.

"He [Lolohea's father] flew in Tuesday morning, he'll be here for the next couple of weeks to enjoy the last ride, no matter what happens," Lolohea said.

"But we never know these days, do we? I'm just buzzing I got on the field again. I'm glad I got to play my part."

World.title: Potential PNG signing helping to heal Cooper Bai's family rift
World.content:
Marcus Bai has explained how he and son Cooper moved past the rift that fractured their family, as the Gold Coast forward edges closer to signing a deal with the PNG Chiefs.

Cooper was warmly greeted by his father at Port Moresby's Jacksons International airport yesterday after being granted permission to explore his options ahead of the opening of the November 1 contracting window.

The 19-year-old has been high on the Chiefs' list of targets since the club got the green light to enter the NRL in the 2028 season, with the forward proving a hit with local crowds in Papua New Guinea across his two-Test international career.

PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry The PNG Chiefs logo brings together elements representative of the country ahead of its NRL debut in 2028.

But Cooper's journey hasn't always been smooth, and last year he invoked the ire of his legendary Kumul father when he turned down a deal with Melbourne Storm to remain at the Titans.

"He promised one thing … and then he went and did the other thing, and I was cranky with him," Marcus told AAP.

"I said you've got to be fair and square, that's not how you treat the clubs and people.

"It's not good for us as a family, I was really pissed off with him for that, and I was really angry at him.

"Now [with the chance to join the Chiefs], I said go and have a look and you and your girlfriend sit down and [think through] before making a decision."

Cooper Bai angered his father Marcus (pictured) by going back on his word with regards to signing for the Storm. (Getty Images: Shannon Morris)

Marcus said Cooper had shown maturity by speaking to the Gold Coast to ask permission to visit the Chiefs.

Cooper was due to visit PNG on a family holiday after he was ruled out of the Kumuls' World Cup campaign with a hamstring injury.

"He's only young. He's still finding his feet, and if he comes here there will be a lot of pressure on him," Marcus said.

"The crowd here are tough, they tell you straight up [if they're not happy]."

The chance for Cooper to join the Chiefs would represent a full circle moment for the Bai family.

Marcus left Papua New Guinea in the 1990s to pursue a career as a professional rugby league player, going on to win titles in the NRL and Super League.

He would likely stand down from the Chiefs board if Cooper was to sign a deal to join the club for its inaugural season in 2028.

"I'm proud of his achievements, it is hard to do what he's done and to be able to have an interest from many clubs, it's pleasing for me as a father," Marcus Bai said.

AAP

World.title: Man United captain branded 'disgrace' for comments following latest loss
World.content:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has been labelled a "disgrace" after questioning manager Michael Carrick's tactics following a Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes said his side failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a "mood of defeat" after conceding early in Thursday morning's 4-1 loss, a result that increased scrutiny on Carrick.

Como opened the scoring in the second minute and United collapsed, with only a stoppage‑time consolation goal from Joshua Zirkzee making the scoreline slightly less severe.

"We started on the wrong foot and they scored very early," Fernandes told TNT Sports. "There was not enough pressure on the ball and not many good movements off the ball. There were many things not going our way.

"It's a decision from the [coaching] staff not to press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence.

Asked if his comments amounted to criticism of Carrick's tactics, Fernandes said: "That's on the manager and staff to see, not me.

"Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

The Manchester United captain was heavily criticised by former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher for his comments.

Carrick raised his arms up in an apology as he approached Manchester United's travelling supporters after the full-time whistle. (Getty Images: Marco Luzzani)

"For Bruno Fernandes to do that, it's a disgrace really," he said on CBS Sports Golazo.

"Last season he got Player of the Year, that was on the back of Michael Carrick becoming the manager, he wouldn't have got that award without Michael Carrick.

"When you think of him as a footballer, he's a talent, but in terms of attitude and the way he goes about things, it's not right at all.

"He's reacted like that because he's been brought off and he's embarrassed tonight by the manager.

"When he talks about pressing … for years, Bruno Fernandes has meant Manchester United can't press because he does things for the crowd.

"I commentate on games watching Man United, and he runs all over the place like a kid in the schoolyard, for the supporters.

"They all think he's working hard, he's not, he's killing the rest of the team.

"Watching him play every week, throwing his arms up at the other players constantly in the game is an absolute disgrace what he's done there, considering how he's performed this season.

"Awful attitude and not what a Manchester United captain should be."

Carrick's position has come under increasing pressure with United now winless in seven matches, and he responded by questioning the players' lack of willingness to run.

"There's a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run and you don't run forward and you don't run back, you ain't gonna win," he said in his press conference when notified of Fernandes's criticism.

"It was more than disappointing," the 45-year-old manager said in a separate interview for TNT Sports. "I think everybody's got to take responsibility for that. I'll take responsibility for the overall team and performance, it stops with me and I'm fine with that.

"But as a supporter of this football club, to see a performance like that is unacceptable, I have to say."

Carrick said his side had failed to show the required intensity.

"It's the motivation and the purpose and the intensity of a game of football that you have to bring. We didn't bring that today," he said. "I've got to apologise for the performance."

Fernandes also questioned United's mentality after the early setback.

"Conceding early makes us go into the game with a mood of defeat," he said.

United have three points from their opening three Champions League matches and host AS Roma in their next fixture in the competition.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Diamonds looking lost and panicked as Constellation Cup woes continue
World.content:
We are halfway through the Constellation Cup and it is hard to know whether to panic about the state of the Diamonds.

Australia finds itself in a 0-2 hole after losing in Auckland 56-50 and in Christchurch 62-50, with two Tests still left to come in Sydney and Melbourne.

This is the last opportunity the Diamonds have to prepare against international opposition without another series scheduled between now and the 2027 home Netball World Cup.

The Diamonds are hoping to defend their Netball World Cup title in Sydney next year. (Getty: Steve Christo)

The Diamonds have looked uncharacteristically lost and panicked, while the coaches have struggled tactically. Some of Australia's greatest ever players are out of form but still getting a starting position, and fans are questioning why more hasn't been done to develop the next generation of talent.

The recent events at the Commonwealth Games probably feed into the worry, seeing the side fall short of the gold medal match for the first time in August.

If the Diamonds concede all four Tests to New Zealand, they are also expected to be knocked off their number one world ranking, a status they've held since 2013.

So, is the series a lost cause? Are injuries to blame? Or should we hold our breath and hope home-crowd advantage swings momentum? Here are the main talking points at the midway point of the Constellation Cup.

Missing key players

Jo Weston's (right) work out front makes it easier for the goal keeper to win ball. (AAP: James Ross)

Australia is dearly missing defenders Sunday Aryang and Jo Weston.

25-year-old Aryang ruptured her ACL in the last Constellation Cup series and is yet to make it back on court. Veteran Weston made herself unavailable for selection to give her body a much-needed break and focus on her Masters studies.

Their work rate at goal defence and wing defence make a huge difference. Weston is a relentless tagger, wearing down the opposition and slowing play outside the circle.

Could she be coaxed into changing her mind? After all, a similar situation happened in 2022, when Weston was originally rested from the series but received an SOS call to cover injury with Australia trailing 2-0. Her team went on to win the final two games at home.

Kate Moloney was ruled out of game one due to a nasty finger injury. (Getty: Ross MacDonald)

The team has also had to rejig its midcourt following injuries to Kate Moloney and Jamie-Lee Price. Moloney was ruled out of the game on Sunday after suffering a finger laceration while trying to catch a ball at training. She returned to play on Wednesday with stitches.

Price appeared in the first match but sustained a calf injury that prevented her from playing in the second. In both instances, head coach Stacey Marinkovich decided to play Liz Watson out of position at centre before subbing her off in the third quarter. It hasn't been the captain's best performance.

Jamie-Lee Price may not be able to return for the rest of the series. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

Whether Price will be able to make it back by Sunday is unclear, but the Diamonds desperately need to do something different defensively. They've been unable to consistently hold up New Zealand's ball speed and the feed into target Grace Nweke.

In Auckland, they were behind on the gain stat 13-6 and in Christchurch it was just as bad, 9-2.

Home-crowd advantage

Silver Ferns smash the Diamonds 3-0 to clinch Constellation Cup The Diamonds were swept aside in Perth by 18 goals, as New Zealand clinch the 2024 Constellation Cup with one game to go.

Since 2014, the Constellation Cup has been played as a four-Test series, granting each country equal hosting rights, and that home-crowd advantage is no joke.

Over the past five series, the team hosting has emerged victorious in 18 of the 20 Tests played.

Because of this, we're unlikely to see either national body agree to hold an uneven number of Tests in the future. Even if it'd be more exciting for fans to see a team win outright than by goal aggregate.

It's certainly been tough going in New Zealand again this year. The Silver Ferns have been the better side in six of the eight quarters and have forced the opposition to make 29 changes, scrambling to find answers.

It's been five years since the Diamonds last won a Test across the ditch. That outing was Marinkovich's second in charge and Watson's first as captain.

In fact, Marinkovich's winning record in New Zealand only sits at seven per cent. But does that really matter if the team wins the overall series, you may ask? Well, in the 10 series preceding her appointment in August 2020, Australia only lost it once.

Australian coaches Stacey Marinkovich and Nicole Richardson were left scratching their heads after the loss. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

In the five completed under her tenure, Australia has conceded it twice. A loss in 2026 would give Marinkovich a 50 per cent Constellation Cup success rate. Although she is contracted through to the end of 2027, there is a lot hinging on these results.

New Zealand last beat the Diamonds in Australia two years ago in Perth to claim the 2024 trophy. It was the first time in history they'd won three consecutive games within the series.

Now there's a real chance it could happen again.

However, if we're to borrow a cricket analogy, it's important to wait till both teams bat before we place our final judgement. Home-crowd advantage tells us there's a possibility we could be sitting here in a week's time in a very different state of mind, with two wins on the board.

High penalties

Umpire Gary Burgess officiates a match at the Netball World Cup. (Twitter: Gary Burgess)

A key area holding the Diamonds back has been the lopsided penalty count.

New Zealand has conceded 100 penalties so far, while Australia has conceded 145. That's a lot of time standing beside your player, unable to contribute to play.

What didn't help in the second game was the repeated offensive contacts called against the shooters, as they pushed off the body of Kiwi defender Kelly Jackson, trying to get free.

Donnell Wallam was called four times in 11 minutes of play. Sophie Garbin was called three times across 50 minutes. Kiera Austin tallied up to 12 penalties to finish as the third-most penalised Diamonds player on the night.

As per the typical etiquette in international netball, two neutral umpires have been appointed to officiate the series: Welsh umpire Alison Harrison and English umpire Gary Burgess.

"We had some offensive contacts, so we've just got to seek some clarification from the umpires as to what it is they're seeing so we can adjust for that in the future," Marinkovich said post-play.

"The fact that we also rotated our whole defence line from wing defence to the keeper, I don't think that we're that ill-disciplined throughout the entire unit and we've got to understand what it is that we're doing so we can adjust.

"In history, for the last four years, we've been penalised in New Zealand and it kind of shifts when we're in Australia … But I don't think our game plan changes too differently."

Silver Ferns captain Karin Burger and Diamonds captain Liz Watson. (AAP: James Ross)

That's an interesting observation as the umpires' calls should be consistent no matter where a game is played. But Silver Ferns captain Karin Burger had a similar thought.

"Obviously, knowing that Australia has the home crowd next and 50/50 calls always tend to go in the home side's way, it means the scrap is going to be even harder," Burger said.

"Later in the series there's going to be more tired bodies and defenders are going to need to be really smart about their line to the ball … so that we're contesting clean ball."

How much it means

The scary part is how much New Zealand is gunning for the trophy.

The Silver Ferns have already been brimming with confidence and head coach Noeline Taurua said they believed the Constellation Cup was just as big a pinnacle as the Commonwealth Games gold they won in August.

"You always have that trans-Tasman rivalry, and you've got to back up four straight outings against the one team," Taurua said.

"It is definitely the battle of the minds and the hearts and the bodies."

ABC Sport will live blog game three of the Constellation Cup in Sydney, starting at 4pm AEDT.

World.title: Scatterbrained Australian approach opens door to South African victory
World.content:
Among those who fret over the ongoing primacy of Test cricket in the face of the T20 onslaught, Australia's tour of South Africa had long shaped as an enticing proposition: the two best sides in the world squaring off, a clutch of veteran tourists confronting ghosts of controversies past, and Australia commencing a year-long run of battles its aging superstars see as legacy-shaping.

Some of that probably distracted us from what a bittersweet prospect it was, too. For how, as anyone glued to this contest in the past two weeks will have asked themselves at some point or other, can a game so awash with money have conspired to deny us regular helpings of this fun and fascinating South African outfit? Of real cricket that matters?

Twenty-four hours ago, it was centurion Temba Bavuma reminding the world not only of his life-affirming resurgence as a batsman, but of the great shame that in the last two years, he's only had eight other opportunities to strut his stuff at Test level.

Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day Steve Smith reaches a major milestone but doesn't return and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve on a disastrous fourth day for the Aussies in Gqeberha. Here are the quick hits from South Africa.

Early on day four at Gqeberha, the focus shifted to beanpole all-rounder Marco Jansen, fresh from his swashbuckling 85 with the bat, now tearing through the Australian batting order like the Grim Reaper. Lurking not so much in the shadows as slightly off to the side of the stage, stirring up drama and intrigue, there was also the imposing figure of Proteas attack leader Kagiso Rabada.

That and a few subtler problems added up to an unmitigated disaster for Australia. Replying to South Africa's declared total of 425, the scatterbrained and frankly embarrassing tourists were skittled for 99 in their first innings and asked to follow on.

By default, Australia fared a little better in the afternoon, finishing the day at 4-156 with Travis Head undefeated on 87. But with its deficit of 170, and a neck injury to Steve Smith — who hasn't appeared to bat yet in the second innings — it will take something truly remarkable for Australia to pull this game out of the fire on the fifth and final day.

The main impression Australia's performance left was of the sheer needlessness of the entire debacle. What was the first innings batting plan, if any? Why were so many batsmen in such a hurry in a scenario from which Australia was never going to win?

Travis Head was the only Australian batter to show a bit of fight in the face of South Africa's onslaught on day four. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

Which is not to take the focus of South Africa's unstinting excellence. Another emblematic figure in that sense was off-spinner Simon Harmer, who many thought should have been dropped for this game.

Instead, he's made big runs, caught everything that has come his way, and chipped in with two key wickets. Australia has had no such unassuming star.
